### [1] [Cost-Effective Automated Judging of Natural-Language Mathematical Proofs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00004)
*Benjamin Grayzel*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates whether inexpensive open-weight language models can reliably grade natural-language mathematical proofs compared to frontier LLMs, finding that some cheap models match top systems’ grading accuracy at much lower cost, especially when using a unanimous-consensus rule across multiple models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Grading natural-language math proofs is costly because it typically requires strong human graders or expensive frontier LLMs as judges. As math-reasoning benchmarks grow, this recurring evaluation cost becomes a bottleneck. The authors aim to determine if cheaper, open-weight models can serve as effective automatic judges, reducing evaluation expenses without sacrificing reliability.

Method: The authors use IMO-GradingBench, a benchmark of mathematical proofs with human-graded pass/fail labels and rubrics. They compare three inexpensive open-weight judge models (GPT-OSS 120B, DeepSeek-V4 Flash, Gemma-4 31B) against frontier LLM judges (Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro). Each model receives a candidate proof, a ground-truth proof, and a grading rubric, and outputs a pass/fail decision. They measure agreement with human labels on a 200-instance validation subset, then scale to the full 1000-instance benchmark. They also explore different ensemble/consensus strategies (e.g., majority vote, unanimous all-three-pass) across the cheap judges, and assess accuracy, precision, and run-to-run variability over multiple runs.

Result: On the 200-instance validation set, all three cheap judge models individually achieve pass/fail agreement rates with human graders that are statistically indistinguishable from the frontier LLMs, despite being up to 100× cheaper per evaluation. The expected best-budget strategy—majority vote among the three cheap judges—performs similarly to the strongest cheap judge but does not surpass it. On the full 1000-instance benchmark, ensemble rules show that the all-three-pass (unanimous agreement) scheme yields the highest agreement with human pass decisions, the best precision, and the lowest variability across four replicate runs.

Conclusion: The study concludes that inexpensive open-weight LLMs can act as competitive automatic judges for grading natural-language mathematical proofs, achieving similar reliability to frontier LLMs at one to two orders of magnitude lower cost. Among ensemble strategies, an all-three-pass unanimity rule across three cheap judges offers particularly strong performance and stability, making it a recommended default deployment choice. However, because this rule was chosen based on post-hoc analysis of the benchmark, the authors caution that it should be independently replicated before being treated as a definitive standard.

Abstract: Grading natural-language mathematical proofs is a recurring cost in evaluating math-reasoning systems, and frontier LLM judges are expensive. We ask whether cheap open-weight models can serve as reliable judges given a candidate proof, a ground-truth proof, and a human-grading rubric. On a 200-instance validation sample of IMO-GradingBench, three cheap judges (GPT-OSS 120B, DeepSeek-V4 Flash, Gemma-4 31B) agree with human pass/fail decisions at rates statistically indistinguishable from Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, at up to $100\times$ lower cost. We had expected a majority vote of the three to be the best budget option; it matched the frontier but did not improve on its strongest member. Extending to the full 1000-instance benchmark and exploring consensus rules, we found that requiring unanimous agreement (all-three-pass) reaches the highest pass-agreement and precision and, on four replicate runs, the smallest run-to-run spread. The headline finding is that cheap judges are competitive with the frontier at one to two orders of magnitude lower cost; as a deployable default we recommend all-three-pass, with the caveat that this rule was identified post-hoc and warrants independent replication.

</details>


### [2] [RubricReviewer: From Direct Critique to Objective and Comprehensive Rubric-Driven Peer Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00005)
*Shuyu Guo,Wenxiang Hu,Yuyue Zhao,Yougang Lyu,Xiaohui Yan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RubricReviewer is a rubric-driven LLM-based review assistant that explicitly generates paper-specific rubrics, then uses both a training-free evidence-gathering agent and a human-aligned trained model to produce more comprehensive, discriminative, and robust reviews than prior systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Peer review systems at major venues face a surge in submissions, creating pressure on reviewers and encouraging use of LLMs as review assistants. Existing LLM-based reviewers either directly map manuscripts to reviews without making the evaluation criteria explicit, or they only partially capture what constitutes a good review: agents that are training-free collect broad evidence but give unfocused critiques, while trained models imitate human judgments, inheriting their noise and uneven coverage. There is a need for a framework that makes evaluation rubrics explicit and paper-adaptive while combining broad evidence gathering with human-aligned discriminative judgment.

Method: The paper introduces RubricReviewer, a fully rubric-driven framework. First, it generates an explicit, paper-adaptive evaluation rubric as an intermediate step rather than implicitly encoding criteria within the review. Then, both the review text and the final assessment are conditioned on this rubric. Architecturally, RubricReviewer integrates two components: (1) Scout, a training-free agent that gathers external evidence and performs broad analysis; and (2) Aligner, a trained model fine-tuned to align with human review standards and to consume and interpret the evidence collected by Scout. The system fuses the outputs of these components to obtain reviews that leverage both supervision sources. The authors evaluate the framework with experiments on real-world submissions and perform ablation studies to understand the contributions of each component.

Result: On real-world submission datasets, RubricReviewer generates reviews that are more comprehensive and more discriminative than existing LLM-based review systems. It also exhibits superior robustness against adversarial prompt-injection attacks, maintaining review quality and integrity in the face of such perturbations. Ablation studies demonstrate that removing or altering any of the core components (explicit rubric generation, Scout, or Aligner) degrades performance, confirming their necessity for the full benefits of the framework.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling paper-adaptive rubrics and separating evidence gathering from judgment can substantially improve LLM-based peer review. By integrating a training-free evidence-gathering agent with a human-aligned trained model, RubricReviewer produces higher-quality, more discriminative, and more robust reviews than prior approaches. The framework addresses structural limitations of existing systems and suggests that rubric-driven, modular architectures are a promising direction for scalable, reliable AI-assisted peer review.

Abstract: Peer review at major venues is under unprecedented submission pressure, motivating the use of large language models (LLMs) as review assistants. Existing LLM-based reviewers, however, face two structural limitations. First, they map manuscripts directly to reviews, leaving the underlying rubric implicit and entangling its derivation with the judgement. Second, the prevailing paradigms each capture only half of a good review: training-free agents gather broad evidence but produce undirected critiques, while training-based reviewers inherit human discriminative judgement together with its noise and uneven coverage. We introduce RubricReviewer, a fully rubric-driven framework that addresses both limitations. It makes rubric generation an explicit intermediate step, so that both review generation and the final assessment are conditioned on paper-adaptive rubrics. It further combines a training-free agent (Scout) that gathers external evidence with a human-aligned trained model (Aligner) that consumes this evidence, fusing the strengths of both supervision sources. Experiments on real-world submissions show that RubricReviewer produces reviews that are markedly more comprehensive and more discriminative than prior systems, and exhibits the strongest robustness against adversarial prompt-injection attacks. Ablation studies further confirm the necessity of each component.

</details>


### [3] [MemoryForge: Synthesize Lifelong Memory for Human-Like LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00007)
*Bohan Tang,Yiwen Guo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes MemoryForge, a framework that gives LLM agents realistic, autobiographical-style memories instead of static persona prompts, leading to more human-like behavior in role-play and user simulation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prompt-based personas usually use short, static textual profiles (e.g., age, job, traits). These lack rich, situational life memories, so LLM agents behave generically and inconsistently, limiting their value in agentic settings like role-play, simulations, and interactive environments. The authors want a way to ground personas in coherent, lifelong experiences so that behavior becomes more nuanced, realistic, and context-sensitive without retraining the base LLM.

Method: They introduce memory-based conditioning, where a frozen LLM is guided by an external autobiographical memory base rather than a short profile description. They formalize the creation of this memory base as customized lifelong memory synthesis and propose MemoryForge. MemoryForge takes a brief target persona description and synthesizes a structured, lifelong memory base using three components: (1) a context generator that creates socio-historical background (time, culture, environment) to ground the persona; (2) a life organizer that arranges events into a developmentally coherent life trajectory consistent with the target identity; and (3) a multi-resolution simulator that generates both high-level temporal summaries and detailed episodic experiences, striking a balance between breadth and depth. These memories are later dynamically retrieved at inference time to condition the LLM’s responses in specific situations.

Result: On benchmarks for role-play (PersonaGym) and user simulation (SimulatorArena), equipping frozen LLMs with the MemoryForge-generated memory base leads to more human-like and persona-faithful behaviors than strong prompt-based descriptive conditioning baselines. Improvements are observed across multiple quantitative metrics and hold across different underlying LLM backbones, indicating the generality of the approach.

Conclusion: Replacing static persona prompts with synthesized autobiographical memory bases and using dynamic memory retrieval makes LLM agents behave more realistically and consistently in agentic tasks. MemoryForge effectively transforms brief persona descriptions into coherent, lifelong memory structures that can steer frozen LLMs, suggesting memory-based conditioning as a promising general paradigm for building more human-like AI agents.

Abstract: Equipping Large Language Models (LLMs) with human-like personas is crucial for agentic applications, such as role-play and user simulation. Traditional prompt-based methods rely on descriptive conditioning by injecting static textual profiles, which often makes agents show generic behaviors due to a lack of realistic life memory. To fill this gap, we introduce memory-based conditioning, a paradigm inspired by the cognitive psychology, which replaces abstract profiles with an autobiographical memory base, enabling frozen LLMs to dynamically retrieve situation-relevant memory to guide their behaviors. We formalize its enabling task as customized lifelong memory synthesis and propose MemoryForge, a novel framework to synthesize such lifelong memory from brief target personas. MemoryForge has three key components: a context generator for socio-historical grounding, a life organizer for developmental coherence toward the target identity, and a multi-resolution simulator that balances broad temporal summaries with high-fidelity episodic experiences. Experiments on PersonaGym for role-play and SimulatorArena for user-simulation, show that the synthesized memory base by MemoryForge enables frozen LLMs to exhibit more human-like behaviors than strong descriptive conditioning baselines across multiple metrics and LLM backbones.

</details>


### [4] [AgentMemBench: A Systematic Benchmark for Evaluating Long-Term Memory Management Strategies in Conversational AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00009)
*Ahmed Cherif*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: AgentMemBench benchmarks five long-term memory strategies for conversational AI and finds that dense external key-value retrieval clearly outperforms alternatives, though at a higher memory footprint.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conversational AI struggles with long-term coherence because models have finite context windows and cannot remember information over thousands of dialogue turns. Many memory mechanisms have been proposed—context windowing, external stores, graphs, summaries, and web search—but they are rarely compared systematically under identical conditions. The paper aims to provide a unified, reproducible benchmark to objectively evaluate and compare these strategies on realistic multi-session and task-grounded dialogue tasks.

Method: The authors design AgentMemBench, a benchmark that standardizes evaluation of five memory strategies: in-context windowing (ICW), external key–value store with dense retrieval (EKV), graph-based episodic memory (GEM), compression-based summarization (CBS), and web-augmented memory (WAM). They test them on three public datasets representing long-term, multi-session, and persona-grounded dialogue with document grounding: LoCoMo, MultiDoc2Dial, and MSC. For 491 annotated question turns, each method must retrieve relevant memories and support answer generation by Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (4-bit) with greedy decoding. The benchmark measures retrieval quality (Recall@k, MRR, nDCG@k), answer quality (F1, faithfulness scored by an LLM judge), and efficiency (memory footprint and latency). They also plug in two existing systems, MemGPT/Letta and HippoRAG, into the same harness for comparison.

Result: The external key–value (EKV) dense retrieval method dominates on all quality metrics, achieving macro Recall@5 of 0.792, MRR of 0.677, Answer F1 of 0.156, and Faithfulness of 0.354. Long-range recall is shown to be critical: on LoCoMo, where relevant turns are many sessions back, ICW, WAM, GEM, and CBS almost completely fail (Recall@5 ≤ 0.005), whereas EKV alone attains 0.573 Recall@5, demonstrating that recency-based windows, summaries, and entity graphs break down over long horizons. CBS performs second-best on retrieval overall with Recall@5 of 0.556. WAM matches ICW for in-corpus recall by design because web results lack dataset provenance. EKV’s superior recall comes with a much larger memory footprint (~5,100 tokens versus ~300 for ICW/WAM), quantifying an explicit accuracy–efficiency trade-off. The two published memory systems (MemGPT/Letta and HippoRAG) are also evaluated, though specific numbers are not given in the abstract.

Conclusion: Long-term conversational memory is best handled, under this benchmark, by dense retrieval over an external key–value store, which substantially outperforms context windowing, graph-based, summarization-based, and web-augmented memory, especially for very long-range recall. However, this quality gain incurs a significant memory footprint and efficiency cost, exposing a core trade-off between accuracy and resource use. AgentMemBench provides a unified, reproducible framework and codebase for comparing memory systems, enabling more rigorous progress on long-term memory for conversational agents.

Abstract: Long-term memory remains a critical bottleneck for conversational AI agents, whose finite context windows cannot support coherent recall across thousands of turns. We present AgentMemBench, a unified, reproducible benchmark evaluating five memory management strategies under identical conditions: in-context windowing (ICW), external key-value store (EKV), graph-based episodic memory (GEM), compression-based summarisation (CBS), and web-augmented memory (WAM). All are assessed across three public datasets covering long-term multi-session dialogue (LoCoMo), task-oriented document grounding (MultiDoc2Dial), and persona-grounded multi-session chat (MSC), using Recall@k, MRR, nDCG@k, Answer F1, an LLM-judge Faithfulness score, Memory Footprint, and Latency over 491 annotated question turns. Generation and judging both use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (4-bit), with greedy decoding for determinism. Our results show that (1) EKV dominates on every quality axis (macro Recall@5 0.792, MRR 0.677, F1 0.156, Faithfulness 0.354); (2) long-range recall is decisive: on LoCoMo, where the gold turn lies many sessions back, ICW, WAM, GEM, and CBS retrieve almost nothing (Recall@5 <= 0.005) while EKV alone reaches 0.573, showing that recency windows, summaries, and entity graphs collapse at long horizons and only dense retrieval scales; (3) CBS is the runner-up on retrieval (0.556); (4) WAM equals ICW on in-corpus recall by construction, since external results carry no in-corpus provenance; and (5) EKV's recall advantage carries a footprint cost (~5,100 vs ~300 tokens for ICW/WAM), an explicit accuracy-efficiency trade-off. We additionally evaluate two published memory systems (MemGPT/Letta, HippoRAG) against the same harness, and release all code, environment, and result artefacts for full reproducibility.

</details>


### [5] [DLLM-TTS: Block Discrete Diffusion Language Model for Text-to-Speech Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00011)
*Wasim Madha,Nityanand Mathur,Hamees Sayed,Apoorv Singh,Sameer Khurana,Akshat Mandloi,Sudarshan Kamath*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Proposes DLLM-TTS, a block-wise discrete diffusion framework over neural audio codec tokens for TTS, achieving fast, high-quality, data-efficient speech synthesis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing TTS systems trade off between quality and efficiency: autoregressive codec LMs are accurate but slow and data-hungry due to sequential decoding and large model sizes, while non-autoregressive models are faster but lose linguistic accuracy. A method is needed that preserves intelligibility and alignment while enabling parallel, efficient generation with moderate model size and data.

Method: Formulate TTS as conditional block discrete diffusion over X-Codec2 neural audio codec tokens. The token sequence is split into blocks; within each block, the model applies masked diffusion, predicting tokens in parallel, while blocks themselves are processed sequentially to retain global structure. The model is conditioned on text to learn both local acoustic coherence and global text-speech alignment. A 0.6B-parameter model is trained on 20K hours of data and evaluated on Seed-TTS-eval.

Result: The DLLM-TTS model attains a real-time factor (RTF) of 0.15, indicating efficient inference, and a 0.6B-parameter model trained on 20K hours of data achieves competitive performance on the Seed-TTS-eval benchmark compared with existing approaches, despite using a relatively modest model size and data scale.

Conclusion: Block discrete diffusion language modeling over neural audio codec tokens is an effective way to perform TTS, combining parallel token prediction (fast inference) with strong linguistic accuracy and text-speech alignment. DLLM-TTS demonstrates that such models can yield practical, data-efficient speech synthesis with competitive quality and real-time performance.

Abstract: Current text-to-speech systems face a trade-off: autoregres- sive codec language models produce highly intelligible speech but require large-scale models and training data and decode tokens sequentially, while non-autoregressive approaches im- prove speed at the cost of linguistic accuracy. We present DLLM-TTS, a framework that formulates TTS as conditional block discrete diffusion over X-Codec2 neural audio codec to- kens. The model decomposes sequences into blocks and applies masked diffusion within each block while processing blocks se- quentially, learning both local acoustic coherence and global text-speech alignment. During inference, parallel token pre- diction within blocks enables efficient generation with a real- time factor (RTF) of 0.15. A 0.6B-parameter model trained on 20K hours achieves competitive performance on the Seed- TTS-eval benchmark, demonstrating that block discrete diffu- sion language models enable practical and data-efficient speech synthesis with parallel generation.

</details>


### [6] [Obshazard-bench: Benchmarking Multimodal Foundation Models for Real-Time Disaster Intelligence from Raw Earth Observation Streams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00012)
*Fengxiang Wang,Qiuyang Yu,Yueying Li,Mingshuo Chen,Chengchi Fei,Kaiyi Xu,Lixin Gu,Wangxu Wei,Junchao Gong,Lipeng Ma,Jiong Wang,Fenghua Ling,Wenlong Zhang,Xue Yang,Wenjing Yang,Ben Fei,Long Lan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose Obshazard-bench, a real-time, observation-driven benchmark to evaluate how well multimodal large language models handle disaster intelligence using raw satellite and ground observations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluations of MLLMs for Earth observation use static, post-processed products that don’t reflect the time-critical, rapidly evolving nature of real-world disasters. This makes it unclear whether MLLMs can truly support operational emergency response.

Method: Create Obshazard-bench, a benchmark that fuses raw, high-frequency satellite sounding streams from multiple sensors with concurrent ground-station data, historical disaster records, and socio-economic indicators. It spans 8 disaster categories, 28 sub-categories, 60+ countries, and 120+ extreme events, with thousands of VQA samples. They define a three-stage taxonomy mirroring operational workflows: (1) Predictive Crisis Anticipation, (2) Active Evolution Reasoning, and (3) Multi-faceted Impact Quantification, then test various general and EO-focused foundation models on it.

Result: When evaluated on Obshazard-bench, both general-purpose and Earth-observation-focused foundation models show major weaknesses in converting raw, multi-channel physical observations into temporally grounded, actionable disaster reasoning across the three stages.

Conclusion: Obshazard-bench exposes a significant gap between current MLLM capabilities and the requirements of real-time, decision-relevant disaster intelligence from raw Earth observation data, indicating a need for new methods and models tailored to operational disaster response.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to interpret Earth observation data, yet their capability to support real-world disaster emergency response remains insufficiently evaluated. Existing remote sensing benchmarks largely rely on static, post-hoc, and expert-processed products, such as gridded reanalysis data, which are difficult to align with operational disaster scenarios where hazards evolve rapidly and decisions must be made under strict time constraints. To bridge this gap, we introduce Obshazard-bench, a real-time, observation-driven benchmark for evaluating disaster intelligence in MLLMs. Unlike image-centric or post-event benchmarks, Obshazard-bench directly integrates raw, high-frequency satellite sounding streams from diverse satellite sensors with concurrent ground-station observations, historical disaster records, and socio-economic indicators, bypassing delayed expert-processing and physical-inversion pipelines. The benchmark covers 8 major disaster categories and 28 sub-categories across more than 60 countries, incorporating over 120 historically documented extreme-event cases and thousands of lifecycle-oriented VQA samples. Moreover, Obshazard-bench further defines a three-stage evaluation taxonomy aligned with the operational disaster workflow: Predictive Crisis Anticipation for pre-disaster risk detection and early forecasting, Active Evolution Reasoning for in-situ disaster tracking and termination prediction, and Multi-faceted Impact Quantification for post-disaster magnitude deduction, humanitarian burden estimation, and socio-economic impact assessment. Experiments on representative general-purpose and Earth-focused foundation models reveal substantial limitations in transforming raw multi-channel physical observations into temporally grounded and decision-relevant disaster reasoning.

</details>


### [7] [What Transfers from Text to Vision? Capability Scaling Laws and Transfer Dynamics for VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00013)
*Ziran Li,Qiang Wang,Zhengyu Chen,Shanglin Lei,Borun Chen,Jingang Wang,Xunliang Cai*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They introduce a capability-driven scaling law that predicts vision-language model (VLM) performance from a low-dimensional summary of an LLM’s text capabilities, enabling principled backbone selection across model families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Backbone choice critically affects VLM performance, but current practice is ad hoc. Existing compute-based scaling laws do not transfer across LLM families and cannot directly predict multimodal performance before training, making backbone sweeps expensive and unprincipled.

Method: They extract a low-dimensional capability score S from many LLM text benchmarks using PCA, then model VLM benchmark accuracy as a function of S with two interpretable parameters per backbone: a transfer rate (how well text capability transfers to multimodal tasks) and an absorption rate (data-scaling efficiency). They train over 150 VLMs built on 34 LLMs from 7 families under a controlled recipe, evaluate them on 200+ text and 50+ multimodal benchmarks, and fit/validate their Capability-Driven Multimodal Scaling Law, also analyzing the correlation structure of text vs multimodal benchmarks.

Result: The proposed scaling law accurately extrapolates VLM transfer rates from small (≤8B) to large (72B) backbones, predicts full VLM training trajectories, and generalizes to held-out LLM families. They find that some text benchmarks are negatively correlated with multimodal performance, base LLMs are better VLM backbones than instruction-tuned ones due to higher absorption and less data-scaling decay, and different model families cluster in distinct regions of the transfer–absorption space.

Conclusion: Textual capability, summarized by a low-dimensional score, is a strong predictor of downstream multimodal performance when coupled with their transfer/absorption model. Their framework provides a principled, quantitative way to choose VLM backbones, revealing that not all text benchmarks are beneficial and that base LLMs are often preferable to instruction-tuned models for VLMs.

Abstract: Choosing the right large language model (LLM) backbone is the most consequential decision when building a vision-language model (VLM), yet it remains fundamentally unprincipled: compute-based scaling laws fail to generalize across model families, and no framework exists for directly predicting VLM performance before training begins. We propose the Capability-Driven Multimodal Scaling Law, the first cross-family framework that predicts VLM benchmark accuracy from directly observable textual capability. Given a low-dimensional capability score $S$ extracted from LLM textual benchmarks via PCA, we model VLM performance as a function of $S$, with a per-backbone transfer rate and an absorption rate that quantifies data-scaling efficiency. To fit and validate the framework, we train over 150 VLMs on 34 LLMs spanning 7 model families under a strictly controlled recipe. Evaluations on more than 200 textual and 50 multimodal benchmarks show that the law accurately extrapolates transfer rate from models up to 8B parameters to 72B-scale backbones, predicts full VLM training trajectories with high fidelity, and generalizes to entirely held-out model families. Beyond the scaling law, our analysis surfaces actionable insights: certain textual benchmarks negatively correlate with multimodal performance, exposing latent benchmark-gaming behavior; base LLMs outperform instruction-tuned counterparts as VLM backbones due to higher absorption rates and lower data-scaling decay; and different model families occupy distinct positions in the transfer--absorption space. The framework turns backbone selection from costly empirical sweeps into a principled, quantitative decision. Code and data are available at https://github.com/wangq-dev/CDMScaling.

</details>


### [8] [Role Steering of Language Models for Social Simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00023)
*Isaac Song,Mohammed Rehan Parwani,Glenn Matlin,Emile Anand,Akhil Theerthala,Arjun Chatterjee,Maria Kostylew,Yonadav G. Shavit,Sebastien Krier,Mark Riedl*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes and tests a workflow for screening role-conditioned language-model agents using activation steering, showing that role-specific directions outperform a generic assistant axis and that steering strength must be tuned per role.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language-model-based social simulations require agents that reliably follow specified roles. Existing persona or role-conditioning methods can be opaque, hard to verify, and may use generic directions (like an assistant axis) that don’t capture fine-grained role behavior. Simulation builders need a systematic, automatic way to check and calibrate role behavior before inserting agents into complex simulations.

Method: The authors design a screening workflow based on activation steering: (1) define a textual role profile; (2) use this profile to extract a role-specific steering direction in model activation space; (3) sweep over four different steering coefficient strengths; (4) query the steered model with a common set of role-agnostic questions; (5) use a separate LLM (GPT-4.1-mini) to compare responses against role references and judge role-profile alignment, lexical diversity, and other metrics. They apply this pipeline to OLMo-3-7B-Instruct across 275 different roles and compare their role-specific steering directions to a prior, more generic assistant-axis direction from persona-vector work.

Result: Role-specific steering directions achieve substantially higher judged role-profile alignment than the assistant-axis baseline, with mean overall scores of 63.2 versus 41.1 across the grid of tested coefficients. Moreover, role-specific steering preserves high lexical diversity at larger coefficients, whereas the assistant-axis control shows a sharp drop in diversity as coefficient strength increases. Role-level analyses show that most roles benefit from increased steering strength, but a notable subset of 38 roles deteriorates across all six evaluated dimensions when steering is applied strongly.

Conclusion: Activation steering with role-specific directions provides an effective way to screen and tune role-conditioned agents for social simulations. A single generic assistant direction is insufficient; instead, steering should be customized per role, and coefficients should be selected on a role-by-role basis to avoid degradation for sensitive roles. The proposed workflow and released code/artifacts offer a practical tool for simulation builders to vet and calibrate role behaviors before deployment.

Abstract: Social simulations built from language-model agents need role-conditioned behavior that can be checked before agents are placed into a simulated population. We introduce an activation-steering screening workflow for role-conditioned agents: define a role profile, extract a role-specific direction, sweep four steering coefficients, evaluate role-profile alignment, and pass or flag each candidate configuration. On OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, we apply the workflow to a mixed 275-role inventory with 228 role-agnostic questions, GPT-4.1-mini prompted role references, and GPT-4.1-mini judges. Role-specific directions receive higher judged role-profile alignment than an assistant-axis directional control from prior persona-vector work, with mean overall scores of 63.2 versus 41.1 across the tested grid. They also preserve high lexical diversity, while the control drops sharply at larger coefficients. The role-level screen is the main practical output: most roles improve as steering increases, but 38 roles decline across all six measured dimensions, showing why simulation builders should choose coefficients per role rather than deploy a uniform high-strength setting. We make our code and evaluation artifacts available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/anonymous-research-code-5F03/.

</details>


### [9] [Exploring More to Solve More: Boosting Diversity in Text Diffusion Models via Entropy-Based Guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00024)
*Jingwei Zhang,Haoyu Lei,Zijin Feng,Jiacheng Sun,Farzan Farnia*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces a training-free Semantic-Aware Kernel Entropy (SAKE) guidance method for text diffusion that improves the fidelity–diversity tradeoff and multi-sample performance on reasoning tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion-style controllable generation works well in continuous domains like images, but extending similar controllability to discrete, sequential text remains difficult. Existing text sampling and guidance methods only adjust token-level probabilities and ignore the global semantic structure and cross-token interactions, which leads to a suboptimal tradeoff between faithfulness (fidelity) and variety (diversity). There is a need for a guidance mechanism that is aware of semantic relations among tokens and their positions, without requiring retraining.

Method: The paper proposes SAKE (Semantic-Aware Kernel Entropy), a training-free guidance method for text generation. It builds a kernel Gram matrix over token embeddings that encodes semantic similarity and relative positional information between tokens. Over this matrix, the method computes the order-2 Rényi entropy as an objective to characterize the semantic spread or concentration of the sequence. By linearizing this entropy objective in the embedding space, they derive a computationally tractable guidance signal that can be injected into the sampling process. This signal adaptively reshapes the token sampling distribution: when the semantic content is redundant, it flattens the distribution to promote exploration; when the content is already diverse, it sharpens the distribution to focus on fidelity.

Result: Experiments show that SAKE yields a better Pareto frontier between fidelity and diversity compared with standard approaches like temperature scaling and other discrete guidance baselines. It especially improves multi-sample performance on reasoning-heavy tasks, including code generation and mathematical problem solving, indicating that semantic-aware entropy guidance leads to more useful and varied candidate outputs.

Conclusion: Semantic-aware entropy-based guidance over token embeddings and their interactions can significantly improve controllable text generation without retraining the underlying model. SAKE adaptively balances exploration and exploitation during sampling, outperforming traditional temperature-based and discrete guidance strategies, particularly on reasoning-intensive tasks. This suggests that modeling global semantic structure is a promising direction for discrete diffusion and guided text generation.

Abstract: Although diffusion models have revolutionized continuous domains like image synthesis through high quality generations and controllable guidance mechanisms, bringing this controllability to the discrete, sequential nature of text remains an open challenge. Meanwhile, current sampling strategies and guidance methods adjust token likelihoods without capturing the broader semantic landscape, leading to a suboptimal balance between fidelity and diversity. In this work, we introduce a novel training-free Semantic-Aware Kernel Entropy (SAKE) guidance method. Our method computes the order-2 Rényi entropy over a kernel Gram matrix that captures both cross-token semantic interactions and relative token positions. By linearizing this objective in the embedding space, we derive a tractable guidance signal that dynamically adjusts the sampling distribution, flattening it to encourage exploration during redundancy and sharpening it for fidelity when diverse. Empirical experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves a superior Pareto frontier between fidelity and diversity, and improves multi-sample performance on reasoning-intensive tasks, such as code and mathematics generation, compared to temperature scaling and discrete guidance baselines.

</details>


### [10] [SLMs as Multi-Agent Routers: A Progressive SFT and Reinforcement Learning Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00030)
*Gayathri V Kondapalli,Alexander Ng,Hirsh Pithadia,Rahul Monish,Harvey Yorke,Amir Kayhani*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a learning-based router that chooses between specialized retrieval agents and generates their parameters, optimizing for actual retrieval relevance rather than just query intent/topic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Specialized retrieval agents often outperform general search, but it is hard to know which agent is best for a specific query. Existing routing methods rely on inferred topic or intent and cannot react when a seemingly appropriate agent returns low-relevance results. There is a need for a routing mechanism that leverages feedback from retrieval performance itself to decide which agent to use and how to call it.

Method: Train a small language model with supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning to (1) select the most suitable retrieval agent and (2) generate structured parameters for downstream tool calls. The RL objective uses a hierarchical reward combining retrieval relevance (e.g., NDCG-based) and query–agent topic alignment, allowing the model to learn which agents work best for which query distributions and when to avoid specialized agents even if they look topically aligned.

Result: On a challenging subset of cases where query topic suggests one agent but retrieval quality is poor (agent–query mismatches), the model reaches NDCG@10 of 0.918, significantly outperforming two intent-only LLM routers (Amazon Nova Lite at 0.539 and Claude Haiku 4.5 at 0.490). Overall, across the full evaluation, the model achieves mean NDCG@10 of 0.771, improving over Nova Lite by +0.177 and over Haiku by +0.219, while also reducing selection latency to 120.1 ms, which is an 82.4% latency reduction compared to Nova Lite.

Conclusion: Incorporating retrieval relevance into the routing objective enables a small LLM to jointly learn agent selection and parameterization that outperform intent-based routing baselines, both in result quality and latency. Learning from retrieval performance lets the model identify when specialized agents are actually harmful despite topical match, leading to better overall retrieval quality at lower cost.

Abstract: Specialised retrieval agents typically surface higher quality results than general-purpose search, but selecting the optimal agent for a given query remains an open problem. Current approaches route queries based on inferred topic or intent, however intent-based selection is fundamentally limited: it does not incorporate signal from retrieved content, and cannot detect when a topically aligned agent produces low-relevance results. We address this by training a small language model via supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning to jointly perform agent selection and structured parameter generation for downstream tool calls, using a hierarchical reward function grounded in retrieval relevance along with query-agent topic alignment. This enables the model to learn task-dependent agent suitability from retrieval performance: which agents reliably yield high-relevance results for which query distributions, and when to redirect queries away from specialised agents despite surface-level topical overlap. On a targeted subset of such agent-query mismatches, the trained model achieves an NDCG@10 of 0.918 compared to 0.539 and 0.490 for two LLM baselines (Amazon Nova Lite and Claude Haiku 4.5) that route on intent alone. Overall, it achieves a mean NDCG@10 of 0.771 (+0.177 over Nova Lite, +0.219 over Haiku) with a mean selection latency of 120.1ms, an 82.4% reduction over Nova Lite.

</details>


### [11] [XL-DocBench: Benchmarking Evidence-Grounded Extra-Long Document Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00036)
*Hongchen Wei,Yuanzhe Wang,Bei Liu,Yifan Yang,Qi Dai,Ruichun Ma,Kai Qiu,Yunsheng Li,Dongdong Chen,Chong Luo,Zhenzhong Chen,Baining Guo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduction of XL-DocBench, a benchmark for extra-long document understanding with human-verified questions spanning up to 2,303 pages across six professional domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM benchmarks focus mostly on short-context or single-page QA, which is insufficient for real-world professional tasks in domains like compliance, clinical, financial, and engineering, where documents are extremely long, answers must be grounded in specific pages, and unsupported answers carry high risk.

Method: The authors construct XL-DocBench by using a tree-guided synthesis pipeline to generate candidate questions, then apply artifact filters and conduct full human verification by 194 domain experts. Each question is annotated with reasoning labels, evidence pages, verification rules, and answer formats, including explicit None-answer cases. The benchmark is designed to require multi-page evidence, cross-document reasoning, and use of tables, charts, and figures.

Result: The resulting dataset contains 1,519 human-verified questions across six professional domains, with contexts up to 2,303 pages. 72.6% of questions require multiple evidence pages, 36.6% involve non-text elements (tables, charts, figures), and 10.9% require evidence from multiple documents. The benchmark provides fine-grained labels for reasoning types, evidence, and verification rules to enable detailed system evaluation.

Conclusion: XL-DocBench fills a gap in long-context evaluation by providing a fully human-verified benchmark tailored to extra-long professional documents, enabling attribution of model failures to specific components like retrieval, evidence integration, or rule following. Empirical results with current systems demonstrate that long contexts, multi-page evidence aggregation, and structured reasoning over professional documents remain challenging for state-of-the-art models.

Abstract: Real-world document tasks often ask professionals to answer questions from annual reports, regulations, clinical guidelines, and technical manuals that span hundreds or thousands of pages. Some questions also require comparing related reports. Reliable long-document understanding is therefore a prerequisite for using LLMs in compliance, clinical, financial, and engineering workflows, where decisions must be traceable to specific evidence pages and the cost of an unsupported answer is high -- yet most existing benchmarks still measure short-context or single-page QA. We introduce XL-DocBench, a fully human-verified benchmark for extra-long document understanding, with 1,519 retained questions from six professional domains and contexts up to 2,303 pages. XL-DocBench goes beyond page-level lookup. 1,103 examples (72.6\%) use multiple evidence pages. The final set also includes 556 questions (36.6\%) that use tables, charts, or figures, and 165 questions (10.9\%) that require evidence from multiple documents. Each question has one of twelve reasoning labels, expert-annotated evidence pages, a typed verification rule, and an answer format, including 218 None-answer cases. We build the benchmark with a tree-guided synthesis pipeline followed by artifact filters and full verification by 194 human experts. By coupling extra-long professional contexts with page-level evidence and typed rules, XL-DocBench fills a gap left by prior single-page, short multi-page, or text-only long-context benchmarks, and lets future work attribute system failures to retrieval, evidence use, or rule following rather than to a single leaderboard score. The results show that current systems still struggle with long contexts, multi-page evidence, and structured reasoning over professional documents.

</details>


### [12] [Trustworthiness Costs of Domain Adaptation in Small Language Models:A Cross-Architecture Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00042)
*Ramesh B. Paramkusham*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Systematic study of how domain adaptation of small language models affects trustworthiness, showing minimal factual calibration change, benefits from adversarially perturbed training data, and potential harms from some safety-preserving strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the under-explored trustworthiness implications (factual calibration and adversarial robustness) when adapting small language models to specialized domains such as healthcare, legal, and finance, especially under resource constraints and safety requirements.

Method: Conduct a large-scale empirical study over 216 configurations, varying three SLM architectures, three target domains, two training data conditions (benign vs adversarially perturbed), and four fine-tuning strategies (baseline LoRA, Safety-DPO, Dark Experience Replay, Task Arithmetic LoRA). Evaluate trustworthiness using TruthfulQA MC2 for factual calibration and HarmBench ASR for adversarial robustness, with three random seeds per configuration.

Result: (1) Baseline QLoRA domain adaptation yields almost no change in TruthfulQA scores across models and domains (mean absolute Delta < 0.02). (2) Adversarially perturbed training data improves domain adaptation quality (loss decreases by ~0.040) without degrading trustworthiness metrics. (3) Safety-preserving methods do not reduce adversarial harm susceptibility: Safety-DPO has negligible effect on ASR, while Dark ER and TA-LoRA substantially increase HarmBench ASR in safety-aligned models, sometimes by more than 0.45.

Conclusion: Domain adaptation of SLMs can preserve factual calibration and benefit from adversarially augmented data, but commonly assumed safety-preserving techniques like replay-based and arithmetic-merge approaches may actually erode adversarial robustness rather than transfer alignment, challenging prevailing assumptions about safety transfer in domain-adapted SLMs.

Abstract: Domain adaptation of small language models (SLMs) has emerged as a practical strategy for deploying capable NLP systems in resource-constrained, high-stakes environments including healthcare, legal services, and financial analysis. While performance gains from parameter-efficient fine-tuning are well characterised, the corresponding impact on trustworthiness (factual calibration and adversarial robustness) remains poorly understood. This paper presents the first systematic cross-domain, cross-architecture empirical study quantifying the trustworthiness cost of domain adaptation across three SLM architectures (TinyLlama 1B, Gemma-2 2B, Llama 3.2 1B), three domains (healthcare, legal, finance), two training-data conditions (benign and adversarially perturbed), and four fine-tuning strategies (baseline LoRA, Safety-DPO, Dark Experience Replay, and Task Arithmetic LoRA, TA-LoRA). Trustworthiness is evaluated through TruthfulQA MC2 (factual calibration) and HarmBench ASR (adversarial robustness) across all 216 experimental configurations with three random seeds. Three principal findings emerge. First, baseline QLoRA domain adaptation produces minimal TruthfulQA MC2 change across all model-domain combinations (mean |Delta TQA| < 0.02). Second, adversarially perturbed training data consistently improves domain adaptation quality (Delta loss approximately -0.040) without worsening trustworthiness benchmarks. Third, none of the three safety-preserving strategies reduced adversarial harm susceptibility: Safety-DPO was effectively neutral (mean Delta ASR < 0.001), while Dark ER and TA-LoRA increased mean HarmBench ASR by +0.171 and +0.155 respectively in safety-aligned models (Gemma-2 2B, Llama 3.2 1B), with individual configurations exceeding +0.45. These results challenge the assumption that replay-based and arithmetic-merge strategies transfer alignment to domain-adapted SLMs.

</details>


### [13] [Predicting Startup Exit from Textual Descriptors - A Computational Linguistics Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00045)
*Alberto M. G. Saruggia,Sebastien Germano*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Study uses only textual descriptors from startup descriptions to predict early-stage startup success (Exit), finding that narrative framing and hyping language have measurable predictive power.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether founder-written textual narratives alone, without financial or contextual data, can predict early-stage startup success, addressing information asymmetry in venture capital decision-making.

Method: Use a VC-curated dataset of 7,419 startups over 20 years; engineer 850 text-based features (startup narrative mapping) from descriptions; build vector embeddings; test for statistical significance; run supervised ML experiments with six models; compare performance, with LightGBM as top performer; analyze importance of specific textual and linguistic features; design a Hyping Score metric.

Result: LightGBM reaches F1 = 0.48 when combining all text-derived features; using raw textual descriptors alone still yields F1 = 0.30, indicating standalone predictive value. Features such as optimized densities of hyping markers (adjectives, jargon, buzzwords) correlate with higher Exit probability, while overly long statements or names correlate with lower Exit probability. A Hyping Score is constructed and shown to be predictive for Exit likelihood in VC contexts.

Conclusion: Founder narrative framing in text holds measurable predictive information about startup Exit outcomes, even absent traditional metrics. Certain linguistic patterns—moderate hype and concise naming—are associated with higher success probabilities. The introduced Hyping Score can support venture capital screening under high information asymmetry, highlighting the importance of how startups describe themselves.

Abstract: This study shows that textual descriptors alone can predict early-stage startup success, defined as Exit, without relying on contextual, financial, or human capital variables. Using venture capital-curated datasets covering 7,419 startups over 20 years, the research isolates text-based framing variables and engineers 850 features through startup narrative mapping. Data subsets and vector embeddings are evaluated for statistical significance, followed by supervised machine learning experiments across six models. LightGBM achieved the highest predictive performance (F1 = 0.48), while textual descriptors alone achieved F1 = 0.30, confirming the standalone predictive value of founder narratives. Feature analysis shows that optimized densities of hyping markers, including adjectives, jargon, and buzzwords, are associated with higher Exit probability, whereas excessive statement or name length reduces it. The study also introduces a quantifiable Hyping Score for venture capital applications, demonstrating that startup framing provides measurable signals for predicting Exit under conditions of high information asymmetry.

</details>


### [14] [Neural Circuit Function Inference with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00059)
*Yijie Yin,Albert Cardona*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces LLantia, an automated LLM-based framework that infers neural cell-type and circuit functions from literature combined with connectome data, demonstrated on the adult fruit fly brain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Connectome mapping has advanced to the point where we now have detailed wiring diagrams of nervous systems (e.g., Drosophila), but interpreting what these circuits do functionally—and how specific cell types contribute—remains difficult, time-consuming, and largely manual. There is a need for systematic, scalable, and explainable tools that can translate static connectivity data plus scattered literature into functional hypotheses about circuits, subcircuits, and cell types to guide experiments.

Method: The authors develop LLantia (LLM automated neural circuit inference and analysis), an automated pipeline that uses large language models to: (1) extract and distill functional descriptions of known neural cell types from the neuroscience literature; (2) integrate these descriptions with anatomical connectivity information from the connectome; and (3) infer functional roles for remaining, previously less-characterized cell types. The method then aggregates cell-type functions into candidate circuit and subcircuit functions, structured hierarchically under different behavioural and physiological contexts, while explicitly linking each inferred function back to specific cell types and literature sources.

Result: Applying LLantia to the adult fruit fly brain, the authors infer functional roles for all defined cell types and for selected larger circuits. They generate a hierarchical catalogue of candidate circuit functions, each broken down into subcircuit descriptions and associated cell types. They report that many of the automated inferences align with existing expert knowledge, and they validate the approach further by cross-checking a subset of predictions against papers that appeared after their original analysis, showing that later experimental work is consistent with LLantia’s earlier functional assignments.

Conclusion: LLantia demonstrates that LLM-based automation can systematically interpret connectomes by inferring plausible functions for both individual cell types and larger neural circuits. The framework yields structured, interpretable hypotheses linked to literature, providing a scalable way to move from wiring diagrams to functional understanding and to prioritize targets and mechanisms for future experimental research.

Abstract: The success of connectome mapping now shifts the challenge of understanding the nervous system to the interpretation of neural circuits. Here, we devise a new automated method, LLantia (LLM automated neural circuit inference and analysis), to systematically infer neural circuit function and the role of its component neural cell types. Our approach distills descriptions of cell type function from the literature and, in combination with the connectome, then infers the function for all other cell types, which serves as a basis for subsequent neural circuit function inference. Results are structured hierarchically, with different possible circuit functions organised under multiple possible behavioural and physiological contexts, and each circuit function composed of subcircuit descriptions alongside relevant cell types to facilitate both backtracking to known, published information and support further experimental research. We illustrate our method by inferring cell type function for all cell types of the adult fruit fly brain and for select broader circuits within, and validate our findings, including by cross-checking with literature published after the release date of our analysis.

</details>


### [15] [LLM-OSDA: An Optimal-Stopping Dynamic Auction for Native Advertising in Multi-Turn LLM Conversations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00123)
*Yan Fang,Jialin Chen,Chun Gan,Hang Yu,Mingjun Nie,Yeyu Zhang,Fengxiang He,Ching Law*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces LLM-OSDA, a dynamic auction mechanism for LLM-native advertising that jointly decides when and which ad to show during a conversation, improving revenue while retaining truthful bidding incentives and user retention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs become interactive platforms, advertising needs to move from fixed ad slots to contextually-timed, in-conversation ad insertions. Existing auction designs only choose winners per response and ignore optimal timing, which is crucial when there is a single native ad opportunity per session. Because the probability of showing an ad and its timing depend on bids, classic auction truthfulness and allocation monotonicity results no longer apply, creating a need for new mechanisms that couple timing and allocation in a principled way.

Method: The authors formulate the problem as a dynamic optimal stopping problem embedded in a cost-per-click auction. They design LLM-OSDA, which combines: (1) a bid-independent LLM layer that predicts contextual click quality and renders ads; (2) a Bellman-optimal stopping policy that decides in each conversational turn whether to show an ad or continue; (3) an allocation rule that awards the ad opportunity based on expected discounted clicks; and (4) envelope-pricing-based payments to support truthful bidding. For practical deployment, they replace the exact Bellman oracle with a learned network, StopNet, that approximates action values and thus the stopping policy.

Result: Theoretically, under an exact Bellman oracle, the mechanism ensures that each advertiser’s expected discounted allocation is monotone in its bid, enabling a payment rule where truthful bidding is a weakly dominant strategy in expectation. With the approximate StopNet, they bound how far incentives deviate from truthfulness in terms of the network’s approximation error, arguing that errors are localized near the stopping boundary. Empirically, on a simulated conversational advertising corpus, LLM-OSDA achieves an 11% net revenue improvement over the best fixed-timing baseline while preserving comparable user retention metrics.

Conclusion: Coupling optimal stopping with auction design enables effective LLM-native advertising that decides both if and when to show an ad within a conversation. LLM-OSDA provides a theoretically grounded, approximately incentive-compatible mechanism that increases platform revenue without sacrificing user engagement. The framework and accompanying StopNet approximation make dynamic, timing-aware auctions practically deployable for LLM-based ad systems.

Abstract: LLM-native advertising embeds sponsored content directly into model-generated responses, shifting the unit of sale from a fixed slot to a moment within an evolving conversation. Existing LLM ad-auction mechanisms primarily operate within a single response, settling the winner but not the timing. The extension is nontrivial: with one native insertion opportunity per session, the stopping time depends on bids, coupling timing with allocation, so static truthfulness arguments no longer apply. We propose the LLM-based Optimal Stopping Dynamic Auction (LLM-OSDA), a dynamic cost-per-click auction that integrates Bellman optimal stopping, winner allocation, and envelope pricing. A bid-independent LLM layer estimates contextual click quality and seamlessly renders the winning ad, while bids enter only the committed auction mechanism. Under an exact Bellman oracle, the expected discounted-click allocation is monotone in each advertiser's bid, and the corresponding envelope payment makes truthful bidding weakly dominant in expectation. For practical deployment, a learned StopNet approximates the Bellman action values. We show that its decisions differ from the optimal policy only near the stopping boundary and bound the resulting incentive loss in terms of its approximation error. Experiments on a simulated conversational advertising corpus show that LLM-OSDA improves net revenue by 11 percent over the strongest fixed-timing baseline while maintaining comparable user retention. Code is at https://github.com/2025Fang2025/llm-osda.

</details>


### [16] [DiffusionGemma Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00146)
*DiffusionGemma Team,Adrien Ali Taïga,James Assiene,Daniele Calandriello,Rahma Chaabouni,João Gante,Tamara von Glehn,Nate Keating,Chris Knutsen,Martin Kukla,Tianlin Liu,Ivan Lobov,Ofir Nabati,João Gabriel Oliveira,Nicolas Perez-Nieves,Nastasia Prutianova,Bobak Shahriari,Jean Tarbouriech,Pavel Tyletski,Çağlar Ünlü,Cindy Wu,Glenn Cameron,Jerome Connor,Sertan Girgin,Maarten Grootendorst,Alon Levkovitch,Eliya Nachmani,Omar Sanseviero,Piotr Stanczyk,Quentin Berthet,Andrew Campbell,Clément Crepy,Valentin De Bortoli,Arnaud Doucet,Romuald Elie,Alexandre Galashov,Klaus Greff,Alexis Jacq,David Ruhe,Yu-Han Wu,Sebastian Flennerhag,Brendan O'Donoghue,George Scrivener,Shantanu Thakoor*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DiffusionGemma is an experimental diffusion-based language model that generates blocks of tokens in parallel, achieving much faster text generation than standard autoregressive models while retaining comparable capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive language models decode tokens sequentially, creating a speed bottleneck, especially at inference time. There is a need for models that can generate text much faster without sacrificing too much capability and that can reuse existing strong AR models instead of training new ones from scratch.

Method: Starting from the mixture-of-experts Gemma 4 model (3.8B active, 25.2B total parameters), the authors fine-tune it with a compute-efficient two-stage pipeline using less than 10% of the original AR training tokens. They convert it into a discrete diffusion model that refines 256-token blocks in parallel. Stage 1 uses supervised fine-tuning to teach bidirectional denoising; Stage 2 combines reinforcement learning and sampler distillation to jointly optimize output quality and inference efficiency. The resulting model can still perform AR decoding, enabling hybrid diffusion-AR possibilities.

Result: DiffusionGemma achieves a new Pareto frontier in the speed–capability trade-off, averaging about 20 output tokens per forward pass and roughly 1,500 tokens per second on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU. It significantly outperforms autoregressive models in speed, even those using advanced speculative decoding, while maintaining strong performance close to the base Gemma 4 model. It preserves key features like thinking mode, multimodal input support, and long-context handling, and its AR performance is only slightly degraded after diffusion fine-tuning.

Conclusion: Discrete diffusion can be successfully applied to large language models to overcome the sequential decoding bottleneck, delivering much faster generation while preserving most of the base model’s capabilities. Fine-tuning an existing AR model with a two-stage denoising and RL-plus-distillation pipeline yields a highly efficient diffusion LLM that still supports AR decoding, pointing toward future hybrid diffusion–autoregressive systems that flexibly trade off speed and performance.

Abstract: We introduce DiffusionGemma, an experimental open-weight language model that uses discrete diffusion to generate text at exceptionally high speed. Rather than decoding one token at a time, DiffusionGemma iteratively refines blocks of 256 tokens in parallel, avoiding the sequential decoding bottleneck of conventional autoregressive (AR) large language models. Instead of training from scratch, we obtain DiffusionGemma by fine-tuning the mixture-of-experts Gemma 4 model with 3.8B activated and 25.2B total parameters. Our compute-efficient two-stage training pipeline uses fewer than 10% of the starting AR model's total training token budget. The first stage uses supervised fine-tuning to teach bidirectional denoising, while the second stage combines reinforcement learning with sampler distillation to jointly improve generation quality and inference efficiency. DiffusionGemma establishes a new Pareto frontier for the trade-off between generation speed and model capability. Averaged across our full evaluation suite, it generates around 20 tokens per forward pass and achieves roughly 1,500 output tokens per second on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU, which is substantially faster than AR models even with state-of-the-art speculative decoding. DiffusionGemma also retains the starting model's support for thinking mode, multimodal inputs, and long contexts. Despite diffusion fine-tuning, it remains capable of AR generation with only minor performance degradation, suggesting a path toward hybrid diffusion-AR decoding.

</details>


### [17] [A Constitution-Grid Instrument for Data-Efficient RL Alignment (C-Guard)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00180)
*Lily Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces methods to more efficiently align RL-trained safety guards facing conflicting objectives of catching harm vs not over-refusing benign prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In RL alignment, safety guards must balance two conflicting goals: detecting real harm and avoiding unnecessary refusals of benign prompts. Existing approaches struggle to train on these conflicting objectives in a data-efficient way, and can silently worsen performance on adversarial attacks while improving benign behavior. The authors aim to systematically manage this tradeoff and improve data efficiency in RL training for safety alignment.

Method: The authors propose C-Guard, a constitution-grid instrument that structures and generates RL training data across cells defined by different conditions or principles. They also introduce C-LIM, a per-cell learnability score that determines how to treat each cell in the grid—whether to prune it, densify it with more data, amend it, or expand it. C-LIM is used to identify unproductive data regions before investing training budget, thus focusing learning on impactful areas.

Result: Using their approach, the authors report that over-refusal on benign prompts is improved (reduced) from 22.4% to 12.8%. However, they find that under-refusal on adversarial attacks can silently worsen from 0.27 to 0.33 if not carefully managed. C-LIM identifies 187 untargeted rows that previously contributed no learning gain, and applying their method raises the learning impact in this region from 0.733 to 0.80.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that structuring RL safety training via a constitution-based grid and guiding data allocation with a learnability metric (C-LIM) improves data efficiency and impact of safety training, while exposing hidden tradeoffs such as worsening robustness on adversarial attacks. The open-sourced code and constitution enable further use and extension of the proposed C-Guard framework.

Abstract: Conflicting objectives are general in RL alignment, and training on them data-efficiently is hard. Training a safety guard with RL means optimizing two objectives that conflict: catch real harm, and do not refuse benign prompts. Our finding is that over-refusal improves 22.4% to 12.8%, while under-refusal on adversarial attacks silently worsens 0.27 to 0.33. We present C-Guard, a constitution-grid instrument that generates the RL training data, and C-LIM, a per-cell learnability score that decides each cell's move: prune, densify, amend, expand. C-LIM flags the dead-weight data region before any training budget is spent: 187 untargeted rows had bought zero gain, and our method lifts the same region's learning impact 0.733 to 0.80. Code and the constitution are open-sourced.

</details>


### [18] [Averaging Bias: Human Faithfulness Annotations are not Locally Faithful](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00205)
*Huajian Zhang,Yiyang Feng,Jiawei Zhou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that human faithfulness labels for summarization exhibit an Averaging Bias: annotators often accept summaries as faithful even when some sentences are unsupported.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Faithfulness evaluation in text summarization typically assumes a strict standard: a summary is faithful only if every sentence is supported by the source. However, common benchmarks only provide a single global faithfulness label per summary. The authors want to know whether these global labels really reflect the strict conjunctive rule or whether human annotators implicitly use a softer, more averaged notion of faithfulness.

Method: The authors re-examine four widely used faithfulness benchmarks by using five large language models as per-sentence judges of factual faithfulness. For each summary, they obtain per-sentence LLM judgments and compare two aggregate interpretations: (1) the strict conjunctive rule (all sentences must be faithful) and (2) the mean of per-sentence scores. They then measure which better correlates with the original global human labels. They also manually inspect summaries labeled as faithful by humans but flagged as partially unfaithful by LLMs to verify the presence of real factual errors.

Result: They find that the global human faithfulness labels align more strongly with the average of per-sentence LLM judgments than with the strict conjunctive rule. Manual review confirms that many summaries labeled as faithful by humans do, in fact, contain local factual errors, validating that the misalignment is not just model noise. This systematic pattern is termed Averaging Bias.

Conclusion: Human-provided global faithfulness labels in widely used summarization benchmarks often embody an Averaging Bias: annotators tolerate some local unfaithfulness as long as most of the summary is faithful. Consequently, these benchmarks do not strictly enforce the commonly assumed all-sentences-must-be-faithful criterion, and future benchmark and annotation designs must be more carefully structured if they are to support trustworthy faithfulness evaluation and training.

Abstract: Evaluation of faithfulness of text summarization treats a model generated summary as faithful only if every of its sentences is supported by the source document: a strict conjunctive rule under which a single unsupported sentence makes the whole summary unfaithful. Yet most faithfulness benchmarks collect only one global human annotation label per summary. We ask whether such global human labels actually implement the conjunctive rule. We hypothesize that annotators may accept a summary as faithful when most sentences are faithful, not only when all are faithful. To test our hypothesis, we use five large language model (LLM) judges as per-sentence raters across four widely used faithfulness benchmarks. We find that global human labels correlate better with the average of per-sentence LLM judgments than with the implementation of the strict conjunctive rule. A manual review confirms that a substantial fraction of summaries labeled faithful by humans contain genuine local factual errors. We call this tendency Averaging Bias. Our results reveal that human labels on widely used faithfulness benchmarks contain measurable Averaging Bias, calling for carefully structured designs for trustworthy human annotations

</details>


### [19] [Bridging the English-Arabic Medical Knowledge Gap: Targeted Low-Rank Adaptation via Causal Layer Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00207)
*Chaimae Abouzahir,Musa Khan,Hala Ali-Hassan,Congbo Ma,Khaled Saleh,Yousra Sadqi,Jihad Mallat,Walid Al-Eisawi,Nizar Habash,Farah E. Shamout*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that Arabic medical knowledge already exists inside LLMs but is blocked from appearing in outputs, and proposes TLoRA, a targeted fine-tuning method on specific layers that fixes this more efficiently than full-model adaptation, plus releases an Arabic clinical dialogue benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs work well for English medical tasks but poorly in Arabic, commonly blamed on lack of Arabic training data. The authors want to check if the problem is actually missing knowledge or a failure to express already-learned knowledge, and then use this mechanistic understanding to design a better adaptation method for underrepresented languages.

Method: They use tuned lens probing and causal activation patching to inspect intermediate representations in LLMs and compare Arabic vs English medical reasoning. Finding a divergence window where Arabic representations differ from English despite containing relevant knowledge, they design Targeted Low-Rank Adaptation (TLoRA), which applies LoRA updates only to a specific subset of layers just before the output head. They train and evaluate this on Arabic medical tasks and also construct the AraClinicDialog benchmark with MSA and dialectal variants created and validated by clinicians.

Result: The analysis shows that Arabic medical information is encoded in intermediate layers but fails to be decoded properly to the output. TLoRA, applied only to the problematic layer window, outperforms full-network LoRA, zero-shot, and few-shot approaches on multiple-choice Arabic medical QA, and performs competitively on short-answer generation and multi-turn Arabic clinical dialogue, despite not being tuned specifically for those tasks. They also provide the new AraClinicDialog benchmark covering MSA and four major dialects.

Conclusion: Performance gaps in Arabic medical LLMs stem less from total lack of knowledge and more from representation-to-output failures. Mechanistic interpretability tools can locate where this breakdown occurs and guide targeted, parameter-efficient adaptation (TLoRA) that is more effective and generalizes across tasks. The release of AraClinicDialog further supports evaluation and development of Arabic medical systems, and the overall framework is promising for other underrepresented languages and domains.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform strongly in English medical tasks but degrade substantially in Arabic, a gap widely attributed to limited training data. We systematically investigate this assumption via tuned lens probing and causal activation patching, and find that Arabic medical knowledge is present in intermediate model representations but fails to surface at the output. This mechanistic insight motivates a targeted adaptation strategy: rather than fine-tuning the full network, we propose Targeted Low-Rank Adaptation (TLoRA), restricted to the layer window where cross-lingual representations diverge, upstream of the output layers where the failure manifests. We evaluate TLoRA on multiple-choice medical QA, where our approach outperforms full-network LoRA, zero-shot, and few-shot baselines. We further evaluate it on short-answer generation and multi-turn clinical dialogue, where it performs competitively without the need for task-specific finetuning. We additionally introduce AraClinicDialog, a clinician-constructed Arabic medical dialogue benchmark in MSA with validated variants across four Arabic dialects. Together, these contributions demonstrate that mechanistic diagnosis can serve as a practical guide for targeted adaptation in underrepresented-language medical LLMs.

</details>


### [20] [A Few Neurons Reveal When LLMs Misuse Tools: Sparse Detection and Selective Steering for Reliable Tool Use](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00218)
*Yutong Ke,Ming Yin,Chongwen Zhao,Kaizhu Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces PRISMS, a method that identifies and leverages a small set of neurons in LLMs to detect and actively control tool-use failures (invalid, missing, and unnecessary tool calls) with high accuracy and very sparse features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic LLMs frequently misuse tools, either by calling them unnecessarily, failing to call them when needed, or issuing invalid tool calls. These errors are costly and undermine reliability, and existing monitoring/steering methods are often dense, expensive, and not robust across models. The authors aim to find compact, interpretable internal signals that both predict such failures and can be used to correct them in a targeted way.

Method: The authors analyze MLP neuron activations in several LLMs (Qwen3, Llama, Gemma) during tool-use tasks and search for neurons whose activations distinguish specific failure types. They then construct PRISMS, a framework that: (1) selects contribution-critical MLP neurons related to each failure mode; (2) trains sparse, L1-regularized linear detectors on these neurons to predict failures (over-calling, missing, invalid calls); and (3) uses the same neuron subset for intervention via activation steering, enabling suppression or elicitation of tool calls based on predicted risk. Detection for over-calling/missing is done at the prompt boundary; validity is detected from the generated tool-call span.

Result: A small number of neurons (1–2 for missing, 2–16 for over-calling, ~128 for validity) is sufficient to detect failures with high ROC-AUC: 0.90–1.00 for over-calling and missing at the pre-generation prompt boundary, and 0.86–0.90 for validity from the tool-call span. These sparse detectors match or outperform dense residual-stream baselines while using 23–627× fewer features. Using the same neuron basis for steering, PRISMS enables accurate bidirectional control of tool use, gating interventions on predicted failure risk. Across six models, PRISMS reduces over-calling from 0.131 to 0.026 (an 80% reduction) and increases tool-required accuracy from 0.689 to 0.831 (+14.2 percentage points).

Conclusion: PRISMS demonstrates that small, failure-specific sets of MLP neurons in LLMs encode enough information to both detect and control tool-use failures in a lightweight, model-agnostic way. By combining sparse probing with targeted activation steering on a shared neuron basis, it provides efficient, selective intervention that improves tool-use reliability across multiple model families, avoiding the blunt side effects of unconditional steering.

Abstract: Agentic LLMs exhibit three consequential tool-use failures: invalid arguments (validity), unnecessary calls (over-calling), and omitted calls when tools are needed (missing). We find that a small, failure-specific set of MLP neurons could distinguish such failures with linearly separable decision boundaries. Building on this observation, we introduce PRISMS (Probing Representations In Support of Monitoring and Steering), a closed-loop framework that shares a failure-specific neuron basis between sparse detection and activation steering. PRISMS selects contribution-critical MLP neurons and fits an L1-regularized detector on their activations. Across six models from the Qwen3, Llama, and Gemma families, over-calling and missing are detected at the pre-generation prompt boundary with ROC-AUC 0.90-1.00, while validity is detected from the generated tool-call span with ROC-AUC 0.86-0.90. These results are achieved with highly sparse readouts: only 1-2 MLP neurons for missing, 2-16 for over-calling, and approximately 128 for validity.
