These sparse detectors match or outperform dense residual-stream baselines using 23-627 times fewer features. The shared neuron basis also supports bidirectional control over tool-calling behavior, suppressing unnecessary calls and eliciting omitted ones. PRISMS therefore gates intervention on predicted failure risk to mitigate the collateral effects of unconditional steering. Across all six models, PRISMS reduces pooled over-calling rate by 80% (from 0.131 to 0.026) while increasing tool-required accuracy by 14.2 percentage points (from 0.689 to 0.831). PRISMS thus provides lightweight failure detection and selective intervention across model families.

</details>


### [21] [Cross-Task Dissociation in Frontier Vision-Language Model Theory of Mind](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00261)
*Kejia Zhang,Youran Sun,Chugang Yi,Haizhao Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper tests whether leading vision-language models (VLMs) show a stable, human-like Theory-of-Mind (ToM) profile across different tasks, and finds they do not: their apparent ToM abilities fragment across paradigms and tend to resemble children or high-functioning autistic adults rather than typical adults, depending on the task.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although large vision-language models often appear to have Theory-of-Mind abilities in isolated benchmarks, it is unclear whether they exhibit a coherent, human-like ToM profile across diverse paradigms. Human ToM performance is structured and relatively stable across tasks and reference groups (e.g., typical adults vs. children vs. HF-ASD adults). The authors aim to test whether frontier VLMs similarly cluster around one human reference group across tasks, or whether their ToM-like behavior breaks apart when probed with distinct, well-validated psychological measures that tap different aspects of mental-state reasoning.

Method: The authors evaluate nine frontier vision-language models on two classic psychology-derived ToM tasks. (1) The Keysar Director Task, which assesses visual perspective-taking in the presence of egocentric interference; they test models without chain-of-thought and also examine the effect of prompting for explicit reasoning. (2) The Frith-Happé animated triangles task, where subjects interpret simple geometric animations and are scored with the Castelli rubric for intentionality attribution, specifically comparing models’ intention scores to human reference distributions: typical-development adults (TD) and high-functioning autistic adults (HF-ASD). They then analyze how each model’s profile positions it relative to these human groups and whether any model consistently aligns with the same human-like profile across both tasks.

Result: On the Director Task without chain-of-thought prompting, the model panel makes the egocentric error on 78% of trials, resembling child performance more than adult performance, and models vary substantially in how often they make this error. Providing reasoning or chain-of-thought prompts substantially improves performance for several models, reducing egocentric errors. On the Frith-Happé triangles, models systematically under-attribute intention: their ToM scores are over three times closer (in the relevant metric) to the HF-ASD adult mean than to the TD adult mean, although their scores on Goal-Directed and Random motion descriptions remain close to the TD profile. Crucially, no single model is closest to TD adults on both tasks: the model that appears adult-like on the Director Task scores more like HF-ASD adults on the triangles, while the model most similar to TD adults on the triangles performs like children on the Director Task.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that current frontier vision-language models do not exhibit a unified, human-like Theory-of-Mind profile across tasks. Instead, their ToM performance is fragmented and task-dependent: they may seem adult-like on one paradigm while resembling children or HF-ASD adults on another. This suggests that apparent ToM competence in VLMs may reflect task-specific heuristics or pattern matching rather than a robust, generalizable understanding of others’ mental states. The paper underscores the importance of multi-task, psychology-informed evaluation to avoid overinterpreting models’ mental-state reasoning abilities and cautions against drawing diagnostic analogies, emphasizing that their analyses are at the group-profile level only.

Abstract: Do frontier vision-language models present a coherent Theory-of-Mind (ToM) profile across tasks, matching the same human reference group, or does that profile fragment from one paradigm to the next? We evaluate a shared panel of nine frontier VLMs on two psychology-derived benchmarks: the Keysar Director Task (visual perspective-taking under egocentric interference) and the Frith-Happé animated triangles scored with the Castelli rubric (intention attribution from pure motion). On the Director Task, without chain-of-thought, the panel makes the egocentric error on 78\% of trials like children rather than adults; variation is substantial across models, and reasoning rescues several models. On the triangles, the panel under-attributes intention: its ToM profile sits more than three times closer to the high-functioning-autistic-adult (HF-ASD) mean than to the typical-development-adult (TD) mean, while Goal-Directed and Random stay near TD. No model is nearest TD on both tasks; the model that looks adult-like on the Director Task falls on the HF-ASD side on the triangles, and the most TD-like model on the triangles is child-like on the Director Task. We report group-level descriptions, not diagnostic labels for any model.

</details>


### [22] [Sixteen models, fewer than two voices: measuring ensemble dispersion where no answer is uniquely correct](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00285)
*Mario Vega-Barbas,Lidia Mora-Valenciano,Iván Pau,Fernando Seoane,Farhad Abtahi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how multiple language models together provide diverse interpretations of psychotherapeutic cases, quantifies each model’s unique “dissent,” and finds that diversity depends more on clinical content and ensemble composition than on model family labels or vignette openness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Decision-makers increasingly rely on ensembles of language models under the assumption that multiple models provide multiple perspectives, but existing measures of diversity and uncertainty are tied to correctness, which doesn’t apply to open-ended psychotherapeutic case interpretations. The authors want to understand where diversity among models actually comes from and how to attribute it to individual models within an ensemble.

Method: The authors use 16 language models from 10 model families to generate 7,082 case formulations for 15 psychotherapeutic vignettes stratified by interpretive openness. They quantify overall semantic diversity using the Vendi Score (the exponential of the von Neumann entropy of a similarity matrix) and introduce a per-model “dissent contribution” defined as the complement of each model’s mean similarity to the rest of the ensemble. They then cross model identity and case, pre-register a hypothesis that model identity explains non-zero variance in dissent, and statistically analyze how dissent varies with model family, scale, panel composition, and case characteristics.

Result: Across ensembles, the average semantic diversity corresponds to about 1.69 distinct case formulations, compared to 1.43 from repeated runs of a single model, confirming added diversity from model ensembles. Model identity significantly structures dissent, but conventional groupings—such as model family and scale—only partially explain these patterns. Scale effects vary idiosyncratically between model pairs, model families form only a few weakly-consistent two-member groupings, and the model that appears most divergent shifts when the ensemble composition changes. Dissent is not aligned with the pre-stratified interpretive openness of vignettes but instead clusters around specific clinical contents of the cases.

Conclusion: Ensembles of language models do yield more diverse psychotherapeutic case formulations than single models, but diversity is a nuanced property of the ensemble’s composition rather than a stable trait of individual models or families. The proposed per-model dissent measure reveals that the “most divergent” model is context-dependent and reflects the ensemble’s structure, not an intrinsic outlier model. Because dissent is organised by clinical content rather than case openness, practitioners should empirically measure, not assume, the diversity provided by model ensembles in complex, correctness-free domains like psychotherapy.

Abstract: Sixteen language models drawn from ten families produced, on average, the semantic diversity of 1.69 distinct formulations of a psychotherapeutic case, against a single-model baseline of 1.43 from one model's own runs. Ensembles place more than one reading before a decision-maker on the premise that several models supply several perspectives. Dispersion over their outputs is measured both as diversity and as uncertainty, and both traditions validate it against a correctness criterion that this task does not admit. Measuring diversity is a solved problem: the Vendi Score, the exponential of the von Neumann entropy of a similarity matrix, is an effective number of distinct elements. What a single aggregate does not say is where the diversity comes from. We define a per-model dissent contribution, the complement of a model's mean similarity to the other members of its ensemble: a magnitude from the same matrix, not a decomposition of the spectral index, whose maximum identifies the most divergent voice. Crossing model and case, we test as a preregistered hypothesis whether model identity accounts for a non-zero share of the variance in dissent, and characterise the structure that test detects. The panel formulated fifteen stratified vignettes, yielding 7,082 formulations for analysis. Model identity was a detectable structuring factor of the dissent that remained, but the usual categories recovered it only partly: scale differences pointed in opposite directions across pairs, family grouped models on only five two-member lines, and the most divergent voice changed with panel composition, so that the surfaced outlier describes the ensemble rather than the model. Dissent did not track the interpretive openness for which the case bank was stratified; it was organised by clinical content instead, leaving the dispersion an ensemble produces a property to measure rather than assume.

</details>


### [23] [Comparing and Modeling Argumentation in German Political Communication across Arenas](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00288)
*Nina Vikhrova,Johannes Kühling,Sebastian Haunss,Sebastian Padó*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They build and analyze a corpus of German political COVID-19 discourse across three arenas to compare how arguments and justifications differ, and run a pilot model to detect argumentative passages automatically.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While deliberation and argumentation are central to democratic politics, existing computational work has mostly ignored how argumentation patterns vary between different political arenas such as plenary debates, committees, and press conferences. There is especially little annotated data to enable systematic comparison and modeling of these differences.

Method: They construct a 17k-sentence corpus from three German political arenas (plenary speeches, committee meetings, press conferences) on a fixed topic (COVID-19). They manually annotate argumentative passages, including both arguments and their justifications, marking their text boundaries and assigning categories to them. They then conduct corpus-based quantitative analysis of argumentation patterns across arenas. Finally, they run a pilot computational study in which models are trained to automatically identify argumentative passages and their boundaries, and they evaluate model behavior, including biases.

Result: Corpus analysis shows an unexpected pattern: justifications invoking domain-specific expertise appear more often in press conferences than in committee meetings, contrary to common assumptions about where expert reasoning dominates. In the modeling pilot, they find that accurately detecting the exact boundaries of argumentative passages is difficult, and that model predictions exhibit confirmation bias, over-predicting argumentation in contexts where it is expected or salient.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that argumentation differs systematically across political arenas in ways that challenge intuitive expectations, and it provides a new annotated corpus as a resource for such comparisons. It also shows that current models struggle with fine-grained detection of argumentative passages and are prone to confirmation bias, indicating that more sophisticated methods and better annotation schemes are needed for reliable computational analysis of political argumentation.

Abstract: Deliberation, involving the formulation and exchange of arguments, forms an integral part of political decision making in democracies. Argumentation patterns however differ substantially across different political arenas, such as plenary speeches and committee meetings. However, despite a lot of interest in argumentation, there is comparatively little computational work on analyzing differences in patterns of political argumentation between arenas.
  Our work addresses this research gap. First, we present a 17k-sentence corpus with annotation for argumentative passages (argument and their justifications, both their boundaries and their categories) across three German political arenas (plenary speeches, committee meetings, and press conferences), keeping the topic (COVID-19) constant. Our analysis of the corpus finds that contrary to expectations, justification by domain-specific expertise is more frequent in press conferences than in committee meetings. Second, we present a pilot study on automatically identifying such argumentative passages. The results show that boundaries are hard to pin down, and models predictions additionally suffer from confirmation bias.

</details>


### [24] [SeDeM: Selective Decompression of Hidden-State Memories for Long-Context Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00311)
*Maryam Haghifam,Jason Cong,Yizhou Sun*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SeDeM is a selective decompression framework that stores compact intermediate hidden states as memory blocks, then selectively decompresses only relevant blocks to support long-context inference more efficiently and accurately than full-context or prior compression baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-context inference with LLMs is computationally expensive due to quadratic self-attention cost and linear growth of KV-cache with sequence length. Even when large context windows are available, models can still fail to reliably use relevant evidence. Existing soft-compression methods typically employ LLMs themselves as compressors and rely on a small set of compact memory tokens both to retain information and to directly condition the decoder, which can limit effectiveness. There is a need for a method that reduces long-context cost while preserving or improving evidence use without forcing the decoder to generate directly from heavily compressed representations.

Method: SeDeM introduces a selective decompression pipeline that decouples compact memory storage from how the decoder is conditioned. First, an LLM processes the long context and intermediate hidden states are extracted from a chosen Transformer layer. A lightweight compressor encodes these hidden states into compact memory blocks. At inference, a query-conditioned selector identifies which memory blocks are likely to contain relevant evidence. A decompressor then expands only the selected blocks back into hidden states compatible with an intermediate layer of the decoder. The decoder continues from that layer using only the decompressed relevant blocks, avoiding full-context self-attention and direct generation from ultra-compressed memory tokens. The selector is trained with block-level evidence supervision so it learns to pick the blocks that matter for answering questions.

Result: On four long-context QA benchmarks, SeDeM outperforms evaluated compression baselines for both 1B and 3B parameter models sharing the same backbone. With the 3B backbone, SeDeM even surpasses full-context fine-tuning on three of the datasets, indicating better use of evidence despite not seeing the entire context at once. Additionally, compared to ICAE, SeDeM achieves lower online time-to-first-token and higher autoregressive decoding throughput, demonstrating significant efficiency gains in generation latency and speed.

Conclusion: SeDeM shows that selectively decompressing only query-relevant portions of a compressed intermediate representation can both reduce the computational cost of long-context inference and improve answer quality. By decoupling compact memory storage from decoder conditioning and training a supervised selector at the block level, SeDeM avoids the weaknesses of prior soft-compression approaches that rely on generating directly from a few compressed tokens. The framework offers a practical direction for scalable long-context LLMs with better evidence utilization and improved latency and throughput.

Abstract: Long-context inference with large language models (LLMs) is costly: self-attention during prefill scales quadratically with sequence length, and the key-value (KV) cache grows with the number of processed tokens. Larger context windows also do not ensure reliable evidence use. Context compression reduces this cost, but many soft-compression methods use LLMs as compressors and rely on compact memory tokens both to preserve information and to condition the decoder. We propose SeDeM, a selective decompression framework that decouples compact memory storage from decoder conditioning. An LLM extracts hidden states from a chosen intermediate Transformer layer, a lightweight compressor stores them as memory blocks, a query-conditioned selector selects relevant blocks, and a decompressor expands only the selected blocks into hidden states compatible with an intermediate decoder layer. Thus, the decoder avoids both full-context processing and direct generation from highly compressed memory slots. On four long-context QA benchmarks, SeDeM achieves higher QA scores than the evaluated compression baselines in both 1B and 3B same-backbone settings, and with the 3B backbone exceeds full-context fine-tuning on three datasets. The learned selector uses block-level evidence supervision during training. SeDeM also reduces online time-to-first-token and improves autoregressive decoding throughput relative to ICAE.

</details>


### [25] [CurveShift: Is Agent Progress Scalar? Separating Level from Shape](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00355)
*Hanwen Xing,Pengyun Wang,BingXu Meng,Kumail Alhamoud,Xiang Li,Jicheng Wang,Xin Yu,Xinyang Han,Xiaomin Li,Philip Torr,Yuexing Hao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper examines whether recent large language model improvements disproportionately benefit harder tasks or are mostly artifacts of metrics and ceiling effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Researchers often summarize LLM progress with single scores, which hide how gains vary by task difficulty and can falsely suggest that models are uniquely improving on hard problems.

Method: The authors analyze METR time-horizon data using Rasch modeling to separate ability from task difficulty, then use LiveCodeBench, a competitive programming benchmark with fixed difficulty ordering and no agentic scaffolding, to measure difficulty-specific gains across 66 dated models and 1,055 problems.

Result: On METR benchmarks, an unchanged difficulty-response curve with rising overall ability explains most of the apparent shift toward harder tasks; on LiveCodeBench, after controlling for overall ability increases, post–Sept 2024 models still show an additional +0.40 logit gain on the hardest problems, boosting solve rates from about 18% to 25%, especially for strong reasoning models on short-horizon tasks.

Conclusion: Much of the perceived improvement on hard tasks is a metric/ceiling artifact rather than a qualitative capability shift, but there remains a measurable, domain-specific hard-task advantage in recent models for difficult competitive programming problems; the authors release a difficulty panel dataset and code for further study.

Abstract: Progress in large language models is often summarized using a single scalar measure, such as a time horizon, a latent ability estimate, or an aggregate benchmark score. These summaries capture the overall performance, but they do not test whether progress is distributed differently across task difficulty. We find that most of the apparent shift in gains toward harder tasks does not reflect a change in the shape of the difficulty-response curve. On METR time-horizon data, a single Rasch model with rising ability reproduces this pattern, so it is largely explained by ceiling effects rather than a qualitative change in capability. This echoes how the choice of metric can make claimed emergent abilities look like a property of the models themselves. We then identify a smaller hard-task effect that survives this control. Isolating it is difficult on agentic benchmarks, because newer models are usually run with newer agentic harnesses, so a gain on hard tasks cannot be assigned to the model or its scaffold. We break the confound with LiveCodeBench, a public competitive programming benchmark that runs no agentic scaffold while pairing dated models with an exogenous difficulty ordering. After accounting for the rise in overall ability, models released after September 2024 still gain on the hardest problems beyond what their easy and medium performance predicts, by about +0.40 logits under our most conservative assumption, raising the hard-problem solve rate from roughly 18% to 25%. The effect is led by the strongest reasoning models and holds for hard tasks that need only short reasoning, not autonomy over long horizons. We present this as a result specific to competitive programming, since our clean identification rests on a single coding benchmark. We release the LiveCodeBench Difficulty Panel (66 dated models x 1,055 problems) and our analysis code.

</details>


### [26] [Deep Research Pretraining via Predictive Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00432)
*Jiang Zhou,Zhiyuan Fan,Xing Wu,Tinghao Yu,Feng Zhang,Lilin Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes Deep Research Pretraining (DRP), an offline method that converts citation and hyperlink structures into synthetic research trajectories to train deep research agents efficiently, improving performance under limited supervised data compared to standard pretraining and SFT alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training deep research agents typically requires expensive, environment-grounded tool-use trajectories where models iteratively search, read, and synthesize information. Collecting such trajectories is costly and requires a live retrieval environment and policy rollouts. The authors are motivated to find a more scalable, offline approach that still teaches models how to navigate evidence, decide what to search, what to read, and how to synthesize information for research-style tasks, especially when supervised agent trajectory data is scarce.

Method: They introduce Deep Research Pretraining (DRP), which leverages naturally occurring evidence structures like scholarly citations and Wikipedia hyperlinks. For each citation-bearing or hyperlinked passage, DRP constructs a proxy research objective, retrieves the linked evidence and graph-related alternatives, and converts these into synthetic search-open-write trajectories. These trajectories simulate the behavior of a research agent (what to search, which documents to inspect, and how to synthesize evidence) without requiring an online environment. They instantiate two datasets: DRP-Paper, based on scholarly citation graphs, and DRP-Web, based on Wikipedia links. Separate Qwen3-14B-Base models are continually pretrained on 1B DRP tokens, then fine-tuned with varying small fractions of 13K real agent trajectories. They also run source-matched and evidence-mismatch control experiments to isolate the effect of evidence-conditioned navigation from domain exposure or format imitation.

Result: Across five independently sampled low-data subsets, both DRP-Paper and DRP-Web models outperform baseline models without DRP on DeepResearch Bench. Under a quarter of the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data, DRP-Web surpasses a no-DRP model trained on the full SFT dataset, and its gains transfer to other benchmarks: ResearchQA, WebWalkerQA, and SimpleQA. When starting from matched low-data SFT checkpoints, the DRP-Web performance advantage remains even after additional agentic reinforcement learning (RL). Control experiments show that these gains cannot be attributed solely to domain exposure or copying an agent format but instead to learning evidence-conditioned navigation.

Conclusion: Deep Research Pretraining (DRP) offers a scalable, offline alternative and complement to traditional trajectory-based training for research agents. By converting citation and hyperlink structures into search-open-write trajectories, DRP effectively teaches models evidence-seeking and synthesis behaviors without online interaction, leading to robust performance improvements in low-data regimes and benefits that persist through subsequent RL. This suggests DRP is a promising direction for improving research agents while reducing reliance on expensive environment-grounded data collection.

Abstract: Deep research agents are often trained on expensive, environment-grounded tool-use trajectories that require repeated retrieval, document inspection, and report evaluation. We introduce Deep Research Pretraining (DRP), an offline framework that derives predictive navigation supervision from naturally occurring evidence structures. Given a citation-bearing or hyperlinked passage, DRP constructs a proxy research objective, recovers linked evidence and graph-related alternatives, and converts them into search-open-write trajectories. This teaches models what to search for, which documents to inspect, and how to synthesize evidence, without a live retrieval environment or executed policy rollout. We instantiate DRP on scholarly citation graphs (DRP-Paper) and Wikipedia hyperlinks (DRP-Web), continually pretrain separate Qwen3-14B-Base models on 1B tokens, and fine-tune them on controlled fractions of 13K agent trajectories. Across five independently sampled subsets at each low-data budget, both variants consistently outperform matched no-DRP models on DeepResearch Bench. With one quarter of the SFT data, DRP-Web even surpasses a fixed no-DRP full-data checkpoint, with gains transferring to ResearchQA, WebWalkerQA, and SimpleQA. Starting from matched low-data SFT checkpoints, the DRP-Web advantage also persists through subsequent agentic RL. Source-matched and evidence-mismatch controls indicate that these improvements arise from evidence-conditioned navigation rather than domain exposure or agent-format imitation. DRP thus provides a promising complementary approach to trajectory-based agent training.

</details>


### [27] [AdaMTP: An Adaptive Training Paradigm for Multi-Token Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00434)
*Ziqiang Cui,Han Shi,Bowei He,Yu Pan,Peiyang Liu,Shengyin Sun,Yankai Chen,Haoli Bai,Yichun Yin,Xue Liu,Chen Ma*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: AdaMTP adaptively chooses how many future tokens to predict based on sequence uncertainty, reducing noisy supervision and improving both quality and speed over standard multi-token prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard multi-token prediction uses a fixed prediction horizon for all positions, ignoring that language and code have uneven information density. When auxiliary heads are forced to predict across high-entropy semantic boundaries (where the future is inherently unpredictable), their errors create noisy, conflicting gradients that harm the shared backbone. The paper is motivated by the need to keep the efficiency benefits of MTP while avoiding degradation of core model capabilities caused by these misaligned, overly aggressive predictions.

Method: The authors introduce AdaMTP, an adaptive multi-token prediction scheme. First, they run an entropy-based segmentation algorithm using the base model’s token-level uncertainty to detect sharp increases in entropy, which are treated as semantic boundaries. These boundaries partition the sequence into variable-length, semantically coherent groups. For each token, they then assign an adaptive prediction depth that does not cross detected boundaries. A dynamically masked MTP loss function zeroes out supervision terms for auxiliary heads whose predictions would cross a boundary, thereby preventing noisy gradients from high-entropy regions from flowing into the backbone representations shared by all heads.

Result: On three different LLM backbones (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Gemma-3-12B), and across tasks including mathematical reasoning, code generation, and general language benchmarks, AdaMTP yields better task performance than standard fixed-horizon MTP. At the same time, it preserves or improves inference speedup relative to standard MTP, demonstrating that adaptively masking predictions at semantic boundaries can mitigate quality–speed trade-offs inherent in conventional MTP training.

Conclusion: Adaptive multi-token prediction that respects sequence predictability provides cleaner supervision than fixed-horizon MTP. By using entropy-based segmentation to avoid predictions that cross semantic boundaries, AdaMTP reduces harmful gradient noise and improves both accuracy and inference efficiency. This suggests that future MTP and acceleration methods should incorporate uncertainty-aware, structure-sensitive training objectives rather than treating all token positions as equally predictable.

Abstract: Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) has emerged as an effective paradigm that augments a shared Large Language Model backbone with auxiliary heads, training the model to predict several future tokens in parallel to enrich its supervision signal and accelerate inference. However, existing training frameworks adopt a rigid, fixed-length prediction horizon, disregarding the highly non-uniform information density of natural language and code. Forcing the auxiliary heads to predict across high-entropy semantic boundaries injects noisy, conflicting training signals; because these heads share the backbone's latent representations, the resulting gradients backpropagate and interfere with the model's core capabilities. We propose AdaMTP, an adaptive training paradigm that dynamically aligns the prediction horizon with the intrinsic predictability of the sequence. At its core, an entropy-based segmentation algorithm leverages the base model to detect sudden surges in uncertainty as semantic boundaries, partitioning sequences into variable-length groups. Each token is assigned an adaptive prediction depth, and a dynamically masked MTP objective suppresses the loss for predictions that cross these boundaries, attenuating the noisy gradients that degrade the backbone. Across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and general benchmarks on three backbones (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Gemma-3-12B), AdaMTP consistently outperforms standard MTP in both task performance and inference speedup.

</details>


### [28] [SERL-SQL: Selective Hindsight Distillation for Text-to-SQL Reinforcement Agentic Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00485)
*Tao Liu,Tao Feng,Xiangheng Li,Jinwang Song,Yifan Li,Xiaoqing Cheng,Dixuan Zhang,Siquan Li,Lin Lan,Hongying Zan,Kunli Zhang,Chao Wu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces SERL-SQL, a reinforcement learning framework that improves multi-turn Text-to-SQL agents by assigning more precise credit to specific SQL and tool actions using execution feedback, leading to state-of-the-art or competitive performance on several benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-turn Text-to-SQL systems use execution correctness as a single trajectory-level reward, which does not clearly indicate which specific SQL decisions caused success or failure. This weak credit assignment limits the effectiveness of reinforcement learning and the ability to learn better query generation strategies from interaction and execution feedback.

Method: SERL-SQL is a selective execution-grounded reinforcement learning framework. It samples on-policy interaction trajectories from a Text-to-SQL agent and uses a separate, training-only teacher model to re-score the student’s actions, incorporating execution feedback. The difference in likelihood between teacher and student (teacher–student likelihood gap) is converted into bounded, masked weights. These weights are applied only to SQL and tool-action tokens to reweight GRPO (a policy-gradient-style) advantages. Thus, the overall RL task reward still guides the optimization direction, while execution-based hindsight focuses credit assignment on the key decision tokens that affected query success.

Result: On major Text-to-SQL benchmarks (BIRD, Spider, and cross-domain evaluations), SERL-SQL attains competitive or strong performance: 76.56% execution accuracy on BIRD-Dev and 89.92% on Spider-Test. Its reward-based candidate selection strategy nearly matches the oracle Best-of-N upper bound and consistently beats more naive consistency-based selection methods, indicating that its execution-grounded rewards effectively identify high-quality SQL candidates produced by the agent.

Conclusion: Selective execution-grounded reinforcement learning, as instantiated by SERL-SQL, enables more precise credit assignment in multi-turn Text-to-SQL. By combining trajectory-level task rewards with localized, execution-informed reweighting of SQL and tool tokens, the framework yields high-quality, reliably selectable query candidates and competitive benchmark performance. This suggests execution-grounded selective credit assignment is a promising direction for improving interactive Text-to-SQL agents.

Abstract: Recent Text-to-SQL systems increasingly rely on multi-turn interaction, execution feedback, and reinforcement learning. However, most existing methods use execution correctness only as a trajectory-level reward, which provides limited guidance for identifying the SQL decisions responsible for success or failure. We propose SERL-SQL, a selective execution-grounded reinforcement learning framework for multi-turn Text-to-SQL agents. SERL-SQL samples on-policy SQL interaction trajectories and uses a training-only teacher to re-score student actions with execution feedback. The resulting teacher--student likelihood gap is converted into bounded, masked weights that reweight GRPO advantages only on SQL and tool-action tokens. In this way, task rewards preserve the optimization direction, while execution hindsight provides localized credit assignment. Experiments on BIRD, Spider, and cross-domain benchmarks show that SERL-SQL achieves competitive performance, reaching 76.56% execution accuracy on BIRD-Dev and 89.92% on Spider-Test. Moreover, our reward-based selection strategy closely approaches the oracle Best-of-N upper bound and consistently outperforms consistency-based selection, showing that SERL-SQL produces high-quality candidates that can be reliably identified by lightweight execution-grounded rewards. Our code will be released at https://github.com/Ffunkytao/SERL-SQL.

</details>


### [29] [The methodology of Constructing the Large-Scale Dataset for Detecting Presuicidal and Anti-Suicidal Signals in Social Media Texts in Russian](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00497)
*Igor Buyanov,Darya Yaskova,Danil Serenko,Danil Shkereda,Andrey Yaskov,Ilya Sochenkov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They create and release a large, annotated Russian social‑media dataset for detecting presuicidal and anti‑suicidal texts, plus baseline classifiers and an explicit annotation methodology.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Suicidal individuals sometimes express their distress and intentions on social media, offering an opportunity for early detection and intervention. However, such posts are buried among a huge volume of irrelevant text, making manual monitoring impractical. Existing resources for Russian are limited, so there is a need for a well‑defined, large‑scale, carefully annotated dataset and clear methodology to support automatic detection of presuicidal and anti‑suicidal signals.

Method: They design a detailed annotation methodology that includes: (1) drafting instructions and a label (class) table for identifying presuicidal and anti‑suicidal signals; (2) conducting an annotation process over social‑media texts; (3) performing verification and post‑annotation correction to improve label quality. Using this protocol, they collect and annotate over 50,000 Russian social‑media posts. They then run baseline text‑classification experiments on different annotation levels to assess model performance. They also compile statistics and document common annotation problems.

Result: The authors obtain a large‑scale Russian dataset (50K+ social‑media texts) annotated for presuicidal and anti‑suicidal signals. They report dataset statistics and identify typical difficulties and ambiguities in annotation. Baseline classification models are trained and evaluated, demonstrating feasible, though not perfect, performance on the various label granularities, thus validating the dataset’s usability for automatic risk‑signal detection.

Conclusion: The paper shows that it is feasible to systematically construct a large and reliable Russian dataset for detecting presuicidal and anti‑suicidal signals from social media. The released data, annotation methodology, code, and baseline models form a foundation for further research and development of automated tools to support earlier identification and help for people at risk.

Abstract: The suicide is a terrifying act of a person who is misled by his own mental state. This problem arises across many countries. Sadly, Russia also has quite high number of persons who committed suicide. Luckily, a subset of these people writes their struggles in social media, allowing a way to find them and help. However, these valuable texts disappearing in many irrelevant texts which is considerably slowing down the decision process about person's suicidal risk. To tackle this problem, in this work we have presented a detailed methodology of building the dataset for detecting texts that describe presuicidal and anti-suicidal signals. This methodology describes the process of instruction and class table creation, the process of annotation, verification and post-annotation correction. Guiding by this methodology, we collect and annotate a large-scale Russian dataset with more than 50 thousand texts from social media. We provide a count statistic of the dataset as well as common problems in annotation. We also conduct basic experiments of building the classification models to show the on go performance on different levels of annotation. Furthermore, we make the dataset, code and all materials publicly available.

</details>


### [30] [The Learning Objective Governs Perceptual Narrowing: A Cross-Lingual, Layer-Wise, Ten-Seed Study of Self-Supervised Speech Encoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00507)
*Sejin Yoo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates what learning objective in neural models best explains perceptual narrowing—the developmental loss of non-native phoneme discrimination in infants—by training a Transformer on speech and testing cross-lingual phoneme discrimination.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Perceptual narrowing is a robust phenomenon in infant language development: infants get better at distinguishing native phonemes while losing sensitivity to non-native ones. However, it is unclear what computational learning objective could give rise to this pattern. Understanding this can link developmental phenomena to concrete optimization goals in representation learning, and clarify the role of architecture versus objective in shaping phonetic representations.

Method: The authors train ~7M-parameter Transformer encoders on both child-directed and read speech, using two main self-supervised objectives: a reconstruction objective (masked mel-spectrogram prediction) and a prediction objective (frame-contrastive prediction). They evaluate phoneme discrimination using ABX tasks in three languages (English, French, Mandarin), running ten random seeds and treating seed as the unit of replication. They probe multiple layers, compare matched vs. mismatched training and test languages, and explore additional objective configurations such as sharpening, compression, consolidation, compositional combinations, and word-level semantic grounding.

Result: 1) The learning objective strongly determines the direction of cross-lingual transfer: reconstruction degrades non-native phoneme discrimination, while prediction improves it, with a substantial and highly significant gap in first-layer Mandarin ABX performance. 2) The observed decline in non-native discrimination under reconstruction reflects both an intrinsic difficulty gradient across phonemic contrasts and a smaller effect of language-specific specialization. 3) Relative to a language-symmetric baseline based on raw mel features, reconstruction can reduce first-layer discriminability below that of the input, whereas prediction enhances it. 4) Models trained on read speech exhibit a much steeper decline in non-native discrimination than those trained on child-directed speech. 5) Typical experimental practice using only three random seeds lacks power to detect these effects reliably, whereas ten seeds reveal them robustly. 6) None of six additional objective variants reproduce the full developmental signature where native discrimination improves while non-native discrimination declines; instead, each objective tends to move all languages in the same direction due to operating on shared representations.

Conclusion: The primary driver of perceptual-narrowing-like changes in learned phonetic representations is the learning objective, not the neural architecture. Reconstruction and prediction objectives shape non-native and native discrimination in opposite ways, but no single tested objective replicates the full developmental pattern of improved native and degraded non-native discrimination simultaneously. This suggests that more complex or multiple interacting objectives may be needed to fully account for infant perceptual narrowing, and underscores the importance of objective choice and sufficient replication (many seeds) in modeling developmental phenomena.

Abstract: Perceptual narrowing---the developmental loss of non-native phoneme discrimination in the first year of life \citep{werker1984}---is a canonical developmental finding, yet \emph{what learning objective produces it} remains open. We train a \(\sim\)7\,M-parameter Transformer encoder on child-directed and read speech and evaluate phoneme ABX in English, French, and Mandarin over ten seeds, the seed as the unit of replication. Six results. \textbf{(1)}~The objective sets the direction of cross-lingual transfer: reconstruction (masked mel-prediction) degrades non-native discrimination, prediction (frame-contrastive) improves it---a same-encoder, same-data gap of \(+0.051\) in first-layer Mandarin ABX (\(p=3\times10^{-8}\)), unanimous in sign across twenty runs. \textbf{(2)}~That decline combines a large arm-intrinsic difficulty gradient with a smaller language-specialization effect (matched vs.\ mismatched \(+0.022\), \(p=10^{-4}\), all four layers). \textbf{(3)}~Against a language-symmetric raw-mel floor, reconstruction pushes the first layer \emph{below} the discriminability of its input; prediction pushes it \emph{above}. \textbf{(4)}~Read speech gives a \(3.6\times\) steeper non-native decline than child-directed speech. \textbf{(5)}~The customary three-seed budget cannot see this reliably: an effect unambiguous at ten seeds is called significant by as few as 70\% of three-seed subsets. \textbf{(6)}~Six objective configurations---sharpening, compression, consolidation, their composition, and word-level semantic grounding in two forms---fail to produce the full developmental signature (native improves \emph{and} non-native declines): a single objective moves both languages the same way because it acts on a shared representation. We conclude that the objective, not the architecture, is the first-order determinant of narrowing-shaped representational change.

</details>


### [31] [Rethinking and formalising the state across languages: a unified computational learning theory account](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00523)
*Mohamed El Idrissi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper reconceptualizes the ‘state’ in Afroasiatic linguistics as a general, system-wide morphosyntactic mechanism that selects grammatical templates, modeling it computationally and linking it to broader dependencies like agreement and case.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditionally, the linguistic notion of ‘state’ (e.g., annexation state) is treated as a peculiar, language-specific phenomenon of Afroasiatic nominal morphology. This fragmented view cannot easily explain why similar patterns recur across different nominal marking systems or how speakers learn and generalize them. The paper is motivated by the need for a unified, formally explicit account of state that ties together diverse nominal marking patterns and connects them to general mechanisms of grammar and cognition.

Method: Within the Template-Based Modular Cognitive framework, the author uses Riffian (a Berber variety) as the main empirical case. They reanalyze nominal marking patterns (previously treated as separate phenomena) via grammatical templates. The ‘state’ is formally modeled as a set-valued function that maps contexts to sets of applicable grammatical templates. A symbolic computational model is built, and a learning algorithm based on finite-set operations is defined to acquire and predict which state-dependent configurations are grammatical.

Result: The model derives a unified explanation of various nominal marking patterns in Riffian as manifestations of a single state mechanism, rather than unrelated rules. The set-valued function correctly predicts state-driven alternations and configurations across the nominal domain. The learning algorithm can, in principle, acquire these patterns from data and anticipate novel, yet grammatical, state-conditioned forms. The framework also extends to determiner–noun structures, showing that these too can be captured within the same template-based mechanism.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that ‘state’ is not an Afroasiatic idiosyncrasy but a general, context-sensitive morphosyntactic selector of grammatical templates in synthetic languages. It provides a uniform account of nominal structure (including determiner–noun combinations) and suggests that state belongs to a broader family of syntactically conditioned dependencies, alongside agreement and grammatical case. This supports a more integrated view of morphosyntax and lexical cognition, where diverse surface phenomena arise from common template-selection mechanisms.

Abstract: The linguistic notion of state has traditionally been restricted to the construct (annexation) state of Afroasiatic languages and treated as a language-specific morphosyntactic phenomenon. This article argues instead that the state is a systemic, context-dependent morphosyntactic mechanism that selects grammatical templates across synthetic languages. Within the Template-Based Modular Cognitive framework, taking Riffian as its primary empirical basis, the proposed theory provides a unified explanation for diverse nominal marking patterns traditionally analysed independently and is formalised as a symbolic computational model in which the state is represented by a set-valued function over grammatical templates. A learning algorithm based on finite-set operations acquires and predicts state-dependent grammatical configurations. Beyond nominal morphology, the framework has broader implications for theories of nominal structure and lexical cognition, in particular offering a unified analysis of determiner-noun structure. These results suggest that the state constitutes one instance of a broader class of syntactically conditioned dependencies that also includes agreement and grammatical case.

</details>


### [32] [S$^4$R: Selective Sampling, Subspaces, and Sparse Reconstruction for Compressed Long-Context KV Caching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00528)
*Jialong Han,You Wu,Kewei Tu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Proposes S^4R, a method to compress KV cache in LLMs via selective low-rank subspaces and sparse reconstruction, achieving up to 5x compression with near-original accuracy on long-context tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs with long context windows require large KV caches, leading to prohibitive memory costs. Existing low-rank compression methods either rely on offline calibration data (less adaptable) or perform costly online full-prompt decompositions (hurting throughput). A new approach is needed that balances adaptability, memory savings, and computational efficiency during decoding.

Method: S^4R constructs low-rank subspaces for KV cache using selectively sampled tokens rather than the full prompt. It employs prompt-aware initialization, building key/value bases from a representative subset of the prompt, which reduces dependence on external calibration data while limiting prefilling cost. During decoding, instead of fully reconstructing the compressed cache at every step, S^4R performs sparse reconstruction, retaining and reconstructing only the most informative positions, and computes attention over this sparsely reconstructed KV representation.

Result: On LongBench and RULER benchmarks with Llama and Qwen model families, S^4R achieves up to 5x KV cache compression while maintaining accuracy close to that of using the full cache.

Conclusion: S^4R provides an effective trade-off between memory compression and model performance, offering the efficiency of fixed compression schemes while preserving the adaptability of prompt-dependent methods. It significantly reduces KV cache memory with minimal accuracy loss on long-context tasks, improving the practicality of long-context LLM deployment.

Abstract: The growth of context window lengths in Large Language Models (LLMs) significantly enhances their long-context capabilities but incurs prohibitive memory costs due to the Key-Value (KV) cache. Although low-rank compression of KV cache is a promising remedy, existing methods face a dilemma: offline approaches depend on external calibration data, whereas online approaches incur substantial compute for full-prompt decomposition and reconstruction. In this paper, we propose S$^4$R, which builds low-rank subspaces from selectively sampled tokens and computes attention over a sparsely reconstructed KV representation. S$^4$R uses prompt-aware initialization to build initial key/value bases from a representative prompt subset, trading off calibration-data dependence against prefilling cost. Because fully reconstructing the cache at every decoding step is prohibitively expensive and hurts throughput, we further adopt sparse reconstruction to retain only informative positions during decoding. Extensive experiments on LongBench and RULER with Llama and Qwen model families show that S$^4$R achieves up to 5$\times$ KV compression with near full-cache accuracy, combining the efficiency of fixed compression with the adaptability of prompt-dependent methods.

</details>


### [33] [Native Multilingual Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Low-Resource Southeast Asian Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00533)
*Sean Gip Lim,William Chandra Tjhi,Hai Leong Chieu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes OSCD, a post-training method that prevents large language models from reverting to English when doing complex reasoning in low-resource languages, significantly boosting math reasoning in Southeast Asian languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large Language Models show strong reasoning in high-resource languages like English but often switch to English internally when asked to reason in low-resource native languages, known as cross-lingual collapse. This harms performance, makes it hard to optimize policies from a cold start in those languages, and typical fine-tuning can cause catastrophic forgetting due to shifting cross-lingual representations. The authors want a way to reliably transfer strong reasoning abilities into low-resource languages without breaking the model’s existing capabilities.

Method: They introduce Onramp-Sequence Cross-Distillation (OSCD), a post-training algorithm. During generative rollouts, it uses an integrated translator agent loop to project the model’s high-resource (English) reasoning trajectories into the vocabulary space of low-resource languages, dynamically translating intermediate reasoning steps that serve as reference samples. In parallel, OSCD performs joint-embedding semantic alignment between reasoning traces in the reference and target languages, reducing representational gaps and maintaining semantic equivalence across languages. This combination stabilizes cross-lingual training and avoids representation drift.

Result: On mathematical reasoning benchmarks AIME25 and HMMT25, applied to native Southeast Asian languages, OSCD delivers up to 3.2× overall improvement in reasoning performance. The joint-embedding semantic alignment component specifically adds up to 6.4% improvement in reducing linguistic bias when compared with approaches that rely only on translation without alignment.

Conclusion: OSCD effectively mitigates cross-lingual collapse in large language models and enables robust mathematical reasoning in low-resource native languages. By combining translation-guided trajectory projection with joint-embedding semantic alignment, it offers a stable and efficient post-training route to transfer high-resource reasoning capabilities to underrepresented languages, outperforming translation-only baselines and alleviating catastrophic forgetting risks.

Abstract: Large Language Models have achieved substantial progress in reasoning capabilities. Yet in low-resource native settings, many suffer from cross-lingual collapse, reverting to English during intermediate steps that require complex logical reasoning. This presents a cold-start bottleneck for policy optimization, whereas standard fine-tuning risks catastrophic forgetting due to cross-lingual representation drift. To address these challenges, we introduce the Onramp-Sequence Cross-Distillation (OSCD), a post-training algorithm that projects high-resource reasoning trajectories into low-resource vocabulary subspaces during generative training rollouts via an integrated translator agentic loop, ensuring the stable and efficient translation of dynamically generated reference samples for fine-tuning. This is coupled with joint-embedding semantic alignment of both reference and target-language reasoning traces, thereby bridging the pairwise cross-lingual representational gaps. Comprehensive evaluations using the AIME25 and HMMT25 benchmarks demonstrate that OSCD yields up to 3.2 times overall improvements in native Southeast Asian languages for mathematical reasoning, of which the joint-embedding semantic alignment component contributes up to 6.4% improvements in linguistic debiasing over translation-only baselines.

</details>


### [34] [DE-NER : Zero-shot Named Entity Recognition via Dialogue Elicitation of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00538)
*Xuankang Zhang,Jiangming Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes DE-NER, a dialogue-based zero-shot NER framework that leverages LLMs’ conversational abilities instead of heavy prompt and demonstration engineering, achieving around 3.75 F1 improvement over strong baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing zero-shot NER methods using LLMs typically convert sequence labeling into question answering. While effective, they rely heavily on hand-crafted prompts and carefully designed demonstrations, which are labor-intensive, brittle, and may not fully utilize the knowledge encoded in LLMs. The authors want a more robust, lower-effort way to tap into LLMs for zero-shot NER.

Method: The authors introduce DE-NER, a dialogue elicitation framework for NER. Instead of treating NER as a single-shot QA task with fixed prompts, DE-NER engages the LLM in a multi-turn dialogue to progressively elicit entities. The framework is designed to minimize human prompt engineering by using generic dialogue patterns that encourage the LLM to reveal its internal knowledge about entity categories and boundaries. It replaces rigid prompt+demonstration templates with an interactive conversation flow tailored for zero-shot extraction.

Result: Across multiple NER benchmarks in zero-shot settings, DE-NER consistently outperforms strong LLM-based QA-style baselines. The reported average performance gain is 3.75 F1 points, indicating that dialogue elicitation yields better entity detection and classification without using task-specific training examples.

Conclusion: Dialogue elicitation is an effective strategy to unlock LLMs’ capabilities for zero-shot NER while reducing reliance on manual prompt and demonstration engineering. DE-NER demonstrates that treating LLMs as conversational partners, rather than static QA engines, improves NER performance across benchmarks. The released code supports reproducibility and further research on dialogue-based information extraction.

Abstract: Recent advancements of zero-shot Named Entity Recognition (NER) establish strong baselines by formulating sequence labeling into question answering where Large Language Models (LLMs) can be naturally adopted. However, existing LLM-based zero-shot NER methods suffer from the limitations of prompt and demonstration engineering. To address these issues with minimal human interventions, we introduce DE-NER, a dialogue elicitation framework which elicits the chatting ability of LLMs to fully extract the knowledge encoded in LLMs. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperform the competitive baselines in zero-shot settings across multiple benchmarks, with an average improvement of 3.75\% F1 points. Codes are released in https://github.com/kkkenshi/DE-NER.

</details>


### [35] [Loanword or Switch? The Annotation Boundary, Not the Model, Drives Kazakh-Russian Code-Switching Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00581)
*Bogdan Savelyev*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper addresses over-labeling of Kazakh-Russian social media text as code-mixed due to Russian loanwords in Kazakh, provides a new gold-standard LID dataset and guidelines, and evaluates several LID models, finding that annotation criteria around loanwords vs. switches are the main challenge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing language identification (LID) tools and simple letter-based heuristics mistakenly tag many Kazakh texts as mixed Kazakh-Russian because Russian loanwords written in the shared Cyrillic script resemble code-switching. This mislabeling distorts research and downstream tasks like sentiment analysis on genuine code-mixed content. There is a need for better resources and standards tailored to this language pair and social media domain.

Method: The authors create a document-level gold-standard LID dataset with specific annotation guidelines that:
1) Treat integrated Russian borrowings as Kazakh
2) Reserve the "mixed" label for actual clause-level code-switching.
They also compile a sentiment dataset consisting only of genuinely mixed texts, intended to be used after LID in a filter-first cascade for sentiment analysis. They then benchmark multiple LID systems—FastText, Lingua, raw and windowed HeLI, character-trigram Naive Bayes, and XLM-R—on a shared LID test set.

Result: Across the shared test set, the evaluated LID models show a range from weak to strong performance. However, even strong model classes struggle around the boundary between loanwords and genuine code-switches, revealing that performance limitations stem less from model architecture and more from how loanwords vs. switches are annotated and conceptualized in the guidelines.

Conclusion: Reliable LID for Kazakh-Russian social text is constrained primarily by the difficulty of distinguishing integrated loanwords from genuine code-switching, not by the choice of model architecture alone. The provided gold-standard LID dataset, annotation guidelines, and mixed-only sentiment pool are intended to support more accurate study and processing of Kazakh-Russian code-mixed data through a filter-first pipeline where LID precedes downstream tasks like sentiment analysis.

Abstract: Off-the-shelf LID and letter heuristics over-label Kazakh-Russian social text as mixed: Russian loanwords inside Kazakh look like code-switching under a shared Cyrillic script. We release a document-level gold LID set whose guideline keeps integrated borrowings as Kazakh and reserves mixed for clause-level switches, plus a mixed-only sentiment pool used after LID in a filter-first cascade. On a shared LID test, FastText, Lingua, raw and windowed HeLI, character-trigram NB, and XLM-R range from weak to strong performance. The gap shows the bottleneck is the loanword-vs-switch annotation boundary, not model class alone.

</details>


### [36] [Writing-System-Level Tokenizer Adaptation for Byte-Level BPE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00582)
*Bohdan Didenko*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose a way to adapt byte-level BPE tokenizers to better support a new, underrepresented language without expanding vocabulary size or retraining from scratch, by inserting new tokens in a way that stays consistent with the original BPE merge rules and keeps most token IDs unchanged.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing pretrained byte-level BPE tokenizers perform poorly on underrepresented languages, causing inefficient segmentations and higher token counts. Simple fixes like replacing the tokenizer or expanding the vocabulary break ID compatibility or grow model parameters. There is a need for a method that improves tokenization for a target language while preserving model-vocabulary size and most token-ID assignments so existing models and infrastructure remain usable.

Method: They formalize the conflict that arises when directly transferring tokens from a language-specific tokenizer into an existing BPE as the merge ordering problem. To address it, they introduce BPE-guided insertion: each new token is constructed so that it is derivable via the target tokenizer’s merge graph, respecting greedy merge ranks. The pipeline includes: (1) script-aware row selection to choose which existing vocabulary rows to repurpose while minimizing damage to other scripts/languages; (2) reconstruction of necessary byte-level prerequisites in the target script; and (3) guided insertion of the transferred tokens so that all added merge rules are reachable under the original BPE’s rank-ordered merging. They then quantitatively evaluate this adapted tokenizer on Ukrainian for Nemotron and GPT-OSS models.

Result: On Ukrainian, the adapted tokenizers reduce token counts by 33.5% and 36.6% compared to the original ones, while changes in token counts for English and a four-language European aggregate remain within 0.05%. The method preserves 78.5% and 77.3% of model-vocabulary entries at the same IDs. Alternative baselines (constraint-matched global and frequency-based removal, and fresh retraining with same-size vocabulary) achieve similar or slightly better compression for Ukrainian but cause noticeably higher token counts for English/European text and lose almost all ID compatibility. The reallocation slightly increases token counts for a Cyrillic micro-aggregate. Structural checks confirm that all newly inserted BPE nodes are reachable by the usual merge process and no preserved ID entries become invalid. They make their tokenizers and code publicly available.

Conclusion: Post-hoc, compatibility-preserving adaptation of BPE tokenizers can significantly improve tokenization efficiency for a new underrepresented language without increasing vocabulary size or retraining a model, and while keeping most token IDs unchanged. Their BPE-guided insertion method ensures that newly added tokens are consistent with the original BPE merge structure, offers a better trade-off between target-language compression and stability on existing languages than naive reallocation or retraining, and is validated both empirically and structurally.

Abstract: Pretrained byte-level BPE tokenizers can segment underrepresented languages inefficiently. Replacing a tokenizer changes the meaning of nearly every token ID, while vocabulary expansion enlarges the model's embedding and output matrices. We study post-hoc adaptation that keeps the model-vocabulary size fixed and preserves most existing token-to-ID assignments as a construction-time compatibility property. Directly transferring tokens from a language-specific tokenizer does not guarantee derivability through the target BPE merge graph: an inserted entry can conflict with the target's greedy merge ranks. We formalize this failure as the merge ordering problem and introduce BPE-guided insertion, which builds each transferred token through a target-reachable decomposition. Our pipeline uses script-aware row selection to limit collateral fragmentation, reconstructs target-script byte-level prerequisites, and applies guided insertion to maintain merge-graph reachability. On Ukrainian adaptations of Nemotron and GPT-OSS, it reduces token counts by 33.5% and 36.6%, keeps changes on English and the evaluated four-language European aggregate within 0.05%, and retains 78.5%/77.3% of original model-vocabulary rows at the same IDs. Constraint-matched global and frequency-based removal achieve similar Ukrainian compression but increase English/European token counts by 0.7-2.2%; fresh same-size retraining compresses Ukrainian slightly more but retains effectively no same-ID rows and increases English token counts by 7.6-8.6%. The reallocation increases token counts on the evaluated three-language Cyrillic micro-aggregate by 6.7%/10.1%. Structural audits find all 28,134/45,398 inserted BPE nodes reachable under ordinary rank-ordered merging and no retained same-ID model-vocabulary entry newly broken. We release all tokenizers and code.

</details>


### [37] [Verification Without Sufficiency: Per-Chunk Filtering Fails on Multi-Hop RAG, and Decomposition Repairs It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00585)
*Randhir Kumar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that standard per-chunk verification in retrieval-augmented generation fails on multi-hop questions and proposes conditioning verification on decomposed sub-questions as an effective fix.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand why verification methods that score each retrieved chunk independently work well for single-hop QA but fail for multi-hop QA, and to find a more reliable verification strategy for complex reasoning tasks.

Method: They empirically evaluate entailment-based per-chunk scoring on multiple single-hop and multi-hop QA benchmarks, run a set of seven control experiments to eliminate alternative explanations for poor performance, and then test a decomposition-based verification approach where verification is conditioned on sub-questions, using both gold and automatically generated decompositions.

Result: Per-chunk entailment verification achieves high AUC (0.951) on single-hop SQuAD but much lower AUCs (0.643, 0.523, 0.560) on multi-hop datasets like HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue; per-chunk gating is consistently worse than no filtering across datasets, model sizes, and prompts. Conditioning verification on decomposed sub-questions dramatically improves entailment performance (e.g., from 0.546 to 0.840 on later hops using MuSiQue's gold decompositions). An automatic decomposer (Qwen2.5-7B) recovers about 31% of this performance gain when given the question plus a retrieved paragraph.

Conclusion: Per-chunk verification fundamentally fails for multi-hop RAG because no single chunk suffices as a premise, and the answer often resides in an unnamed paragraph. Effective verification must be conditioned on decomposed sub-questions; existing iterative retrieval systems already generate such decompositions and should retain and exploit them for verification instead of discarding them.

Abstract: Verification for retrieval-augmented generation usually scores each retrieved chunk and drops the ones that fail. We show this cannot work for multi-hop questions, and show what does. Per-chunk scoring assumes one chunk is a sufficient premise for the answer. Multi-hop questions are built so that none is, and the paragraph carrying the answer is the one the question does not name. Entailment scoring reaches 0.643, 0.523 and 0.560 AUC on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA and MuSiQue, against 0.951 on single-hop SQuAD. Seven controls rule out model capacity, premise length, hypothesis template, decision threshold, retriever, answer-matching criterion and prompt. End to end across three datasets, three generator sizes and two prompts, per-chunk gating is significantly worse than not filtering at all in every cell, and its penalty grows with generator capability. The repair is to condition verification on the decomposed sub-question rather than the original query. Using MuSiQue's gold decomposition, entailment on a later hop rises from 0.546, which is chance, to 0.840, a paired lift of +0.355 with a bootstrap interval of [0.331, 0.382]. An off-the-shelf Qwen2.5-7B decomposer, given the question and the top retrieved paragraph, reaches 0.637 and captures 31% of that ceiling; decomposing without retrieval reaches 0.533, below the original question. Iterative retrieval systems already produce such decompositions and discard them before verifying.

</details>


### [38] [A Heuristic Perspective on Debiasing Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00622)
*Tian Lan,Yemin Wang,Chuancheng Shi,Xiangyu Wu,Zesheng Shi,Yuan Wang,Jiang Li,Guanglai Gao,Xiangdong Su*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces HEIMAT, an automatic, heuristic-based framework to reduce social biases in language models efficiently and in a scalable way, while preserving their language understanding ability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language models inherit and express social biases learned during pre-training, which can cause social harm. Existing debiasing methods are computationally expensive, hard to scale to large models, and often need manually annotated data confined to specific cultures and bias types. There is a need for an automated, scalable, culture-agnostic debiasing approach that maintains model performance.

Method: HEIMAT is a two-step framework. First, in the bias disclosure step, it uses simple template-based heuristic prompts to elicit and expose biases from the language model itself, generating context prompts that capture biased behavior. Second, in the debiasing fine-tuning step, it fine-tunes the model by minimizing the Jensen-Shannon divergence between predictions associated with these context prompts, encouraging the model to produce more balanced outputs and thereby reducing bias without heavy manual annotation.

Result: Experiments show that HEIMAT significantly mitigates biases across different cultural settings and bias categories. At the same time, it preserves the model’s natural language understanding capabilities, indicating that its debiasing does not come at a large cost to core task performance.

Conclusion: HEIMAT offers a practical, scalable, and largely automatic approach to debias language models. By using heuristic prompts for bias discovery and a Jensen-Shannon-divergence-based fine-tuning objective, it reduces cultural biases while maintaining NLU performance, overcoming key limitations of prior debiasing methods tied to heavy computation and manual annotation.

Abstract: Language models (LMs) often acquire various biases during pre-training and may express them in interactions, potentially causing social harm. Existing methods often rely on counterfactual augmentation or representation projection. These strategies remain limited in practice due to their high computational costs and difficulty in scaling to larger models. Additionally, many of these strategies require manual data annotation, narrowing their scope to specific cultures and bias categories. To overcome these limitations, we propose HEIMAT, a HEurIstic-style autoMATic debiasing framework for LMs. HEIMAT consists of two main steps: bias disclosure and debiasing fine-tuning. In the first step, it uses simple templates to construct heuristic prompts, which are applied to reveal model biases and generate corresponding context prompts. In the second step, it fine-tunes the model by minimizing the Jensen-Shannon divergence of predictions on these context prompts to reduce bias. Extensive experiments show that HEIMAT effectively mitigates bias in different cultures while maintaining the model's natural language understanding (NLU) performance.

</details>


### [39] [TreeProbe : A Tibetan Medicine Benchmark for Cultural Bias in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00640)
*Jin Zhang,Linyu Li,Weili Jiang,Yuqing Cai,Yutong Liu,Guanquecairang,Yongbin Yu,Jingye Cai,Nyima Tashi,Gadeng Luosang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces TreeProbe, a benchmark based on the Tibetan medicine Tree of Medicine framework to quantitatively measure cultural bias and ontology drift in large language models’ reasoning about Tibetan medicine.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models are being considered for reducing global health inequities, but they mainly reflect dominant high-resource biomedicine and offer poor, distorted coverage of Tibetan medicine, a major traditional medical system with its own rigorous theory. There is currently no quantitative, culturally grounded benchmark to assess how LLMs handle Tibetan medical knowledge or how they drift toward external medical ontologies.

Method: The authors construct TreeProbe, a cultural-bias benchmark aligned with the indigenous Tree of Medicine framework of Tibetan medicine. It consists of 4,719 expert-adjudicated items spanning 467 diseases and 10 subtasks mapped along the three roots (major divisions) of the Tree of Medicine. They then evaluate several representative LLMs on this benchmark to analyze performance, types of errors, and systematic ontology drift patterns toward other medical systems.

Result: LLMs perform poorly in native Tibetan medical contexts and frequently exhibit systematic external ontology drift, i.e., forcing Tibetan medical concepts into non-native frameworks. Models differ in their drift target: some align more with biomedicine, while others are biased toward TCM-like reasoning, influenced by their pretraining data and superficial similarities between TCM and Tibetan medicine.

Conclusion: TreeProbe offers the first structured, quantitative diagnostic benchmark for Tibetan medicine grounded in its own theoretical framework. It reveals that current LLMs are not epistemically faithful to Tibetan medicine and tend to reframe it through external medical ontologies. The benchmark can support the development and evaluation of medical AI systems that are both linguistically inclusive and epistemically fair across medical knowledge traditions.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly viewed as a potential means of mitigating global health inequities, yet their outputs often reflect dominant high-resource medical traditions and provide limited coverage of traditional medical knowledge systems. Tibetan medicine, one of the world's four major traditional medical systems, has an independent and highly structured theoretical framework. When models lack grounded understanding of Tibetan medicine, they may fall back on dominant epistemic systems and distort the native knowledge structure during reasoning. However, quantitative tools for evaluating cultural bias in Tibetan medicine remain largely absent. To address this gap, we introduce TreeProbe, the first cultural-bias benchmark organized around the native Tree of Medicine framework in Tibetan medicine. It contains 4,719 expert-adjudicated items covering 467 diseases and 10 subtasks along the three roots. Experiments on representative LLMs show that current models remain limited in native Tibetan medical contexts and exhibit systematic external ontology drift. Further analysis reveals that models diverge in whether they drift toward biomedical or TCM reasoning, shaped by pretraining data composition and surface resemblance between TCM and Tibetan medicine. TreeProbe provides a diagnostic benchmark for developing medical AI systems that are both linguistically inclusive and epistemically fair. Code and data are available in an anonymous repository at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TreeProbe/.

</details>


### [40] [Select-And-Extract: A Lightweight Plugin for Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00658)
*Chenming Tang,Jiawei Han*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces SANE, a lightweight plugin to improve retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) by addressing both retrieval and reading failures using LM-based candidate selection and blueprint-guided evidence extraction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG systems often fail either by not retrieving the right information (retrieval failure) or by failing to use the retrieved information correctly (reading failure). Existing structured indexing methods don’t generalize well, and query-time structuring methods are heavy and LM-expensive. There is a need for a simple, efficient method that improves both stages without large overhead.

Method: SANE augments a standard RAG pipeline with two components: (1) For retrieval failure, it first retrieves a broad pool of candidates using a semantic retriever, then uses an LM to re-rank/select top candidates based on short synopses of each candidate, improving recall. (2) For reading failure, it performs blueprint-guided query-time evidence extraction, distilling each selected document into compact, structured key information tailored to the question, which is then passed to the generator LM for final answering.
