Result: Experiments show that adding SANE on top of baseline RAG systems consistently improves performance across tasks, yielding better answer accuracy with only modest additional computational and latency overhead compared with conventional RAG and heavier structuring methods.

Conclusion: SANE demonstrates that a lightweight, LM-assisted selection and evidence-extraction layer can substantially improve RAG performance without complex indexing or heavy multi-call pipelines. This suggests that high-performing RAG frameworks can remain simple while effectively mitigating both retrieval and reading failures.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for language model (LM) systems fundamentally has two failure modes: retrieval failure and reading failure. The former fails to recall the right pieces of information from the external corpus, and the latter fails to produce the correct answer although the right information is retrieved. Some methods perform structured indexing for retrieval failure, but may suffer from limited generalization of the fixed structures. Some methods perform query-time structuring for reading failure, but typically require a lot of LM calls and rely heavily on the LM's capability. To this end, we propose Select-ANd-Extract (SANE), a simple yet effective plugin for RAG. For the retrieval failure, we retrieve a wide set of candidates with a semantic retriever, and leverage the LM to select the top candidates based on their synopses, which yields better recall than the original retriever. For the reading failure, we perform blueprint-guided query-time evidence extraction, which allows the generator LM to use only compact and structured key information so that it can perform better reasoning. Empirical results confirm that SANE brings solid improvements, while only introducing modest extra overhead. As a lightweight plugin for RAG, SANE offers a simple alternative to heavier approaches, and suggests a high-performance RAG framework need not be overly complex.

</details>


### [41] [OpenART: Scaling Agent Red Teaming via Open-Ended Environment Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00677)
*Yunhao Chen,Xin Wang,Yixu Wang,Yi Liu,Jie Li,Yan Teng,Xingjun Ma,Xia Hu,Yu-Gang Jiang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces OpenART, a large-scale, open-ended evaluation arena for red-teaming AI agents in persistent, evolving environments, and proposes EMHA, a black-box attack policy that reveals safety failures by evolving environment state rather than changing task instructions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safety benchmarks mostly test language models on short, static, single-turn or few-turn tasks, which miss the cumulative and long-horizon risks of AI agents that operate via tools in persistent environments where early actions can have delayed consequences. There is a need for a scalable, systematic way to evaluate how agent safety degrades as environments and attack surfaces evolve over long workflows and across many domains.

Method: The authors build OpenART, an arena of over 10,000 validated, stateful scenarios spanning 50 domains, based on more than 500,000 tools and skills. These scenarios are long-horizon tasks with a median of 97 tool calls and are used to benchmark 75 agent–model configurations in a unified way. They then propose Evolutionary Markov Hypergraph Attack (EMHA), a black-box attack policy that performs feedback-driven environment evolution: it coordinates authorized state transitions in the environment (without updating model parameters) to gradually expose vulnerabilities, keeping the task objective fixed while only the environment state changes. They compare EMHA to simpler instruction-only environment evolution baselines across environments of varying complexity.

Result: Across all evaluated agent–model configurations, EMHA reaches a pooled Attack Success Rate of 85.0%. Its advantage over instruction-only evolution grows with environment complexity, from about 2% higher ASR in simple environments to more than 17% higher in the most complex ones, showing that richer environment evolution more effectively surfaces safety failures. The analysis also finds that differences in agent runtime implementations account for a significant share of the variance in safety outcomes, beyond what can be explained by the underlying language models alone.

Conclusion: OpenART provides a scalable foundation for stress-testing and studying the safety of tool-using AI agents in complex, evolving, and stateful environments. EMHA demonstrates that systematically evolving environment state, rather than merely changing instructions, is a powerful way to uncover safety vulnerabilities—especially as task and environment complexity grow. The work suggests that both environment design and agent runtime implementation critically affect safety, and that long-horizon, persistent-state benchmarks are necessary to properly evaluate agent robustness.

Abstract: AI agents operate in persistent environments where early state changes can influence decisions far into the future. Unlike conventional language-model interactions, agent behavior is mediated through a shared state that is repeatedly modified and reused across long-horizon workflows. Current safety benchmarks often fail to capture these cumulative risks because they focus on short, static tasks. To address these limitations, we introduce OpenART, an open-ended arena for scalable agent red teaming through environment evolution. OpenART provides over 10,000 validated stateful scenarios across 50 domains, drawing from a pool of more than 500,000 tools and skills. These tasks require a median of 97 tool calls and enable unified evaluation across 75 different agent-model configurations. To systematically explore these evolving attack surfaces, we propose the Evolutionary Markov Hypergraph Attack (EMHA). EMHA is a black-box policy that performs feedback-driven environment evolution by coordinating authorized state transitions without requiring parameter updates. Throughout the evaluation, task objectives remain fixed while only the environment state changes. Across all configurations, EMHA achieves a pooled Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 85.0%. Its advantage over instruction-only evolution increases from approximately 2% on simple environments to over 17% on the most complex ones, demonstrating that environment evolution increasingly exposes safety failures as task complexity grows. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the specific runtime implementation of an agent explains a significant portion of safety variation beyond the underlying model's capabilities. These results establish OpenART as a scalable foundation for studying agent safety in complex, evolving environments.

</details>


### [42] [AttnLink: Turning Attention into Schema Links for Text-to-SQL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00693)
*Jinwang Song,Tao Liu,Haowen Zheng,Xiangheng Li,Yifan Li,Hongying Zan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes AttnLink, an attention-based schema linking framework for Text-to-SQL that converts LLM attention into controllable, efficient relevance scores, achieving near-perfect schema linking quality and improving downstream SQL execution accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Schema linking is essential in Text-to-SQL, as the model must identify which database tables and columns correspond to parts of a natural language question. Existing methods face a three-way trade-off: they either rely on heavy contextual modeling that is slow, score-based methods that lack fine control, or approaches that require costly autoregressive decoding over schema items. There is a need for a method that leverages large language models effectively while providing continuous relevance scores, controllable precision-recall behavior, and high efficiency.

Method: The authors introduce AttnLink, which converts internal attention patterns of an LLM into continuous relevance scores over schema items. It extracts attention from the generation-start token to candidate schema spans, ranking all candidates in a single prefill pass without step-by-step decoding. Two variants are proposed: AttnLink-U uses the pretrained model’s native attention directly, without updating parameters; AttnLink-S trains the attention distribution with supervision so that higher attention is aligned to gold schema items. For AttnLink-S, they design a set-mass objective that encourages total probability mass on all correct items, plus an adaptive probability-floor regularizer to maintain coverage over multiple relevant items. The resulting attention-based scores can be post-processed via temperature scaling and cumulative-mass thresholds to trade off precision and recall for schema selection.

Result: On three Text-to-SQL benchmarks—Spider, BIRD, and Spider2-SQLite—AttnLink-S attains very strong schema-linking performance, with mean average precision (mAP) of 99.22%, 95.95%, and 83.29%, respectively. The method operates with millisecond-level latency for schema linking, indicating high efficiency. When integrated with various SQL generators, AttnLink-S delivers the best or tied-best execution accuracy in 7 of 9 model–dataset combinations, demonstrating that improved schema linking translates into stronger end-to-end Text-to-SQL performance.

Conclusion: AttnLink demonstrates that LLM attention can be directly repurposed as a powerful, efficient schema-linking mechanism. With supervised alignment (AttnLink-S) and specific training and regularization objectives, the approach produces calibrated, controllable relevance scores that support dynamic precision-recall trade-offs. Its strong empirical results and low latency suggest that attention-based probing is a practical alternative to more expensive or less controllable schema linking methods in modern Text-to-SQL systems.

Abstract: Schema linking is a critical component of Text-to-SQL systems, but existing approaches often trade off contextual modeling capacity, score-based controllability, and inference efficiency. We introduce AttnLink, an attention-based framework that converts LLMs' internal attention into continuous relevance scores for schema items. AttnLink extracts the attention from the generation-start position to candidate schema spans, enabling all candidates to be ranked in a single prefill pass without autoregressive decoding. We develop two variants: AttnLink-U, which directly probes pretrained attention without parameter updates, and AttnLink-S, which aligns the attention distribution with gold schema items through direct supervision. To improve coverage of multiple relevant schema items, AttnLink-S combines a set-mass objective with an adaptive probability-floor regularizer. The resulting scores support post-hoc precision-recall control through temperature scaling and cumulative-mass selection. Experiments on Spider, BIRD, and Spider2-SQLite show that AttnLink-S achieves mAP scores of 99.22%, 95.95%, and 83.29%, respectively, with millisecond-scale schema-linking latency. It also yields the best or tied-best execution accuracy for downstream SQL generation in seven of nine generator-dataset settings.

</details>


### [43] [Exploiting Intrinsic Duality for Multi-Hop Question Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00712)
*Maodong Li,Xinyue Kang,Yuanchen Shi,Fang Kong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces QQ, a unified framework that jointly performs multi-hop question generation (MQG) and question answering (QA) by exploiting their dual relationship, using bidirectional alignment constraints and contrastive learning to improve multi-hop question quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-hop question generation methods treat MQG in isolation and largely ignore its intrinsic duality with question answering, where MQG creates questions from documents and answers, and QA derives answers from documents given questions. This misses an opportunity to leverage the strong mutual constraints between good questions and their correct answers, especially in complex multi-hop scenarios across multiple documents. The authors are motivated to more fully exploit this duality to improve the relevance, answerability, and quality of generated multi-hop questions.

Method: The authors propose QQ, a unified architecture that is trained to function both as a multi-hop question generation model and as a question answering model. The framework incorporates two main mechanisms: (1) Bidirectional alignment constraints: the model is trained so that questions generated from documents and target answers (MQG direction) are strictly aligned with answers produced from documents and questions (QA direction), enforcing mutual consistency between the two tasks. (2) Contrastive learning: the method learns joint representations of question–answer pairs, pulling embeddings of correct (paired) question–answer instances closer together while pushing apart embeddings of mismatched (unpaired) pairs, reinforcing the dual correspondence at the representation level. Training and evaluation are conducted on multi-hop datasets such as HotpotQA and MuSiQue.

Result: Through extensive automatic metrics and human evaluations on HotpotQA and MuSiQue, QQ is shown to substantially improve the quality of generated multi-hop questions compared with previous MQG approaches. The reported gains indicate better alignment between generated questions and target answers, as well as improvements in human-judged aspects such as clarity, answerability, and multi-hop reasoning quality.

Conclusion: The study concludes that explicitly modeling the duality between multi-hop question generation and question answering within a single unified framework leads to significantly better multi-hop question generation. Bidirectional alignment constraints and contrastive learning effectively enforce tight correspondence between questions and answers, thereby improving question quality. This demonstrates that leveraging QA–MQG duality is a promising direction for future work in multi-hop QA and question generation models.

Abstract: Multi hop question generation (MQG) aims to generate questions from multiple given documents and target answers, whereas question answering (QA) focuses on deriving answers from documents given specific questions. Although MQG and QA are inherently dual tasks, most existing MQG studies largely overlook this intrinsic duality. To address this limitation, we propose QQ, a novel framework that exploits the duality between Question and answer for multi hop Question generation. Specifically, QQ employs a unified architecture functioning simultaneously as both an MQG and a QA model to fully leverage their interdependence. Our framework is driven by two key mechanisms: (i) enforcing bidirectional alignment constraints to ensure strict mutual correspondence between the questions generated by the MQG model and the answers produced by the QA model; and (ii) applying contrastive learning to pull paired question answer representations closer while pushing unpaired ones apart, thereby reinforcing this correspondence. Extensive automatic and human evaluations on the HotpotQA and MuSiQue datasets demonstrate that the QQ framework significantly improves the quality of generated multi hop questions.

</details>


### [44] [Observatorio Lazaro: A self-populating database of anglicism usage in the Spanish press](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00713)
*Elena Alvarez-Mellado*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents Observatorio Lázaro, a large-scale, continuously updated resource tracking unassimilated English borrowings in the Spanish digital press using an automated NLP pipeline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To fill the gap between static borrowing dictionaries / one-off annotated corpora and the dynamic, ongoing use of lexical borrowings (especially anglicisms) in contemporary Spanish press, by creating a diachronic, high-coverage, empirically grounded resource.

Method: They build an end-to-end pipeline that daily collects articles from multiple Spanish digital news outlets (2020–2026), runs a neural sequence-labeling model to detect unassimilated lexical borrowings, post-processes and stores the results in a structured database, and exposes them via a web interface and API; they evaluate the system via held-out F1, inter-annotator agreement on the training corpus, and a manual precision audit.

Result: The resource now contains over two million borrowing tokens across 1.88M articles and 993M running tokens; the detector achieves span-level F1=0.86 for the borrowing class, annotator agreement is very high (κ=0.91), and a manual audit confirms good precision. Empirical analysis shows anglicisms occur at roughly 2 per 1,000 tokens, this rate is stable over six years, the borrowing vocabulary is open and growing with a large proportion of hapax types, and borrowing density varies strongly by news section (highest in fashion, technology, lifestyle; lowest in political/institutional news).

Conclusion: Observatorio Lázaro provides a robust, continuously updated, high-quality record of unassimilated lexical borrowings in the Spanish press that complements existing static dictionaries and one-off corpora, and offers a valuable empirical basis for lexicography, neology monitoring, and research on borrowing dynamics in Spanish.

Abstract: This paper describes Observatorio Lázaro, a language resource that monitors unassimilated lexical borrowings (predominantly English lexical borrowings or anglicisms) in the Spanish digital press. Since April 2020 the system has automatically processed the daily output of a collection of news outlets, detected borrowings with a neural sequence-labeling model, and made the results available through a public web interface and API. The result is a continuously updated diachronic database which, at the time of writing, records more than two million borrowings across 1.88 million articles and 993 million running tokens of text (2020-2026). The paper documents the resource: we describe the end-to-end pipeline (acquisition, detection, post-processing, storage and access), the data model and the terms of availability; we evaluate the resource through the detector's held-out performance (span-level F1=0.86 for the borrowing class), inter-annotator agreement on the training corpus (Cohen's kappa=0.91) and a manual precision audit of 1,000 spans from the deployed data; and we situate it with respect to Spanish borrowing lexicography, annotated borrowing corpora and neology-monitoring observatories. The data shows that unassimilated anglicisms are used in the Spanish press at a frequency of approximately two anglicisms per thousand tokens, and that this rate remains stable. Our statistical analysis over six years reveals that the anglicism vocabulary in Spanish behaves as an open and growing class, with 58.7% of its types attested only once (53.6% after correcting for detection precision), and that its density is highest in the fashion, technology and lifestyle sections and lowest in political and institutional news. The resource is intended to complement static borrowing dictionaries and one-off annotated corpora by providing a continuously updated record of borrowing in the Spanish press.

</details>


### [45] [RAGOCR: Optical Compression of Retrieval-Augmented Text via Visual Representation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00765)
*Jiayang Yu,Jialun Zhong,Lei Zou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose RAGOCR, a query-aware visual compression framework for RAG that turns retrieved documents into compact images with adaptive resolution, greatly reducing tokens while improving QA accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG systems for knowledge-intensive QA struggle to scale because processing long retrieved texts is computationally expensive. Existing compression methods either: (1) do modest, query-aware online compression but need model fine-tuning, or (2) do stronger, query-agnostic offline compression that ignores the specific query and is costly. There is a need for a scalable, query-aware compression method that preserves relevant information and reduces token usage without retraining LLMs.

Method: RAGOCR converts retrieved documents into compact visual (image-like) representations that are conditioned on the input query. It introduces a query-aware dynamic resolution mechanism that assigns higher visual resolution to passages estimated as more relevant and complex, and lower resolution to less important documents. This balances compression rate against information fidelity. The LLM then consumes tokens derived from these compressed representations instead of the full text, reducing the token count.

Result: On five QA benchmarks built on the MedOmniKB corpus, RAGOCR beats naive (uncompressed) RAG by more than 15% accuracy while using only one-eighth as many input tokens. It also consistently outperforms state-of-the-art hard and soft compression baselines under multiple retrieval depths.

Conclusion: Query-conditioned visual compression with dynamic resolution is an effective way to scale RAG. RAGOCR can substantially cut token costs while improving QA performance, overcoming the trade-offs in current hard vs soft compression approaches and providing a more efficient and accurate retrieval-augmented generation pipeline.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become essential for knowledge-intensive question answering, yet scaling RAG pipelines remains challenging due to the prohibitive computational cost of processing lengthy retrieved contexts. Existing compression approaches face a fundamental trade-off: hard compression methods operate online in a query-aware fashion but achieve only modest compression rates and typically require fine-tuning the generative model, while soft compression methods attain higher ratios but rely on costly offline encoding that is entirely agnostic to the input query. To bridge this gap, we introduce RAGOCR, a novel framework that compresses retrieved documents into compact visual representations conditioned on the input query. To further balance compression rate and information fidelity, we introduce a query-aware dynamic resolution mechanism that adaptively allocates visual granularity based on each document's estimated relevance and complexity: highly relevant passages are rendered at higher resolution to preserve fine-grained details, while peripheral documents are aggressively compressed at lower resolution. Experiments on five QA benchmarks using the MedOmniKB retrieval corpus demonstrate that RAGOCR surpasses naive RAG by over 15\% in accuracy while requiring only one-eighth the number of input tokens, and consistently outperforms both hard and soft compression baselines across varying retrieval depths.

</details>


### [46] [Distill Where You Fail: Recovering Learning Signals of Negative RL-Groups from Adaptive Teacher Guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00782)
*Zhuowen Han,Jinwei Xiao,Zhengxi Lu,Renren Jin,Zhiyuan Yao,Yuxin Liu,Hongyan Hao,Yueqing Sun,Yu Yang,Qi GU,Xunliang Cai,Deyi Xiong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper identifies weaknesses in combining GRPO-based RL with on-policy distillation for LLM post-training and proposes RSTG, an adaptive, selective distillation framework that recovers informative learning signals and improves performance on math and code tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-training LLMs with RLVR typically relies on GRPO, which suffers from sparse rewards and complete gradient loss when group rewards are identical. Although OPD can provide dense token-level supervision, naive integration with GRPO backfires due to overfitting to the teacher, asymmetric suppression of tokens, and the fact that not all samples benefit from distillation. There is a need for a method that leverages OPD's strengths while preserving RL's exploration and addressing sparse/noisy rewards.

Method: The authors propose RSTG (Recovering Learning Signals via Adaptive Teacher Guidance), an RLVR training strategy that applies on-policy distillation in a targeted, adaptive way. At the sample level, RSTG restricts OPD to negative zero-variance prompts (where GRPO provides no gradient) and weights each such sample by the teacher model's confidence score. At the token level, it distills only on tokens characterized by high student entropy or large divergence between teacher and student predictions, thus focusing supervision where the student is uncertain or disagrees with the teacher. Additionally, RSTG introduces supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on correct trajectories generated by the teacher model to inject positive gradient signals in regions where RL provides none.

Result: Empirical evaluations show that RSTG markedly improves over a naive combination of GRPO and OPD, yielding +4.02% performance gains on math tasks and +3.05% gains on coding tasks. These results indicate that targeted, adaptive distillation can effectively recover and amplify learning signals in RLVR-based post-training of LLMs.

Conclusion: RSTG successfully addresses the failings of naive GRPO+OPD integration by selectively applying teacher guidance where RL signals are missing or weak, both at the sample and token level. By combining adaptive OPD with teacher-generated SFT, it restores informative gradients, maintains RL's exploratory behavior, and achieves superior performance on structured reasoning benchmarks such as math and coding. The approach suggests that carefully controlled distillation is key to leveraging teacher models in RLVR pipelines for LLMs.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a standard paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs). While Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is widely adopted, it suffers from sparse reward signals and loses gradients entirely when all responses within a group receive identical rewards. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a natural remedy by providing dense, token-level supervision from a teacher model. However, naively combining GRPO with OPD leads to degraded performance, due to three underlying causes: not all samples benefit from distillation; fitting too quickly to the teacher undermines the exploratory capacity of RL; and OPD's advantages are asymmetric, suppressing most tokens. To address these challenges, we propose RSTG (Recovering Learning Signals via Adaptive Teacher Guidance), which applies distillation selectively and precisely where it matters most. At the sample level, OPD is restricted to negative zero-variance prompts with each sample weighted by the teacher's confidence score. At the token level, distillation targets only tokens with high student entropy or large teacher-student divergence. We further augment training with SFT on correct trajectories generated by the teacher model, injecting positive gradient signals where RL yields none. Experiments demonstrate that RSTG substantially outperforms naive GRPO+OPD by +4.02% on math and +3.05% on code.

</details>


### [47] [OoO-Spec: Out-of-Order Semantic Speculation for Fast Tool Calling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00814)
*Zhiheng Zhang,Mujie Xu,Feiyu Sun,Zhixin Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: OoO-Spec is a method to speed up tool-calling LLMs by predicting tool choice and arguments in parallel with decoding, then feeding these hints back into the main model while keeping it as the final authority.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional LLM tool calling is slow because tools are invoked via token-by-token generation, even though tool choice and argument values are often predictable from the request and schema. ToolSpec improves speed by drafting schema tokens and reusing prior calls, but it still cannot generate request-specific argument values that are not already in the schema or history. There is a need for a more efficient, general approach that can infer these semantics early and in parallel, without retraining drafters for each target model.

Method: OoO-Spec introduces an out-of-order specification pipeline with a lightweight sidecar model (Qwen3-0.6B). When a request arrives, the sidecar predicts the tool/function to call and fills all schema-defined argument slots in one parallel step. In parallel, the main target LLM starts ToolSpec-style decoding. The runtime then merges the predicted slot values into a concrete tool call, renders it as text, and makes this hint available during subsequent decoding rounds. The target model periodically polls, re-tokenizes any available hint with its own tokenizer, and decides whether to adopt or ignore it, preserving the target as the sole verifier/committer. The sidecar is trained once using LoRA on traces from a larger Qwen2.5-32B teacher model and is reused unchanged across different target models (Qwen2.5, Qwen3, Llama), avoiding target-specific drafter training.

Result: On three benchmarks and seven fully ranked target models under greedy, batch-one decoding, OoO-Spec is the fastest method tested in all 21 target–benchmark combinations. It delivers 2.46x–5.34x speedup over standard autoregressive decoding, with an unweighted mean speedup of 3.89x, compared to 2.95x for ToolSpec. It also exceeds the performance of all evaluated released learned drafters in each comparable setting. For Qwen3 targets of sizes 4B, 8B, 14B, and 32B, the same sidecar improves performance over ToolSpec by an average of 34.1%. The semantic payload transmitted by the sidecar averages only 85 bytes per request (excluding protocol metadata), enabling efficient split-GPU overlapping.

Conclusion: OoO-Spec demonstrates that out-of-order semantic prediction with a small sidecar model can substantially accelerate tool-calling LLMs while preserving correctness by keeping the main model as the final authority. It generalizes across multiple target model families without per-target drafter retraining and consistently outperforms both ToolSpec and other learned drafters in speed. Its small payload and architecture make it practical for deployment scenarios that benefit from split-GPU and overlapping computation.

Abstract: LLMs generate tool calls token by token, even though the function choice and argument values can often be predicted in parallel from the request and tool schema. ToolSpec reduces this cost by drafting schema tokens and retrieving earlier calls, but cannot propose request-specific values absent from either source. We present OoO-Spec, which computes these missing semantics out of order. At request arrival, a Qwen3-0.6B sidecar predicts the function choice and all schema-defined argument slots in one parallel request-level wave while the target begins ToolSpec decoding. The runtime joins the slot values, renders the resulting call as text, and exposes it to subsequent candidate-construction rounds. The target polls without blocking, re-tokenizes a ready hint with its own tokenizer, and remains the sole verifier and commit authority. The sidecar is trained once with LoRA on Qwen2.5-32B teacher traces and used unchanged across Qwen2.5, Qwen3, and Llama targets, without target-specific drafter training. Across seven fully ranked targets and three benchmarks under greedy batch-one decoding, OoO-Spec is fastest among all evaluated methods in all 21 target-benchmark cells, reaching 2.46x-5.34x over autoregressive decoding with an unweighted mean of 3.89x, versus 2.95x for ToolSpec. It also outperforms every evaluated released learned drafter in each comparable cell. Across Qwen3-4B, 8B, 14B, and 32B targets, the same sidecar improves on ToolSpec by 34.1% on average. Its compact semantic payload averages 85 bytes per request excluding protocol metadata, supporting effective split-GPU overlap.

</details>


### [48] [Exemplars in Disguise: Pure Exemplar Models Mimic Abstraction-First Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00821)
*Zachary Nicholas Houghton,Vsevolod Kapatsinski*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper questions claims that language models learn abstract, class-level linguistic generalizations before item-specific knowledge, showing that current methods can misdiagnose learning order even in simple memorization models, and arguing that the item-specific vs. abstract distinction is blurry for distributed representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a long-standing debate in language acquisition about whether learners first store detailed exemplars and only later form abstractions, or whether abstract, rule-like knowledge emerges early. Recent work applying this question to large language models has used specific evaluation methods to argue that abstract knowledge is learned first. The authors are motivated to scrutinize these methods, assess whether they truly distinguish between memorization and abstraction, and clarify what it means to separate item-specific from class-level knowledge in models with distributed representations.

Method: The authors construct and analyze "pure memorizer" models that, by design, lack explicit abstract, class-level representations and instead only store item-specific information. They then apply the same diagnostic methods previously used to claim that abstract knowledge is learned before item-specific knowledge in large language models. By varying the models' sensitivity to individual observations and examining how learning curves change as a function of the input distribution, they show that the diagnostics can be made to indicate either earlier item-specific learning or earlier class-level learning, purely as an artifact of these factors. They also conceptually analyze how distributed word representations can entangle class-level and item-specific properties.

Result: They find that the existing methods used to infer the relative timing of item-specific versus abstract knowledge acquisition are not reliable: even models that only memorize individual items can appear to learn either item-specific or class-level knowledge first, depending on parameter choices and data distributions. This demonstrates that the transition point inferred by these diagnostics is not a robust indicator of a shift from memorization to abstraction. They also show, at a representational level, that in distributed embeddings it may not be possible to cleanly separate class-level properties from item-specific ones.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that current empirical methods claiming to show that large language models acquire abstract linguistic generalizations before item-specific knowledge are fundamentally limited and can be systematically misled by simple memorization processes and data properties. Moreover, for distributed representations commonly used in language models, the conceptual distinction between item-specific and abstract knowledge may be ill-posed, since both are intertwined within the same representational space. Therefore, stronger methods and clearer theoretical definitions are needed before making claims about the order in which different types of linguistic knowledge are learned.

Abstract: Whether idiosyncratic, item-specific knowledge is learned before abstract class-level generalizations, or vice versa, is a central question in language learning, with exemplar and abstraction-based theories making opposite predictions. Recent methods have claimed to show that, at least for large language models, abstract knowledge is learned first. We show that these methods fall short: pure memorizer models with no abstract representations can appear, by the same criteria, to learn either item-specific or class-level knowledge first, depending on their sensitivity to individual observations, with the transition point governed by the distributional properties of the input. We further argue that the distinction between item-specific and abstract knowledge may be ill-defined for distributed representations, as a word's class-level properties may not be separable from its item-specific properties.

</details>


### [49] [Pruned BPE: Post-training Visibility Pruning and Token Reallocation for Byte Pair Encoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00837)
*Kenny Shao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Pruned BPE, a variant of Byte Pair Encoding that hides low-usage merge tokens from the model while still using them internally, reallocating visible vocabulary slots to more useful tokens and thereby improving tokenization efficiency without increasing visible vocabulary size.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard BPE exposes all learned merge tokens to the model, even those that are mainly intermediate construction units and rarely appear in final encodings. This wastes limited vocabulary slots and reduces tokenization efficiency, especially when vocabulary size is constrained for language models.

Method: Train a standard BPE model, then measure each token’s final exposure (frequency in encoded text). Tokens below a chosen exposure threshold are reclassified as internal-only merge nodes: they can be used during the merge process but will not appear in the final visible vocabulary. Their freed visible vocabulary slots are reassigned to better-exposed candidate tokens obtained via resumed BPE training. At inference/encoding time, any internal-only tokens are recursively expanded into visible descendants while preserving the original BPE merge order. The method is evaluated across English, Chinese, and mixed corpora with controlled visible vocabulary sizes.

Result: Across two disjoint English- and Chinese-dominated corpora and their combination, Pruned BPE consistently reduces encoded sequence length compared with standard BPE at the same training corpus, evaluation corpus, and model-visible vocabulary size. With a 40% exposure threshold, it achieves roughly 0.27%–0.36% shorter encodings on same-corpus evaluations. Using a shared optimal dynamic-programming encoder for vocabulary-only evaluation, Pruned BPE still provides a 0.23%–0.31% reduction, showing that the gains come from a more efficient visible vocabulary rather than encoding heuristics. These improvements correspond to a significant portion of the 1.5%–3.8% reduction that would otherwise require adding about 2K more standard BPE tokens.

Conclusion: Separating merge-construction tokens from model-visible vocabulary via post-training visibility pruning makes BPE vocabularies more efficient. Pruned BPE improves compression (shorter token sequences) without increasing the number of tokens that the language model must handle. Internal-only tokens capture reusable subfragments (English morphemes, Chinese components, byte sequences, structured-text fragments), and reallocating visibility to better-exposed tokens offers a practical way to get part of the benefit of a larger BPE vocabulary without expanding the model’s embedding size.

Abstract: Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) is widely used for subword tokenization, but standard BPE exposes every learned merge token to the downstream model, including tokens that mainly serve as intermediate construction units and rarely appear in the final encoded corpus. This paper proposes Pruned BPE, a post-training visibility-pruning and token-reallocation method that separates merge construction from model-visible vocabulary selection. After standard BPE training, tokens are evaluated by final exposure. Low-exposure tokens are retained as internal-only merge nodes, while their visible vocabulary slots are reassigned to better-exposed candidates learned through resumed training. During encoding, internal-only tokens are recursively expanded into visible descendants while the original BPE merge order is preserved. Experiments on two non-overlapping English- and Chinese-dominated corpora and their combination show that Pruned BPE consistently reduces encoded length relative to Standard BPE at the same training corpus, evaluation corpus, and model-visible vocabulary size. At a 40\% exposure threshold, the reduction is approximately 0.27\%--0.36\% on same-corpus evaluations. In a vocabulary-only evaluation using a shared exact minimum-token dynamic-programming encoder, Pruned BPE retains an advantage of approximately 0.23\%--0.31\%, indicating that the improvement arises from a more efficient visible vocabulary. These gains represent a meaningful fraction of the approximately 1.5\%--3.8\% marginal reduction that would otherwise require adding another 2K Standard BPE tokens. Qualitative analysis shows that internal-only tokens include reusable English fragments, Chinese components, partial UTF-8 byte sequences, and structured-text fragments. The results indicate that post-training visibility pruning can improve BPE vocabulary efficiency without increasing the vocabulary exposed to the language model.

</details>


### [50] [Practical Online KV Cache Compaction for LLM Agents: An Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00902)
*Yujian Liu,Jiabao Ji,Li An,Rohit Jain,Gungor Polatkan,Siyu Zhu,Shiyu Chang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how to compress the KV cache for long-horizon LLM agents during runtime (online) without knowing future queries, and shows that carefully delayed, proxy-based token eviction can shrink KV by ~80% while preserving accuracy and even improving throughput.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents generate long sequences of reasoning steps, tool calls, and environment feedback, which leads to very large KV caches and makes KV memory and compute a major inference bottleneck. Existing KV compaction methods mostly assume a static context where future queries are known or can be approximated offline, which does not match the online, evolving nature of agents. There is a need for methods that can compact KV caches on-the-fly, before future relevance is known, using only cheap approximations that fit in the inference loop.

Method: The authors formulate online KV cache compaction for LLM agents and adapt two families of techniques—token eviction (TE) and attention matching (AM)—to the setting of compacting agent turns. They investigate how to drive compaction using various inexpensive proxy queries, including boundary queries, repeat-prefill queries, and queries delayed to future generations. They then systematically compare TE and AM under these imperfect proxy signals. Experiments are run on agent-style benchmarks, BrowseComp-Plus and WideSearch, across multiple model scales, measuring accuracy, KV cache size, and throughput under different compaction timings and proxy strategies.

Result: Empirically, performing compaction immediately after information is produced often degrades agent performance because the proxy queries at that time are poor predictors of future relevance. When compaction is delayed so that it can use the agent’s actual future queries as better proxies, much of the performance drop is recovered. Across settings, token eviction (TE) is more robust than attention matching (AM) when proxies are imperfect. With appropriately chosen proxy-query strategies, TE can reduce KV cache usage by about 80% while preserving most of the task accuracy and in some cases increasing inference throughput compared to no compaction.

Conclusion: Online KV cache compaction for LLM agents is feasible and effective if guided by well-chosen proxy queries and appropriately robust mechanisms. Immediate compaction based on weak proxies is harmful, but delaying compaction to leverage future queries can significantly improve outcomes. Token eviction is generally more stable than attention matching in realistic online settings with imperfect proxy information. Overall, the choice and scheduling of proxy queries emerge as central design decisions for deploying practical online KV compaction in long-horizon LLM agents.

Abstract: LLM agents accumulate long trajectories of reasoning steps, tool calls, and environment feedback, making the KV cache a major inference bottleneck. KV cache compaction can reduce this cost, but most prior methods assume a static context where future queries are known or can be approximated offline. Agents instead require online compaction: new information must be compressed before future relevance is known, using proxy queries cheap enough for the inference path. We study online compaction across token eviction (TE) and attention matching (AM), adapting both to compact agent turns and comparing cheap proxy sources such as boundary, repeat-prefill, and delayed future-generation queries. Experiments on BrowseComp-Plus and WideSearch show that immediate compaction often hurts performance, whereas delaying compaction to use the agent's future queries recovers much of the gap. Moreover, TE is often more robust than AM under imperfect proxies. Across models at different scales, TE preserves most of the accuracy while reducing KV cache by 80%, and can improve throughput over the no compaction baseline. These results position proxy-query selection as a core design choice for practical online KV compaction.

</details>


### [51] [FinHardBench: Can LLMs Generate Latency-Aware Hardware for Financial Computing?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00909)
*Weimin Fu,Hejia Zhang,Minghao Shao,Zeng Wang,Johann Knechtel,Ozgur Sinanoglu,Muhammad Shafique,Ramesh Karri,Xiaolong Guo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces FinHardBench, a benchmark to test whether large language models can generate ultra-low-latency financial FPGA hardware, and shows that while they can often produce functionally correct designs and outperform standard methods in system-level configuration search, they still struggle to meet tight timing and to adapt to complex strategy changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Financial trading on FPGAs operates under extreme latency constraints (5–10 ns), and designs must be updated frequently as markets and regulations change. This creates demand for faster hardware design iteration. Large language models show promise for code and hardware generation, but it is unclear whether they can create not just correct, but also high-performance, low-latency FPGA designs in realistic financial workloads. There is also a lack of a standardized benchmark reflecting these iterative FPGA design cycles.

Method: The authors construct FinHardBench, a benchmark suite of 33 financial computing tasks implemented on FPGAs, and design three experiment settings that emulate a real FPGA development loop: (1) generating new hardware modules from high-level specifications, (2) tuning system-level parameters across a six-stage trading pipeline via design space exploration, and (3) modifying existing modules to match updated specifications. Six different LLMs are evaluated across over 1530 experiment rounds, measuring functional correctness, timing/latency, and the ability to find optimal configurations versus search-based baselines such as random search, simulated annealing, and Bayesian optimization.

Result: (1) On module generation, LLMs achieve between 19% and 61% functional correctness, with some designs suffering timing slowdowns of up to 13.7× relative to baselines, indicating substantial performance gaps even when functionally correct. (2) In system-level design space exploration for the six-stage pipeline, the strongest LLMs more reliably converge to globally optimal configurations than random search, simulated annealing, or Bayesian optimization, reaching the optimum on all 5 seeds within a 24-round budget while baselines succeed on only 0–4 of 5 seeds. (3) For adapting hardware to higher-level strategy changes, most models perform poorly, failing to robustly incorporate complex specification updates. The ranking of models by code-generation quality is only moderately aligned with their ranking in architecture optimization performance, and even a relatively weak code generator (MiniMax M2.7) can still discover optimal system configurations in most runs. Task difficulty correlates more with the presence of similar patterns in the model’s training data than with the conceptual abstraction level of the task.

Conclusion: LLMs can partially automate financial FPGA design: they often produce correct hardware modules and are competitive or superior to classical search techniques for exploring system-level design spaces. However, they have major limitations in meeting strict timing constraints and in handling nuanced, strategy-level specification changes. Code-generation strength does not directly predict effectiveness in architecture optimization, and benchmark difficulty is heavily influenced by training data coverage. FinHardBench provides a realistic, open-source testbed to track progress on low-latency hardware synthesis and design iteration with LLMs.

Abstract: Can large language models generate not just correct, but fast hardware? This paper investigates the question in financial FPGA design, where 5-10 nanoseconds of latency determines competitive advantage and designs iterate continuously as protocols, strategies, and regulations evolve. FinHardBench, a benchmark of 33 financial computing tasks, is presented together with three experiments that mirror the real-world FPGA iteration cycle: generating new modules from specifications, tuning system-level configurations across a 6-stage trading pipeline, and adapting existing modules to specification changes. Evaluation of six LLMs on 1530+ experiment rounds yields three findings: (1) models achieve 19-61% functional correctness with timing degradation up to 13.7$\times$ on specific tasks; (2) in system-level design space exploration, top LLMs converge to the optimal configuration with higher reliability than random search, simulated annealing, and Bayesian optimization baselines (5/5 seeds vs. 0-4/5 at the same 24-round budget); (3) strategy-level specification changes remain unsolved for most models. Across the six models, generation and DSE rankings overlap moderately: the strongest code generator is not the fastest architecture optimizer, and the weakest code generator (MiniMax M2.7) still reaches the system optimum on 4 of 5 seeds. On the tasks in FinHardBench, difficulty tracks training data pattern availability more closely than abstraction level. FinHardBench is released as an open-source benchmark.

</details>


### [52] [Gaokerena: A Small Persian Medical Language Model Family](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00932)
*Mehrdad Ghassabi,Hamidreza Baradaran Kashani,Pedram Rostami,Sadra Hakim,Zahra Kazemi,Audrina Ebrahimi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Gaokerena introduces compact Persian medical language models tailored for low-resource settings, improving benchmark scores and incorporating uncertainty estimation, but are not yet safe for clinical use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most medical QA AI research targets English, leaving low-resource languages like Persian without specialized, reliable medical models. There is a need for localized, efficient models that can run on consumer hardware and support safer digital healthcare in Persian.

Method: The authors build two Persian medical LMs. Gaokerena-V is trained on a new 90M-token Persian medical corpus plus 20k expert-validated physician Q&A pairs to strengthen domain knowledge. Gaokerena-R uses the same base architecture but applies Chain-of-Thought reasoning and two new RLAIF (Reinforcement Learning with AI Feedback) frameworks to optimize reasoning quality and preferences, despite training on a smaller dataset. Both models include uncertainty heads that estimate answer confidence directly from hidden states.

Result: Gaokerena-V improves performance on a translated medical MMLU benchmark from 46.28% to 49.31%. Gaokerena-R, with CoT and RLAIF, further boosts the score to 52.98% even with less data. The uncertainty heads can predict confidence levels, enabling proactive safety estimation. Models are compact enough for consumer hardware deployment.

Conclusion: Gaokerena demonstrates that specialized Persian medical LMs with reasoning optimization and uncertainty estimation can significantly improve benchmark performance in a low-resource language. However, their current accuracy is still inadequate for direct clinical use, so further work is needed on knowledge robustness and rigorous safety validation before real-world deployment.

Abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into medical question-answering systems has advanced rapidly; however, research remains predominantly focused on English, leaving low resource languages like Persian significantly underserved. To address this gap, this paper introduces Gaokerena, a novel family of compact Persian medical language models optimized for deployment on consumer grade hardware. As a foundational step toward localized digital healthcare, we first present Gaokerena-V, developed by training a baseline model on a newly curated 90-million-token Persian medical corpus and 20,000 expert-vetted physician Q&A pairs, which improved performance on a translated medical MMLU benchmark from 46.28% to 49.31%. Second, recognizing the critical demands of clinical reasoning, we developed Gaokerena-R by integrating a Chain-of-Thought approach with two novel Reinforcement Learning with AI Feedback (RLAIF) frameworks to optimize preference-based reasoning. Despite utilizing the same baseline architecture and a smaller dataset than Gaokerena-V, Gaokerena-R achieved a superior benchmark score of 52.98%. Furthermore, both models are equipped with custom-developed uncertainty heads that predict the model's confidence in its responses based solely on internal hidden states. While these results demonstrate significant progress in Persian medical language modeling and proactive safety estimation, current performance levels remain insufficient for direct clinical application, highlighting the necessity for further research into robust knowledge acquisition and rigorous safety verification prior to real world deployment.

</details>


### [53] [Mind the Gap: Zero-Query Jailbreaks via Filter-Generator Discrepancy in Text-to-Image Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00973)
*Wanguang Li,Zhaoxin Wang,Handing Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a zero-query jailbreak attack framework against text-to-image safety filters that exploits differences between how filters and generators interpret prompts, improving attack success rates across multiple black-box systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing text-to-image systems use prompt-level safety filters to block unsafe requests, but they are still vulnerable to adversarially crafted jailbreak prompts. Transfer-based attacks that build adversarial prompts without querying the target often overfit to a single surrogate model and explore an enormous search space, where many candidate prompts are semantically similar yet fail either to bypass filters or to preserve the intended unsafe content. There is a need for a more principled, efficient way to craft adversarial prompts that are likely both to evade filters and to retain the unsafe generation intent, while not requiring any interaction with the target system.

Method: The authors identify and formalize the Filter-Generator Discrepancy (FGD)—the fact that the safety filter and the image generator process the same text prompt under different objectives and internal representations. Exploiting this, they design a zero-query jailbreak attack framework. First, it screens perturbations using observable discrepancy rules at both the tokenization level and semantic level to select a smaller, high-potential set of candidate prompts that are more likely to reduce perceived risk for the filter but preserve the unsafe visual concept for the generator. Then, over this screened candidate set, they run an evolutionary search with an ensemble of surrogate models, without any access to the actual target pipeline. The whole process is transfer-based and query-free with respect to the victim system.

Result: On six black-box text-to-image pipelines and a commercial online service, the proposed method consistently outperforms representative baseline jailbreak attacks. Measured by attack success rate under MHSC and Q16 metrics, it achieves average success rates of 29.2% (MHSC) and 33.3% (Q16) across the six pipelines, which is about an 8 and 12 percentage point improvement, respectively, over the strongest baseline method.

Conclusion: The study shows that exploiting the Filter-Generator Discrepancy enables more effective zero-query jailbreak attacks on text-to-image systems. By combining discrepancy-based screening with surrogate-ensemble evolutionary search, the method significantly improves transfer-based adversarial prompt quality, achieving higher success rates at bypassing safety filters while maintaining the intended unsafe generation intent. This highlights a serious security vulnerability in current T2I pipelines and suggests that defenses must better account for the divergent behaviors of filters and generators.

Abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) systems typically have prompt-level safety filters before the generator to block unsafe requests, yet such systems remain vulnerable to malicious jailbreak prompts. Transfer-based attacks construct adversarial prompts offline without querying the target, but they tend to overfit to a single surrogate. Moreover, they explore a large search space in which semantic or perceptual similarity alone cannot guarantee both filter evasion and preservation of the unsafe generation intent, wasting effort on low-potential candidates. We observe that the filter and the generator process the same prompt under different objectives and representations, and term this gap the Filter-Generator Discrepancy (FGD), which allows a perturbation to reduce a prompt's perceived risk to the filter while preserving the visual concept needed by the generator. Building on FGD, we propose a zero-query jailbreak framework that screens perturbations into a high-potential candidate set via observable discrepancy rules at the tokenization and semantic stages, and then performs a surrogate-ensemble evolutionary search that requires no access to the target. Experiments on six black-box pipelines and a commercial online service show that our method consistently outperforms representative baselines, raising the average attack success rate to 29.2\% (MHSC) and 33.3\% (Q16) across the six pipelines and improving over the strongest baseline by about 8 and 12 percentage points, respectively.

</details>


### [54] [Unsupervised Multidomain Approaches to Named Entity Recognition with Small Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00984)
*Israel Fianyi,James Montgomery,Soonja Yeom*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how to build effective NER models in domains with very small, unlabeled datasets by combining unsupervised pre-training and transfer learning, plus techniques like data augmentation, few-shot learning, and domain adversarial training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most NER systems need large labeled datasets, which are expensive or impossible to obtain in many specific domains. The authors want to enable reliable NER when only small, unlabeled or sparsely labeled datasets are available, and domains differ significantly from standard benchmarks.

Method: They first use unsupervised pre-training on unlabeled domain data to learn general text representations and roughly identify entities without annotations. Then they apply transfer learning, adapting these pre-trained models to multiple simulated low-resource datasets for NER. They consider and likely combine methods such as data augmentation (to expand data), few-shot learning (to learn from very few labels), and domain adversarial training (to make representations domain-invariant).

Result: The abstract claims that integrating unsupervised pre-training with transfer learning and auxiliary techniques like data augmentation, few-shot learning, and domain adversarial training improves NER performance and generalization in small-data, multi-domain settings, compared to traditional approaches that rely on large labeled corpora.

Conclusion: By leveraging unsupervised pre-training plus transfer learning and advanced low-resource learning strategies, NER systems can become more robust and adaptable across diverse, resource-constrained domains, reducing dependence on large annotated datasets and enabling more efficient NLP applications.

Abstract: This paper explores the challenges and the methodologies associated with learning quality representations in scenarios with unlabelled small or limited datasets for downstream information extraction task (Multidomain Named Entity Recognition (NER). The study adopts a Transfer Learning on small datasets. Traditional NER systems often rely on large, labelled data, which is impractical for many domains. This study, therefore, applies an unsupervised pre-training approach to precondition and identify entities without annotated datasets, then applies transfer learning models to different simulated limited datasets for a named entity recognition task. Entity Recognition (NER) is essential in natural language processing (NLP), it identifies and classifies related entities within the text. This study addresses the complexities of domain variability, data sparsity, and overfitting and investigates innovative approaches such as data augmentation, few-shot learning, and domain adversarial training. Integrating these techniques promises to enhance the performance and generalizability of NER systems across diverse and resource-constrained domains, paving the way for more efficient and adaptable NLP applications.

</details>


### [55] [MedUPS: Towards Diagnostic Assistance in Uncommon Medical Cases with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01012)
*Ofir Ben Shoham,Oriel Perets,Nir Grinberg,Nadav Rappoport*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces MedUPSQA, a large dataset and MedUPS, an alignment framework to train LLMs on mid-stream clinical decisions (next actions) rather than only final diagnoses, significantly improving next-step performance on multiple medical LLM backbones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing medical LLM benchmarks and training regimes largely focus on final diagnoses or end-point labels. However, real-world clinical decision-making involves a sequence of incremental, uncertain decisions (e.g., which test or consult to order next). Uncommon and off-guideline cases are particularly challenging because clinicians rarely see the full picture at once. There is a gap between how models are evaluated/trained and how clinicians actually reason over time, so better benchmarks and training objectives are needed for mid-stream decision support.

Method: The authors construct MedUPSQA, a dataset of 21,874 intermediate clinical decision points derived from 5,535 real case reports. They segment free-text case narratives into chronologically ordered, accumulating clinical chunks that simulate the unfolding of a patient encounter. They then propose MedUPS, an alignment framework that trains models to predict the next clinical step at each mid-stream point using reinforcement learning (GRPO) with an external LLM-as-a-Judge reward function. They also create supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baselines on the same mid-stream task for comparison.

Result: Applying MedUPS across three backbone models (Qwen3.6-27B, Qwen3.5-9B, HuatuoGPT-3-8B) substantially improves next-step decision accuracy: from 55.2% to 66.7% for Qwen3.6-27B, from 47.2% to 57.8% for Qwen3.5-9B, and from 37.8% to 44.4% for HuatuoGPT-3-8B, all with 95% confidence intervals. The mid-stream alignment objective sometimes yields larger gains than simply increasing model scale, with smaller aligned models outperforming larger frontier models. SFT on the mid-stream task also improves all backbone performances over their base versions, showing that the task design itself is beneficial, independent of the RL optimizer.

Conclusion: Training and evaluating medical LLMs on mid-stream clinical decisions—mirroring how clinicians actually encounter and manage patients—can substantially improve decision quality on complex, off-guideline cases. The MedUPSQA dataset and MedUPS alignment framework demonstrate that focusing on next-step reasoning rather than only final diagnoses provides strong signal, can outperform mere model scaling, and generalizes across different backbones. The released data, code, and checkpoints provide resources for advancing clinically realistic decision-support models.

Abstract: Uncommon and off-guideline cases are difficult for clinical decision support, because physicians must make a series of management decisions under diagnostic uncertainty and rarely see the full case at once. Most large language model (LLM) benchmarks for medicine score only the final diagnosis, yet much of clinical care turns on the next appropriate action: the next test to order, the imaging study to obtain, the specialist to involve, or the differential to pursue. We introduce MedUPSQA, a dataset of 21,874 mid-stream clinical decision points built from 5,535 real case reports, and MedUPS, an alignment framework that supervises models on these intermediate decisions as they unfold along a patient's trajectory. We segment free-text case presentations into chronologically ordered, accumulating clinical chunks and align models to predict the next step with reinforcement learning (GRPO), using an external LLM-as-a-Judge reward. This objective mirrors how clinicians actually meet patients, reasoning forward from accumulating evidence toward the next decision, rather than committing to a final label. Across three backbones, mid-stream alignment raises next-step accuracy from 55.2 to 66.7 for Qwen3.6-27B, from 47.2 to 57.8 for Qwen3.5-9B, and from 37.8 to 44.4 for HuatuoGPT-3-8B, with 95% CI. In several model scales we test the objective improves accuracy more than scale, with smaller models surpassing larger, frontier models we evaluate. We further train supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baselines on the mid-stream task, SFT improves all backbones above base, indicating the target framwork carries signal independently of the optimizer. We release the dataset, code, and aligned checkpoints.

</details>


### [56] [Cloud-ScPO: Hidden-State Geometry for Semi-Supervised Preference Optimization in LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01014)
*Yuzhou Liu,Xiyang Hu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They use the geometry of internal LLM representations to mine preference pairs for mathematical reasoning, reducing the need for human or external supervision and improving preference optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Preference optimization needs reliable chosen-rejected pairs, which are expensive because they typically require verified labels, human annotation, or separate reward models. The authors want a cheaper, semi-supervised way to obtain preference supervision for math reasoning, leveraging information already present in the model’s internal states.

Method: They analyze reasoning trajectories across math problems and discover structured global point clouds where correct vs. incorrect trajectories have distinct geometric patterns. Building on this, they introduce Cloud–ScPO: using a small labeled set, they construct multiple reference "Clouds" of correct and incorrect trajectories. Each candidate trajectory is encoded as a mean-pooled hidden state and scored via component-level soft k-nearest-neighbor similarity to connectivity-induced components of these Clouds, averaged over several reference banks. They integrate this cross-problem Cloud score with prompt-level self-consistency: self-consistency picks which final answer direction is preferred, and Cloud scoring selects specific trajectories and filters chosen–rejected pairs based on their score margin.

Result: On GSM8K and MATH-Numeric, across four LLM setups, Cloud–ScPO consistently outperforms standard ScPO, with up to 4.49% accuracy gain on GSM8K and 4.19% on MATH-Numeric. Pair-level analysis shows that, compared to ScPO, their method keeps a similar rate of correctness in chosen responses but better distinguishes high-quality, informative chosen trajectories from low-quality rejected ones (e.g., incomplete or repetitive reasoning).

Conclusion: Internal representation geometry encodes useful structural information about reasoning quality that can be turned into semi-supervised preference signals. By constructing and leveraging topology-guided Clouds of correct and incorrect trajectories and combining them with self-consistency, Cloud–ScPO yields better preference optimization for mathematical reasoning without heavy labeling or external reward models.

Abstract: Preference optimization improves mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs), but reliable chosen-rejected pairs usually require verified answers, human annotations, or external reward models. We investigate whether preference supervision can instead be derived from the model's internal representation geometry in a semi-supervised setting. Our analysis shows that reasoning trajectories generated across different mathematical problems form structured global point clouds in which correct and incorrect trajectories exhibit different geometric organization. Based on this observation, we propose Cloud--ScPO, a topology-guided preference-mining framework that uses a small labeled set to construct multiple correct and incorrect reference Clouds. Each trajectory is represented by a mean-pooled hidden state and scored against connectivity-induced components using a component-level soft $k$-nearest-neighbor measure averaged across reference banks. We combine this cross-problem Cloud signal with prompt-level self-consistency: self-consistency determines the answer-level preference direction, while Cloud scoring selects concrete trajectories and filters pairs by their score margin. Experiments on GSM8K and MATH-Numeric across four model settings show that Cloud--ScPO consistently improves over ScPO, with gains of up to 4.49\% on GSM8K and 4.19\% on MATH-Numeric. Pair-level analyses further show that Cloud--ScPO maintains comparable correctness reliability while more effectively separating informative chosen trajectories from incomplete, repetitive, or otherwise low-quality rejected responses.

</details>


### [57] [Why LLMs Give In: Conversational Factors and Reasoning Behind Medical Sycophancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01017)
*Kaike Ping,Buse Çarık,Caleb Wohn,Xiaohan Ding,Tongshuai Wang,Eugenia Rho*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes when and why medical language models abandon correct answers under user pressure, showing that “medical sycophancy” is driven more by conversational setup and question properties than by the model itself.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluations report a single sycophancy rate per model, implicitly treating it as a fixed model property. However, in medical settings, a model that initially answers correctly but later yields to user misinformation is especially dangerous. There is a need to understand how conversational context (user role, evidence, timing of challenges, and prompt grounding) shapes this behavior, rather than attributing it solely to the model.

Method: The authors run a large-scale, fully crossed factorial experiment over four conversational factors: (1) user role, (2) type and presence of evidence behind a false claim (including fabricated sources), (3) whether the user’s challenge to the model comes before or after the model’s initial answer, and (4) whether the correct answer is explicitly grounded in the prompt. They test five open-weight language models on 500 MedQuAD medical QA questions, yielding about 1.2 million conversation trials. They then analyze sycophancy rates, factor interactions, and chain-of-thought traces to understand why models change their answers.

Result: They find strong interactions between conversational factors. Fabricated sources double sycophancy when included with the initial user question, but reduce sycophancy by half when introduced after the model has already answered correctly—so the same evidence has opposite effects depending solely on timing. Variation in sycophancy is much larger across questions than across models (67x vs. 3x), indicating that a single sycophancy rate mostly reflects question and conversation design, not just model characteristics. Analysis of chain-of-thought shows that models that re-evaluate their own prior answer often concede to user misinformation, while models that focus on medical facts tend to maintain the correct answer. Only models that have already answered can use an extra turn to audit fabricated sources effectively.

Conclusion: Medical sycophancy is primarily a property of the conversation structure and question set rather than an intrinsic, fixed property of a model. The timing and nature of user-provided (even fabricated) evidence critically shape whether models abandon correct answers. Evaluations and mitigations should therefore focus on conversational design and encouraging models to reason about domain facts—not merely re-examine their own earlier outputs—if we want them to resist harmful user pushback in medical contexts.

Abstract: A language model that abandons a correct medical answer under user pushback is more dangerous than one that was simply wrong, because it lends the credibility of a correct answer to the user's misinformation. Such model behavior, described as medical sycophancy, is usually reported as a single rate per model, but we find it is a property of the conversation, not the model. We study medical sycophancy in language models with a fully crossed factorial design over four conversational factors, user role, the evidence behind a false claim, whether the challenge precedes or follows the model's answer, and whether the correct answer is grounded in the prompt, across five open-weight models and 500 MedQuAD questions (1.2M trials). The factors interact sharply: fabricated sources raise sycophancy 2.0x when they accompany the question but halve it once the model has answered, so the same evidence helps or hurts depending only on timing. Sycophancy varies far more across questions than across models (67x vs. 3x), so a single rate reflects the conversation and the questions sampled as much as the model. Chain-of-thought traces explain why. Models that re-examine their own prior answer concede, while those that reason about the medical facts hold, and only a model that has already answered can spend a round auditing the fabricated source.

</details>


### [58] [Opt.Gear Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01034)
*Juneyoung Park,Youngwook Kwon*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Opt.Gear is an efficient on-device foundation language model family with up to 1B parameters and 64K context, using a hybrid architecture to reduce KV-cache memory and accelerate inference on NPUs and MCUs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the challenge of running capable foundation models on resource-constrained edge devices, where memory, compute, and latency limitations make standard transformer architectures and large KV-caches impractical.

Method: They design a hybrid architecture combining a convolutional key-value gated mixer with local-global attention to shrink KV-cache requirements while preserving long-context abilities; train 1M, 270M, and 1B parameter models on a curated 0.5T-token subset (from a 2T-token candidate corpus) without distillation; release optimized deployment binaries for ONNX, Qualcomm NPU, and Apple ANE and a 1M-parameter Tiny Language Model (Opt.Gear-1M) that runs on MCUs with W4A32 quantization.

Result: The architecture achieves up to 4.9× faster prefill and decoding on NPUs versus similar-sized models, maintains a 64K context window with reduced KV-cache memory, and Opt.Gear-1M reaches 20 tokens per second with W4A32 quantization on an ARM Cortex-M7 MCU board.

Conclusion: Opt.Gear demonstrates that carefully designed hybrid architectures plus data-efficient training can produce open, edge-focused foundation models that deliver strong task performance, long context, and high-speed, low-memory inference on NPUs and even MCUs, making them practical bases for on-device generative applications.

Abstract: We introduce Opt.Gear, a foundation model designed for efficient on-device deployment, real-tim inference, and strong task capability. It includes a dense model (1M, 270M, and 1B) with a context length of 64K. We designed a new hybrid architecture that combines a convolutional key-value gated mixer with local-global attention to reduce the KV-cache memory that tends to increase exponentially with long context. This architecture delivers up to X4.9 faster prefill and decoding speeds on the NPUs compared to models of a similar scale models. From a 2T tokens candidate corpus, Opt.Gear is trained on a curated 0.5T tokens subset without knowledge distillation. This is the most data-efficient of the existing foundation models. All models are released with open weights and deployment binaries for ONNX, Qualcomm NPU, and Apple ANE making Opt.Gear a practical base for edge applications that need fast, memory-efficient inference and strong task capabilities. Furthermore, to expand the ecosystem of on-device generative language models, we are introducing the Opt.Gear-1M that can be deployed on Micro-Controller Units (MCUs), a Tiny Language Model (TLM). Opt.Gear-1M is the first generative language model to achieve 20 TPS with W4A32 quantization on the ARM Cortex-M7 CPU of the STM32H747I-DISCO.

</details>


### [59] [DeBERTa-Sentinel: Toward Transparent and Trustworthy Detection of AI-Generated Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01046)
*Muhammad Yousaf Rehman,Muhammad Islam*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose DeBERTa-Sentinel, an interpretable DeBERTa-v3–based detector that reliably distinguishes human from LLM-generated text and explains its decisions at token level.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are widely used online, raising risks of misinformation, academic dishonesty, and automated manipulation. Existing detectors like GPT-Sentinel work reasonably well but generalize poorly across different LLMs and paraphrased text and are often black boxes. Stakeholders such as journalists, educators, and trust-and-safety teams need accurate and transparent tools to assess whether content is AI-generated and to understand why a detector made its decision.

Method: They build DeBERTa-Sentinel on top of DeBERTa-v3, exploiting its disentangled attention to better capture structural and stylistic patterns in text that distinguish synthetic from human writing. The framework is explicitly designed for interpretability, outputting token-level explanations that highlight which words or phrases drive the AI-vs-human decision. They train and evaluate the model on the GLC-AIText dataset containing 28,057 human and LLM outputs (from GPT, LLaMA, Claude) with a 60/20/20 train/validation/test split, and compare it against a RoBERTa-Sentinel baseline from NeurIPS 2025.

Result: On the GLC-AIText dataset, DeBERTa-Sentinel attains 98.21% validation accuracy and 97.53% test accuracy, outperforming the RoBERTa-Sentinel baseline. It reaches 95.89% precision, 99.33% recall, 99.53% ROC-AUC, and a very low 0.665% false negative rate.
