The interpretability analysis shows that the model consistently flags markers such as academic-style phrasing and formal transitions as indicative of AI-generated text.

Conclusion: DeBERTa-Sentinel is a high-performing, interpretable detector for AI-generated text that generalizes across multiple LLMs and provides token-level rationales, addressing key shortcomings of prior black-box detectors. By improving accuracy, reducing false negatives, and providing explanations that stakeholders can audit, it contributes to more trustworthy and human-centric use of AI in online environments.

Abstract: The rapid spread of large language models (LLMs) across the web raises concerns about misinformation, academic integrity, automated content manipulation, and risks to vulnerable online communities. Existing transformer-based detectors, such as GPT-Sentinel, show promise but struggle to generalize to diverse model outputs and paraphrasing attacks, limiting their role in building trustworthy web ecosystems. This work introduces DeBERTa-Sentinel, a responsible AI-generated text detection framework leveraging DeBERTa-v3's disentangled attention to capture subtle structural irregularities in synthetic content. A central design principle is transparency: unlike black-box commercial detectors, DeBERTa-Sentinel exposes token-level explanations of its decisions, enabling affected stakeholders journalists, educators, and platform trust and safety teams to audit, challenge, and contextualize detection outcomes. Using the GLC-AIText dataset of 28,057 human and LLM-generated samples (GPT, LLaMA, and Claude) with a 60-20-20 split, DeBERTa-Sentinel achieves 98.21\% validation accuracy and surpasses the RoBERTa-Sentinel baseline from NeurIPS 2025, achieving 97.53\% test accuracy, 95.89\% precision, 99.33\% recall, and 99.53\% ROC-AUC, and maintaining a 0.665\% false negative rate. The model's interpretability reveals linguistic markers such as academic phrasing and formal transitions associated with synthetic text, directly supporting stakeholder needs for verifiable, auditable content-authenticity decisions. By advancing responsible detection methods that reduce bias and enhance explainability, DeBERTa-Sentinel promotes trustworthy, ethical, and human-centric AI systems. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Galileo-Galili/HUMAN-VS-AI-TEXT-DETECTION.

</details>


### [60] [Attend to Your Own Thoughts: Breaking the Barrier for Post-Training Quantization of Reasoning LLMs through the Lens of 1.58-Bit Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01078)
*Shigeng Wang,Chao Li,Yangyuxuan Kang,Jiawei Fan,Anbang Yao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ScaleQ-1.58 is a ternary post-training quantization framework for reasoning LLMs that preserves strong performance on math, coding, and reasoning tasks by calibrating with the model’s own chain-of-thought traces (AYOT).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ternary PTQ methods like CAT-Q severely degrade the reasoning performance of LLMs on hard math and coding benchmarks because standard calibration ignores the chain-of-thought behavior these models were trained to exhibit. There is a need for a scalable, data-efficient quantization approach that maintains reasoning quality, works across model sizes and architectures, and reduces calibration cost.

Method: The authors introduce Attend to Your Own Thoughts (AYOT), a calibration strategy where, for a set of calibration questions, the full-precision target LLM first generates its chain-of-thought (reasoning traces) and final answers. These generated traces plus answers are then concatenated with the original questions and used as the context during ternary post-training quantization. AYOT is combined with the existing learning-based differentiable ternarization framework CAT-Q to form ScaleQ-1.58. The approach is evaluated across model sizes (up to 235B), both dense and MoE architectures, and multiple task types, while varying the number of calibration tokens.

Result: With only 4M calibration tokens, a ternary Qwen3-1.7B quantized by ScaleQ-1.58 recovers over 90.52% of the performance of BitNet b1.58 2B4T across four math and coding tasks. A ternary Qwen3-4B quantized with ScaleQ-1.58 outperforms the prior baseline by an absolute 8.97% while using 1,000,000x fewer calibration tokens. Performance scales positively with model size up to 235B parameters, generalizes to both dense and MoE models, extends to a broad range of tasks (math, coding, scientific and commonsense reasoning, basic generation), and continues to improve as more calibration tokens are used. AYOT also shows effectiveness beyond ternary, at other quantization bit-widths.

Conclusion: Incorporating the model’s own chain-of-thought outputs into the calibration process is crucial for preserving reasoning performance under ternary PTQ. The proposed ScaleQ-1.58 framework—AYOT combined with CAT-Q—provides a scalable, data-efficient, and architecture-agnostic solution that maintains strong performance on challenging reasoning tasks, improves with model and data scale, and generalizes across bit-widths. This suggests that reasoning-aware calibration should be a key component of future quantization methods for LLMs.

Abstract: We propose ScaleQ-1.58, a scalable ternary post-training quantization (PTQ) framework for reasoning LLMs. Its core insight stems from an empirical finding: although modern LLMs are typically trained to exhibit chain-of-thought reasoning capabilities, in the PTQ regime, even the latest CAT-Q method based on learning-based differentiable ternarization still leads to performance collapse on challenging mathematics and coding tasks when using conventional calibration schemes that ignore the model's reasoning process. Driven by this finding, we introduce a simple calibration approach, Attend to Your Own Thoughts (AYOT), where reasoning traces and final answers generated by the pre-trained high-precision target LLM on a proper set of calibration samples are used as the context input during the ternarization process, along with the corresponding questions. ScaleQ-1.58 is formed by simply integrating AYOT with CAT-Q, which demonstrates several scaling properties: (1) with only 4M calibration tokens, Qwen3-1.7B ternarized by ScaleQ-1.58 reaches over 90.52% of the performance of the prior best BitNet b1.58 2B4T averaged over 4 mathematics and coding tasks, and our ternary Qwen3-4B shows an absolute gain of 8.97%, while requiring 1,000,000x fewer calibration tokens for quantization; (2) ScaleQ-1.58 generalizes well to both dense and MoE architectures, with performance improving as model scale increases (up to 235B parameters); (3) ScaleQ-1.58 demonstrates strong generalization across tasks of varying difficulty levels, including mathematics, coding and scientific logic reasoning, as well as commonsense reasoning and basic language generation; (4) its performance continues to improve as the number of calibration tokens increases. Notably, AYOT also exhibits strong generalization ability across other quantization bit-widths. Code will be available at https://github.com/IntelChina-AI/BitTern.

</details>


### [61] [Morphology Aware Reversible Semantic Tokenization and Hierarchical Word Composition for Tamil Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01153)
*Anand Murugan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a morphology-aware Tamil tokenizer and a hierarchical word composer that better align with Tamil’s rich morphology, improving translation quality and efficiency over standard subword tokenizers under the same model and training budget.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional statistical subword tokenizers (e.g., BPE) segment text without regard to morphological or grammatical structure, which is particularly problematic for morphologically rich languages like Tamil, where single orthographic words bundle many grammatical categories. This misalignment can hurt machine translation quality and efficiency, especially for small models with limited capacity. The authors aim to test whether explicit morphology and hierarchical word composition can yield better translation performance and shorter effective sequences than widely used Indic tokenizers, under a strictly controlled, fixed-model setting.

Method: They extend the open-source ThamizhiMorph Tamil morphology analyzer/generator into a full morphology system comprising 12 finite-state transducers. These analyze words into lemmas plus grammatical feature bundles, with character and byte-level fallbacks to ensure exact text reconstruction. On top of this, they define: (1) a flat morphology tokenizer that directly uses analyzed morphemes/features as tokens, and (2) a learned hierarchical word composer that builds words from sub-tokens while preserving the original byte sequence. They also design a signal-preserving semantic tokenizer. They compare these systems against several strong baselines (Sarvam-1, AI4Bharat IndicBERTv2, BrahmicTokenizer-131K) using the same NMT architecture: an 18.97M-parameter encoder-decoder, 69,591 Tamil–English training pairs, 40k updates, fixed optimizer, positional encoding, generation, and target-side tokenization. Evaluation uses a 3,539-sentence protected IN22 and FLORES+ test set with BLEU, chrF++, COMETKiwi, and analyses of sequence length, global source states, and estimated FLOPs.

Result: The morphology-flat tokenizer yields the best pooled translation scores: 10.63 BLEU, 35.26 chrF++, and 0.6276 COMETKiwi. Compared to the strongest external tokenizer baseline (from AI4Bharat), these represent relative gains of 7.2% (BLEU), 3.2% (chrF++), and 2.6% (COMETKiwi). The hierarchical word composer also outperforms AI4Bharat, scoring 10.30 BLEU, 34.88 chrF++, and 0.6241 COMETKiwi, corresponding to 3.8%, 2.1%, and 2.0% relative improvements. In terms of efficiency, the composer cuts mean global source states from 71.48 to 29.08 (a 59.3% reduction) and is estimated to save 9–21% inference FLOPs depending on decoder caching. Its remaining quality deficit relative to morphology-flat is concentrated on longer FLORES+ sentences.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling Tamil morphology in the tokenizer improves translation quality when the model size and training conditions are held fixed, demonstrating that linguistically structured tokenization can be beneficial over purely statistical subword methods for a morphologically rich language. Furthermore, the hierarchical word composer offers a favorable trade-off: it substantially shortens effective sequence lengths and reduces estimated inference cost while still outperforming strong external baselines, though it lags slightly behind the flat morphology tokenizer on longer sentences. Overall, morphology-aware and hierarchical tokenization strategies provide a practical path to better accuracy–efficiency trade-offs for Tamil NMT under tight model budgets.

Abstract: Statistical subword tokenizers can process arbitrary text, but their units need not align with lexical or grammatical structure. This is especially important for Tamil, where a written word may encode stem changes, case, number, tense, agreement, voice, clitics, and linked verbs. We present a Tamil morphology system extending the open-source ThamizhiMorph analyzer and generator, together with a byte-exact semantic tokenizer and a learned hierarchical word composer. Twelve finite-state transducers analyze words into lemmas and grammatical features, while character and byte fallbacks preserve exact reconstruction.
  We compare a flat morphology tokenizer, a signal-preserving word composer, and tokenizers based on Sarvam-1, AI4Bharat IndicBERTv2, and BrahmicTokenizer-131K. All systems use the same 69,591 Tamil-English training pairs, 18.97-million-parameter encoder-decoder, 40,000 updates, target tokenizer, optimizer, positional method, and generation settings.
  On a protected 3,539-row IN22 and FLORES+ evaluation, morphology-flat achieves the best pooled scores: 10.63 BLEU, 35.26 chrF++, and 0.6276 COMETKiwi. Relative to AI4Bharat, the strongest external-tokenizer baseline, these are improvements of 7.2%, 3.2%, and 2.6%. The word composer scores 10.30, 34.88, and 0.6241, improving on AI4Bharat by 3.8%, 2.1%, and 2.0%.
  The composer reduces mean global source states from 71.48 to 29.08, a 59.3% reduction, and is estimated to require 9-21% fewer inference FLOPs depending on decoder caching. Its remaining quality gap is concentrated in longer FLORES+ sentences. These results show that explicit Tamil morphology improves translation under a fixed small-model budget, while hierarchical composition substantially reduces sequence length and estimated inference cost.

</details>


### [62] [PlainMedScale: A Corpus of Multi-Level Simplified Medical Texts in German and English](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01158)
*Bruno Brocai,Ilaria Papagno,Mayumi Ohta*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PlainMedScale is a bilingual (German/English) medical corpus organized into four graded comprehensibility levels, enabling nuanced study of medical text difficulty beyond simple expert vs. lay distinctions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing medical corpora usually distinguish only between expert and layperson language, which is too coarse to reflect the full range of texts patients encounter (e.g., detailed reference vs. simple access information). Research also lacks resources to test whether readability metrics and large language models (LLMs) handle a more fine-grained continuum of difficulty. The authors want to fill this gap with a topic-aligned, multi-level corpus.

Method: They construct a corpus from several medical sources: MSD professional and consumer articles, Gesund.Bund, Apotheken Umschau Einfache Sprache, and the NHS. Texts are organized into four tiers, each linked to a communicative function: reference, explanation, decision support, and access. The corpus is topic-aligned across languages and levels. Using this resource, they conduct two pilot studies: (1) evaluating how well existing readability metrics, trained on two registers, generalize across the four-level gradient; and (2) prompting a state-of-the-art open-weight LLM to generate Plain Language versions of texts and assessing whether difficulty is effectively reduced.

Result: They obtain a structured, topic-aligned bilingual corpus spanning four distinct comprehensibility levels. In their pilot experiments, they find that many standard readability metrics fail to generalize when applied across all four levels of difficulty. They also find that a state-of-the-art open-weight LLM, even when instructed to produce Plain Language output, still partially maintains the difficulty level of its input text rather than fully simplifying it.

Conclusion: PlainMedScale offers a more nuanced, function-based gradient of medical text comprehensibility than previous binary expert–lay corpora. The initial experiments show that both widely used readability formulas and current open-weight LLMs have limitations when dealing with this richer difficulty spectrum. The released code and data provide a foundation for further research on medical text simplification, readability modeling, and patient-centered communication across languages.

Abstract: We introduce PlainMedScale, a topic-aligned medical corpus spanning four levels of comprehensibility in German and English, drawn from MSD (professional and consumer), Gesund.Bund, Apotheken Umschau Einfache Sprache, and the NHS. The four tiers correspond to distinct communicative functions --- reference, explanation, decision support, and access --- and move beyond the binary expert--lay contrast of prior corpora. In two pilot studies enabled by the alignments, we show that many readability metrics established on two registers fail to generalize across the full gradient, and that a SOTA open-weight LLM prompted for Plain Language still partially preserves the difficulty of its input. Code (https://github.com/GS-Uni-Heidelberg/PlainMedScale) and data (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21728290) are made available.

</details>


### [63] [Does Machine "know" interpersonal pragmatics? Evidence from MARBERT's learning of emoji pragmatics in Arabic digital discourse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01174)
*Mohammed Q. Shormani*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how well an Arabic Transformer model (MARBERT) can learn and predict the interpersonal pragmatic functions of emojis in Arabic digital discourse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is limited work on how NLP models capture nuanced interpersonal functions of emojis—such as politeness and solidarity—especially in Arabic digital discourse. Existing research focuses mostly on sentiment, not on richer pragmatic or relational meanings. The authors aim to fill this gap and to connect interpersonal pragmatics theories with computational modeling.

Method: The authors collect 8,504 Arabic Facebook posts that contain emojis, then manually annotate them for five interpersonal pragmatic functions: Politeness, Respect, Solidarity, Empathy, and Encouragement. They fine-tune the Arabic Transformer model MARBERT on this labeled dataset. They use a mixed-methods approach: quantitative evaluation using accuracy and F1-scores, and qualitative interpretation using speech act theory, politeness theory, and rapport management theory to analyze how the model handles different functions.

Result: MARBERT achieves 93% accuracy, a micro F1 of 0.61, and a macro F1 of 0.56 on unseen data for classifying emoji-related interpersonal functions. Politeness and Respect are recognized more accurately than Solidarity, suggesting that more explicit, less context-dependent functions are easier for the model to capture than highly implicit, context-sensitive ones.

Conclusion: Transformer-based models like MARBERT can learn patterns of face management and relational communication encoded in emojis, performing well above chance on interpersonal pragmatic functions in Arabic digital discourse. However, they still struggle with subtle, highly contextual social meanings (e.g., Solidarity). The study offers a new computational approach to emoji pragmatics and strengthens the bridge between interpersonal pragmatics and NLP in the study of digital communication.

Abstract: This study examines Transformer-based models' ability to learn emoji pragmatics in Arabic digital discourse (ADD), providing evidence from MARBERT's behavior with interpersonal pragmatic functions (IPFs). A corpus of 8,504 unique emoji-posts collected from Facebook via Python was used in the study. These posts were manually annotated, developed, and labeled for five IPFs: Politeness, Respect, Solidarity, Empathy, and Encouragement. A mixed-method approach was employed comprising statistical methods and interpretative analyses involving speech act theory, politeness theory, and rapport management theory. MARBERT was fine-tuned to model these context-dependent pragmatic functions. Findings demonstrate MARBERT's ability to learn these IPFs, achieving strong performance on unseen data, with an accuracy of 93%, a micro F1-score of 0.61, and a macro F1-score of 0.56, demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing interpersonal functions beyond conventional sentiment analysis. Function-level evaluation showed that Politeness and Respect were identified more accurately than Solidarity, reflecting differences in the explicitness and contextual dependence of IPFs. The study concludes that Transformer-based models learn patterns of face management and relational communication but remain challenged by highly implicit social meanings. It contributes a novel computational approach to modeling emoji pragmatics and advances the integration of interpersonal pragmatics with NLP for digital communication research.

</details>


### [64] [When Words Divide: Diachronic Ideological Polarization in Political Discourse on Social Media](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01176)
*Roy Yitzchak,Noa Lavie,Ella Rabinovich*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how ideological polarization in Reddit political discussions changes over time by comparing how different political communities semantically frame concepts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While political polarization online is widely discussed, most computational studies only take snapshots or focus on emotional tone rather than how meanings and framings diverge over time. Understanding the long-term evolution of ideological polarization in language can shed light on how political divisions deepen and spread in online communities.

Method: The authors build temporally aligned, community-specific word embeddings from Reddit political discussions. They then measure polarization as the semantic divergence between embeddings of the same political concepts across opposing political communities at different time periods, analyzing both individual concepts and broader topics.

Result: They find that ideological polarization on Reddit has increased substantially over the study period. This increase is evident at the level of specific political concepts and entire topics, indicating widening semantic distance in how different communities talk about politics.

Conclusion: The study concludes that ideological polarization in online discourse is not just about sentiment but also about increasingly divergent semantic framings of political ideas. Their embedding-based framework offers a scalable way to track the temporal dynamics of ideological polarization in large-scale social media data.

Abstract: Political polarization has become a defining feature of online discourse, yet its long-term evolution remains poorly understood. We present a longitudinal analysis of ideological polarization in Reddit discussions by measuring semantic differences in the language used by opposing political communities. We construct temporally aligned community-specific word embeddings and quantify ideological polarization as the semantic divergence of political concepts over time. Our analysis shows that ideological polarization has increased substantially during the study period, both at the concept- and topic-level. Unlike prior computational work, which has largely focused on cross-sectional analyses or affective dimensions of polarization at a single point at time, our approach captures the evolution of ideological differences in semantic framing. The proposed framework provides a scalable method for studying the temporal dynamics of ideological polarization in large-scale social media discourse.

</details>


### [65] [ShiJianBench: From Dialogue to Decision for Long-Horizon Evaluation of Investment Advisors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01204)
*Jie Gong,Maowei Jiang,Zhiwei Liu,Yang Qiao,Wenxi Wu,Mengxi Xiao,Enze Zhang,Ziyan Kuang,Yankai Chen,Caishuang Huang,Meng Zhou,Xiku Du,Xue Liu,Guojun Xiong,Min Peng,Qianqian Xie,Sophia Ananiadou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents ShiJianBench, an offline benchmark to evaluate conversational investment advisors by simulating long-term investor behavior under historical market conditions, revealing that good responses do not always mean effective long-horizon guidance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluations of conversational investment advisors largely focus on single-turn response quality or final observed outcomes, making it hard to understand or audit how an advisor’s language shapes investor behavior over time as markets change. There is a need for a trajectory-level, behavior-aware evaluation framework that can isolate advisor effects under consistent market feedback and distinguish between high-quality sounding advice and truly effective long-horizon interventions.

Method: The authors build ShiJianBench, an offline evaluation framework centered on a multi-agent investor simulator that interacts with conversational advisors over fixed historical market data. The simulator models investors with explicit evolving state variables, motive-based deliberation, long-term memory, and updates grounded in the dialogue with the advisor. It is calibrated using aggregate behavioral data from 7,199 real users. Advisor policies are then tested against this simulator and assessed via investor-side (e.g., trajectory outcomes), service-side, and content-side metrics, all subject to a strict compliance filter to ensure only permissible advice is considered.

Result: Using Chinese fund-market data from 2021–2026, the experiments show that a subset of LLM-based advisors consistently outperform others, forming a stable leading group. These advisors provide more personalized content while achieving competitive investor-side trajectory performance under the simulator, all within compliance constraints. The benchmark surfaces differences across models that are not apparent from single-step response quality alone.

Conclusion: ShiJianBench demonstrates that evaluating conversational investment advisors requires trajectory-aware, behavior-centric benchmarks rather than only response-level metrics. The work establishes a practical offline protocol to study how advisor language affects evolving investor states and decisions, highlighting a systematic gap between generating high-quality answers and delivering effective long-term interventions, and motivating future research on long-horizon evaluation and design of financial advisory systems.

Abstract: Conversational investment advisors influence not only what users know, but also how they make subsequent decisions as market conditions evolve. Existing evaluations primarily assess response quality or observed outcomes, leaving the long-horizon pathway from advisor language to investor behavior difficult to audit. We introduce ShiJianBench, an offline framework for evaluating conversational investment advisors through matched investor trajectories under fixed historical market feedback. At its core is a multi-agent investor simulator with explicit evolving state variables, motive-driven deliberation, long-term memory, and dialogue-grounded updates. The simulator is calibrated against aggregate behavioral patterns from 7,199 real users, and advisor policies are evaluated using separate investor-side, service-side, and content-side metrics under a hard compliance gate. Experiments on Chinese fund-market traces from 2021 to 2026 identify a stable leading group of LLM advisors that combines substantially stronger personalized content with competitive investor-side trajectory outcomes. These results reveal a systematic distinction between producing a high-quality response and delivering an effective long-horizon intervention, motivating trajectory-aware evaluation of conversational advisors.

</details>


### [66] [Evaluating VLMs on Multimodal Aristotelian Persuasion Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01238)
*Khondoker Ittehadul Islam*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates Vision Language Models (VLMs) on complex persuasion-related tasks using the ImageArg dataset, finding Qwen models particularly strong on Logos, Ethos, and Pathos detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLMs have excelled on many benchmarks, but their ability to handle complex, bias-laden persuasive content has not been systematically studied. The authors aim to fill this gap by grounding evaluation in Aristotle’s persuasion model (Logos, Ethos, Pathos) to better understand VLMs’ performance on higher-level reasoning and rhetorical tasks.

Method: The authors use the ImageArg datasets annotated for three persuasion dimensions—Logos, Ethos, and Pathos—to benchmark multiple VLMs. They specifically analyze detection performance on each persuasion type, with a focus on models from the Qwen family, and compare F1 scores across tasks and models.

Result: Qwen-family models outperform others on these persuasion detection tasks. Qwen3 achieves notably high F1 scores on Logos and Pathos detection, while Qwen2 is particularly competitive on the more challenging Ethos detection task.

Conclusion: Current VLMs, especially Qwen models, show promising capability in recognizing complex persuasive strategies in visual–textual data, though Ethos detection remains more difficult. The released code supports further research into evaluating and improving VLMs on nuanced, bias-prone persuasive reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated exceptional performance across various tasks. However, they have not yet been thoroughly evaluated on more complex tasks. The Persuasion Model, conceived by Aristotle, resembles a triangle shape, which highlights its inherent challenges related to personal biases. To assess the progress of VLMs on these complex tasks, we use the ImageArg datasets, focusing on the Logos, Ethos, and Pathos detection tasks. Our findings indicate that models from the Qwen family achieve improved F1 scores, with Qwen3 performing exceptionally well on the Logos and Pathos tasks, while Qwen2 exhibits competitive performance on the more complex Ethos detection task. We release the code to foster research in this direction.

</details>


### [67] [DeltaFlow: Noise-Adaptive Bidirectional Gated Delta Networks for Embedded Language Flows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01240)
*Guangfu Guo,Xiaoqian Lu,Linsey Pang,Weiran Yao,Haolin Chen,Kunpeng Liu,Long Cheng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DeltaFlow is an efficient, bidirectional Gated Delta Network architecture for continuous language denoising that outperforms full-attention ELF models in perplexity and speed while using fewer training tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Embedded Language Flows (ELF) rely on full, non-causal attention at every denoising step, which is computationally expensive, especially for long sequences, due to repeated quadratic attention costs. Gated Delta Networks are a more efficient recurrent alternative but their standard causal (unidirectional) nature cannot use both left and right context, which is crucial for ELF-style denoising. The paper aims to design a model that preserves the efficiency advantages of GDNs while enabling bidirectional context and stability across noise levels.

Method: The authors propose DeltaFlow, a noise-adaptive bidirectional Gated Delta Network backbone for continuous language denoising. Two architectural variants are studied: DeltaFlow-A, which alternates left-to-right and right-to-left recurrent scans across layers, and DeltaFlow-P, which runs forward and backward scans in parallel within each layer. They add noise-adaptive memory control to modulate how hidden states evolve as a function of the noise level and introduce scheduled Temporal State Consistency (TSC) to keep internal representations stable when denoising across nearby noise levels. The model is trained and evaluated as the backbone for an SDE-based language denoiser and compared against full non-causal attention ELF baselines.

Result: On OpenWebText with a 32-step stochastic differential equation sampler, DeltaFlow-P reduces generated perplexity from 24.218 (full-attention ELF baseline) to 21.228 while maintaining similar unigram entropy, despite being trained on 36B tokens versus 45B for the baseline. In a denoiser-only throughput benchmark at sequence length 16k, DeltaFlow-P achieves a 2.72x speedup compared with the full-attention ELF model. These results indicate both better quality (lower perplexity) and significantly higher efficiency (speed and token usage).

Conclusion: DeltaFlow demonstrates that bidirectional, noise-adaptive Gated Delta Networks can serve as an effective and efficient replacement for dense, non-causal attention in continuous language denoising. By enabling bidirectional context, controlling memory based on noise, and stabilizing hidden states across noise levels, DeltaFlow achieves better perplexity and substantially higher throughput than full-attention ELF baselines, making it a promising backbone for scalable, long-context language denoising systems.

Abstract: Embedded Language Flows (ELF) rely primarily on full non-causal attention for iterative denoising, repeatedly incurring quadratic sequence-mixing cost at each sampling step. Gated Delta Networks (GDNs) provide an efficient recurrent alternative, but their standard causal formulation cannot directly capture the bidirectional context required by ELF. We introduce DeltaFlow, a noise-adaptive bidirectional GDN backbone for continuous language denoising. We study two variants: DeltaFlow-A, which alternates scan directions across layers, and DeltaFlow-P, which performs parallel forward and backward scans within each layer. We further introduce noise-adaptive memory control and scheduled Temporal State Consistency (TSC) to stabilize hidden representations across nearby noise levels. On OpenWebText, using a 32-step stochastic differential equation sampler, DeltaFlow-P reduces generated perplexity from 24.218 for the full-attention ELF baseline to 21.228 while maintaining comparable unigram entropy, with 36B training-token exposure compared with 45B for the baseline. In a denoiser-only benchmark, DeltaFlow-P achieves a 2.72x throughput speedup over the full-attention baseline at a sequence length of 16k. These results show that DeltaFlow is a promising alternative to dense attention for efficient continuous language denoising.

</details>


### [68] [RestoreKV: Recovering Full-Cache Behavior Under Aggressive Query-Agnostic KV Cache Eviction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01247)
*Changwoo Baek,Seungjun Shin,Kyeongbo Kong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduce RestoreKV, a query-agnostic KV cache eviction method with learned restoration to mitigate performance degradation under tight KV budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing query-agnostic KV cache eviction methods focus only on selecting which KV pairs to retain, and suffer severe performance collapse when KV budgets are tight. There is a need for a method that can better preserve model performance by not only selecting but also reconstructing lost contextual information within the same memory budget.

Method: RestoreKV augments standard KV eviction by adding a small number of learnable restore tokens that, after context prefill, attend once to the full KV cache using LoRA-adapted attention to generate a compact, context-dependent restore cache. The usual importance scorer and eviction rule are left unchanged. The LoRA adapters are then disabled for all subsequent queries and decoding. The system is trained via parameter-efficient self-distillation from a frozen full-cache teacher model, tuning only about 0.4% of parameters and requiring no task-specific finetuning.

Result: Across four model backbones and four long-context benchmarks, RestoreKV consistently reduces the performance degradation caused by KV compression. For example, on Qwen3-4B with a 5% KV budget, it improves the KVzip score on RULER-4K from 38.2 to 73.2, and it improves 59 out of 60 paired, budget-matched configurations spanning five base eviction methods. When combined with KVzip+ on the KVPress Benchmark, RestoreKV attains 86.4 RULER accuracy at 16× compression, adding under 0.5% one-time cache construction overhead in a 32K-context setup.

Conclusion: RestoreKV demonstrates that complementing selection-based KV eviction with a learned restoration stage can substantially mitigate the performance collapse seen under aggressive KV compression, all while respecting the same overall KV budget and adding minimal runtime overhead. The shared restore mechanism generalizes across contexts and tasks without task-specific tuning, making it a practical, parameter-efficient enhancement for long-context LLM inference.

Abstract: Query-agnostic KV cache eviction compresses a context once and reuses the resulting cache for arbitrary future queries, but performance can collapse under tight budgets. Existing methods primarily improve which original KV pairs are retained. We introduce RestoreKV, which complements this selection-based formulation with learned restoration under the same total KV budget. Our key insight is that, although the information lost through eviction is context-specific, the mechanism for generating its compact complement can be shared across contexts. After context prefill, a few restore tokens attend to the full KV cache in a single LoRA-adapted pass, generating a compact, context-conditioned restore cache. The base importance scorer and eviction rule remain unchanged, and the adapters are disabled for all subsequent queries and decoding. RestoreKV is trained through parameter-efficient self-distillation from the frozen full-cache model, optimizing only $0.4\%$ of the parameters and requiring no task-specific tuning. Across four backbones and four long-context benchmarks, RestoreKV substantially reduces compression-induced degradation. On Qwen3-4B, it improves 59 of 60 paired, budget-matched settings across five base eviction methods; at a $5\%$ budget, it raises KVzip from $38.2$ to $73.2$ on RULER-4K. Applied to KVzip+, RestoreKV reaches $86.4$ RULER accuracy at $16\times$ compression on the KVPress Benchmark, while adding less than $0.5\%$ one-time cache-construction overhead in a 32K-context evaluation. Our project page is available at https://paper.pnu-cvsp.com/RestoreKV/

</details>


### [69] [ACE-GraphRAG: Agentic Context Engineering for Hierarchical GraphRAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01269)
*Yongfeng Huang,Yuren Lai,Ruiying Chen,Haoyu Huang,Mingming Zhao,James Cheng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ACE-GraphRAG is an agentic context-engineering layer for Hierarchical GraphRAG that adaptively builds query- and task-specific contexts using parallel retrieval and policy-based refinement, outperforming fixed GraphRAG and RAG baselines on multi-hop QA and summarization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Hierarchical GraphRAG organizes knowledge at multiple granularities but uses largely fixed rules for constructing the context passed to the generator. This causes a representation–inference gap: rich multi-resolution graph representations are not fully exploited because the same context-construction procedure is used regardless of query type, task, or graph topology. The authors aim to close this gap by making context construction adaptive, query-aware, and task-aware, so that retrieval and aggregation better align with what the current question actually requires.

Method: The authors introduce ACE-GraphRAG, an inference-time context policy layer on top of Hierarchical GraphRAG. They treat context construction as a policy over several choices: (1) gap-aware refinement of an initial context, (2) selecting and combining retrieval branches, and (3) adapting to task and graph topology. A core mechanism, Parallel Differential Retrieval, runs two complementary retrieval branches in parallel: a depth-oriented, factual branch and a breadth-oriented, semantic branch. These branches acquire additional evidence, represented as increments that are merged with the initial context while keeping track of provenance and abstraction level. They define two variants: Full-ACE, which applies a uniform policy within each task family, and Adaptive-ACE, which dynamically selects task- and topology-specific policies per query.

Result: On benchmarks including HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and four UltraDomain subsets, ACE-GraphRAG (Full-ACE) consistently outperforms baseline RAG and GraphRAG systems on both multi-hop question answering and query-focused summarization. Adaptive-ACE further improves performance on multi-hop QA and is preferred to Full-ACE across all four UltraDomain subsets. Additional ablation experiments and analyses over graph topologies indicate that the gains come from the policy-based, adaptive context construction rather than just adding more retrieval.

Conclusion: Context construction in RAG over hierarchical graphs should be viewed and implemented as a query- and task-dependent inference policy, not a fixed retrieval-and-aggregation pipeline. By introducing an agentic policy layer (ACE-GraphRAG) with parallel, differential retrieval and task/topology-aware adaptation, the approach closes part of the representation–inference gap and yields better performance on complex multi-hop QA and summarization tasks.

Abstract: Hierarchical Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) organizes corpus knowledge at multiple levels of granularity, yet fixed context construction may fail to translate these multi-resolution representations into a context suited to the current query. We identify this mismatch as the representation--inference gap. We propose Agentic Context Engineering for Hierarchical GraphRAG (ACE-GraphRAG), an inference-time context policy layer that supplements and adapts the initial context for generation. ACE-GraphRAG formulates context construction as a policy over gap-aware refinement, retrieval branches, and task-conditioned adaptation. Parallel Differential Retrieval acquires supplementary evidence from depth-oriented factual and breadth-oriented semantic branches. These evidence increments are consolidated with the initial context while preserving provenance and abstraction levels. Full-ACE applies the full policy uniformly within each task family, whereas Adaptive-ACE selects task- and topology-specific policies for individual queries. We evaluate ACE-GraphRAG on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and four UltraDomain subsets across multi-hop QA and query-focused summarization. Full-ACE outperforms the evaluated RAG and GraphRAG baselines across both task families, while Adaptive-ACE further improves multi-hop QA and is preferred over Full-ACE on all four UltraDomain subsets. Ablation and topology analyses support treating context construction as a query- and task-dependent inference policy rather than a fixed procedure.

</details>


### [70] [ArabicDialectSafety: A Dialect-Aware Benchmark for Arabic Content Safety Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01291)
*Wajdi Zaghouani,Md. Rafiul Biswas,Kholoud Khalil Aldous,Mabrouka Bessghaier*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces ArabicDialectSafety, a curated dataset and evaluation framework for safety detection across six Arabic dialects, showing that a fine-tuned MARBERTv2 model outperforms frontier LLMs in both binary and fine-grained harm classification, while identifying weaknesses on low-resource Maghrebi dialects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a lack of robust, dialect-aware safety evaluation resources and benchmarks for Arabic, especially for non-standard dialects. Existing safety tools and models, including large language models and Arabic-specialized systems, struggle with dialectal variation and fine-grained harm categories, limiting their reliability for real-world safety-critical applications in the Arabic-speaking world.

Method: The authors construct ArabicDialectSafety, a human-curated dataset of 25,071 Arabic prompts labeled by dialect (MSA, Syrian, Egyptian, Algerian, Palestinian, Moroccan) and seven granular harm categories. They design a dual-task evaluation framework for (1) binary safe/unsafe detection and (2) granular harm classification. They then benchmark seven supervised and generative models, including MARBERTv2 and several frontier LLMs, and analyze how dialect conditioning at different stages (e.g., representation level) impacts performance, with special focus on low-resource Maghrebi dialects. They further evaluate seven frontier LLMs as response generators, measuring unsafe generation rates on harmful dialectal prompts.

Result: Fine-tuned MARBERTv2 achieves the best performance with Macro-F1 of 0.95 on binary safe/unsafe detection and 0.90 on granular harm classification, significantly outperforming prompted frontier LLMs, including Arabic-focused models. Dialect conditioning is most effective when applied at the representation level. Nonetheless, there are notable performance gaps for Maghrebi dialects (Algerian and Moroccan), reflecting their low-resource status. When used as generators, seven frontier LLMs exhibit unsafe generation rates under 5% on harmful dialectal Arabic prompts.

Conclusion: ArabicDialectSafety provides a new, dialect-aware benchmark for Arabic safety evaluation, demonstrating that a fine-tuned encoder model (MARBERTv2) currently surpasses frontier LLMs on both binary and fine-grained harm detection across dialects. However, dialectal disparities—especially for Maghrebi varieties—remain, underscoring the need for more dialect-balanced data and methods. The public release of the dataset and code aims to catalyze further research on robust, dialect-sensitive Arabic safety systems.

Abstract: We present ArabicDialectSafety, a human-curated Arabic safety dataset of 25,071 prompts covering six Arabic varieties: Modern Standard Arabic, Syrian, Egyptian, Algerian, Palestinian, and Moroccan. The dataset is annotated with dialect labels and seven fine-grained harm categories. We introduce a dual-task evaluation framework for binary safe/unsafe detection and granular harm classification across dialects. Benchmarking seven supervised and generative models, we find that fine-tuned MARBERTv2 achieves the strongest performance, with Macro-F1 scores of 0.95 for binary classification and 0.90 for granular classification, substantially outperforming prompted frontier LLMs, including Arabic-specialized models. Our analyses show that dialect conditioning is most effective when integrated at the representation level, while significant performance gaps remain for low-resource Maghrebi dialects. We further evaluate seven frontier LLMs as response generators on harmful dialectal Arabic prompts and observe unsafe generation rates below 5 percent across models. We release the dataset and code upon acceptance to support future research on dialect-aware Arabic safety evaluation. Warning: This paper contains examples of harmful and potentially offensive content included solely for research purposes.

</details>


### [71] [CrossLex: A Source-Grounded Benchmark for Cross-Jurisdictional Legal Reasoning in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01292)
*Xiaocui Yang,Xican Tan,Shoujie Chen,Shihan Xiao,Keke Tong,Xinyu Zhou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CrossLex is a benchmark to test whether LLMs can handle the same legal fact pattern differently across jurisdictions and ground their answers in correct legal sources.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM legal benchmarks mostly test generic legal QA and do not examine whether models understand that identical facts can yield different legal outcomes under different jurisdictions. There is a need for an evaluation suite that explicitly targets cross-jurisdictional legal reasoning and checks grounding in authoritative legal sources.

Method: The authors build CrossLex, a legal-source-grounded benchmark covering 55 aligned legal issues across China, California, and Germany in domains like contract, consumer, criminal, family, and labor law. They construct same-fact scenarios, create jurisdiction-specific questions, answers, and citations, and have legal professionals review all content. They define three tasks: (T1) single-jurisdiction reasoning, (T2) joint cross-jurisdiction comparison, and (T3) fine-grained cross-jurisdiction evaluation. They also introduce the Grounded Joint metric that evaluates both answer correctness and quality of legal-source grounding, and then run multiple LLMs on the benchmark.

Result: CrossLex comprises 6,149 instances organized into 385 fact groups, each with aligned issues and authoritative citations. Experiments on several state-of-the-art LLMs show that while models often reach correct legal conclusions, they frequently fail to provide accurate, jurisdiction-appropriate legal citations, especially in cross-jurisdictional settings.

Conclusion: CrossLex exposes a gap between LLMs’ ability to answer legal questions and their ability to ground those answers in correct, jurisdiction-specific legal sources. The benchmark and the Grounded Joint metric provide a standardized way to evaluate and drive progress on source-grounded, cross-jurisdictional legal reasoning in future research.

Abstract: Legal reasoning is inherently jurisdiction-dependent: the same facts can call for different legal rules and yield different conclusions across legal systems. Yet existing benchmarks rarely evaluate whether large language models (LLMs) can recognize such jurisdiction-specific variation, especially when identical fact patterns lead to divergent legal outcomes.We introduce CrossLex, a same-fact, legal-source-grounded benchmark for evaluating cross-jurisdictional legal reasoning in LLMs across three jurisdictions: China, California, and Germany. Built from authoritative legal sources, CrossLex aligns 55 legal issues spanning contract, consumer, criminal, family, and labor law, and constructs jurisdiction-aligned questions paired with answers and supporting citations. In total, CrossLex contains 6,149 instances organized into 385 fact groups, with all legal issues, answers, and cited authorities reviewed by legal professionals.To disentangle basic legal knowledge from cross-jurisdictional reasoning, CrossLex defines three complementary tasks: single-jurisdiction reasoning (T1), joint cross-jurisdictional comparison (T2), and fine-grained cross-jurisdictional evaluation (T3). We further propose Grounded Joint, a metric that jointly assesses answer correctness and legal-source grounding, and provide a unified evaluation for streamlined benchmarking. Extensive experiments on representative LLMs show that, although current models can often answer legal questions correctly, they struggle to provide accurate cross-jurisdictional legal citations.We hope that CrossLex will facilitate future research on source-grounded cross-jurisdictional legal reasoning.

</details>


### [72] [RH-RAG: Trustworthy Long-Form Generation for Privacy-Constrained Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01311)
*Raj Shekhar Singh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RH-RAG is a privacy-preserving, multi-agent RAG framework using local LLMs to generate long, coherent, and factually grounded documents from internal reports, rivaling proprietary cloud systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Organizations with sensitive internal data often cannot use cloud-based LLM APIs due to privacy and security constraints. While local open-weight models are safer, they struggle with long-form generation: standard RAG pipelines on smaller models lack global planning, lose coherence over long documents, and accumulate factual errors and hallucinations. The paper is motivated by the need for a framework that can: (1) run fully on consumer-grade local hardware, (2) plan and generate long documents coherently, and (3) maintain strong factual grounding and trustworthiness without relying on external cloud services.

Method: The paper proposes RH-RAG, a multi-agent retrieval-augmented generation framework designed for local deployment. It decomposes long-form generation into three coordinated agents: (1) Planner Agent: uses high-level semantic summaries and a dual-level retrieval index to build a global outline for the target document; (2) Writer Agent: generates each section incrementally, guided by the outline and a bounded coherence memory to maintain consistency across sections while fitting within smaller model context limits; (3) Checker Agent: applies natural language inference-based factual verification against retrieved evidence and runs an attestation-driven revision loop to detect hallucinations and trigger targeted rewrites. The system is supported by a dual-level index: a high-level index for planning over summaries and a fine-grained index for detailed, section-level retrieval, enabling efficient operation on consumer-grade hardware.

Result: Across tasks in literary, financial, and legal domains, RH-RAG outperforms both standard flat RAG and hierarchical RAG baselines in factual accuracy, semantic coherence, and overall document-level alignment with the source material. Its reliability approaches that of proprietary cloud-based LLM systems, despite using smaller, locally run models, and it maintains strict data privacy because all computation occurs on local hardware.

Conclusion: RH-RAG demonstrates that a carefully designed multi-agent RAG architecture can overcome many limitations of smaller local models for long-form generation. By separating planning, writing, and checking, and combining this with a dual-level retrieval index, the framework delivers more factual, coherent, and trustworthy long documents while preserving privacy. This suggests that organizations with sensitive data can achieve near cloud-level performance in long-form generation using only local, open-weight models.

Abstract: Generating long-form content from extensive internal reports remains challenging for organizations operating under strict privacy and security constraints, where proprietary cloud-based LLM APIs are often not viable. While locally deployed open-weight models offer a privacy-preserving alternative, existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approaches on smaller models frequently lack effective global planning and accumulate factual inconsistencies over long outputs. To address these limitations, we present RH-RAG, a multi-agent framework for secure and trustworthy long form generation using local language models. RH-RAG decomposes generation into three coordinated stages: a Planner Agent that constructs a global document outline from high-level semantic summaries, a Writer Agent that incrementally generates coherent section-wise content using bounded coherence memory, and a Checker Agent that mitigates hallucinations through natural language inference-based factual verification and an attestation-driven revision loop. The framework further employs a dual-level retrieval index that supports efficient planning and fine-grained contextual generation on consumer-grade hardware. Evaluations across literary, financial, and legal domains demonstrate that RH-RAG consistently improves factual grounding, semantic coherence, and document-level alignment compared to standard and hierarchical RAG baselines, while achieving reliability competitive with proprietary cloud-based systems without compromising data privacy.

</details>


### [73] [BiCAA: Bidirectional Credit Assignment for Search-Augmented Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01321)
*Yibin Huang,Bin Xu,Hailong Cao,Conghui Zhu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes BiCAA, a bidirectional credit assignment framework that provides dense, stepwise rewards for multi-step search agents, improving stability, reducing redundant search, and achieving strong QA performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multi-step search for complex reasoning QA, standard GRPO gives rewards only on final answers, leading to sparse, outcome-only supervision. This causes unstable training and inefficient, redundant search behaviors, because the agent receives no guidance on which intermediate steps are useful or harmful.

Method: The authors introduce process rewards that evaluate each search step according to two criteria: (1) whether it brings in new evidence that helps solve the problem, and (2) whether it constitutes an efficient, pivotal decision in the reasoning trajectory. They then design BiCAA, a bidirectional credit assignment framework that combines two signals: forward solvability gain (how much a step improves answer plausibility) and hindsight success criticality (how necessary a step was for the final success, measured via outcome-based criticality scoring). These two signals are modulated, aggregated, and fused with the final outcome reward to guide policy optimization.

Result: On search-augmented QA benchmarks, BiCAA leads to more stable policy optimization, reduces redundant search behavior, and achieves competitive performance relative to baselines using only outcome rewards.

Conclusion: Incorporating bidirectional process rewards into reinforcement learning for search-augmented QA agents allows finer-grained supervision of intermediate reasoning steps, which stabilizes training, encourages efficient search trajectories, and yields strong overall QA performance.

Abstract: Multi-step search is a fundamental capability for search agents, enabling them to iteratively acquire, refine, and integrate external evidence for complex reasoning QA. However, vanilla GRPO allocates rewards exclusively based on the model's final outputs, yielding outcome-only supervision with no supervisory signals for intermediate reasoning steps. Such sparse supervision easily causes training instability and redundant search behaviors on multi-step search tasks. To mitigate this limitation, we adopt process reward to deliver stepwise supervision signals. For this process reward, we propose two complementary criteria to judge each search step: whether the step yields new evidence to facilitate problem solving, and whether it forms an efficient, pivotal intermediate decision within the overall reasoning trajectory. Building on this insight, we propose BiCAA: a bidirectional credit assignment framework that delivers dense, distinguishing process rewards for search-augmented agents. BiCAA builds bidirectional process rewards by fusing two complementary signals: forward solvability gain and hindsight success criticality. The former quantifies step-wise improvements in answer plausibility, while the latter evaluates each step's necessity for final success via hindsight outcome-based criticality scoring. We modulate and aggregate the two signals and then fuse them with the outcome reward. Experiments on search-augmented QA benchmarks show that BiCAA stabilizes policy optimization, reduces redundant search behavior, and achieves competitive performance.

</details>


### [74] [Can Language Models Identify Shadow Trading Targets? An NLP Evaluation of SEC Enforcement Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01322)
*Sarah Wilson,Michael MacKay,Anthony Marello,Trinav Bhattacharyya*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper tests whether large language models (LLMs) can identify economically linked peer firms ex ante, as required by the SEC’s “shadow trading” theory, and finds little empirical support that LLM-based similarity predicts peer firms’ abnormal returns around M&A announcements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Shadow trading liability assumes insiders can foresee which peer firms will move when MNPI about a related firm is revealed, yet the SEC currently infers those links ex post using surveillance. The authors want to know whether such economic linkages are visible ex ante in mandatory disclosures, and whether modern NLP (especially LLMs) can operationalize this in a systematic, testable way. The answer bears on both the practicality and fairness of enforcing shadow trading and on broader questions about market surveillance and constitutional constraints.

Method: The authors construct a two-stage LLM pipeline to measure semantic similarity between firms based on Item 7 (MD&A) sections from 10‑K filings. They assemble 30 M&A events across five industries, then: (1) use an LLM to embed or interpret MD&A text to score pairwise semantic similarity between the target firm and candidate peers; (2) compute announcement‑day abnormal stock returns for those peers; and (3) test whether similarity ranks correlate with abnormal return ranks within each event. They also conduct a case study of SEC v. Panuwat, checking whether the pipeline recovers Incyte as a top peer of Medivation.

Result: In the Panuwat case, the pipeline does rank Incyte among the closest peers to Medivation, providing a sanity check. However, across the full sample of 30 M&A events and 217 peer observations, semantic similarity shows essentially no relationship with announcement‑day abnormal returns. The pooled within‑event rank correlation is only +0.07 with a non‑significant permutation p‑value of 0.37. The mean per‑event Spearman correlation is +0.05, with a 95% confidence interval of [-0.08, +0.18], which statistically rules out any moderate positive association. Case‑level qualitative review yields mixed evidence: roughly equal numbers of events support or contradict the hypothesized relationship. They also note that Incyte did not fall within the standard mid‑cap range at the relevant time, challenging the SEC’s “mid‑cap oncology” framing.

Conclusion: The study finds that, at least with their LLM pipeline and dataset, publicly available MD&A text does not reliably encode the kind of economic linkages that would allow ex ante identification of shadow‑trading‑relevant peer firms via NLP. This weakens the empirical foundation of the SEC’s shadow trading theory, suggesting that insiders’ ability to identify such peers is not obvious from disclosures and that even sophisticated NLP struggles to replicate it. The results raise concerns about the fairness and constitutional implications of enforcing shadow trading based on ex post inferences from large‑scale financial surveillance.

Abstract: Shadow trading -- trading in a peer firm's securities on the basis of material nonpublic information (MNPI) about an "economically linked" company -- is a novel and contested theory of insider trading liability, first prosecuted in SEC v. Panuwat (2023). Enforcing it requires identifying economically linked firms ex ante, a determination the SEC makes only after the fact using mass market surveillance infrastructure. We ask whether NLP can do what the SEC's theory presumes insiders already know: identify peer firms ex ante from publicly mandated disclosures. Using a two-stage LLM pipeline applied to Item 7 (Management's Discussion and Analysis) sections of SEC 10-K filings, we score semantic similarity across 30 M&A events spanning five industries and relate similarity to announcement-day abnormal stock returns. On the Panuwat fact pattern itself the pipeline recovers Incyte among the closest peers, a sanity check on the one case with a known outcome. Across the full dataset, however, we find no association: pooling 217 peer observations, the within-event rank correlation between similarity and abnormal return is +0.07 (permutation p = 0.37), and the mean per-event Spearman correlation is +0.05 with a 95% confidence interval of [-0.08, +0.18] -- narrow enough to exclude any moderate relationship rather than merely failing to detect one. A case-level reading agrees: 14 of 30 events support the hypothesis, 12 contradict it, and 4 are ambiguous. We also find that Incyte fell outside the standard \$2B-\$10B mid-cap band on the day before the announcement, complicating the "mid-cap oncology" category the SEC invoked. These results are exploratory and bound to this pipeline, corpus, and return measure, but they put pressure on the empirical premise of shadow trading enforcement and bear on constitutional questions surrounding the SEC's financial surveillance infrastructure.

</details>


### [75] [LongChart VQA: A Comprehensive Benchmark for MLLMs with Complex Multi-Chart Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01328)
*Ziyan Xiao,Yinghao Zhu,Wenting Zhang,Heaju Kim,Lequan Yu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces LongChart, a benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models on complex multi-chart reasoning using a latent-graph-based synthesis pipeline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks focus mainly on single-chart perception and only simple relationships between charts, which fail to test the emerging ability of multimodal LLMs to reason across multiple charts, perform multi-step inference, and handle long context windows needed in complex agentic tasks.

Method: The authors design a data synthesis pipeline that uses latent graphs to generate consistent, valid multi-chart scenarios and associated questions. Using this pipeline, they construct LongChart, a visual question answering benchmark in which each VQA set averages 6.5 images (charts) and 31.2 questions. They then evaluate 10 state-of-the-art multimodal LLMs under varying reasoning patterns, with and without auxiliary tools, and under different image perturbations to analyze performance factors.

Result: Across 10 state-of-the-art multimodal LLMs, accuracy drops and becomes more variable as the computational and reasoning complexity of the tasks increases. Performance is also affected by reasoning strategies, use of auxiliary tools, and robustness to image perturbations, though detailed numbers are not provided in the abstract.

Conclusion: LongChart effectively exposes current limitations of multimodal LLMs in complex multi-chart reasoning. The observed accuracy degradation with growing computational complexity underscores the need for improved methods in long-context, multi-step, and multi-chart reasoning, and positions LongChart as a challenging benchmark for future research.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are rapidly evolving with expanded context windows and stronger reasoning capabilities, enabling multi-chart understanding and multi-step inference. These abilities are increasingly important as MLLMs are adopted in complex agentic tasks. However, existing benchmarks largely emphasize single-chart perception, while simple chart-to-chart connections are insufficient to evaluate these capabilities. To capture multi-chart complexity while ensuring consistency and validity, we design a synthesis pipeline supported by latent graphs. Building on this pipeline, we introduce LongChart, a benchmark whose VQA sets contain an average of 6.5 images and 31.2 questions. We evaluate 10 state-of-the-art MLLMs and examine three factors that influence performance: reasoning patterns, auxiliary tools, and robustness to image perturbations. Our results show that MLLM accuracy decreases and varies substantially as computational complexity increases, highlighting directions for future research in multi-chart reasoning.

</details>


### [76] [Prompt-Induced Waste in Large Reasoning Models: A Preregistered Two-Harness Benchmark of Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01347)
*Sarel Weinberger,Amir Hozez*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper empirically studies how different prompt wordings and agent harness designs affect the token cost and success of large reasoning models used as coding agents, finding that many "think more"-style prompts greatly increase cost without improving correctness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As large reasoning models are increasingly used as autonomous coding agents, their operational cost (tokens spent on reasoning, tools, and turns) becomes significant. Practitioners widely use prompting tricks like "think step by step" or "compare several approaches" to improve accuracy, but there is little causal, systematic evidence on how such prompt formulations actually affect cost and success in realistic coding-agent setups. The paper aims to fill this gap with controlled experiments.

Method: The authors design a preregistered benchmark of 24 deterministic coding tasks with hidden evaluators and run them through two real coding-agent harnesses across six large reasoning models. They compare multiple prompt templates (e.g., multi-approach, generic deep-thinking cues, a bounded-efficiency template) and measure reasoning tokens, total cost per successful solution, and correctness. The study includes several phases: screening, stress tests, holdout tasks, replications, and cross-provider comparisons, totaling 4,643 valid runs. They also analyze the impact of harness design, misleading architectural hints, irrelevant prose, and provider-side caching.

Result: Prompt wording significantly affects reasoning cost: asking models to develop and compare several approaches inflates reasoning tokens by 2.4–7.4x without improving correctness; generic “think deeply” cues increase deliberation by 1.6–2.2x; and a bounded-efficiency template that specifies scope, acceptance criteria, and a stop condition is roughly cost-neutral in success rate and can halve reasoning tokens. Harness choice has an even larger impact: the same model-task-prompt triplet is 5–30x more expensive per success under one harness (Claude Code) than another (pi) due mostly to larger static prefixes and more agent turns. Misleading architectural hints prove more harmful and costly than adding irrelevant prose. Provider-side caching lowers billed costs without changing the model’s behavior, showing it should not be conflated with true efficiency gains. Replication on additional models (Kimi-K3, Claude Sonnet 5) confirms the main directions of these effects but highlights model-specific sensitivity to “thinking” and “certainty” cues.

Conclusion: Prompt phrasing and agent harness design have substantial, measurable effects on the computational cost of coding agents, frequently increasing token usage by multiples without improving task success. Instructions that encourage extensive or multi-path reasoning are often wasteful, whereas structured, bounded-efficiency prompts can maintain performance while reducing deliberation. Because harness architecture and provider-level features like caching heavily influence apparent cost, they must be considered when claiming efficiency improvements. The work suggests practitioners should critically evaluate prompt and harness design rather than reflexively adding “think more” style instructions.

Abstract: Large reasoning models used as coding agents incur costs from deliberation, tool calls, and repeated agent turns, yet the causal effect of prompt wording on this spend has not been measured systematically. We present a preregistered benchmark across six large reasoning models, two real agent harnesses, and 24 deterministic coding tasks with hidden evaluators. Across 4,643 valid runs, including screening, stress, holdout, replication, and cross-provider studies, we find that prompt formulation can multiply reasoning cost without improving correctness. Asking the model to develop and compare several approaches is the most consistently wasteful instruction, increasing reasoning tokens by 2.4-7.4x across all models. Generic "think deeply" cues also increase deliberation by 1.6-2.2x, while a bounded-efficiency template specifying scope, acceptance criteria, and a stop condition is cost-neutral and can halve reasoning. Harness choice matters even more: identical model-task-prompt triples cost 5-30x more per success under Claude Code than under pi, mainly because of larger static prefixes and more turns. Misleading architectural hints are far costlier than irrelevant prose, and provider-side caching reduces billed cost without changing behavior, so it must not be treated as efficiency. Replications on Kimi-K3 and Claude Sonnet 5 preserve the main effect directions while revealing model-specific sensitivity to thinking and certainty cues. Overall, prompt wording and harness design materially affect agent cost, often with no gain in task success.

</details>


### [77] [HopRefusalBench: Diagnosing Refusal Failures in Search-Augmented Agents for Multi-Hop Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01358)
*Jianan Xie,Xin Sun,Zhongqi Chen,Xing Zheng,Qiang Liu,Bowen Song*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: HopRefusalBench is a benchmark to study how search-augmented LLM agents handle unanswerable multi-hop questions, revealing that even top models often fail to stop and refuse properly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Search-augmented LLMs can solve many knowledge-intensive tasks, but their behavior on fundamentally unanswerable multi-hop questions is not well understood. Existing abstention benchmarks focus mainly on single-hop or surface-level issues and cannot expose failures that appear only after seemingly correct intermediate reasoning and retrieval. There is a need for a controlled, systematic way to analyze when and how such models should refuse to answer in complex multi-hop search scenarios.

Method: The authors construct HopRefusalBench, a controlled benchmark of 889 unanswerable multi-hop questions derived from KILT-grounded entity paths. They systematically vary three types of unanswerability—answer unknown, false premise, and underspecified context—across three positions in the reasoning chain: root, middle, and terminal. This design allows separate observation of premise verification, intermediate-bridge validation, and terminal stopping. They further define a taxonomy of final outcomes (target-aware refusal, pseudo-refusal, hallucinated completion, search-budget exhaustion) and introduce trajectory-level metrics such as post-trigger continuation and token waste. Ten cutting-edge proprietary and open-weight LLMs are evaluated in search-augmented mode on this benchmark.

Result: The best-performing model achieves only a 42.9% target-aware correct halting rate (TCHR), showing that even frontier models often fail to stop appropriately when questions are unanswerable. Root and middle unanswerability cases are harder than terminal ones, indicating difficulty in early detection of invalid or impossible paths. Models perform best on questions with false premises and worst on underspecified questions. Despite low TCHR, when models do produce explicit refusal-like responses, 84.7–98.4% of them correctly diagnose why the question is unanswerable. Failures typically manifest as hallucinated answers or exhaustion of the search budget instead of clean refusals.

Conclusion: Refusal behavior in multi-hop search is both challenging and insufficiently addressed by current systems. HopRefusalBench exposes that the main bottleneck is not recognizing unanswerability—models often identify the right rationale—but rather committing to a correct non-answer at the right time. The benchmark and associated taxonomy/metrics offer a foundation for more rigorous evaluation and for improving the reliability and safety of search-augmented LLM agents in knowledge-intensive, multi-hop settings.

Abstract: Search-augmented large language model agents are increasingly capable of solving knowledge-intensive tasks, but their behavior when a multi-hop question is fundamentally unanswerable remains poorly understood. Existing abstention benchmarks largely expose defects at the surface of single-hop queries and therefore cannot reveal failures that emerge only after valid intermediate reasoning and retrieval. We introduce HopRefusalBench, the first controlled benchmark of refusal within multi-hop search, comprising 889 unanswerable questions constructed from KILT-grounded entity paths. It crosses three causes of unanswerability (answer unknown, false premise, and underspecified context) with root, middle, and terminal topologies, making premise verification, intermediate-bridge validation, and terminal stopping separately observable. We further propose a final-outcome taxonomy spanning target-aware refusal, pseudo-refusal, hallucinated completion, and search-budget exhaustion, together with source-aware trajectory metrics for post-trigger continuation and token waste. Across ten frontier proprietary and open-weight models in search-augmented mode, the best model achieves a target-aware correct halting rate (TCHR) of only 42.9%. Root and middle items are consistently harder than terminal items, and all models attain their highest TCHR on false premises and their lowest on underspecified questions. Yet when pooled across categories, 84.7--98.4% of each model's explicit refusal-like responses identify the correct rationale, localizing the main bottleneck to committing to an appropriate non-answer; failed trajectories instead diverge into hallucination or search-budget exhaustion. These results establish refusal in multi-hop search as a consequential evaluation problem and provide a foundation for diagnosing and improving the reliability of search-augmented agents.

</details>


### [78] [EviSD: Evidence-Conditioned Self-Distillation for Search-Augmented Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01359)
*Jianan Xie,Xin Sun,Zhongqi Chen,Xing Zheng,Shu Wu,Bowen Song,Liang Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: EviSD introduces an evidence-conditioned self-distillation framework that improves outcome-based RL for search-augmented language agents by providing fine-grained, evidence-aware credit assignment to individual actions, yielding higher QA accuracy with minimal changes to generated tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Outcome-based reinforcement learning for search-augmented language agents can leverage verifiable final answers, but its trajectory-level credit assignment is coarse: it treats all actions in a multi-step search trajectory similarly, failing to identify which specific actions or evidence contributed most to the final correct answer. This leads to suboptimal learning signals for search actions and answer generation. The authors aim to design a method that uses richer supervision (supporting evidence and golden answers) to refine credit assignment at the action level while maintaining the benefits of outcome-based RL and without adding inference-time cost.

Method: The authors propose EviSD, an evidence-conditioned self-distillation framework. It treats instance-level supporting evidence as privileged information for search actions and golden reference answers as privileged information for answer-generation actions. During training, the model plays two roles: (1) a student that samples actions (search and answer tokens) from the original context without privileged information; and (2) a teacher that re-scores these same actions under an action-aligned context augmented with privileged evidence or answers. EviSD then converts the teacher–student score difference into a bounded correction term applied to the GRPO (outcome-based RL) advantage, and this correction is applied only to the spans corresponding to generated actions. This yields localized, evidence-aware guidance while preserving the overall gradient direction specified by the outcome reward, and it avoids auxiliary distillation losses or any modification to inference-time behavior.

Result: On seven question-answering benchmarks and with three different backbone models across scales and generations, EviSD consistently attains the best macro-average Exact Match (EM) scores in all evaluated configurations. It surpasses the strongest competing methods by 1.3–2.3 EM points, while modifying only 6.7%–15.1% of the response tokens, demonstrating that small, targeted adjustments guided by privileged evidence can yield substantial performance gains.

Conclusion: EviSD effectively addresses the coarse trajectory-level credit assignment issue in outcome-based RL for search-augmented language agents by leveraging supporting evidence and golden answers as privileged signals within a self-distillation framework. By translating teacher–student discrepancies into bounded adjustments to outcome-derived advantages, focused only on action tokens, it improves QA performance without extra inference-time cost or additional training objectives. The results indicate that localized, evidence-conditioned guidance can significantly enhance search and answer quality while keeping the majority of the model’s behavior unchanged.
