Abstract: Outcome-based reinforcement learning enables search-augmented language agents to learn from verifiable final answers, but its trajectory-level credit cannot distinguish the contributions of individual actions in a multi-turn search process. We propose EviSD, an evidence-conditioned self-distillation framework that uses instance-level supporting evidence as privileged information for search actions and golden answers as complementary privilege for answer actions. During training, the student samples actions from the original context, while the same model re-scores them as a privileged teacher under an action-aligned context. EviSD converts the detached teacher--student gap into a bounded correction to the outcome-derived GRPO advantage and applies it only to generated action spans. This design localizes privileged guidance while preserving the update direction determined by the outcome reward, without an auxiliary distillation objective or any change at inference time. Across seven question-answering benchmarks and three backbones spanning model scales and generations, EviSD achieves the highest macro-average Exact Match in all evaluated settings, outperforming the strongest compared methods by 1.3--2.3 points while modulating only 6.7%--15.1% of response tokens. Code is available at https://github.com/JiananXie/EviSD.

</details>


### [79] [Language Equality has a Price: A Systematic Investigation of Multi-turn LLM Performance for EU-24+](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01395)
*Sherzod Hakimov,Karl Osswald,Jelle Psurek,Eszter Bukovszky,A. Altar Lüser,David Schlangen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates large language models as goal-directed dialogue agents across 30 languages via self-play games, finding commercial models vastly outperform open-weight ones and that non-English languages remain more costly and lower-performing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To move beyond static, English-centric, or preference-based benchmarks and assess how well LLMs function as interactive agents across many languages using a scalable, language-agnostic evaluation setup.

Method: Use multi-turn, goal-directed dialogue games in self-play as an evaluation paradigm that is reference-free and programmatically scored. Localize only prompts and word lists to support 30 languages, then evaluate nine open-weight and commercial LLMs on their game performance, comparing scores across languages and models.

Result: Commercial LLMs outperform all open-weight models in every one of the 24 official EU languages. Some open-weight models score under 40 points on average across EU-24. Commercial systems remain strongest even in low-web-text languages. Region-specific models (e.g., Chinese-developed) are relatively strong in their home language but still fall short of top US commercial systems. Across models and languages, non-English languages are on median 31% more expensive to run and achieve 10% lower scores than English.

Conclusion: Current open-weight models do not yet provide strong, broad multilingual performance, while commercial models achieve better but still unequal coverage. Linguistic parity is possible but cannot be achieved from public web crawls alone, and even where coverage exists, non-English languages receive worse and more expensive service than English.

Abstract: We evaluate large language models (LLMs) as language agents playing goal-directed dialogue games in self-play across 30 languages: the 24 official EU languages plus six others. Unlike static or preference-based evaluation, this paradigm is multi-turn, reference-free and programmatically scored, and because the game mechanics are language-agnostic it extends to a new language by localising a fixed set of prompt and word-list files. Evaluating nine open-weight and commercial LLMs, we find that no open-weight model covers the EU-24 well: in every official language both commercial systems outscore every open-weight model, and the two weakest average below 40 points across the EU-24. The commercial systems stay ahead even in languages with four orders of magnitude less public web text, showing that linguistic parity is achievable, but not from public crawls alone. A model's home region lifts it without closing the gap: Chinese is the strongest of all 30 languages for two Chinese-developed models, yet the best Chinese score of any model belongs to a US commercial system. Coverage is also not parity of service. Pooled over models and languages, the median non-English language costs 31% more to run than English, and scores 10% lower.

</details>


### [80] [When Retrieval Helps and Distracts: Evaluating Evidence-Generating LLMs for Biomedical Claim Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01409)
*Pritam Deka,Prabhjot Singh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They evaluate and improve biomedical fact-checking systems that must generate high-quality evidence, introducing a new diagnostic metric to understand when retrieval helps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing biomedical fact-checking often only predicts labels (supported/contradicted/not addressed) and lacks high-quality, faithful, and complete evidence generation; the community also lacks a unified benchmark and diagnostic tools to understand retrieval’s true utility across different biomedical sources.

Method: They build CARE-XAI, a unified benchmark combining five biomedical and health fact-checking datasets, and systematically compare multiple system types—base instruction LLMs, retrieval-augmented LLMs with PubMed, fine-tuned LLMs, label-only LLMs, and biomedical encoder-based classifiers—under a shared evaluation protocol. They also introduce Bio-GRACE, a diagnostic metric that normalizes against gold reference evidence to quantify how much benefit retrieved evidence provides for making decisions, and use it to analyze retrieval behavior and utility across sources.

Result: Biomedical encoder classifiers perform best on verdict-only prediction, while fine-tuned LLMs perform best at generating evidence. PubMed-based retrieval helps evidence generation and decision quality for sources closely aligned with PubMed (e.g., PubMedQA, SciFact), but can hurt performance on broader public health claims. Bio-GRACE reveals that the usefulness of retrieval is strongly dependent on the source and that high retrieval recall or high lexical overlap with reference evidence does not necessarily translate into better fact-checking decisions.

Conclusion: Verdict-only models and evidence-generating models have different strengths in biomedical fact-checking, and retrieval should be applied selectively rather than uniformly across tasks and sources. Bio-GRACE provides a more faithful way to evaluate retrieval utility than standard metrics like recall or lexical overlap, highlighting that effective biomedical fact-checking requires nuanced evidence generation and task-aware retrieval strategies.

Abstract: Biomedical fact-checking systems must do more than predict whether a claim is supported, contradicted, or unaddressed: they should also produce evidence that is faithful, complete, and useful for verification. We study this evidence-generation setting on CARE-XAI, a unified benchmark spanning five biomedical and health fact-checking sources. We compare base instruction LLMs, PubMed retrieval-augmented LLMs, fine-tuned LLMs, label-only LLMs, and biomedical encoder classifiers under a shared evaluation protocol. Biomedical classifiers remain strongest for verdict-only prediction, while fine-tuned LLMs are the strongest evidence-generating systems. PubMed retrieval is mixed: it helps PubMed-aligned sources such as PubMedQA and SciFact, but can distract models on broader public-health claims. We introduce Bio-GRACE, a gold-reference-normalized diagnostic for measuring whether retrieved evidence recovers the decision benefit of reference evidence. Bio-GRACE shows that retrieval utility is source-dependent, motivates selective retrieval, and exposes why retrieval recall and lexical evidence overlap are insufficient for biomedical fact-checking.

</details>


### [81] [QR-Erase: Efficient Subspace-Based Machine Unlearning with Layer Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01422)
*Tyler Lizzo,Larry Heck*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: QR-Erase is a fast, SVD-free machine unlearning framework that removes task-specific information from models using pivoted QR decomposition, achieving strong forgetting with minimal loss of other capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Machine unlearning should remove specific knowledge from large models without full retraining, but current methods either harm unrelated capabilities (optimization-based) or require expensive SVD computations (subspace-based). There is a need for an efficient, accurate, and scalable unlearning method suitable for modern foundation models.

Method: The paper proposes QR-Erase, which uses pivoted QR decomposition to estimate task-specific subspaces directly from model parameters and then projects out these components to forget the target task. A variant, Layer-Localized QR-Erase, restricts modifications to layers where task-specific information is most concentrated. Theoretical analysis shows that pivoted QR recovers the important subspace with bounded error and converges to the SVD solution under a spectral gap condition. The approach also exploits low-rank structure and layer localization for further efficiency and effectiveness.

Result: QR-Erase consistently outperforms optimization-based unlearning methods in the tradeoff between forgetting target information and retaining other capabilities, and its performance is within 5% of SVD-based methods across evaluation metrics. Additional gains are obtained by focusing on low-rank and layer-localized structure, e.g., cutting speech forget-set accuracy from 53.1% to 15.7%.

Conclusion: Accurate recovery of task-specific subspaces is sufficient for effective machine unlearning, meaning that full optimal SVD-based reconstruction is unnecessary. Pivoted QR provides a computationally efficient and broadly applicable alternative to SVD for subspace-based unlearning in large foundation models, enabling strong forgetting with limited collateral damage to other tasks.

Abstract: Machine unlearning seeks to remove targeted information from trained models without requiring costly retraining. Existing optimization-based methods often degrade unrelated capabilities, while subspace-based approaches rely on computationally expensive singular value decompositions (SVD). We introduce QR-Erase, a subspace-based framework that uses Pivoted QR decomposition to identify and remove task-specific representations directly from model parameters. We further propose Layer-Localized QR-Erase, which restricts updates to layers containing the highest concentration of task-specific information. We show that Pivoted QR provides accurate subspace recovery with bounded error, and that under a mild spectral gap condition, the recovered subspace approaches the optimal SVD solution. Across task-level, cross-lingual, and speech unlearning, QR-Erase achieves a stronger forgetting-retention tradeoff than optimization-based methods while remaining within 5% of SVD across all metrics. Exploiting low-rank and layer-localized structure further improves forgetting (for example, reducing speech forget-set accuracy from 53.1% to 15.7%). These results demonstrate that accurate subspace recovery, rather than optimal reconstruction, is sufficient for effective unlearning and provides an efficient and general alternative to SVD-based methods for modern foundation models.

</details>


### [82] [PALMs: Using Multi Construct-Grounded Rationales for Modeling Population Preferences in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01458)
*Priyanka Dey,Brihi Joshi,Preyashi Poddar,Jieyu Zhao,Emilio Ferrara*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Population Aligned Language Models (PALMs), LLM variants tuned to reflect the psychological values, beliefs, and cultural norms of specific national populations, achieving better alignment and downstream performance than existing baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard and even culture-specialized LLMs struggle to faithfully represent diverse populations because they mainly learn from surface-level response distributions or simple demographic conditioning, failing to capture deeper, systematic variation in values, beliefs, and cultural norms across groups. This limits the reliability of LLM-based user simulation, personalization, and social reasoning, especially when models are expected to stand in for specific populations in evaluations or applications.

Method: The authors build Population Aligned Language Models (PALMs) for five national populations (USA, India, Brazil, France, Italy). They first synthesize rationales grounded in established psychological and cultural constructs (e.g., personality traits, values, norms, moral foundations). These construct-grounded rationales serve as latent supervision during preference tuning, guiding the model toward responses that reflect the target population’s characteristic patterns rather than just matching survey-like aggregates. They compare this construct-grounded preference learning against demographic prompting and survey-based fine-tuning, and evaluate models across four dimensions—personality, values and beliefs, cultural norms, and morality—plus several downstream tasks (personalized reward modeling, population simulation, and social reasoning) without task-specific tuning.

Result: Across the four alignment dimensions, PALMs consistently outperform all baselines, including existing culture-specialized models, with an average 8.59% relative improvement over the best baseline across the five populations. The construct-grounded rationale approach yields better population alignment than both demographic prompting and direct survey-response fine-tuning, indicating richer inductive bias from psychological and cultural constructs. On downstream tasks without task-specific supervision, PALMs beat the best baselines by 5.19% in personalized reward modeling and 6.34% in population simulation, and transfer well to social reasoning benchmarks.

Conclusion: Grounding preference tuning in psychological and cultural constructs and using synthesized rationales as latent supervision produces LLMs that more faithfully reflect specific populations than methods based only on demographics or survey distributions. These Population Aligned Language Models offer a stronger, more generalizable representation of population-specific values, beliefs, norms, and morality, leading to improved performance in user simulation, personalization, and social reasoning tasks. The released models, datasets, and code provide a framework for building better population-aligned LLMs for other groups and applications.

Abstract: Large language models are being extensively used to simulate individual user behavior, yet faithfully representing a population requires capturing the systematic variation in values, beliefs, and cultural norms that distinguish one group from another. We introduce Population Aligned Language Models (PALMs), a suite of models each aligned to specific populations, covering five countries: USA, India, Brazil, France and Italy. PALMs are created by synthesizing rationales grounded in psychological and cultural constructs and using these as latent supervision during preference tuning for population-specific alignment. Evaluated across four dimensions: personality, values and beliefs, cultural norms, and morality, PALMs consistently outperform baselines, including culture-specialized models, achieving an average of 8.59% relative improvement over the best baseline across all five populations. Notably, construct-grounded rationales outperform both demographic prompting and survey-based fine-tuning, suggesting that grounding preference learning in psychology and culture provides a richer inductive signal than surface-level response distributions. We further demonstrate strong generalization to downstream applications with- out task-specific supervision: outperforming best baselines by 5.19% in personalized reward modeling, 6.34% in population simulation, and showing strong transfer to social reasoning tasks. Datasets and code are available at: https://github.com/limenlp/PALMs.

</details>


### [83] [Retrieval Augmented Biomedical Question Answering with Weak Question Recovery and Neural Reranking for BioASQ Task 14b](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01468)
*Xueying Zhao,Lee Mai,Balaji Anandganesh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They built a robust biomedical QA pipeline for BioASQ that improves retrieval and answer quality using advanced ranking, recovery for hard questions, and cleanup/validation steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Biomedical question answering depends heavily on finding and ranking relevant PubMed documents, but many questions, especially difficult ones, suffer from weak retrieval, poor ranking, and noisy snippets, which hurt answer generation and competition performance.

Method: They design a multi-stage QA pipeline: (1) retrieve documents from PubMed; (2) apply fine-tuned MiniLM-based semantic reranking, Reciprocal Rank Fusion, and feature-based relevance scoring to reorder documents; (3) detect weak or difficult questions and trigger a "weak-question recovery" strategy that uses semantic query expansion, relationship-aware augmentation, and selective merging of additional retrieval results; (4) perform post-retrieval pruning to remove redundant or low-relevance snippets while still keeping enough evidence; and (5) use OpenBioLLM for answer generation, followed by output validation and post-processing for consistent, submission-ready outputs across BioASQ phases.

Result: On BioASQ evaluation batches, the pipeline’s recovery and cleanup components significantly improve retrieval robustness and MAP@10, particularly on difficult questions with initially poor retrieval performance.

Conclusion: A carefully engineered biomedical QA pipeline that couples advanced retrieval/reranking with targeted recovery for hard queries, evidence pruning, and LLM-based answer generation yields more robust performance and better ranked results for BioASQ tasks, while validation/post-processing improve reliability in competition settings.

Abstract: This work presents DS@GT ARC BioASQ team's work for a biomedical question answering pipeline, integrating multi-source query expansion, neural reranking, retrieval refinement, and OpenBioLLM-assisted answer generation. The system combines PubMed retrieval with fine-tuned MiniLM-based semantic reranking, Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), and feature-based relevance scoring to improve document ranking quality. To address challenging queries with weak retrieval performance, we introduce a conditional weak-question recovery strategy that applies semantic expansion, relationship-aware augmentation, and selective result merging. A post-retrieval pruning stage further removes redundant or low-relevance snippets while preserving evidence coverage for downstream answer generation. Experimental results on BioASQ evaluation batches demonstrate that the proposed recovery and cleanup strategies substantially improve retrieval robustness and MAP@10 performance on difficult question sets. The final system also incorporates output validation and post-processing steps to ensure formatting consistency and submission reliability across BioASQ phases.

</details>


### [84] [Two-Stage Bengali Sentiment Classification: Domain Adaptation Through Continual Learning and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01471)
*MD Shaikh Rahman,Syed Maudud E Rabbi,Muhammad Mahbubur Rashid*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose SentiBanglaBERT, a Bengali sentiment analysis framework that adapts to news data efficiently and offers interpretable predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sentiment analysis in Bengali is hard due to its low-resource status, lack of domain-specific data (e.g., news), and morphological complexity, which existing models don’t fully exploit or explain.

Method: They use a two-stage framework: (1) domain-adaptive continual pretraining of a Bengali language model on news-style data, and (2) parameter-efficient fine-tuning via LoRA for sentiment classification, plus SHAP-based analysis to interpret which linguistic/morphological features drive predictions.

Result: Experiments show that SentiBanglaBERT achieves performance on par with strong baselines, while also providing more stable results and richer interpretability through SHAP analyses of morphological cues.

Conclusion: Domain-adaptive continual pretraining combined with efficient fine-tuning and SHAP interpretability is an effective, resource-efficient strategy for sentiment analysis in morphologically rich, low-resource languages like Bengali.

Abstract: Understanding sentiment in low-resource languages remains a key challenge for Natural Language Processing (NLP), particularly when domain-specific data is scarce. In this work, we present SentiBanglaBERT, a two-stage Bengali sentiment classification framework combining domain-adaptive continual pretraining and parameter-efficient fine-tuning. The approach enables contextual adaptation to news-style data while remaining computationally efficient through Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). Beyond performance, SentiBanglaBERT integrates SHAP-based interpretability, offering linguistic insights into how Bengali morphological cues, such as negation suffixes and aspectual markers, influence sentiment predictions. Experiments demonstrate stable performance comparable to strong baselines while providing greater transparency and interpretive depth. This framework highlights the potential of domain-adaptive continual learning as a foundation for interpretable, resource-efficient NLP in morphologically rich, underrepresented languages.

</details>


### [85] [Discriminative Axis, Not Data Volume: What a Contrastive Corpus Teaches an Audio Embedding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01560)
*Abdul Basit Tonmoy*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Corpus size alone doesn’t ensure a contrastive multimodal audio embedding will learn desired attributes; corpus structure determines which attributes are encoded.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In contrastive representation learning for multimodal audio-text models, practitioners usually scale the dataset when important attributes (e.g., emotion, lexical content) are missing from the learned embeddings. However, it is unclear whether simply increasing corpus size is sufficient for the model to encode specific attributes like prosody or emotion, or whether other factors such as dataset structure and negative-sample separability play a more critical role.

Method: The authors start from a frozen-base multimodal embedding model and add a lexical-speech fine-tuning round, then evaluate its impact on two tasks: zero-shot keyword spotting and speech-emotion recognition. They compare several training settings: (1) lexical-speech round alone, (2) fine-tuning on a small, prosody-controlled corpus where sentence content is fixed but prosody varies, and (3) exposure-matched fine-tuning on a mined corpus whose captions explicitly name emotions but vary in scene content. They analyze how each setup affects performance on keyword spotting and emotion recognition, and conduct controlled interventions on caption similarity and caption diversity to test causal effects of corpus structure on the learned representations.

Result: Adding the lexical-speech round dramatically improves zero-shot keyword spotting performance (by 76 points) but substantially harms speech-emotion recognition (by 14 points). Fine-tuning on a small prosody-controlled corpus of 7,442 clips not only recovers the lost emotion performance but surpasses the pre-speech level, at the cost of about five points in keyword accuracy. In contrast, fine-tuning on 29,428 mined clips with captions that explicitly mention emotions, under matched exposure, produces a negligible change in emotion performance (-0.0007). Intervention experiments show that simply increasing caption similarity does not restore emotion encoding. However, collapsing caption diversity so that emotion becomes the only axis along which in-batch samples can be separated recovers emotion by 8.9 points across three random seeds, with a smaller but consistent gain on a non-acted corpus, while keyword performance degrades correspondingly.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates that for contrastive audio-text embeddings, corpus structure—specifically, how in-batch negatives can be separated—determines which attributes are encoded, more than corpus size or the explicit presence of relevant vocabulary in captions. An attribute like emotion or prosody is learned only when it is necessary to distinguish samples within the contrastive objective, such as when sentence content is held constant and prosody is the primary differentiating factor. Simply scaling the dataset or adding emotion words to captions without controlling structural separability is insufficient. Therefore, effective representation learning for specific audio attributes requires designing datasets where those attributes are the critical separating signals among training examples.

Abstract: Scaling the corpus is the default remedy when a contrastive representation lacks an attribute. We report a case where it does nothing, and identify what does: adding a lexical-speech round to a frozen-base multimodal embedding model raises zero-shot keyword spotting by 76 points while reducing speech-emotion recognition by 14. The loss is not a capacity limit: fine-tuning on 7,442 clips from a prosody-controlled corpus recovers emotion past its pre-speech level at a five-point keyword cost. Nor is it data volume: 29,428 mined clips whose captions explicitly name emotions, at matched exposure, move emotion by -0.0007. The difference is structural: a contrastive objective encodes an attribute only when the in-batch negatives cannot be separated without it; the controlled corpus holds sentence content fixed, so prosody is the only separating signal, whereas mined captions name emotion yet remain separable by scene content. Intervention on the same audio confirms causality: raising caption similarity does not recover emotion, but collapsing caption diversity so that emotion becomes the only separating axis recovers it by 8.9 points across three seeds, with a smaller, same-signed gain on a non-acted corpus, while keyword accuracy trades back. Corpus structure, not size or caption vocabulary, controls what a contrastive audio embedding encodes.

</details>


### [86] [DocNavRAG: Document-Structured Graph RAG with Stateful Evidence Construction for Complex Document Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01565)
*Dongyang Xie,Yao Tian,Hao Zhang,Yifei Yuan,Tieyun Qian,Ming Zhong,Jiawei Jiang,Yuanyuan Zhu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DocNavRAG is a retrieval-augmented generation framework that lets an agent navigate a structured graph of document hierarchies and cross-document links to gather sufficient evidence for complex QA, outperforming strong baselines in answer quality and context sufficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RAG approaches struggle with complex questions over large, long, or multiple documents because they either rely on repeated ad hoc search (agentic RAG over weak interfaces) or on rigid, fixed graph traversals (GraphRAG). These limitations make it hard to systematically assemble complementary evidence from different sections or documents, leading to incomplete or low-quality answers in long- and multi-document QA tasks.

Method: The paper proposes DocNavRAG, which first represents documents as hierarchies (e.g., document → sections → passages) and augments these with cross-region relations to form a navigable graph across and within documents. It then exposes explicit graph operations—such as locate, navigate, expand, and fetch—that an agent can use step-by-step instead of repeatedly searching from scratch. During this process, DocNavRAG maintains an evolving evidence state that tracks what has been found so far and uses it to guide subsequent navigation and retrieval until there is enough evidence to answer the question.

Result: On four benchmarks targeting long- and multi-document question answering, DocNavRAG achieves higher answer quality and better context sufficiency compared to strong RAG baselines, with average improvements of 7.8% in answer quality and 17.7% in context sufficiency over the strongest competing system.

Conclusion: By turning document structure and inter-document relations into an explicit navigable graph and coupling it with agent-style operations and an evolving evidence state, DocNavRAG enables more targeted, cumulative evidence gathering for complex QA. This structured navigation approach offers a more effective alternative to both fixed graph traversals and unstructured agentic search, leading to substantially better answers and more adequate supporting context on challenging long- and multi-document benchmarks.

Abstract: Answering complex questions over large document collections requires assembling complementary evidence across sections and documents. GraphRAG offers structured retrieval but typically uses fixed traversal, while agentic RAG operates over weakly structured interfaces. Our key insight is that agents should navigate document structure within and across documents rather than repeatedly search from scratch. We introduce DocNavRAG, which organizes document hierarchies and cross-region relations into a navigable graph, exposes graph operations for locating, navigating, expanding, and fetching, and maintains an evolving evidence state to guide retrieval until sufficient evidence is collected. Across four long- and multi-document QA benchmarks, DocNavRAG improves answer quality and context sufficiency over the strongest baseline by 7.8\% and 17.7\% on average.

</details>


### [87] [Characterizing Treatment-Context Medication Evidence Across Clinic Notes and Structured EHR Medication History](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01570)
*Mingyang Jiang,Congning Ni,Weixin Liu,Zhijun Yin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates why medication information in clinical notes often disagrees with structured EHR medication records, and shows that much of the mismatch is due to normalization, terminology, and timing differences rather than true contradictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical notes and structured EHR medication tables should, in principle, reflect the same patient treatments, but they frequently disagree at the level of recorded medications. This discordance complicates research, quality measurement, and clinical decision support that rely on accurate medication data. There is a need to understand and reduce these discrepancies by improving how free-text notes are converted into normalized medication representations and how they are compared with structured records.

Method: The authors propose a note-grounded pipeline that constructs high-quality medication references from clinical notes using large language model (LLM) assistance, together with targeted and random human review for validation. They apply deterministic medication normalization, including lexical cleanup and curated alias mappings, to convert text mentions into canonical medication labels. They then perform semantic and temporal comparisons of these normalized note-derived medications with the structured EHR medication history, and evaluate normalization performance on a patient-level held-out test set to avoid overfitting to the cohort.

Result: On 5,403 held-out medication mention rows, exact canonical agreement between mentions and reference standards increased from 0.7226 with naive surface-exact matching to 0.8429 after applying lexical cleanup and curated alias mappings. In a random audit of previously unaudited data, canonical-label agreement for valid medication mentions reached 0.9210, but accurate attribution of treatment actions (e.g., prescribing vs. other contexts) was lower at 0.5326. In the full-cohort comparison of notes vs. structured EHR, only 16.44% of note-derived medication rows had exact same-visit overlap with structured data, whereas 55.17% had same-visit semantic overlap and 90.34% had overlap within the same visit or within ±30 days. After broad project-level mapping, only 3.97% of note-derived rows had no structured overlap. An ontology-based sensitivity analysis using OMOP showed that strict no-overlap on the held-out set decreased from 43.99% to 36.68% after incorporating a development-derived alias supplement.

Conclusion: A large fraction of apparent mismatches between medications documented in clinical notes and those in structured EHR tables is attributable to normalization issues, terminology variations, and timing differences rather than genuine inconsistencies. Using an LLM-assisted, ontology- and alias-augmented normalization pipeline significantly improves agreement and reveals that truly unmatched medications are far fewer than suggested by naive comparisons. This has implications for more reliable use of EHR data in research and clinical applications.

Abstract: Clinic notes and structured electronic health record (EHR) medication history often contain different medication information. Same-visit disagreement between these sources may result from note-side normalization errors, differences in terminology or timing, or actual differences in documentation. We developed a note-grounded approach that uses large language model (LLM) assisted reference construction, targeted and random human review, deterministic medication normalization, and semantic and temporal comparisons with structured medication history. We evaluated all normalization results on a patient-level held-out test set to limit adaptation to the study cohort. On 5,403 held-out mention rows, exact canonical agreement improved from 0.7226 with surface-exact matching to 0.8429 after lexical cleanup and curated alias mapping. In a random audit of previously unaudited rows, canonical-label agreement was 0.9210 among evaluable valid medication mentions, whereas treatment-action attribution was lower at 0.5326. In the full-cohort characterization analysis, only 16.44% of note-derived rows had same-visit exact overlap with structured medication history, but 55.17% had same-visit semantic overlap, 90.34% had same-visit or +/-30-day overlap, and only 3.97% remained in the strict no-structured-overlap bucket under broad project-level mapping. An ontology-backed sensitivity analysis further showed that held-out strict Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP)-backed no-overlap fell from 43.99% to 36.68% after a development-derived alias supplement. These results show that note-to-structured-medication mismatch can arise from normalization errors, differences in terminology, and differences in documentation timing.

</details>


### [88] [Semantic Alignment of AI Models: Concept Collapse, Checkpoint Dynamics, and Cross-Lingual Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01585)
*Tyler Ashoff,Jordan Rodu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes using topological methods to compare language model embedding spaces with interpretable structures like ontologies and knowledge graphs, enabling richer benchmarks of semantic understanding and cross-lingual phrase comprehension.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Benchmarking language models is hard because typical outcome-based tests don’t directly assess how models conceptualize language, open-source benchmarks quickly saturate, and many benchmarks leak into training data. There is a need to go beyond pure output evaluation and understand the internal semantic structure of models to see how they relate and organize abstract concepts, including across languages.

Method: The authors apply topological analysis techniques to high-dimensional embedding spaces of language models. They rigorously compare these spaces to low-dimensional, interpretable baselines such as ontologies and curated knowledge graphs, effectively building multi-modal alignment tests between model embeddings and structured human knowledge representations.

Result: They show that topological methods can successfully align and compare language model embedding spaces with ontologies and knowledge graphs, yielding interpretable measures of how well a model’s semantic organization matches these baselines and enabling tracking of model adaptations over time and across languages.

Conclusion: Topological, multi-modal alignment methods provide a principled way to benchmark language models beyond traditional outcome reasoning, enabling more interpretable analysis of semantic structure, better tracking of model evolution, and more robust testing of phrase understanding in multiple languages.

Abstract: Language model benchmarking is a difficult task. Outcome reasoning alone does not test the model's conceptualization of language and popular open-source benchmarks are quickly saturated or ingested as training data. It is important to test the model's output, but augmenting these tests by characterizing semantic structure gives more insight to how models relate abstract concepts. However, the high dimensional embedding spaces are not easy to interpret. This work demonstrates how topological methods can be used to rigorously compare these spaces to low dimensional and interpretable baselines like ontologies and curated knowledge graphs. These multi-modal alignment tests make it possible to track model adaptations and test phrase understanding across multiple languages.

</details>


### [89] [PICTURE: Enhancing Theory-of-Mind in Large Language Models by Revealing, Not Hiding, Characters' Lack of Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01598)
*Eojin Jeon,SangKeun Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes PICTURE, a prompting method that lets LLMs perform Theory of Mind reasoning using free-form explanations instead of rigid event-hiding formats, and shows it improves performance on false-belief tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing NLP approaches to Theory of Mind typically rely on event hiding (removing events unknown to a character) before question answering. While this perspective-taking step helps model what each character knows, it requires strict, structured outputs, which cause performance degradation and limit practicality. The authors are motivated to find a more flexible, free-form way for LLMs to do perspective-taking without explicitly hiding events, while still preventing the model from using information that characters should not know.

Method: The authors first analyze why event-hiding-based methods degrade performance, focusing on their rigid output format. They then hypothesize that LLMs can internally inhibit use of unknown events if the character’s lack of knowledge is stated explicitly in the reasoning process. Based on this, they design PICTURE, a prompting strategy that guides LLMs to produce free-form Chain-of-Thought explanations that explicitly mention what a character does not know. They empirically validate the hypothesis and evaluate PICTURE on Theory of Mind false-belief tasks, comparing it to existing prompting baselines.

Result: Experiments on false-belief Theory of Mind benchmarks show that making lack-of-knowledge explicit allows LLMs to avoid relying on hidden events, even when those events are present in the context. The PICTURE prompting method achieves an average improvement of 7.3% over existing prompting methods on these tasks, demonstrating more accurate character-belief reasoning without requiring structured event-hiding outputs.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that explicit representation of a character’s ignorance within free-form Chain-of-Thought is sufficient for LLMs to inhibit use of inaccessible events, removing the need for rigid event-hiding steps. PICTURE provides a practical, higher-performing prompting method for Theory of Mind reasoning, and highlights that controlling how knowledge and ignorance are verbalized in prompts can substantially improve LLM ToM performance.

Abstract: Simulating human-like Theory of Mind (ToM) has been a longstanding problem in natural language processing (NLP). To address this, existing works introduce a reasoning step of event hiding (a.k.a. perspective-taking), where events unknown to a character are removed before question answering. However, resorting to event hiding for ToM reasoning presents a performance degradation issue due to the strict output format constraints involved in event hiding. To mitigate this issue, we propose generating perspective-taking outputs as free-form explanations without event hiding, but this poses a notable yet underexplored challenge: LLMs need to inhibit responses to events unknown to characters, because the absence of event hiding exposes LLMs to these events throughout reasoning. To address this challenge, we hypothesize and empirically verify that LLMs can achieve such inhibition if a character's lack of knowledge about events is made explicit during reasoning. Based on this finding, we introduce PICTURE, a new prompting method that enables LLMs to generate a character's lack of knowledge within free-form Chain-of-Thought (CoT). Experimental results show that PICTURE outperforms existing prompting methods by an average of 7.3% on false-belief tasks.

</details>


### [90] [Not the Dimension, the Norm: What Matters in Gradient-Free Weight Perturbation of Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01624)
*Taeyeong Kim,Ahhyun Kim,TaeHyeon Kim,Unggi Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates what aspects of random weight perturbations matter for gradient-free adaptation of language models and finds that the key factor is the overall perturbation norm, not which weights or subspace are perturbed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gradient-free adaptation methods for language models currently perturb all weights, which is inefficient compared to parameter-efficient fine-tuning approaches that only modify a small number of parameters. It is unclear whether full-weight perturbation is actually necessary and which properties of perturbations drive performance, because prior work changed multiple factors at once (search space, scale, aggregation), obscuring causal effects.

Method: The authors use a controlled experimental pipeline for gradient-free adaptation where they hold fixed how candidate perturbations are scored and aggregated, and systematically vary only one factor at a time: (1) the dimensionality of the search (number of perturbed parameters), (2) the choice of subspace/basis in which perturbations are applied (e.g., SVD frame vs random frame), and (3) the perturbation norm/scale. They compare performance of full-weight search against low-dimensional perturbations (12–16 scalars) across 49 combinations of models and benchmarks, and analyze how different bases and scales affect outcomes, including comparisons based on Grassmann overlap between subspaces.

Result: They find that perturbing only a small frozen frame of 12–16 scalars performs close but consistently worse than full-weight search, lagging by an average of 1.8 accuracy points and losing in 36 out of 49 model-benchmark cells. Performance is not meaningfully explained by the search dimension or by the specific choice of basis: even a random frame with only chance-level overlap with an SVD-based frame performs similarly, as long as a single global scale factor is matched. At large perturbation scales, directions derived from SVD degrade first (“collapse”) while random directions remain viable. Across seven different models, the usable range of perturbation norms is tight, varying by less than a factor of five, and performance is relatively flat within this safe range.

Conclusion: The decisive factor for gradient-free adaptation performance is the perturbation norm (how strongly weights are perturbed), not which particular subspace or basis is used. There exists a relatively small, model-agnostic safe range of perturbation norms that transfers across scales and model families. This reframes the design problem for gradient-free methods: instead of carefully choosing which subset of weights or subspace to perturb, practitioners should focus on calibrating the perturbation magnitude—"how hard to shake" the model—since that is where real failure modes arise.

Abstract: Adapting a language model to a task no longer requires training all of its weights, and a line of parameter-efficient methods has driven the trainable count from billions down to a handful of scalars. Gradient-free adaptation, which samples random weight perturbations and keeps the ones that score well, has not followed that trajectory and still perturbs every entry of the weight tensor. It is unknown whether that full-weight search is necessary, and more fundamentally which property of a perturbation makes it work at all, because existing methods vary the search space, the perturbation scale, and the aggregation together. We resolve this by intervening on one factor at a time inside a fixed pipeline, holding candidate scoring and voting constant while we vary the search dimension, the subspace that carries the perturbation, and its norm. Perturbing a frozen frame of 12 to 16 scalars stays 1.8 accuracy points behind full-weight search on average across 49 model-benchmark cells, trailing it in 36 of them. Neither the dimension nor the choice of basis explains that performance. A random frame whose Grassmann overlap with the SVD frame is at chance level performs identically once a single scale factor is matched, and at large scales the SVD directions collapse first. What survives is the perturbation norm, whose usable range closes within a factor of five across seven models and stays flat inside. The perturbation norm is therefore the one factor with a failure mode, and its safe region transfers across scale and family. The design question narrows from which subspace to perturb to how hard to shake.

</details>


### [91] [Human-LLM Alignment in Language Attitudes Toward Non-Native Japanese](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01629)
*Naho Orita,Hayato Ogawa,Daisuke Kawahara*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper compares how humans and large language models (LLMs) evaluate native (L1) vs. non‑native (L2) Japanese emails, finding that LLMs partially replicate human biases but with some important differences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used to evaluate human writing in consequential settings like hiring and academic assessment, there is concern that they may replicate or even amplify biases against non‑native speakers. Existing work focuses mostly on English and often lacks a principled framework to quantify such attitudes. This paper is motivated by the need to systematically measure whether, and how, LLMs inherit native speakers’ language attitudes toward L2 writers, specifically in Japanese, and to provide a general framework for auditing these biases across languages.

Method: The authors draw on the language attitudes framework, which distinguishes dimensions such as fluency, status, and solidarity. They compile parallel sets of Japanese emails written by native (L1) and non‑native (L2) speakers. Human Japanese raters evaluate these texts along the three dimensions, producing baseline measures of native speaker attitudes. Then, six different LLMs are tasked with judging the same texts on the same dimensions. The authors compare the size and structure of the L1–L2 gaps in human vs. LLM ratings, and analyze where the models align with or diverge from human patterns, including sensitivity to learners’ L1 backgrounds.

Result: Human Japanese raters rated L2 emails significantly lower than L1 emails on fluency, status, and solidarity, with the fluency gap being about twice as large as the gaps in status and solidarity. The six LLM judges replicated the direction of this bias (L2 < L1) and, in five cases, also replicated the ordering of gaps across dimensions (largest in fluency, smaller in status and solidarity). However, LLMs differed in two notable ways: they consistently underestimated the solidarity gap, which is the most socially grounded dimension, and they showed differential evaluations based on learners’ L1 backgrounds, even though human raters did not differentiate in this way.

Conclusion: LLMs inherit native speakers’ language attitudes toward non‑native writing in a structured but attenuated form: they reproduce the direction and relative structure of human biases but with reduced magnitude on socially grounded dimensions like solidarity and with additional, model‑specific differentiation across learner L1 backgrounds. The study demonstrates that the language attitudes framework is an effective, ready‑made tool for auditing LLM biases across languages beyond English, and highlights the need for careful evaluation and mitigation when LLMs are used as judges in high‑stakes contexts involving L2 writers.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly evaluate human writing in high-stakes domains such as hiring and academic assessment, putting non-native speakers at particular risk. Drawing on the language attitudes framework, we compared human and LLM evaluations of parallel L1- and L2-written Japanese emails on three dimensions: fluency, status, and solidarity. Japanese raters rated L2 texts significantly lower on all three dimensions, with a fluency gap roughly twice the size of the status and solidarity gaps. Six LLM judges reproduced the direction of this bias, and five reproduced its ordering across dimensions. The models diverged from humans in two ways: all understated the solidarity gap, the most socially grounded dimension, and all differentiated among learner L1 backgrounds where humans did not. LLM judges thus reproduce native speakers' language attitudes in a structured yet attenuated form, and the language attitudes framework offers a ready-made yardstick for auditing them beyond English.

</details>


### [92] [RING: Retrieval-Internalized Generation for Continual Large-Scale Knowledge Injection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01630)
*Shicheng Xu,Liang Pang,Liyi Chen,Zihao Wei,Jingcheng Deng,Yan Gao,Yi Wu,Yao Hu,Huawei Shen,Xueqi Cheng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RING is a training and architectural framework that internalizes retrieval into an LLM via a Mixture-of-Memory Experts, learning to search its own parametric memory instead of using an external retriever, achieving RAG-level or better performance with lower serving complexity and latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves factuality by accessing external documents at inference, but this adds latency, infrastructure complexity, and dependence on an explicit retriever. Existing methods that inject knowledge into model parameters still typically rely on fixed or rule-based retrieval components. There is a need for a system that can (1) absorb large-scale, genuinely new knowledge into an LLM after pretraining, (2) retrieve over this knowledge efficiently without external search at serving time, and (3) learn the retrieval policy directly from downstream task signals rather than hand-designed heuristics, while matching or beating RAG on accuracy and efficiency.

Method: RING introduces a Mixture-of-Memory Experts architecture where a dedicated Knowledge Expert stores newly injected information. Training has three stages: (1) Continued pre-training with Dual Causal Attention to inject and organize new corpora into the Knowledge Expert’s parameters and attention patterns. (2) Supervised fine-tuning to instill an explicit "search-then-answer" behavior, teaching the model how to route queries through its parametric memory before generating answers. (3) Reinforcement learning with hierarchical rewards to optimize the routing and search policy over internal memory, so the model learns which memory experts to consult and how to attend to them, directly from task performance. The authors also provide a theoretical view of RING as a search-free approximation to the standard RAG objective, and they build a new benchmark, News-2025, composed of news articles that post-date the base LLM’s pretraining cutoff to evaluate true post-hoc knowledge injection without leakage.

Result: On the News-2025 benchmark and other evaluations, RING achieves accuracy that matches or surpasses both (a) traditional search-based RAG systems and (b) prior parametric knowledge-injection baselines. At the same time, it reduces inference-time latency and engineering overhead by eliminating the need for an external retriever, instead relying on learned parametric search over internal memory experts. Empirical results indicate that RING can successfully internalize large-scale new knowledge and leverage it via its learned retrieval policy.

Conclusion: RING demonstrates that retrieval-like behavior can be internalized into an LLM through a Mixture-of-Memory Experts architecture and a three-stage training pipeline, obviating external retrievers at inference. By learning a retrieval policy via reinforcement learning and structuring attention with Dual Causal Attention, the model can approximate classical RAG behavior in a purely parametric, search-free way. The framework effectively injects and utilizes new, post-training knowledge while matching or outperforming RAG and other baselines on both accuracy and efficiency, suggesting a promising direction for low-latency, knowledge-rich language models without external retrieval infrastructure.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves factuality but adds latency and engineering overhead at serving time. We propose RING (Retrieval-Internalized Generation), a holistic paradigm spanning both architecture and training that injects large-scale external knowledge into a \textit{Mixture-of-Memory Experts} and learns parametric search over this internal memory via reinforcement learning, removing the external retriever entirely. Training proceeds in three stages: continued pre-training injects new corpora into a Knowledge Expert via our novel \textit{Dual Causal Attention}; supervised fine-tuning teaches a ``search-then-answer'' pattern; and reinforcement learning with hierarchical rewards optimizes the routing-and-search policy over the parametric memory. Unlike prior parametric injection methods that pair internal memory with a fixed or rule-based retriever, RING {learns} its retrieval policy directly from task signals. We further frame RING theoretically as a search-free approximation to the classical RAG objective. To evaluate large-scale injection of genuinely {new} knowledge without test-time leakage, we further construct News-2025, a benchmark built from news strictly post-dating the base LLM's pretraining cutoff. RING matches or surpasses both search-based RAG and parametric injection baselines in accuracy and efficiency.

</details>


### [93] [Does Accuracy Equal Evidence? Reasoning Faithfulness under KV Cache Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01631)
*Mengting Ai,Jingrui He,Yue Guo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that KV cache compression can keep a model’s final answers correct while silently degrading the underlying reasoning, revealing an “answer‑evidence gap.”


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most KV cache compression work focuses on preserving final-answer accuracy, assuming that if answers stay correct, the supporting reasoning is also preserved. For large reasoning models, this assumption might be wrong and can be risky in settings where trustworthy reasoning and evidence are important (e.g., scientific, clinical, or long-context tasks). The authors want to rigorously test whether compression preserves not just answers, but also the usability and faithfulness of the reasoning trace.

Method: They introduce a fixed-trace replay protocol that holds the reasoning content fixed and checks whether different compression schemes preserve enough information from an already-generated reasoning trace for the model to keep working correctly. They evaluate ten token-eviction-based KV cache compression methods and one quantization method on three large reasoning models across multiple domains: mathematical reasoning, scientific QA, clinical calculation, and long-context retrieval. They define and measure several metrics: final-answer accuracy, answer-chain consistency (whether the answer matches the chain-of-thought), and perturbation faithfulness (whether perturbing the reasoning has the expected effect on answers).

Result: Token-eviction KV compression methods can maintain high final-answer accuracy but significantly reduce answer-chain consistency and perturbation faithfulness, indicating that the model’s visible reasoning becomes less reliable even when answers remain correct. In contrast, a coverage-preserving quantization method is much less affected on these reasoning metrics while achieving compression, suggesting the main problem is not compression per se but selective loss of access to parts of the reasoning trace due to token eviction.

Conclusion: The standard practice of evaluating KV cache compression only by final-answer accuracy is inadequate for reasoning models because correct answers can be preserved while the quality and faithfulness of their supporting reasoning degrade. This phenomenon, termed the answer-evidence gap, arises particularly with token-eviction methods that discard parts of the reasoning trace. Compression schemes that preserve coverage of the reasoning trace, such as appropriate quantization, better maintain reasoning faithfulness, so future work should evaluate and design KV compression with reasoning quality—not just accuracy—in mind.

Abstract: KV cache compression is commonly evaluated by final-answer accuracy, implicitly assuming that preserving the answer also preserves the reasoning that supports it. We test this assumption for large reasoning models and show that it can fail: under compression, correct answers and the validity of their visible supporting rationales can be preserved at different rates. We study this failure with a controlled fixed-trace replay protocol, which holds reasoning content fixed and isolates whether compression preserves usable information from an already available trace. We evaluate ten token-eviction KV compression methods and one quantization method on three models across mathematical reasoning, scientific QA, clinical calculation, and long-context retrieval. We measure final accuracy, answer-chain consistency, and perturbation faithfulness. Across tasks, token-eviction methods can preserve competitive final-answer accuracy while substantially degrading chain support or perturbation faithfulness. We call this the answer-evidence gap. A coverage-preserving quantization control is substantially less affected, suggesting that the failure is tied less to KV memory reduction itself than to losing access to parts of the reasoning trace. Code is available at https://github.com/famous-blue-raincoat/Safe_KV_Compress.

</details>


### [94] [Style Wins, Substance Loses: A Diagnosis of LLM-as-Judge in Idea Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01666)
*Fengxian Ji,Yuke Li,Jingpu Yang,Juanfan Wu,Fan Zhang,Zhexuan Cui,Yu Xie,Min Peng,Qianqian Xie,Xiuying Chen,Zhuohan Xie*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces SciStyleBench, a benchmark to test and reduce how much LLM judges are biased by writing style instead of true scientific content.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based reviewers are increasingly used to evaluate scientific ideas, but it is unclear whether their scores reflect real scientific merit or are unduly influenced by superficial writing style. This uncertainty threatens the fairness and reliability of automated or assisted peer review, funding decisions, and idea triage systems. The authors aim to systematically diagnose and mitigate this stylistic bias so that evaluations depend on substance rather than presentation.

Method: The authors build SciStyleBench with three components. (1) SciStyleStage: a controlled evaluation setup where the same underlying scientific ideas are perturbed into multiple writing styles across three scenarios: no external context, fixed-domain context, and open-domain retrieval context. It covers 600 ideas, 15 style variants, and 9,000 evaluation instances per setting. (2) SciStyleMetrics: new quantitative metrics—Style Bias Index (SBI) to measure sensitivity of scores to style changes, Substance Recognition Rate (SRR) to measure the judge’s ability to favor more substantive ideas, and Adversarial Win Rate (AWR) to measure robustness under adversarially styled comparisons. (3) SciStyleExtractor: a plug-and-play module that first predicts a text’s style type and deviation, then performs style-conditioned evaluation to factor out stylistic effects, aiming to make the judgment focus on content. They run LLM judges with and without SciStyleExtractor on SciStyleBench and compute the proposed metrics.

Result: Baseline LLM judges (without mitigation) show strong sensitivity to writing style and limited ability to distinguish actual scientific substance across stylized variants of the same idea. With the SciStyleExtractor module, stylistic bias is reduced: the Style Bias Index drops from 0.566 to 0.501, while both Substance Recognition Rate and Adversarial Win Rate increase substantially—from 0.504 to 0.759 and from 0.554 to 0.899, respectively. This indicates better invariance to style alongside improved discrimination of substantive quality.

Conclusion: LLM-based scientific idea evaluation is meaningfully affected by superficial stylistic presentation, which can compromise fairness and reliability. SciStyleBench offers a systematic way to detect and quantify this bias, and the SciStyleExtractor module shows that incorporating explicit style modeling can reduce stylistic bias while improving attention to substantive content. Robust automated idea evaluation should therefore aim for style invariance paired with strong sensitivity to scientific substance, and SciStyleBench can serve as a benchmark to develop and test such methods.

Abstract: However, whether these judges truly evaluate the scientific substance of ideas or are influenced by superficial stylistic presentation remains an open question. To address this question, we propose SciStyleBench, a unified three-component benchmark for diagnosing and mitigating stylistic bias in LLM-based idea evaluation: (i) First, SciStyleStage, a three-stage evaluation environment that applies controlled stylistic perturbations to fixed scientific content across three settings no context, fixed-domain context, and open-domain retrieval context, covering 600 scientific ideas and 15 style variants, with 9,000 evaluation instances per setting; (ii) Second, SciStyleMetrics, a set of quantitative measures, including Style Bias Index (SBI), Substance Recognition Rate (SRR), and Adversarial Win Rate (AWR), to characterize how stylistic variation affects scoring stability, substance discrimination, and ranking robustness; (iii) Third, SciStyleExtractor, a plug-and-play evaluation module that separates presentation style from scientific content by predicting style type and deviation before style-conditioned evaluation, enabling us to assess whether style awareness reduces stylistic bias. Experiments on SciStyleBench show that direct LLM judges remain sensitive to writing style and struggle to distinguish scientific substance. In contrast, SciStyleExtractor reduces SBI from 0.566 to 0.501 while increasing SRR and AWR from 0.504 and 0.554 to 0.759 and 0.899, respectively. These results suggest that robust idea evaluation requires invariance to stylistic variation without sacrificing sensitivity to scientific substance. Overall, SciStyleBench provides a systematic framework for identifying, quantifying, and mitigating stylistic bias in scientific idea evaluation.

</details>


### [95] [Learning What to Remember: Test-Time Training via Context Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01672)
*Zixuan Wang,Xingyu Dang,Rui-Jie Zhu,Zixin Wen,Hengyu Fu,Wenhao Chai,Jason D. Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose TTCD, a test-time context distillation framework, to better use limited memory for long-context language modeling by supervising a short-window model with a long-window teacher via hidden-state matching, improving long-context performance and enabling continual pre-training at inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-context methods and test-time training approaches either just retain more tokens or optimize for short-term reconstruction/adaptation without explicitly preserving information that will be useful for future predictions. Memory capacity is limited, so models need a principled way to decide what to store for later use. The authors aim to design a mechanism that allocates memory to context that will matter for downstream token prediction, and that can be applied both when training from scratch and when adapting pre-trained transformers.

Method: They introduce Test-Time Context Distillation (TTCD), where a long-window teacher model supervises a short-window student at test time. The student has fast weights that can be updated online. The training signal is the discrepancy between the hidden states of the teacher (which sees a long context) and the student (with short context), serving as a dense self-supervised objective that nudges the student to memorize information important for future tokens. They focus on an in-place variant, IP-TTCD, which reuses existing MLP parameters as the fast weights instead of adding separate memory parameters. TTCD is used both when pre-training from scratch and as a lightweight augmentation for continual pre-training of existing transformers during inference.

Result: On long-context language modeling benchmarks, IP-TTCD consistently outperforms baselines including DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, sliding-window attention, and standard TTT when models are pre-trained from scratch. Additionally, applying IP-TTCD to pre-trained transformers via continual pre-training during inference improves their ability to handle long contexts without heavy architectural changes.

Conclusion: TTCD provides an effective self-supervised test-time training framework for long-context modeling by explicitly optimizing memory allocation for future prediction utility. The in-place IP-TTCD variant shows strong empirical gains and can endow existing transformers with long-context capabilities through lightweight continual adaptation. The authors see this as a step toward more general architectural continual learning, where models can update internal parameters online to better exploit long sequences.

Abstract: Effective long-context modeling is not merely about retaining more of the past, but about preserving the information that may prove relevant later. Test-time training (TTT) is an appealing approach that performs online parameter updates for long-context modeling, yet existing TTT methods only optimize either reconstruction or online adaptation objectives without considering the future utility of retained information. In this work, we propose \textbf{T}est-\textbf{T}ime \textbf{C}ontext \textbf{D}istillation (TTCD), a TTT framework that introduces a self-supervised objective for allocating limited memory capacity for future use. Specifically, TTCD uses a long-window teacher to supervise the fast weights of a short-window student, where the hidden-state discrepancy between them offers a dense, self-supervised signal guiding the model to memorize the contextual information crucial for future token predictions. We focus on an in-place variant: In-Place TTCD (IP-TTCD), which uses the existing MLP parameters as the fast weights. Experiments on long-context language modeling tasks show IP-TTCD consistently outperforms DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, sliding-window attention, and TTT when pre-trained from scratch. Furthermore, IP-TTCD allows pre-trained transformer models to adapt their parameters during inference through continual pre-training, gaining long-context capabilities with only a lightweight architectural augmentation. Our results position TTCD as a step toward architectural continual learning.

</details>


### [96] [Understanding Sparse Attention Selectivity in Long-Context Foundation Models via Counterfactual Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01676)
*Xingyu Ren,Youran Sun,Chugang Yi,Haizhao Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates how sparse attention mechanisms in long-context models alter the influence of specific content, introducing an auditing framework that reveals sparsification can significantly and non-obviously change content influence without affecting aggregate accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sparse attention is heavily used to make long-context models efficient, but there is no systematic way to measure how dropping attention blocks changes which pieces of input actually affect the output, raising safety, reliability, and interpretability concerns.

Method: The authors analyze Block Sparse Flash Attention (BSFA) via route replay across multiple architectures, then design a dense-calibrated counterfactual auditing setup using specially constructed probe “cards” (Gold, Poison, Benign) placed in symmetric layouts. They vary compression ratios and compare several sparsification mechanisms—BSFA, block-top-k selection, and KV-cache eviction—to measure how each changes the influence (logit impact) of different content blocks.

Result: They show that changing BSFA routes alters model decisions in the majority of tested settings (13/16) without label flips under identity replay, confirming a causal sparsification effect. The audit reveals two competing phenomena—signal concentration, where Gold and Poison blocks are preferentially preserved over Benign ones, and integration loss, where discarded blocks break cross-block attention and sharply reduce influence. Compression strength modulates which effect dominates, with higher compression often increasing sparse amplification and sometimes reversing its sign. Different sparsification arms exhibit consistent qualitative behavior, confirming that content influence is systematically distorted in ways not captured by standard accuracy metrics.

Conclusion: Sparse attention does more than speed up inference: it reshapes which content influences the model’s outputs, through a mix of signal concentration and integration loss that depends on the compression level. As these effects are not visible from aggregate accuracy alone, the authors propose their open auditing framework—applicable to any model exposing block identities—as a necessary tool for evaluating and monitoring sparsified long-context systems.

Abstract: Sparse attention is widely deployed in long-context serving stacks, yet no framework audits how discarding blocks changes the influence of specific content on model output. We first establish that the phenomenon is real and causal: Block Sparse Flash Attention (BSFA) route replay across four architectures changes output decisions in 13 of 16 cells, with zero identity-replay label flips. We then introduce a dense-calibrated counterfactual audit using matched probe cards---Gold (carrying the correct answer label), Poison (carrying a target wrong label), and Benign (filler only)---under six-layout position symmetry, isolating the sparsification-specific effect.
  Two patterns compete. Signal concentration: the selector preserves Gold and Poison blocks far above filler-matched Benign blocks (G$\approx$P$\gg$B across all model--task pairs). Integration loss: discarding blocks severs cross-block attention---confirmed by an ablation where isolating the probe block collapses its influence from 4.48 logits to zero. Compression ratio governs the balance: a full sweep from mild ($c=0.25$) to aggressive ($c=0.75$) compression across four model--task pairs reveals that three of four cells move toward stronger sparse amplification at higher compression, with two exhibiting sign reversals.
  Three independent arms---BSFA route replay, controlled block-top-$k$, and KV-cache eviction---converge: sparsification changes content influence in ways aggregate accuracy cannot detect. We provide an open measurement framework deployable on any model exposing block identities.

</details>


### [97] [PGMem: Tightly Coupled Persona-Memory Graph for Lifelong Personalized Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01708)
*Wonjun Choi,Yerim Kim,Yukyung Lee,Susik Yoon*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces PGMem, a persona-memory graph that tightly links user personas to supporting dialogue events, improving long-term personalized dialogue agents’ retrieval and performance over existing memory systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing dialogue agent memory systems store user personas as flat profiles detached from the conversational events that generated them. This weak linkage causes two problems: (1) a memory-persona validity gap, where it’s hard to tell whether current personas are still supported by recent interactions, and (2) a persona-aware retrieval gap, where the system struggles to fetch the most relevant and up-to-date persona information during conversation. The authors aim to create a memory structure that keeps personas grounded in concrete, time-evolving evidence from dialogue history.

Method: The authors propose PGMem, a heterogeneous persona-memory graph where nodes represent both events and persona statements, and edges are typed to capture provenance (how persona nodes originate from events) and evidence (which events support, update, or contradict persona nodes). At inference time, PGMem performs query-time expansion from seeds that are relevant to the current dialogue query and ranks retrieved persona signals based on evidential validity, i.e., how well they are supported by linked events. They evaluate PGMem on three benchmarks using small language models as backbones and compare against summary-based memory, persona-aware memory, graph-structured memory, and agentic memory approaches.

Result: On three different benchmarks, PGMem consistently outperforms several strong baselines, including summary-based memory, persona-aware memory, existing graph-structured memory, and agentic memory systems. The performance gains are especially pronounced as the dialogue context length increases, indicating that PGMem scales better with long-term interaction histories than alternative methods.

Conclusion: PGMem’s persona-memory graph effectively reduces the mismatch between stored personas and underlying dialogue events, leading to more valid and useful persona representations for long-term personalized dialogue agents. By grounding persona signals in evidential connections to past events and using evidential validity during retrieval, PGMem enhances the agent’s ability to leverage evolving user personas, and shows robust gains over existing memory architectures, particularly in longer-context scenarios.

Abstract: Long-term personalized dialogue agents must track user preferences as their personas evolve. Existing memory systems organize past events well, but store personas as flat profiles detached from the events that justify them. This loose coupling leads to the memory-persona validity gap and the persona-aware retrieval gap. We propose PGMem, a heterogeneous persona-memory graph that connects event and persona nodes through typed provenance and evidence edges, keeping each persona signal traceable to the events that support or revise it. At retrieval time, PGMem expands from query-relevant seeds and ranks signals by evidential validity. Across three benchmarks with small language model backbones, PGMem consistently outperforms summary-based, persona-aware, graph-structured, and agentic memory baselines, and improves performance as the context grows. The source code of PGMem is available at https://github.com/wonjunchoi23/pgmem/

</details>


### [98] [TIDES: A Longitudinal Bilingual Dataset for Modeling Multi-Party Social Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01724)
*Heechan Lee,Jeonggyu Kang,Junho Myung,Jaywoong Jeong,Juho Kim,Joseph Seering*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces TIDES, a longitudinal, naturalistic group-conversation dataset and shows that fine-tuning on it improves next-speaker prediction but not necessarily human-perceived quality of generated dialogue.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard LLMs perform poorly on complex multi-party conversations, partly because existing datasets are short, artificial, and lack long-term social dynamics. The authors aim to create a dataset that better reflects real-world team interactions over time so models can learn structural and social aspects of group dialogue.

Method: Collect a high-resolution, semester-long corpus of 12 university project teams’ in-person meetings (in English and Korean), with detailed socio-structural annotations such as interaction types, emergent roles, and team development stages. Train and fine-tune models for next-speaker prediction on this dataset and compare performance against a bigram baseline, proprietary zero-shot models, and prior state-of-the-art models on another meeting corpus (AMI). Conduct human evaluations of generated dialogue quality.

Result: Fine-tuning on TIDES improves next-speaker prediction accuracy by 13.8 percentage points over a bigram baseline (to 64.53%) and reaches performance similar to strong proprietary zero-shot models. On the AMI Meeting Corpus, the model is within 2.1 percentage points of state-of-the-art performance while using ~42% less training data. However, human evaluators tend to prefer outputs from un-fine-tuned (vanilla) models over those fine-tuned on TIDES, indicating that structural prediction gains do not translate directly into perceived naturalness or coherence.

Conclusion: TIDES enables more accurate modeling of team interaction structure and next-speaker prediction in multi-party conversations and is data-efficient relative to prior work. Yet, improved structural modeling alone does not guarantee better human-perceived dialogue quality, highlighting a gap between structural prediction metrics and conversational naturalness. Future work should focus on integrating structural modeling with generation objectives that directly target natural, coherent, and contextually appropriate multi-party dialogue.

Abstract: Group conversations are fundamental to human collaboration, yet standard large language models (LLMs) still struggle with the complexities of multi-party interaction. This challenge persists in part because existing group conversation datasets are often limited to short-term lab settings with contrived tasks, failing to capture the long-term social dynamics of real-world teams. To bridge this gap, we introduce TIDES, a high-resolution longitudinal dataset tracking 12 university project teams over a full semester.
