Comprising 75,971 utterances in both English and Korean from in-person meetings, TIDES provides a naturalistic record of teams working on self-managed projects. Our socio-structural annotations-covering interaction types, emergent roles, and development stages-allow for modeling of team evolution over months. Experiments show that fine-tuning on TIDES improves next-speaker prediction by 13.8 percentage points over a bigram baseline (64.53%) and yields performance comparable to strong proprietary zero-shot models. The model also comes within 2.1 percentage points of the published state of the art on the AMI Meeting Corpus while using approximately 42% less training data. However, human evaluations suggest that better next-speaker prediction does not necessarily yield more natural or coherent utterances, as fine-tuned models were generally less preferred than vanilla models. This potential mismatch motivates further study of how structural modeling can support natural multi-party generation.

</details>


### [99] [Constructing Parallel Multidimensional Chromatic Lexicons for Corpus-Assisted Analysis of Russian and English Texts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01752)
*Larisa Nikitina*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper develops reusable chromatic lexicons for Russian and English and shows, via a pilot poetry corpus study, that they enable fine-grained, quantitative comparison of colour usage across authors and languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing corpus tools for studying colour in literature are limited, often focusing only on basic colour words, lacking multidimensional semantic information (like hue, saturation, temperature) and multilingual coverage. This constrains researchers’ ability to systematically compare colour usage across languages and authors, especially in literary texts with rich, nuanced visual description. The authors aim to fill this methodological gap by creating transparent, replicable resources and procedures that can support corpus-assisted, contrastive analysis of chromatic lexis.

Method: The authors compiled two chromatic lexicons: 224 Russian and 141 English entries. They gathered colour vocabulary from specialised colour resources and prior research, aligned and compared the language inventories, manually checked translations, and accounted for language-specific morphology. Each entry was tagged with chromatic dimensions (hue, saturation, temperature) and included both clear colour terms and more general visual descriptors. To test the lexicons, they built small, purposive poetry corpora (Bely and Dickinson), extracted all lexicon matches, and manually classified each match as Confirmed_chromatic, Ambiguous_visual, or Excluded. They ran a strict analysis (confirmed only) and then a sensitivity analysis (confirmed + ambiguous) to assess the robustness of findings to coding decisions.

Result: The pilot corpus study showed substantial quantitative differences between Bely and Dickinson in the frequency and distribution of chromatic lexis and visual descriptors, and across hue, saturation, and temperature categories. Confirmed chromatic terms appeared 3.4 times more often in the Bely corpus than in the Dickinson corpus. The sensitivity analysis suggested that including borderline ambiguous items did not overturn the main patterns. The lexicons successfully captured multidimensional chromatic behavior in the texts and facilitated cross-linguistic comparison.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that multidimensional, language-specific chromatic lexicons enable more precise and nuanced corpus-assisted analysis of colour in literary texts than approaches limited to basic colour terms. The authors provide a transparent, replicable procedure for building and applying such lexicons, highlighting their analytical value for cross-author and cross-language comparisons. The resulting Russian and English chromatic lexicons are reusable tools that can support further research on colour and visual description in literature and potentially other text types.

Abstract: This article addresses the relative scarcity of research tools for the corpus-assisted linguistic analysis of colour terms in literary texts. It describes the development of two multidimensional chromatic lexicons: one for Russian (224 entries) and one for English (141 entries). Lexicon construction involved sourcing colour vocabulary from specialised resources and research literature, comparing the two language inventories, manually checking translated candidates, and addressing language-specific morphological features. In addition to identifying colour terms and visual descriptors, the lexicons classify entries according to hue, saturation, and temperature. To demonstrate their practical application, a pilot study was conducted on purposively sampled corpora of poetry by Andrei Bely (20,373 tokens) and Emily Dickinson (28,479 tokens). All retrieved matches were checked in context and classified as Confirmed_chromatic, Ambiguous_visual, or Excluded. The analysis was implemented in two main stages: a strict analysis including confirmed chromatic lexis only, followed by a sensitivity analysis incorporating both confirmed and ambiguous chromatic lexis to determine whether coding decisions about borderline cases affected the main findings. The quantitative results indicated marked differences in the use of colour terms, visual descriptors, hue, saturation, and temperature. Specifically, the analysis revealed that confirmed chromatic terms occurred 3.4 times more frequently in the sampled Bely corpus than in the Dickinson corpus. These findings demonstrate the analytical value of a multidimensional approach, with the main contribution of this study being a transparent and reusable procedure for constructing and applying multilingual chromatic lexicons.

</details>


### [100] [RADAR: Rubric-Aware Dependency and Redundancy Analysis for LLM-as-Judge Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01810)
*Divyansh Singh,Reza Davari,Afra Mashhadi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces RADAR, a framework to detect and measure coupling between rubric criteria in LLM-as-judge evaluations before running large, expensive evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current rubric-based LLM-as-judge pipelines typically assume evaluation criteria are independent, but in reality improving one criterion can systematically affect others, leading to distorted aggregate scores and potentially flawed deployment decisions. There is a need for a lightweight way to detect these inter-criterion couplings early.

Method: RADAR takes an evaluation rubric, automatically generates targeted synthetic probes for each criterion, scores each probe along all criteria using an LLM-as-judge setup, and then computes a directional coupling matrix that reveals which criteria co-score and in what direction and strength. The approach is run as a small-scale preflight diagnostic before full evaluation.

Result: Across three evaluation settings—NVIDIA HelpSteer2, SumPubMed, and Yale-Salesforce SummEval—RADAR, using only a small number of probes per criterion, closely matches human-measured inter-criterion correlation structures with Pearson correlation above 0.84. It outputs actionable diagnostics about how criteria interact.

Conclusion: RADAR can reliably estimate redundancy, hierarchical relationships, and aggregation sensitivity among rubric criteria with minimal probing, giving practitioners practical audit signals about rubric design and criterion coupling before committing to large-scale LLM-as-judge evaluations.

Abstract: Rubric-based LLM-as-judge pipelines often assume that evaluation criteria provide independent signals. In practice, however, criteria can be behaviorally coupled: improving one criterion may systematically change scores on another, distorting aggregate scores used in model-release or product-update decisions. We introduce RADAR, a lightweight preflight diagnostic framework for estimating such coupling before large-scale evaluation. Given a rubric, RADAR generates targeted synthetic probes, scores each probe on all criteria, and produces a directional coupling matrix that shows which criteria co-score and how. We validate RADAR on three industry-relevant evaluation settings: NVIDIA HelpSteer2, SumPubMed, and the Yale-Salesforce SummEval benchmark. Using only a small number of probes per criterion, RADAR recovers human inter-criterion correlation structure (Pearson r > 0.84) and provides practitioners with concrete audit signals about redundancy, hierarchy, and aggregation sensitivity before committing to large-scale judging.

</details>


### [101] [Divergent large language model predictions from convergent representations in ambiguous word pairs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01816)
*K. Jack Scott,Narun Pat,Veronica Liesaputra*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes how decoder-only transformers disambiguate word meanings, showing that semantic distinctions peak in middle layers, become less visible in late-layer embeddings, yet still strongly control outputs—raising concerns for using late-layer embeddings in semantic applications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how large language models internally resolve lexical ambiguity (homonyms and polysemes), and to reconcile an emerging puzzle: internal embedding similarities often correlate poorly with model behavior despite strong task performance. This has practical importance because many downstream applications rely on late-layer embeddings and cosine similarity for semantic search, retrieval, and clustering.

Method: They conduct layer-by-layer analyses of three decoder-only transformer models of increasing size (GPT-2-Small-117M, Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-32B). For ambiguous words, they compare representation separation across layers and compute KL divergence between next-token distributions. They run activation patching to causally test whether late-layer representational differences drive outputs, and perform single-layer ablations to probe how vulnerable disambiguation is to disruptions at each layer.

Result: Across models and for both homonyms and polysemes, semantic representations of different senses separate most strongly in middle layers, then partially reconverge in later layers, even while the KL divergence between their predictive distributions is highest in the final layers. Activation patching shows that altering late-layer activations causally changes disambiguation decisions, and ablations reveal that models reach similar disambiguation performance even though the specific layers they depend on differ qualitatively.

Conclusion: Decoder-only transformers maintain semantic distinctions needed for lexical disambiguation, but these distinctions become increasingly obscured to standard embedding similarity metrics in late layers. Consequently, embedding-space similarity can look high even when output behavior differs strongly. This helps explain the mismatch between internal similarity and behavior and suggests caution for embedding-based methods that rely on late-layer cosine similarity for semantic tasks like search, retrieval, and clustering.

Abstract: In this work we investigate how decoder-only transformers resolve lexical ambiguity through layer-by-layer analysis of three models spanning three parameter sizes (GPT-2-Small-117M, Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-32B). For both homonyms and polysemes, we find that representations become maximally distinct in middle layers, then partially reconverge in late layers, while the KL divergence between their next-token predictions reaches its maximum in the final layers. The activation patching experiment provides causal evidence that late-layer representational differences directly determine outputs despite apparent increased similarity in embedding space. Our single-layer ablation experiment indicates that models achieve equivalent disambiguation despite qualitatively different layer-wise vulnerabilities. These findings offer a mechanism for recent observations where models' internal embedding similarities show low correlation with their behavioural outputs despite strong performance. The semantic distinctions therefore remain present but become increasingly invisible to similarity measures over the embeddings, with implications for embedding-based methods such as semantic search, retrieval, and clustering that rely on late-layer cosine similarity.

</details>


### [102] [Analyzing Speech Condition Effects in Dysarthric ASR: A Layer-wise Probing Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01865)
*Darwin Jelestin Muthu,Navya Gupta,Wei Lin Tay,Zhengchen Zhang,Daniel Wang Zhengkui,Rong Tong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They probe a transformer ASR encoder on Mandarin dysarthric speech, show how disordered articulation alters layer-wise representations, and use these insights to design efficient, layer-aware adaptation that nearly matches full fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ASR models perform poorly on dysarthric speech, but we lack understanding of how such disordered articulation affects internal representations. This gap limits our ability to design targeted, parameter-efficient adaptations, especially for low-resource settings like Mandarin dysarthric ASR.

Method: They conduct a layer-wise probing study of a transformer ASR encoder on Mandarin dysarthric speech under three conditions with matched transcripts: original dysarthric recordings, zero-shot TTS resynthesis conditioned on the dysarthric speaker, and unconditioned TTS. They probe for phoneme boundary and identity information and recognition difficulty across layers, analyze tone-related errors, and measure cross-condition similarity. Using these insights, they test parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategies (single-layer LoRA and partial-layer adaptation) at different depths.

Result: Probing shows a hierarchy: phoneme boundaries remain weakly represented for dysarthric speech at all layers, phoneme identity emerges in higher layers, and recognition difficulty is captured in the deepest layers. Tone remains a major and persistent error source in Mandarin. Representation similarity between conditions diverges more in deeper layers, indicating dysarthria mainly disrupts higher-level representations. Guided by this, single-layer LoRA at layer 7 and adapting only layers 5–8 reach within 3.5% and 2.48% relative WER of full-encoder adaptation, while adapting only upper layers is less beneficial.

Conclusion: Disordered articulation in dysarthric Mandarin speech primarily affects high-level ASR encoder representations, with persistent weaknesses in phoneme boundary encoding and tone modeling. Layer-wise representation analysis can directly inform where to adapt a model: mid-layer, subset adaptation (layers 5–8) or single-layer LoRA can nearly match full fine-tuning, making dysarthric ASR more practical in low-resource settings. This motivates layer-aware, parameter-efficient adaptation strategies grounded in internal representation diagnostics.

Abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) performance degrades sharply on dysarthric speech, yet how disordered articulation reshapes a model's internal representations is underexplored. We present a layer-wise probing analysis of a transformer ASR encoder on Mandarin dysarthric speech under three transcript-matched conditions: original dysarthric speech, speaker conditioned zero-shot TTS resynthesis, and unconditioned TTS. The probes reveal a task-dependent hierarchy: phoneme boundary information stays weak for dysarthric speech at every layer, phoneme identity becomes recoverable toward the upper layers, and recognition difficulty is encoded in the deepest layers. Tone-sensitive evaluation shows Mandarin lexical tone is a persistent error source. Cross-condition similarity divergence grows with depth, indicating that disordered speech affects high-level representations more than low-level acoustic features. Guided by these findings, single-layer LoRA at layer 7 and adaptation on subset layers 5-8 achieve performance within 3.5% and 2.48% relative margins of full encoder adaptation, respectively, while upper-layer adaptation is less effective for dysarthric speech. These findings link representation analysis to parameter-efficient fine-tuning and motivate layer-aware adaptation for low-resource Mandarin dysarthric ASR.

</details>


### [103] [CRISP: Critical Step Perception for Training Efficient Deep Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01867)
*Haosi Mo,Zihao Yan,Ruiqing Zhang,Zhongli Li,Hexuan Deng,Xuebo Liu,Min Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CRISP is a framework to train efficient LLM-based deep search agents by identifying which tool-use steps are truly necessary and pruning redundant ones, thus shortening interaction trajectories without hurting answer quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep search agents built on LLMs can answer complex questions by interacting with search and browsing tools over multiple steps, but they often generate long, redundant trajectories with many unnecessary tool calls. Existing efficiency methods penalize tool use uniformly, which can discourage both wasteful and essential evidence-gathering steps, hurting accuracy. There is a need for a way to distinguish critical tool interactions from redundant ones so that agents can become more efficient without losing necessary evidence.

Method: CRISP introduces critical step perception into training deep search agents. First, it uses Backward Evidence Induction: a strong model inspects a completed search trajectory in reverse from the final answer, labeling each tool-interaction step as critical if it provides or preserves evidence needed for that answer. These step-wise labels are then distilled into a smaller critical-step recognizer model that can classify steps over full trajectories in a single forward pass. During policy optimization, CRISP applies an efficiency-aware reward that selectively penalizes redundant interactions while preserving critical ones, and this reward shaping is applied only to trajectories that successfully reach the correct answer.

Result: On the BrowseComp and HLE-Verified benchmarks, CRISP-trained agents keep final-answer accuracy on par with strong baselines while significantly reducing the number of interaction turns. Specifically, the method reduces average tool-interaction steps by 15.1% on BrowseComp and 33.2% on HLE-Verified, demonstrating that it can substantially improve interaction efficiency without sacrificing performance.

Conclusion: CRISP shows that explicitly modeling which tool-using steps are critical for obtaining the final answer enables more efficient deep search agents. By labeling and recognizing critical steps via backward evidence induction and then applying targeted reward shaping only on successful trajectories, the framework reduces redundant search and browsing interactions while maintaining accuracy. This suggests a promising direction for building more cost-effective and responsive LLM-based agents that rely on external tools.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly extended into deep search agents that solve complex questions through multi-step interaction with external search and browsing tools. However, existing agents often incur substantial computational and interaction costs, generating lengthy trajectories that contain redundant queries, inefficient exploration, and irrelevant observations. Existing efficiency-oriented methods usually encourage agents to use tools less frequently, but treating all tool interactions uniformly may also suppress steps that gather necessary evidence. In this paper, we propose CRISP, a framework for training efficient deep search agents through critical step perception. Unlike prior efficiency methods that uniformly penalize tool use, CRISP distinguishes interactions that gather necessary evidence from redundant ones and shapes the training reward to preserve the former while pruning the latter, improving efficiency without sacrificing the evidence needed for correct answers. Specifically, CRISP first constructs critical-step labels with Backward Evidence Induction: starting from the final answer, a strong model traverses a completed search trajectory backward and judges whether each tool-interaction step provides or preserves evidence for the final answer. We then distill these step-wise judgments into a smaller critical-step recognizer, enabling full-trajectory analysis in a single pass. During policy optimization, an efficiency-aware reward is applied only to successful rollouts. Experiments on BrowseComp and HLE-Verified show that CRISP maintains competitive final-answer accuracy while reducing average interaction turns by 15.1% and 33.2%, respectively, demonstrating substantial improvements in interaction efficiency.

</details>


### [104] [TRAM: Enhancing Multimodal Reasoning with Trajectory-Derived Auxiliary Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01922)
*Kang Liu,Zijing Wang,Yongkang Liu,Mengjie Zhao,Xiaocui Yang,Shi Feng,Yifei Zhang,Daling Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes TRAM, a training-free auxiliary memory mechanism that improves long-horizon reasoning in multimodal large reasoning models by maintaining and re-injecting compact representations of prior reasoning steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As MLRMs perform multi-step visual reasoning, they tend to underutilize information derived earlier in the reasoning trajectory, especially task-specific relations and constraints, leading to errors. Existing methods focus mainly on preserving visual grounding, neglecting the retention and integration of intermediate reasoning products, which motivates a method that explicitly maintains and reuses this reasoning-derived information.

Method: The authors first conduct attribution analysis showing that correctness correlates more with retention of reasoning-derived information than with image attribution alone. They then introduce TRAM (TRajectory-derived Auxiliary Memory), a training-free decoding-time mechanism that: (1) consolidates completed reasoning segments into a compact latent memory; (2) updates this memory online via fast and slow recurrent streams; and (3) feeds the memory back into selected decoder layers through a lightweight residual pathway, augmenting standard decoding without retraining the base model.

Result: Applied to four different multimodal large reasoning models across eight benchmarks covering mathematical, scientific, and general visual reasoning tasks, TRAM consistently improves performance compared with vanilla decoding, demonstrating better handling of long reasoning trajectories without additional training cost.

Conclusion: Maintaining an explicit, trajectory-derived auxiliary memory during decoding helps MLRMs better retain and integrate intermediate reasoning products over long contexts, leading to more reliable visual reasoning. TRAM offers a simple, training-free mechanism that can be plugged into existing models to enhance long-horizon multimodal reasoning.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Reasoning Models (MLRMs) have achieved strong performance on tasks requiring visual understanding and multi-step inference. However, as reasoning trajectories grow, models may become less effective at using information established earlier in the context, increasing the risk of reasoning errors. Existing approaches primarily address this problem by sustaining visual grounding throughout reasoning. However, reasoning also transforms visual observations into task-specific relations, constraints, and intermediate conclusions whose influence may weaken over long trajectories. Our attribution analysis suggests that correctness is not consistently separated by image attribution alone, but is more closely associated with whether trajectories retain and integrate such reasoning-derived information across stages. Motivated by this, we introduce TRAM (TRajectory-derived Auxiliary Memory), a training-free method that augments standard decoding with an auxiliary memory pathway derived from the model's own reasoning trajectory. TRAM consolidates completed reasoning into a compact latent memory, updates it online through fast and slow recurrent streams, and feeds it back into selected decoder layers through a lightweight residual pathway. Experiments across four MLRM variants on eight benchmarks show that TRAM improves performance over vanilla decoding on mathematical, scientific, and general visual reasoning tasks without additional training.

</details>


### [105] [Automatic Annotation of Ancient Greek Vowel Length](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01935)
*Albin Thörn Cleland,Eric Cullhed*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents the first general-purpose automatic tool to mark long vs. short vowels (macronization) in Ancient Greek text, using rule-based inheritance plus a small transformer model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ancient Greek NLP resources typically omit phonemic vowel length for alpha, iota, and ypsilon, although length is crucial for phonology and prosody. Manually marking vowel length (macronizing) is difficult due to context dependence and the huge number of word forms, and no large-scale, publicly available macronized corpus exists. A general macronizer is therefore needed, both for linguistic work and to create training data for machine learning models.

Method: The authors build a rule-based macronizer that operates over input in CoNLL-U format (lemma, POS, morphology). It uses a set of recursive modules so that rarer inflected forms inherit vowel-length markings from more common forms of the same lexeme. This rule-based system then generates large-scale labeled data, on which a small character-level transformer model is trained. The neural model learns to infer macronization even in cases not explicitly covered by the rule system. They evaluate on a manually macronized gold-standard corpus including both verse and prose, and assess impact on downstream tasks like verse scansion.

Result: The character-level transformer trained on the rule-based macronizer’s output attains accuracy on a gold-standard macronized benchmark that matches or improves upon the rule-based system itself, including better generalization to previously unmarked cases. Applying automatic macronization also improves performance on prosodic NLP tasks, such as automatic verse scansion, demonstrating downstream utility.

Conclusion: A practical, general-purpose Ancient Greek macronizer is achievable by combining rule-based inheritance over morphological annotations with a lightweight neural model trained on its output. This approach fills a major resource gap for Ancient Greek, produces high-quality vowel-length annotation, and measurably benefits prosody-related NLP tasks. The framework can serve as a foundation for further improvements and for creating large, macronized corpora for research and applications.

Abstract: Prior work in Ancient Greek NLP relies on corpora that do not disambiguate the phonemic vowel length of alpha, iota, and ypsilon, together known as the dichrona. Depending on lexeme, morphology, sandhi, syntax, and conventions of period, genre, and verse form, each of these letters can represent either a long or a short vowel. Deciding and marking the correct length is known as "macronizing", a long-tail problem given the sheer mass of word forms and the context dependency of individual instances. No macronized corpus of Ancient Greek is publicly available at scale, so a stand-alone macronizer is needed. While previous work has shown how to build a static, corpus-bespoke vowel-length dictionary, the present paper constructs the first general-purpose macronizer for arbitrary Ancient Greek input. Given input carrying lemma, part-of-speech, and morphological annotation in the standard CoNLL-U format, a set of recursive modules lets less common word forms inherit markup from more common forms of the same lexical word. The macronizer's chief application is generating training data for machine learning: we show that a small character-level transformer trained on the macronizer's own output learns to generalize past the cases the rule-based system leaves unmarked, matching or exceeding its accuracy on a gold-standard, manually annotated benchmark of verse and prose. We also show that macronization can improve downstream prosodical NLP tasks like verse scansion.

</details>


### [106] [Look Ahead Before You Distill: Future Trajectory Validation of Teacher Guidance for Agentic On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01953)
*Chishui Chen,Yaoyou Fan,Te Sun,Yi Yang,Chenghao Sun,Delin Mao,Hongbo Qiao,Zuowei Zhang,Junxi Wang,Chenxing Sun,Yangen Hu,Lu Pan,Xuyang Liu,Linfeng Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces FutureBridge-OPD, a method to improve on-policy distillation for multi-turn agentic tasks by selectively using short teacher rollouts at high-disagreement states to decide when teacher guidance is actually beneficial for the student’s future trajectory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard on-policy distillation gives teacher supervision on states visited by the student, which helps reduce the mismatch between training and inference distributions. However, in multi-turn agentic tasks, small student deviations compound over time, leading the agent into regions where the teacher’s guidance is less relevant or effective. Moreover, not all high-disagreement states are equally good for distillation; some guidance may help, others may hurt, and this depends on how the future trajectory evolves. This creates a need for a mechanism that can evaluate the *future impact* of teacher guidance before committing to it.

Method: FutureBridge-OPD (FTB) identifies high-disagreement states between teacher and student during interaction. At such a state, it briefly lets the teacher take over for a short “bridge” segment of the trajectory. Then, it lets the student continue from the end of that bridge and compares how many positive distillation signals (i.e., states where the teacher provides beneficial supervision) arise along that future student continuation versus under the teacher’s own trajectory. If the teacher bridge increases the density of positive distillation signals, it is considered beneficial and used as supervision; otherwise, it is rejected. This procedure adaptively decides when and where to apply teacher guidance in on-policy distillation.

Result: On three multi-turn benchmarks—ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld—using Qwen3-32B as the teacher and Qwen3-1.7B as the student, FTB achieves substantial performance gains. It improves average performance by 16.6 points over vanilla on-policy distillation (OPD) and by 7.6 points over TCOD. The method also shows robustness across different student sizes and alternative teacher configurations.

Conclusion: FutureBridge-OPD addresses the compounding deviation issue in multi-turn on-policy distillation by evaluating the *trajectory-level* impact of teacher guidance at high-disagreement states via short teacher bridges. By accepting only those bridges that increase the density of positive distillation signals for the subsequent student trajectory, FTB selectively leverages teacher supervision where it is most useful. Experiments across multiple benchmarks and model scales indicate that this approach consistently outperforms prior OPD variants, suggesting it is a practical improvement for training agentic language model students from stronger teachers.

Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides teacher supervision on states visited by the student, reducing the distribution gap between training and inference. However, in multi-turn agentic tasks, student deviations may accumulate over time, gradually moving the trajectory away from states where teacher guidance remains effective. Our quantitative analysis further shows that high-disagreement states offer promising opportunities for teacher guidance, but determining whether such guidance is beneficial requires examining its effect on subsequent student trajectories. We propose FutureBridge-OPD (FTB), which executes a short teacher bridge at a high disagreement state and uses the resulting student continuation to assess whether the bridge increases the density of positive distillation signals relative to the teacher. On ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, under the main Qwen3-32B teacher to Qwen3-1.7B student setting, FTB outperforms vanilla OPD and TCOD by an average of 16.6 and 7.6 points, respectively, and remains effective across student scales and teacher settings. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenChiShui/FutureBridge-OPD.

</details>


### [107] [CompanionBench: A Theory-Anchored, Real-World-Grounded Benchmark for AI Emotional Companionship](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02046)
*Yao Liu,Guangjia Chai,Yuming Huang,Jihao Huang,Lei Wang,Junchen Wan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CompanionBench is a bilingual, real-data-grounded benchmark to evaluate LLM companions on nuanced relational capabilities, correcting for judge bias and revealing weaknesses obscured by single empathy scores.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM companions are increasingly used in sensitive, personally consequential contexts, but existing evaluations are shallow: they rely on hand-written or fully simulated scenarios, compress complex relational skills into one empathy score, and ignore systematic judge biases like leniency toward familiar models or inconsistent scoring over time. This makes it hard to know whether companion agents provide genuinely supportive, safe relationships. The paper aims to build a more rigorous, theory-driven, and realistic benchmark that captures fine-grained socio-emotional abilities and yields trustworthy rankings across languages and models.

Method: The authors construct CompanionBench, an interactive bilingual (Chinese-English) benchmark grounded in de-identified real-world companion interactions. They design personas, histories, and events from actual data, and train a user simulator whose behavior branches via a hidden disclosure gate that depends on the agent’s responses—controlling interaction complexity without scripting dialogue. Drawing on 25 theories from psychology and counseling, they define ten distinct capabilities (including four rarely or never graded before: holding ambiguity, selfobject responsiveness, positive resonance, and calibrated challenge). Agents are evaluated along two axes: (1) a subjective rubric rating these ten capabilities, scored by a cross-family panel of judges to reduce same-family favoritism, and (2) an objective, deterministic measure of whether the agent’s behavior earns deeper user disclosure. To correct for judge bias, they apply Item Response Theory to disentangle agent quality from judge severity. They ensure bilingual robustness and release 500 parallel Chinese-English pairs plus evaluation code.

Result: The benchmark yields highly reproducible model rankings across languages (Spearman rho ≈ 0.996 in Chinese and 0.953 in English). Evaluating 28 LLM agents reveals nuanced, capability-level performance differences that are invisible when using a single aggregate empathy score. Notable weaknesses commonly observed include emotion regulation and calibrated challenge, while the capability of holding ambiguity is especially discriminative among models. Role-play–oriented agents tend to perform relatively poorly, suggesting that immersive conversation alone does not guarantee relational competence. A key failure pattern across agents is the tendency to offer superficial warmth instead of substantive, tailored relational support that fosters deeper user disclosure.

Conclusion: CompanionBench provides a more valid, fine-grained, and realistic framework for evaluating LLM companions by leveraging psychological theory, real-world data, interactive branching simulations, and bias-aware scoring. It challenges prior practices that collapse relational competence into a single empathy metric and rely on simplistic scripted scenarios. The benchmark shows that many current agents underperform on critical relational skills—especially handling ambiguity, regulating emotions, and delivering calibrated challenge—and that immersive role-play does not equate to genuine supportiveness. By releasing a bilingual dataset and evaluation tools, the work lays groundwork for rigorous, cross-lingual assessment and targeted improvement of LLM companions’ socio-emotional capabilities.

Abstract: LLM companions are deployed at scale in personally consequential settings, yet poorly evaluated. Existing benchmarks use hand-authored scenarios and prompted simulators, aggregate empathy into one score, and overlook judge biases such as same-family favoritism and scale drift. We introduce CompanionBench, an interactive bilingual benchmark. To our knowledge, it is the first companion benchmark to ground both its scenarios and a trained user simulator in de-identified real-world data. A hidden disclosure gate branches each persona's trajectory on the agent's own behavior, controlling the interaction state space without scripting dialogue. We operationalize ten capabilities derived from 25 theories across psychology and counseling, four of them not graded explicitly by prior work: holding ambiguity, selfobject responsiveness, positive resonance and calibrated challenge. Agents are assessed on two complementary axes: a subjective ten-capability rubric and a deterministic measure of whether deeper disclosure was earned. A cross-family panel dilutes same-family favoritism; an Item Response Theory model separates agent quality from judge severity. Theory fixes what to measure and how personas are structured; real data supply events, history, and profiles -- coverage from theory, authenticity from data. Rankings are reproducible in both languages (rho = 0.996 ZH / 0.953 EN). Evaluating 28 agents reveals capability-level differences obscured by aggregate scores. Emotion regulation and calibrated challenge remain common weaknesses; holding ambiguity discriminates most. Role-play agents rank near the bottom: immersion does not imply relational competence. Across agents, the dominant failure mode is substituting surface warmth for substantive relational support. We will release 500 Chinese-English parallel pairs and the evaluation code.

</details>


### [108] [TextNCA: Neural Cellular Automata for Language Modeling via Hierarchical Local Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02050)
*Avni Mittal,Avinash Anand,Ashutosh Kumar,Dikshant Kukreja,Kritarth Prasad,Sushane Dulloo,Erik Cambria,Timothy Liu,Zhengkui Wang,Rajiv Ratn Shah*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper studies whether a strictly local, iterated, weight-shared Neural Cellular Automaton (NCA)-style primitive can support language modelling, using a 1D windowed-attention model (TextNCA), and finds that the main performance driver is the hierarchical narrow-to-wide window schedule, with iteration providing a smaller, bounded benefit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformers use global, non-local attention and layer-wise parameterization, making it unclear how much of their language modelling power depends on global context vs. structured local computation and iteration. Neural Cellular Automata offer a very different, strictly local and weight-shared computation paradigm. The authors want to understand: (1) can such an NCA-style primitive support competitive language modelling? and (2) among locality, iteration, and weight sharing, which aspects actually matter most for performance? To answer this, they introduce a text-specific NCA model and treat it as an analytical probe rather than a competitor to Transformers.

Method: They define TextNCA, a 1D causal windowed-attention implementation of a Neural Cellular Automaton, and a hierarchical variant (Hier-TextNCA) that processes text in three stages with increasing attention window sizes (w ∈ {8, 32, 128}). Each stage runs T_s iterations with shared weights. They train on WikiText-103 with ~30M parameters and 60k training steps. To dissect which architectural properties matter, they compare: (1) the full hierarchical TextNCA to parameter-matched Transformers, (2) a non-iterating sliding-window Transformer that follows the same narrow-to-wide schedule, and (3) ablations that reverse, flatten, or otherwise disrupt the monotone narrow-to-wide schedule. They also vary the number of iterations T_s, test the presence/absence of a GRU gate and per-step embeddings, and explore training with random T_s to see if it enables iteration-count control at inference time.

Result: Hier-TextNCA underperforms parameter-matched Transformers on WikiText-103 (PPL 60.3 vs. 52.8 for a 6-layer and 44.7 for a 12-layer Transformer). However, a non-iterating sliding-window Transformer that uses the same hierarchical narrow-to-wide schedule achieves perplexity within +4.1 PPL of Hier-TextNCA, indicating that the schedule—rather than iteration or strict NCA structure—is the dominant performance factor. Disrupting the monotone narrow-to-wide schedule (reversing, flattening, or breaking it) severely harms performance, adding between +16.7 and +70.8 PPL. Iteration brings a smaller, bounded improvement on top of the schedule, with best performance at T_s = 4 and degradation for larger iteration counts (a U-shaped curve). The GRU gating mechanism and learned per-step embeddings are necessary for iteration to provide a benefit. Training with random T_s permits inference-time tuning of the iteration count but significantly worsens overall perplexity.

Conclusion: Strictly local, iterated, weight-shared NCA-style computation can support language modelling but is not competitive with standard Transformers at similar scale. The primary source of its modelling power lies in the hierarchical narrow-to-wide window schedule, which a non-iterative model can largely replicate. Iteration confers only a modest, optimal-at-4-steps benefit that depends on specific architectural components (GRU gate and per-step embeddings) and degrades when overused. Thus, in this NCA-inspired setting, scheduling of context expansion is more critical than the raw iterative cellular-automaton-style computation itself. The work serves as a controlled analysis of which NCA-inspired ingredients actually matter for language modelling, rather than as a proposed replacement for Transformers.

Abstract: Can a strictly local, iterated, weight-shared computation primitive support language modelling, and which of those three properties actually drives the model's behaviour? We define \textsc{TextNCA}, a 1D causal windowed-attention realisation of the Neural Cellular Automaton primitive, and study a hierarchical variant that cascades three stages with windows $w \in \{8, 32, 128\}$ and $T_s$ shared-weight iterations per stage, all on WikiText-103 at roughly 30M parameters and 60k training steps. The model does not match a parameter-matched Transformer at this scale (Hier-TextNCA $60.3$ vs.\ Transformer-6L $52.8$ and Transformer-12L $44.7$ PPL), so we treat it as an analytical probe rather than a proposed alternative. The behaviour we observe is largely explained by the staged narrow-to-wide schedule: a non-iterating sliding-window Transformer that reuses the same schedule comes within $+4.1$ PPL of the iterated model, while reversing, flattening, or breaking the monotonic ordering of the schedule costs between $+16.7$ and $+70.8$ PPL. Iteration adds a smaller bounded benefit on top of the schedule, with a clear optimum at $T_s{=}4$ and a U-shaped degradation beyond it. The GRU gate and learned per-step embeddings are required for that benefit to appear, and training with random $T_s$ yields an inference-time iteration-count knob at the cost of substantially higher absolute PPL. We position the work as a controlled reading of which parts of NCA-style computation carry the weight in language modelling.

</details>


### [109] [CAVE: Competence-Aware Visual Boundary Evidence Alignment for Video Temporal Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02078)
*Wei Jia,Zhicong Lu,Yu Chen,Xiang Wang,Shuai Li,Wenqian Lv,Jiayue Cao,Huaxing liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They improve video temporal grounding in large vision-language models by aligning predicted timestamps with boundary-level visual evidence using a new RL-based framework called CAVE.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LVLM-based video temporal grounding methods using reinforcement learning mostly reward only the correctness of the final predicted time interval. This ignores whether the visual evidence the model attends to near the temporal boundaries actually supports those timestamps, causing misalignment between visual attention and predicted boundaries, which the authors find is common across benchmarks.

Method: They propose Competence-Aware Visual Boundary Evidence Alignment (CAVE). First, they add boundary-specific evidence tokens to explicitly capture visual evidence at start and end boundaries. These tokens are initialized via a lightweight supervised warm-up that structures their generation and assigns distinct boundary semantics. Then, during reinforcement learning, they introduce a visual boundary evidence alignment reward that encourages these evidence tokens to focus attention on frames within the ground-truth boundaries, aligning visual evidence with temporal boundaries. Additionally, they design a performance-aware gating mechanism that adaptively controls the strength of evidence supervision: it keeps strong evidence guidance when localization is poor and gradually relaxes it as localization becomes accurate to avoid over-constraining boundary refinement.

Result: On several public video temporal grounding benchmarks, adding CAVE to LVLMs yields consistent performance gains over baseline RL-based methods, demonstrating better alignment between visual evidence and predicted boundaries and overall improved temporal localization accuracy.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling and rewarding boundary-level visual evidence alignment within RL improves video temporal grounding in LVLMs. The CAVE framework, with boundary evidence tokens, alignment rewards, and competence-aware gating, effectively reduces evidence-timestamp misalignment and enhances localization performance across benchmarks.

Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have achieved substantial performance gains in Video Temporal Grounding (VTG) through reinforcement learning (RL). However, existing methods primarily rely on outcome correctness rewards that evaluate only the final predicted intervals, leaving boundary-related visual evidence and its correspondence with timestamp predictions insufficiently constrained. In this paper, we delve into timestamp prediction and its underlying boundary-level visual evidence, showing prevalent misalignment between visual evidence and predicted timestamps across widely used benchmarks. To address this issue, we propose Competence-Aware Visual Boundary Evidence Alignment (CAVE), which augments localization optimization with boundary-specific visual evidence rewards to mitigate evidence-timestamp misalignment. Specifically, to explicitly represent the boundary-specific visual evidence, CAVE introduces boundary-specific evidence tokens and initializes their structured generation and distinct boundary semantics through a lightweight supervised warm-up. During RL, the visual boundary evidence alignment reward reinforces the visual attention of special evidence tokens within the ground-truth boundaries, thereby promoting alignment between visual evidence and temporal boundaries. Moreover, performance-aware gating for evidence supervision is designed to adaptively retain evidence guidance for poorly localized groups while reducing it once localization becomes sufficiently accurate to avoid over-constraining fine-grained boundary refinement. Extensive experiments on several public VTG benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

</details>


### [110] [Cross-Domain Hybrid OPD for Generalizable Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02101)
*Hongzhan Chen,Xiaoyu Liu,Dengming Zhang,Minzhou Huang,Dongliang Xu,Jingcheng Xie,Dongxiang Fang,Bowen Qin,Minsheng Hao,Yaozong Shen,Xiaojun Quan,Mona Zhou,Haosheng Zou,Jeff Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose a training framework for a search-specialized RL agent that avoids losing general-purpose abilities by combining agentic RL with expert distillation, achieving both strong search and broad general intelligence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Specializing language models for search with reinforcement learning often causes an alignment tax: improved search behavior but degraded general-purpose abilities, which weakens their value as universal assistants. The authors want a way to train a search-specialized agent that retains or improves its broad capabilities instead of trading them off.

Method: They build on the Hunyuan3 architecture and introduce a hybrid training strategy: (1) agentic reinforcement learning to train an autonomous search agent capable of sophisticated planning and iterative retrieval over dynamic information sources; (2) a cross-domain expert On-Policy Distillation (OPD) pipeline, where multiple expert models specialized in different general-purpose domains are distilled into the search-specialized student model. This joint procedure is designed so that specialization and general capability are optimized together rather than in conflict.

Result: Experiments show that the resulting Yuanbao search agent reaches competitive performance on search tasks while at the same time consistently improving its general-purpose capabilities compared to baselines that suffer from alignment tax.

Conclusion: By combining agentic RL for search with cross-domain expert on-policy distillation, the training framework behind Yuanbao can specialize a model for search without sacrificing—and even enhancing—its general intelligence, offering a practical balance between specialized execution and broad generalization for real-world search scenarios.

Abstract: Recent advances in Reinforcement Learning (RL) have substantially improved the capabilities of autonomous search agents, enabling sophisticated planning, and iterative retrieval over dynamic information sources. However, optimizing language models for specialized search behaviors often incurs an alignment tax, where gains in search performance come at the expense of general-purpose capabilities, limiting their effectiveness as universal assistants. In this technical report, we present the training framework behind the Yuanbao search agent, designed to achieve search specialization without sacrificing general intelligence. Built upon the Hunyuan3 architecture, our framework combines agentic reinforcement learning for autonomous search with a cross-domain expert On-Policy Distillation (OPD) pipeline. Experts specializing in complementary general-purpose domains are distilled into the search-specialized student, restoring and further enhancing its broad capabilities. Rather than treating specialization and general capability as competing objectives, our hybrid training strategy jointly optimizes both, effectively mitigating the alignment tax. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the resulting model achieves competitive search performance while consistently improving its general-purpose capabilities, providing a favorable balance between specialized execution and broad generalization in real-world search scenarios.

</details>


### [111] [IACM-RL: Intent-Aware Context Management and Reinforcement Learning for Complex Tool Invocation under Dynamic Intent Fluctuations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02110)
*Dingwei Zhu,Jiahan Li,Chengjun Pan,Yunxian Yang,Yunbin Zhao,Yunke Zhang,Zhonghang Lu,Zhuohui Sheng,Chenhao Huang,Jiahang Lin,Yajie Yang,Junlin Shang,Shichun Liu,Yuhui Wang,Honglin Guo,Junjie Ye,Xin Guo,Jiazheng Zhang,Ming Zhang,Shihan Dou,Zhiheng Xi,Tao Gui,Qi Zhang,Xipeng Qiu,Xuanjing Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces IACM-RL, a reinforcement-learning framework that makes tool-using language models robust to noisy, changing user intents over long interaction horizons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In real-world environments, user intents and constraints change over time and are often noisy or inconsistent. Existing tool-use methods for language models mostly assume clean, static instructions and only use simple history scanning or compression for robustness. Under realistic, fluctuating contexts, outdated constraints stay in the context window, distracting the model and causing severe failures such as drifting away from the user’s true current goal or getting stuck in infinite tool-calling loops. The paper aims to address this gap by explicitly modeling and handling dynamic, evolving intent in long-horizon tool invocation.

Method: The authors propose IACM-RL, centered around explicit intent and context management. (1) They build DynamicIntent, a data-generation pipeline that creates trajectories exhibiting 13 types of fine-grained intent fluctuation scenarios, and they define a five-dimensional diagnostic metric suite to evaluate robustness under such dynamics. (2) They design a BeliefState-based Self-Generated Context Manager (CM) that maintains an internal belief state of the current user goal, tracks how it changes over time, and marks outdated parameters with structural stale flags so that obsolete constraints can be isolated from current decision-making. (3) They train the policy via reinforcement learning using a hierarchical intent-driven reward signal that encourages correct goal tracking and tool usage, supplemented by three auxiliary losses: action calibration (aligning predicted actions with desired ones), CM extraction (learning to generate high-quality context management outputs), and state distillation (transferring useful belief-state representations into the policy).

Result: On three benchmarks—DynamicIntent, BFCL-V3, and τ²-Bench—the proposed IACM-RL framework substantially outperforms baseline methods. It notably decreases the frequency of infinite API call loops and errors caused by using stale or outdated context, and it shows better generalization to out-of-domain scenarios compared with prior approaches.

Conclusion: Explicit belief-state tracking and structured context management, optimized via reinforcement learning with auxiliary objectives, can markedly improve the robustness of tool-using language models to noisy, evolving user intents. By generating challenging dynamic-intent benchmarks and demonstrating gains across multiple datasets, the paper argues that robust long-horizon tool invocation requires moving beyond passive history scanning to active, stateful intent modeling.

Abstract: Executing long-horizon tool invocations in real-world environments is severely challenged by dynamic user intent noise. Existing methods attempt robustness via implicit history scanning or text compression, yet predominantly assume perfect instructions in simplistic scenarios. Inevitably, under fluctuating contexts, obsolete constraints dilute model attention, triggering catastrophic intent deviation and infinite API loops. To resolve this, we propose IACM-RL, a comprehensive framework for robust tool invocation. First, we introduce the DynamicIntent pipeline, synthesizing trajectories across 13 fine-grained fluctuation scenarios, paired with a five-dimensional diagnostic metric suite. Second, IACM-RL deploys a BeliefState-based Self-Generated Context Manager that proactively tracks shifting goals and isolates overwritten parameters using structural stale flags. To autonomously internalize this state-tracking capability, we optimize the policy using a hierarchical intent-driven reward alongside three auxiliary losses (action calibration, CM extraction, and state distillation). Experiments on DynamicIntent, BFCL-V3, and $\mathrmτ^2$-Bench demonstrate that IACM-RL significantly outperforms baselines, reducing infinite loops and stale context errors while enhancing out-of-domain generalization.

</details>


### [112] [From Chains to Trees: Parent-Conditioned Drafting for Semi-Autoregressive Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02123)
*Zixian Li,Tong Li,Chi Xie,Xiaohui Song,Haonan Lu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper improves speculative decoding for LLMs by turning DSpark’s linear draft into a branching tree, using the existing Markov head to explore multiple likely continuations per parent token without retraining, leading to higher token acceptance and faster inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Semi-autoregressive speculative decoding methods like DSpark only yield speedups when drafted tokens are accepted by the target model. DSpark’s linear block decoding wastes potential because a mismatch early in the block invalidates the rest, especially for large blocks. The authors aim to exploit the conditional structure already captured by DSpark’s Markov head to better use the verification budget and increase effective acceptance without extra training or backbone passes.

Method: They propose Parent-Conditioned Drafting Tree (PCTree). Starting from DSpark’s one-pass parallel backbone, PCTree uses the pretrained Markov head to independently score multiple candidate children per concrete parent token, forming a tree of possible continuations instead of a single chain. Given a fixed verification budget, the method allocates verification to the most probable paths in this tree, effectively converting DSpark’s linear draft into a branching structure while keeping the backbone computation unchanged.

Result: On Qwen3 models with 4B, 8B, and 14B parameters across nine benchmarks and a draft block size B=7, PCTree yields additional speedups over standard autoregressive decoding that are 3.1%–29.5% better than matched DSpark. On Qwen3-4B with GSM8K and a larger block size B=16, it increases the mean accepted token length from 9.41 to 11.16 and improves mean AR speedup from 6.14× to 6.60× over three runs, demonstrating better utilization of drafted tokens and end-to-end inference gains.

Conclusion: Parent-conditioned branching can transform the conditional modeling capacity already present in semi-autoregressive drafters like DSpark into practical inference speedups. By turning a linear draft into a drafting tree using only inference-time changes and no retraining or extra backbone passes, PCTree improves token acceptance rates and overall decoding speed across multiple model sizes and benchmarks.

Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference only when drafted continuations survive target-model verification. Semi-autoregressive drafters such as DSpark predict an entire token block with one backbone forward and refine it with a lightweight Markov head. However, DSpark decodes this block as a single chain, so an early mismatch invalidates the remaining suffix and limits the benefit of large draft blocks.
  We show that the conditional structure already learned by DSpark can support multiple parent-consistent continuations without retraining or additional backbone passes. We introduce Parent-Conditioned Drafting Tree (PCTree), which uses the pretrained Markov head to score alternative children separately for each concrete parent and allocates a fixed verification budget to the most probable paths. This converts DSpark's linear draft into a tree while preserving its one-pass parallel backbone.
  Across Qwen3-{4B,8B,14B} and nine benchmarks, at $B{=}7$, measured speedup gains over autoregressive (AR) decoding, relative to matched DSpark, range from $3.1\%$ to $29.5\%$. On Qwen3-4B GSM8K at $B{=}16$, PCTree increases mean acceptance length from $9.41$ to $11.16$ and three-run mean AR speedup from $6.14{\times}$ to $6.60{\times}$. These show that parent-conditioned branching can turn conditional capacity already present in a semi-autoregressive drafter into end-to-end inference gains through an inference-only change.

</details>


### [113] [The Role of Disfluencies in Speech Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02138)
*Maike Züfle,Maria Teleki,Fabian Retkowski,Vilém Zouhar,Oliver Grabner,Alexander Waibel,James Caverlee,Jan Niehues*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that removing speech disfluencies (like false starts) in translation harms meaning, introduces a multilingual benchmark with annotated disfluencies, and demonstrates decoding strategies to better preserve them without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most speech translation and SpeechLLM systems are trained on clean, edited text, so at inference they tend to delete disfluencies such as filled pauses and false starts rather than translate them. However, in real-world conversations these disfluencies can carry important pragmatic or semantic information. The field lacks systematic evaluation resources to understand how this “cleaning” affects translation quality across languages and models, and it is unclear which types of disfluencies are most harmful when dropped.

Method: The authors construct Uh-Mazing, a benchmark built from the Switchboard corpus of conversational English. They annotate disfluencies (e.g., filled pauses, discourse markers, false starts, self-repairs) and obtain human translations from English into eight target languages. Using this benchmark, they evaluate multiple speech translation architectures and SpeechLLMs, measuring how different disfluency types impact translation quality. They analyze error patterns to see whether models omit or mistranslate disfluencies and experiment with inference-time decoding strategies—without model retraining—to encourage better preservation of disfluent material.

Result: Across eight target languages and several model architectures, the study finds that false starts and self-repairs are the main sources of translation-quality degradation when disfluencies are removed or mishandled, whereas filled pauses and discourse markers have comparatively minor impact. When models fail to preserve a disfluency, they typically omit it entirely instead of producing an incorrect translation. Adjusted decoding strategies at inference time can significantly reduce this loss of disfluency information without any additional training or fine-tuning of the models.

Conclusion: Cleaning conversational speech before or during translation is not harmless: certain disfluencies, especially false starts and self-repairs, encode important meaning that current systems frequently drop, leading to measurable quality loss. A fine-grained, multilingual benchmark such as Uh-Mazing enables systematic analysis of these effects. Moreover, targeted inference-time decoding methods can partially correct this behavior without retraining, suggesting a practical path toward more faithful speech translation that preserves pragmatically relevant disfluencies. The benchmark and released code provide a foundation for future work on disfluency-aware speech translation models.

Abstract: Current speech translation systems, including SpeechLLMs, are trained on cleaned text and tend to strip disfluencies like filled pauses and false starts rather than translate them. We show this comes at a cost: disfluencies carry meaning that gets lost when speech is cleaned up. To study this systematically, we introduce Uh-Mazing, a benchmark of human-translated, disfluency-annotated Switchboard speech covering English into eight target languages. Across these languages and several architectures, we find that false starts and self-repairs, not filled pauses or discourse markers, drive most of the translation-quality loss, and that models which fail to preserve a disfluency tend to omit it rather than mistranslate it. We show inference-time decoding can mitigate this without retraining, and release the benchmark and code.

</details>


### [114] [Self-Improving Large Language Models via Progressive Experience Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02139)
*Shijie Ren,Xiting Wang,Meng Li,Yujie Guo,Yunhang Yao,Ziheng Peng,Xunlong Wang,Yuetan Chen,Haoyang Zhou,Yunlong Liang,Fandong Meng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes SPEE, a unified post-training framework that distills interaction experience into model parameters to enable self-improving LLMs, outperforming existing test-time and training-time self-evolution methods on math reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current self-improvement approaches for LLMs are fragmented: test-time methods can leverage interaction traces but cannot update model weights, while training-time methods can optimize parameters but lack an explicit representation and accumulation of reusable experience. There is a missing intermediate stage—experience distillation—that can bridge explicit experience extraction and implicit policy optimization.

Method: The authors introduce SPEE (Self-Progressive Experience Evolution), a two-stage post-training framework. First, an experience evolution stage reflects over multi-interaction trajectories to extract, verify, refine, and progressively evolve transferable experience, storing it in a global experience pool that incorporates both successes and failures while filtering low-utility or post-hoc rationalized patterns. This distilled experience then guides a privilege-based On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) step that internalizes the experience into the model’s policy. Second, an implicit policy optimization stage uses reinforcement learning, with rewards, to further optimize the model, using the distilled experience as priors to explore better strategies.

Result: On five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and across three model sizes, SPEE consistently outperforms both test-time self-evolution approaches (which only adapt at inference) and training-time self-evolution baselines (which only optimize parameters without explicit experience evolution).

Conclusion: Experience distillation is a crucial missing component for self-improving LLMs, and SPEE provides an effective unified framework to realize it. By explicitly evolving a global experience pool and then internalizing it via self-distillation and RL, models can more reliably convert interaction trajectories into persistent capabilities, leading to superior performance on challenging reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) capable of self-improvement require not only effective policy optimization, but also a principled mechanism for transforming transient interaction experience into persistent model capabilities. Existing self-improvement paradigms remain fragmented: test-time methods can explicitly extract experience but cannot internalize it into model parameters, whereas training-time optimization methods can update model parameters but lack an explicit mechanism for accumulating transferable experience. Bridging these two paradigms requires a critical intermediate stage that remains underexplored, namely \emph{experience distillation}. To address this gap, we propose \textbf{SPEE} (\textbf{S}elf-\textbf{P}rogressive \textbf{E}xperience \textbf{E}volution), a unified post-training framework that sequentially performs explicit experience evolution followed by implicit policy optimization. During explicit experience evolution, SPEE reflects on trajectories collected from multiple interactions to extract, verify, and progressively evolve transferable experience, which is subsequently internalized into the policy through privilege-guided On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD). During implicit policy optimization, reward-driven reinforcement learning leverages these internalized priors to explore novel solution strategies. In the experience evolution stage, a continuously evolving global experience pool consolidates knowledge from both successful and failed trajectories, filters out low-utility experience, and mitigates post-hoc rationalization induced by individual trajectories. Experiments on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that SPEE consistently outperforms both test-time and training-time self-evolution baselines across three model scales. The source code is available at https://github.com/rrrsj/SPEE.

</details>


### [115] [Domain-Specific Evaluation of Text-to-Speech Systems: A Multi-Metric Benchmarking Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02235)
*Ali Jafar,Amal Sarmad,Shifa Yousaf,Maryam Bashir*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes and demonstrates a reproducible, multi-metric benchmarking framework to evaluate modern TTS systems across speech domains, focusing on a low-resource language.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While neural TTS quality has improved, there is no comprehensive, standardized way to jointly evaluate perceptual quality, speaker similarity, and acoustic fidelity across different speech domains, especially for low-resource and underrepresented languages. This gap makes it difficult to compare systems fairly, understand domain-specific weaknesses (e.g., emotional speech), and advance TTS for these languages.

Method: The authors design a multi-metric evaluation framework combining subjective and objective measures. They apply it to a low-resource language across four domains (Formal, Conversational, Literary/Storytelling, Emotional). Four state-of-the-art TTS systems (Indic-Parler-TTS, MMS-TTS, Microsoft Edge TTS, Google Gemini TTS) are evaluated. Subjective tests include MUSHRA listening tests and ABX discrimination tests; objective metrics include speaker similarity scores using Resemblyzer and acoustic fidelity measures via mel-cepstral distortion (MCD) and F0 RMSE, computed over 960 audio pairs. All scripts, tables, and Colab notebooks are made publicly available for reproducibility.

Result: Across the four TTS systems and four domains, performance varies substantially by domain. Emotional speech is the hardest to synthesize well, showing the worst acoustic metrics (mean MCD 12.03 dB and mean F0 RMSE 889 cents), while conversational speech exhibits the best overall acoustic fidelity. The framework successfully differentiates systems and domains in a fine-grained way using both subjective and objective metrics.

Conclusion: The proposed framework offers a reproducible, multi-dimensional way to benchmark modern TTS systems, especially for low-resource languages and different speech domains. Emotional speech remains a major challenge, whereas conversational speech is comparatively well handled. By releasing all evaluation assets, the work aims to standardize TTS evaluation practices and support future research targeting domain- and language-specific improvements.

Abstract: Recent advances in neural text-to-speech (TTS) systems have substantially improved speech naturalness and intelligibility across many languages. However, comprehensive evaluation methodologies that jointly assess perceptual quality, speaker similarity, and acoustic fidelity across diverse speech domains remain limited, particularly for low-resource and underrepresented languages. This paper presents a reproducible, multi-metric benchmarking framework for systematic evaluation of modern TTS systems through domain-specific analysis. The proposed framework integrates complementary subjective and objective evaluation protocols and is demonstrated through a comprehensive case study on a representative low-resource language spanning four speech domains: Formal, Conversational, Literary/Storytelling, and Emotional. Four state-of-the-art TTS systems -- Indic-Parler-TTS, MMS-TTS, Microsoft Edge TTS, and Google Gemini TTS -- are evaluated using MUSHRA listening tests, ABX discrimination tests, speaker similarity scoring with Resemblyzer, and acoustic analyses based on mel-cepstral distortion (MCD) and F0 RMSE over 960 audio pairs. Results reveal substantial variation in TTS performance across speech domains, with emotional speech consistently presenting the greatest synthesis challenge (mean MCD 12.03 dB; mean F0 RMSE 889 cents), while conversational speech achieves the highest overall acoustic fidelity. Beyond the empirical findings, this work provides a reproducible evaluation framework, publicly releasing evaluation scripts, result tables, and executable Colab notebooks to support standardized benchmarking and future research on TTS evaluation for low-resource languages.

</details>


### [116] [An Evidence-Grounded Retrieval-Augmented Transformer Framework for Health Misinformation Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02310)
*Isah M. Bukar,Bala Mairiga Abduljalil,Bashir Saleh Maina,Abdulbasit Hassan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes and evaluates a retrieval-augmented transformer framework for verifying health-related claims in Nigeria, showing that a BERT-based model performs best but that limited evidence resources currently constrain the benefits of retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Health misinformation spreads quickly online and can seriously undermine outbreak response, especially in developing countries where timely, locally relevant verification is scarce. Existing automated misinformation detection systems mainly use global biomedical resources and therefore miss local epidemiological, linguistic, and contextual nuances, making them less effective for countries like Nigeria. The authors aim to build a more context-aware, evidence-driven verification system that uses trusted international and national health authorities while being tailored to local diseases and information ecosystems.

Method: The authors design a retrieval-augmented transformer framework that first retrieves semantically relevant evidence from a curated corpus of documents from the World Health Organization and the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention, and then feeds the claim and retrieved evidence into a transformer-based classifier to label the claim as true, false, or misleading. They compile and manually annotate a dataset of 67 Nigerian health claims related to COVID-19, Lassa fever, cholera, measles, and monkeypox, using local fact-checking sources as ground truth. Three transformer architectures and a retrieval-augmented configuration are trained and compared, focusing on classification performance metrics such as accuracy and weighted F1-score.

Result: Among the tested models, a BERT-based transformer achieves the highest performance, with accuracy of 71% and a weighted F1-score of 0.66 on the annotated Nigerian health-claims dataset. The retrieval-augmented version does not outperform the plain transformer models, largely because the current evidence repository from WHO and NCDC is limited in size and coverage, which restricts the quality and completeness of retrieved evidence.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that transformer-based models can effectively support health misinformation verification in a Nigerian context, even with relatively small datasets, and that carefully curated, authoritative knowledge sources are critical for improving reliability. While the present retrieval augmentation does not yet yield performance gains, the framework is a promising foundation for future systems that combine richer, locally relevant evidence with advanced language models to provide context-aware, evidence-driven verification in Nigeria and other resource-constrained environments.

Abstract: The rapid spread of false and misleading health information through digital platforms has become a major public health challenge, particularly during infectious disease outbreaks where delayed verification can influence public behaviour and hinder effective disease control. Although recent advances in automated health misinformation detection have shown encouraging results, most existing approaches rely heavily on global biomedical resources and often fail to capture the local context needed to verify claims in developing countries. This study presents a retrieval-augmented transformer framework designed to verify health-related claims using trusted evidence from the World Health Organization and the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention. The framework combines semantic evidence retrieval with transformer-based classification to determine whether a claim is true, false, or misleading. To evaluate the proposed approach, a manually annotated dataset of 67 verified health claims covering coronavirus disease, Lassa fever, cholera, measles, and monkeypox was compiled from Nigerian fact-checking sources.
  Three transformer models and a retrieval-augmented configuration were evaluated. The Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers model achieved the best performance, with an accuracy of 71% and a weighted F1-score of 0.66. Although retrieval augmentation did not improve classification performance because the current evidence repository was limited in size and coverage, the findings highlight the importance of comprehensive and authoritative knowledge sources for reliable health misinformation verification. The proposed framework provides a practical foundation for developing context-aware and evidence-driven health misinformation verification systems for Nigeria and other resource-constrained settings.

</details>


### [117] [Can AI Agents Simulate A/B Test Outcomes? A Validation Framework for Agentic Experimentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02345)
*Stefan Hut,Lorenzo Masoero*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes using AI agents to simulate A/B tests (Simulated RCTs) as a faster, cheaper pre-screening tool before running real online experiments, and develops a framework and calibrations that substantially improve prediction accuracy and precision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Running traditional A/B tests is costly in traffic, time, and engineering resources. With increasingly powerful behavioral AI models, the authors ask whether these models can act as stand-ins for real users to forecast experimental outcomes, so that only the most promising variants are shipped to live traffic. However, there is no formal framework to quantify and decompose the errors involved in such simulations or to validate how well they recover real-world treatment effects.

Method: The authors define Simulated Randomized Controlled Trials (S-RCTs), where AI agents replace human users in an RCT framework. They derive a two-layer error decomposition that separates (1) agent approximation error (how well the model mimics user behavior) from (2) subsampling error (variance from finite samples of agents/contexts). The framework is agent-agnostic and can work with specialized or general-purpose foundation models. Empirically, they apply S-RCTs to 67 historical marketing A/B tests, first using an off-the-shelf foundation model as the simulation engine, then introducing a two-phase pre-period calibration protocol and a within-subject design (same agent exposed to both arms) to reduce bias and variance in the simulated treatment effect estimates.

Result: Using an off-the-shelf foundation model, S-RCTs recover the correct direction of treatment effects in 70% of the 67 historical marketing experiments but tend to overestimate effect magnitudes.
