After applying the two-phase pre-period calibration, the squared prediction error (net of irreducible measurement noise) decreases by about 77×. Additionally, adopting a within-subject design in the simulations reduces standard errors of the estimated effects by approximately 2.4×, leading to more precise estimates.

Conclusion: AI agents can provide useful, though imperfect, signals about the outcomes of online experiments before committing real user traffic. With appropriate calibration and experimental design (e.g., within-subject S-RCTs), simulated RCTs can achieve substantial gains in accuracy and precision over naive approaches, making them potentially valuable as a pre-screening or decision-support tool. The approach is flexible across models, but current limitations remain, and the authors outline contexts where agentic simulation is most likely to be beneficial rather than a replacement for real A/B testing.

Abstract: A/B testing remains the standard for rolling out new features in the technology industry. Each experiment, however, consumes real traffic, engineering effort, and weeks of wall-clock time. Can AI agents---conditioned on behavioral profiles and contextual descriptions of the intervention---simulate outcomes accurately enough to vet candidate treatments before committing live traffic? We formalize this question as a \emph{Simulated Randomized Controlled Trial} (S-RCT) and derive a two-layer error decomposition that separates agent approximation error from subsampling error, enabling targeted improvements to each. The framework is agent-agnostic: any behavioral model---from a fine-tuned specialist to a general-purpose foundation model---can serve as the simulation engine. Validated on 67 historical marketing A/B tests, a baseline S-RCT using an off-the-shelf foundation model captures directional signal (sign overlap 0.70) but systematically overshoots effect magnitudes. A two-phase pre-period calibration protocol reduces the squared prediction error (after removing irreducible measurement noise) by ${\sim}77\times$; a within-subject design---where each agent is exposed to both arms---reduces standard errors by ${\sim}2.4\times$. We discuss limitations of the current approach and identify applications where experimenters stand to benefit from agentic signals.

</details>


### [118] [Global Optimization and Inference-Time Region Grafting for Agentic Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02353)
*Donghyeok Koh,Gyuwan Kim,Jinyeong Bak,Seung-Hoon Na,Tao Yang,Haneol Jang,Cheoneum Park*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: GRAFT is a method for adapting parts of an already-optimized agentic workflow at inference time using label-free execution-quality signals, without retraining or re-optimizing the whole workflow, leading to better performance across several tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agentic workflow optimization methods fix the workflow before execution, so they cannot adapt when parts of the workflow fail or underperform for specific inputs. Fully re-optimizing the workflow at inference time for each input would be too computationally expensive. There is a need for a method that can locally adapt workflows per instance, using signals available at execution time, while preserving the benefits of a globally optimized workflow.

Method: The authors propose GRAFT, a framework that starts from a globally optimized workflow and then, for each input, selectively considers local alternative sub-workflows (regions). Without any parameter training, GRAFT scores these local alternatives using label-free execution-quality metrics (signals derived from the behavior of the system rather than ground-truth labels). It only accepts replacements that improve local quality and maintain consistency with the rest of the workflow, thus enabling instance-wise local adaptation without recomputing or re-optimizing the whole workflow structure.

Result: Across diverse tasks including mathematical reasoning, code generation, multi-hop question answering, and knowledge-intensive QA, GRAFT outperforms the prior state-of-the-art workflow optimization approach MaAS by an average of 3.85 points under matched optimizer and executor conditions. Additionally, swapping in a stronger executor model on top of the same globally optimized workflow yields further performance gains, without needing to redo the workflow optimization.

Conclusion: An optimized workflow should be viewed not as a static, once-and-for-all structure, but as an adaptable execution policy that can be locally modified at inference time using label-free quality feedback. GRAFT demonstrates that preserving the global workflow while selectively replacing underperforming regions can significantly improve performance, is computationally efficient, and continues to pay dividends as executors improve.

Abstract: Recent advances in agentic workflow optimization automate workflow design through task-specific workflow search or input-conditioned architecture selection. However, they determine the workflow before execution and cannot adapt failed workflow regions using execution-time label-free quality signals. Naively enabling such inference-time adaptation through whole-workflow re-optimization would be computationally prohibitive. To tackle this challenge, we introduce GRAFT, which preserves a globally optimized workflow while locally replacing only selected regions for each input. Without parameter training, GRAFT evaluates region-level alternatives using label-free execution-quality signals and accepts only replacements that improve local quality while preserving workflow-level consistency, thereby enabling instance-wise adaptation without whole-workflow re-optimization. GRAFT applies without modification across a range of tasks spanning mathematical reasoning, code generation, and multi-hop and knowledge-intensive question answering. Under matched optimizer and executor settings, it improves over the strongest prior workflow-optimization method, MaAS, by 3.85 points on average. Replacing only the executor with a stronger model yields further gains without re-optimizing the global workflow. This suggests that an optimized workflow is not merely a static optimization artifact, but an adaptable execution policy that can evolve with inference-time feedback and stronger executors.

</details>


### [119] [ScrambleToolBench: Agents Search Exhaustively Even When Their Own Map Points to the Next Step](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02358)
*Vernon Toh,Navonil Majumder,Zhengyuan Liu,Nancy F. Chen,Soujanya Poria*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They introduce ScrambleToolBench, a benchmark where agents must learn scrambled tools purely via interaction, showing that current language-model agents can discover behaviors but adapt poorly to changing tool mappings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most existing tool-use benchmarks leak semantic information (names, descriptions, static schemas), so agents can exploit prior knowledge instead of genuinely inferring how unfamiliar tools behave, which is unrealistic for open-world autonomous operation. The authors want a setting that isolates behavioral reasoning and tests whether agents can discover and revise models of tools based solely on interaction, especially when the environment changes over time.

Method: They design ScrambleToolBench, an interactive terminal-based benchmark that hides semantic cues about tools and requires agents to complete a continuous curriculum of tasks. Tool behaviors are scrambled, forcing trial-and-error discovery. The environment includes dynamic phenomena—mapping drift (tool-behavior remapping), stochastic action failures, and time-limited execution windows—so agents must update their hypotheses as conditions change. They then evaluate state-of-the-art language model agents with different settings (e.g., varying test-time reasoning and persistent memory) on this benchmark.

Result: Language model agents can often discover initial tool behaviors, but struggle substantially when the environment undergoes structural changes like mapping drift. Rather than using principled, deductive strategies (e.g., cycle tracing to detect remappings), agents tend to stick with outdated beliefs or resort to expensive brute-force search. Increasing test-time reasoning mainly expands this search effort instead of enabling smarter inference. Adding persistent memory reduces some error accumulation but does not solve the core difficulty of efficiently recognizing and adapting to structural changes.

Conclusion: ScrambleToolBench exposes a significant gap between current language-model agents’ ability to discover tool behaviors and their ability to adapt those beliefs as tools and environments change. Existing agents display belief inertia and brute-force strategies instead of robust, deductive behavioral reasoning, even with more reasoning time or persistent memory. The benchmark thus provides a targeted way to study and improve adaptive behavioral reasoning in open-world tool use.

Abstract: To operate robustly in open-world environments, autonomous agents should be able to infer the behavior of unfamiliar systems through interaction alone, even in the absence of documentation. However, existing tool-use benchmarks expose semantic tool schemas in static environments, allowing agents to rely on prior knowledge rather than autonomous discovery. To address this limitation, we introduce ScrambleToolBench, an interactive terminal benchmark designed to isolate behavioral reasoning. By removing semantic cues and enforcing a continuous task curriculum, the benchmark requires agents to uncover hidden tool behaviors entirely through trial-and-error interaction. The benchmark further introduces dynamic challenges, including mapping drift, stochastic action failures, and temporal execution windows, to evaluate whether agents can revise and adapt their hypotheses as the environment changes. Our evaluation of state-of-the-art language models reveals that successful initial discovery does not translate into robust adaptation. When faced with structural changes such as mapping drift, agents fail to use deductive strategies such as cycle tracing, and instead exhibit belief inertia or fall back to exhaustive search. Increasing test-time reasoning only amplifies this expensive brute-force search rather than enabling deductive recovery. While equipping agents with persistent memory reduces compounding errors, they remain unable to efficiently infer structural changes, highlighting a gap in current agent reasoning.

</details>


### [120] [Fast and Accurate Quotation Attribution in Literary Texts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02359)
*Gaspard Michel,Hugo Attali,Elena V. Epure*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They introduce an efficient encoder-based method (“joint scoring”) for attributing quotations to speakers in novels, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy much faster than existing methods and LLMs, and release it in a tool called ModernBookNLP.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quoting attribution in literary texts is still difficult: existing independent-prediction models are fast but not accurate enough, while LLM-based solutions are accurate but computationally too expensive for large-scale literary analysis. There is a need for a method that is both highly accurate and efficient on long novels.

Method: They formulate quotation attribution as a joint scoring problem over a large shared context window using an encoder-based architecture. Instead of predicting each quotation’s speaker in isolation, the model processes many quotations and candidate speakers together, leveraging long-range context and anaphora resolution signals already present in pretrained encoders. They evaluate on the PDNC corpus of 35,000+ manually annotated quotations from 22 English novels and integrate their best model into a modified BookNLP pipeline (ModernBookNLP).

Result: On the PDNC corpus, the joint scoring model achieves 94.5% overall attribution accuracy, setting a new state of the art. It processes novels about 20× faster than standard independent-prediction methods and over 1000× faster than LLM-based approaches on an A100 GPU. Representation analyses show improvements especially on hard cases where long-range anaphoric information is crucial.

Conclusion: Joint scoring over a shared large context window is an effective and computationally efficient way to attribute quotations in novels, surpassing prior methods in both accuracy and speed. Pretrained encoders already encode useful long-range anaphora signals, and leveraging them jointly yields strong gains. The released ModernBookNLP system makes the method accessible for large-scale literary studies.

Abstract: Attributing quotations to their speakers in literary texts remains an open challenge. Standard methods, which independently predict a speaker mention for each quotation, are efficient but still limited in accuracy. In contrast, large language model (LLM) approaches achieve strong performance, but their computational cost limits their use in large-scale literary analysis. We propose an encoder-based efficient formulation that resolves multiple quotation attributions within a shared, large context window. Using our new formulation, \textit{joint scoring}, we report state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on the Project Dialogism Novel Corpus (PDNC), comprising more than 35,000 manually annotated quotations from 22 English novels. Our best model reaches 94.5\% overall attribution accuracy while processing novels $20\times$ faster than comparable standard methods and more than $1000\times$ faster than LLM-based approaches on an A100 GPU. An analysis of models' representations suggests that joint scoring improves on challenging attribution examples by preserving long-range anaphora resolution signal, an information that we found already present in pretrained encoders. To facilitate adoption, we release ModernBookNLP, a modified fork of BookNLP that replaces its quotation attribution model with our best system available at https://github.com/gasmichel/ModernBookNLP_QA/.

</details>


### [121] [PredAct-Bench: Benchmarking Tool-Augmented Dialogue under Controlled Tool Noise](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02372)
*Abdulrahman AlRabah,Xiaocheng Yang,Dilek Hakkani-Tür,Abdussalam Alawini*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces PREDACTBENCH, a benchmark to evaluate how dialogue agents using imperfect prediction tools support human decision-making in education, focusing on trust and reliance under noisy conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most LLM benchmarks assume perfectly accurate tools and ignore that, in real high-stakes settings like education, healthcare, and finance, tools are noisy and human trust in AI is uncertain. There is a need to systematically evaluate how AI assistants behave when their tools are statistically imperfect and when humans might over- or under-rely on them, particularly in multi-step decision-making tasks.

Method: The authors construct PREDACTBENCH, an education-focused benchmark where LLM-based dialogue agents interact with users while leveraging noisy predictive tools to support intervention decisions (e.g., about students). They define episode-level metrics—Relative AI-Reliance (RAIR) and Relative self-reliance (RSR)—that extend prior trust calibration notions to multi-turn dialogue. They then test 13 closed- and open-source LLMs on two educational datasets (OULAD and PREDACT-CS) and run a human study with instructors and TAs to see how well models help teachers calibrate their reliance on AI suggestions under noisy conditions.

Result: Experiments on OULAD and PREDACT-CS, plus a human study, show that state-of-the-art LLMs do not adequately manage uncertainty or expose tool noisiness to users. Instead of fostering appropriately calibrated reliance, models often fail to prevent over-reliance on incorrect predictions or hallucinated information when tools are imperfect.

Conclusion: PREDACTBENCH reveals that current LLMs, when paired with noisy tools, are not yet reliable decision-support partners for teachers because they fail to promote appropriate human reliance. The benchmark and proposed RAIR/RSR metrics provide a structured way to evaluate and improve LLM-based decision-support systems in education, with implications for designing better AI assistance in other high-stakes domains.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in task-oriented dialogue systems that support multi-step decision-making in high-stakes domains such as education, healthcare, and finance. However, existing benchmarks typically assume perfectly accurate tool outputs, overlooking the reality that deployed systems must operate with noisy tools and human decision-makers whose trust in the agent is itself uncertain. Such conditions are common in practice, for example, a clinician using a diagnostic prediction tool or an advisor relying on a model that forecasts student outcomes from historical records. We introduce PREDACTBENCH, a benchmark for evaluating dialogue agents paired with statistically imperfect tools, using education as a measurable testbed where ground truth outcomes and clear intervention decisions are available. First, we build a benchmark for AI-assisted human decision-making, where the AI uses noisy predictors to help guide a user. Second, we introduce episode-level Relative AI-Reliance (RAIR) and Relative self-reliance (RSR) metrics, extending prior trust calibration framework to multi-turn dialogue. Third, we evaluate 13 state-of-the-art closed and open source LLMs on two educational datasets, OULAD (real assessment trajectories from the UK Open University) and PREDACT-CS (60 courses with real final grade outcomes and synthetically generated weekly score trajectories), alongside a human study with instructors and teaching assistants. We find that when tools are noisy, SOTA models are supposed to provide visibility to teachers so that they do not over-rely on wrong suggestions or hallucinations, but current models fail to do that. We offer PREDACTBENCH to help build better LLMs as AI decision support systems to help teachers.

</details>


### [122] [Training-Free versus Training-Based Intent Classification in LLMs: Accuracy, Robustness, and Failure Modes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02415)
*Nan Chen,Zhouhao Yang,Soufiane Hayou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how well training-free vs training-based methods can classify user intent (e.g., math, coding, general text) from LLM prompts, finding that both work well on easy tasks, training-based wins on hard tasks, and training-free is more robust to tricky prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Intent classification is crucial for routing user prompts to specialized LLMs, which boosts accuracy and efficiency. However, it is unclear when simple, training-free methods based on internal LLM representations are sufficient and when more complex, trained classifiers (like MLPs or linear probes) are necessary. The authors aim to systematically compare these approaches across varying task difficulties and robustness conditions.

Method: They perform a systematic empirical study that compares two lightweight, training-free intent classification methods—both using statistics of internal LLM representations—against training-based classifiers, specifically MLP classifiers and linear probes. The evaluation spans simple and hard intent distinctions (e.g., broad domains like math vs coding vs natural language, and finer-grained ones like Java vs Python), and tests robustness to mixed-intent and adversarial prompts.

Result: (1) On easy intent classification benchmarks such as distinguishing mathematics, coding, and natural language prompts, both training-free and training-based approaches achieve near-saturated performance. (2) On harder intent classification tasks that require fine-grained distinctions (like Java vs Python), training-based classifiers significantly outperform the training-free baselines. (3) On robustness tests involving mixed-intent prompts and adversarially crafted inputs, training-free methods generally show better robustness than the training-based methods.

Conclusion: Training-free methods using internal representation statistics are surprisingly strong for coarse-grained intent classification and offer robustness advantages, making them attractive when labels or training budgets are limited or robustness is a priority. However, for fine-grained or more challenging intent distinctions, training-based classifiers (MLPs and linear probes) provide superior accuracy, so practitioners should choose methods based on the difficulty and robustness requirements of their routing task.

Abstract: Intent classification in Large Language Models (LLMs) involves categorizing user prompts into predefined classes. For instance, given a user prompt, the system must determine whether it primarily concerns mathematics, coding, or general text processing. Such classification enables routing prompts to specialized models optimized for specific domains, improving both accuracy and computational efficiency. In this work, we conduct a systematic study comparing training-free vs training-based approaches for intent classification. For this purpose, we consider two lightweight, training-free methods based on statistics of internal representations and compare them against MLP classifiers and linear probes. Our comprehensive empirical evaluation reveals that 1) Both training-free and training-based methods saturate easy benchmarks (mathematics vs. coding vs. natural language), 2) Training-based classifiers have an advantage on harder classification tasks (e.g. Java vs Python), and 3) Training-free methods are generally more robust to mixed-intent and adversarial prompts.

</details>


### [123] [CTRAG: An In-Context Retrieval-based Framework for Automated Compliance Checking using LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02472)
*Muhammad Roman,Karen Rafferty,Barry Devereux*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CTRAG is an automated RAG-based system for checking regulatory compliance by matching regulatory control questions with company documents, improving accuracy and reducing manual effort.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual regulatory compliance checking is slow, inconsistent, and especially difficult when compliance is indirect via third-party services like cloud providers. There is a need for a more automated, reliable way to verify compliance across domains like finance, privacy, and cybersecurity using unstructured documentation.

Method: The paper introduces CTRAG, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline tailored for compliance checking. It uses adaptive chunking of documents, dynamic retrieval settings, and in-context learning. CTRAG automatically extracts control questions from regulatory texts, retrieves relevant content from company documentation (including evidence of third-party-based compliance), and uses LLM-based reasoning to determine compliance status.

Result: In empirical tests and a real-world POC at a Big Four firm, CTRAG achieved an F1-score of 78% and recall of 85% in its final configuration. This reduced missed non-compliance cases and lowered manual reviewer workload compared with traditional manual checks.

Conclusion: CTRAG demonstrates that specialized RAG pipelines can reliably automate large parts of regulatory compliance verification, including cases involving third-party services. It improves accuracy, reduces effort, and can strengthen trust and risk management in highly regulated environments.

Abstract: Trust is fundamental in modern regulatory ecosystems, and compliance checking plays a critical role in fostering that trust. Regulatory compliance verification is essential for businesses operating in highly controlled environments, as it ensures alignment with sector-specific guidelines across domains such as financial reporting, data privacy, and cybersecurity. Manual compliance testing, however, is often time-intensive and prone to inconsistencies, particularly when compliance depends indirectly on third-party services such as cloud providers, where vendors rely on external providers to meet regulatory standards. In this paper, we present CTRAG, a novel Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline designed for automated compliance checking. CTRAG employs advanced strategies, including adaptive chunking, dynamic retrieval configurations, and in-context learning, to improve the precision and relevance of compliance assessments. By extracting control questions from regulatory texts and cross-referencing them with unstructured company documentation, CTRAG achieves highly accurate, document-informed compliance verification, even in cases of indirect compliance through third-party services. Empirical evaluations demonstrate significant improvements, with CTRAG achieving an F1-score of 78% and a recall of 85% in the final deployed configuration, ensuring minimal missed non-compliance cases while reducing manual reviewer effort in a real-world deployment. To validate CTRAG value, we developed and deployed a POC within a Big Four professional services firm, applying it to real-world cases and cross-checking results against manual compliance reports. These findings highlight CTRAG potential to streamline compliance workflows, mitigate risks, and enhance regulatory trust in complex, high-stakes environments.

</details>


### [124] [Cultural Awareness is Represented but Not Decoded: Tracing Mythological Knowledge across 18 Open-Source LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02486)
*Iaroslav Chelombitko,Ekaterina Chelombitko,Mika Hämäläinen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Paper studies why open-source LLMs default to Greco-Norse gods (Zeus, Jupiter, Thor) and fail on less-represented mythologies, and finds the problem lies in the decoder readout, not internal representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs show cultural bias: they easily recall deities from dominant Western mythologies but struggle with counterparts in Finnish, Slavic, Egyptian, or Chinese traditions. The authors want to understand *where* in the model this bias arises—whether the model’s internal representations already encode diverse cultures but the output layer collapses them, or whether the issue is in the representations themselves. This matters for diagnosing and fixing cultural bias in LLMs.

Method: They construct a cross-cultural dataset of mythological entities aligned via Thompson motifs, spanning multiple traditions. Using 18 open-source LLMs from 8 architecture families, they apply four main analysis techniques: (1) linear probing to test whether culture-specific information is linearly decodable from hidden states; (2) logit lens to inspect token logits layer-by-layer; (3) activation patching to see how manipulating intermediate activations affects outputs; and (4) output extraction to analyze final token predictions. They compare English prompts versus prompts in each culture’s native language and introduce tests for language-conditioned behavior.

Result: Hidden residual stream activations clearly encode cultural distinctions between mythological entities, beating a simple name-string baseline, showing that internal representations differentiate cultures. However, the decoder tends to map culturally specific tokens to dominant-tradition deities (e.g., Zeus-like answers) instead of the correct local figures. Errors correlate strongly within a given prompt language but diverge across languages, indicating the decoder’s behavior is gated by the language of the input. They provide per-entity analyses and predictions for all 18 models.

Conclusion: The main locus of cultural default bias in these LLMs is the readout/decoder rather than the internal representations: models internally distinguish less-represented mythologies but the output layer collapses them to dominant Western figures, especially in English prompts. Decoder behavior is strongly conditioned on prompt language. The authors release a framework, dataset, and analysis tools to study and potentially correct such language- and culture-conditioned readout failures in LLMs.

Abstract: Open-source LLMs reliably name Zeus, Jupiter, and Thor, but recover their counterparts in less-represented traditions like Finnish, Slavic, Egyptian, or Chinese mythology far less consistently. We ask where inside the model this cultural default is produced. On a parallel cross-cultural substrate of Thompson-motif entities, we instrument 18 open-source LLMs from 8 architecture families with linear probing, logit lens, activation patching, and output extraction. The residual stream cleanly distinguishes cultures, well above a name-string baseline, yet the decoder collapses culturally-specific tokens onto dominant-tradition ones. The failure is at readout, not at representation. Asking the same question in the target culture's native language versus English produces failures that cluster within language but decouple across language: the decoder is gated on prompt language. We release a per-entity (probe, output) decomposition framework, a citation-anchored cross-cultural ground truth, a within- versus cross-mode correlation test for language-conditioned readout, and per-entity predictions for all 18 models.

</details>


### [125] [LiveMem: Maintaining Memory State Continuity in Long-Running LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02515)
*Zhichen Liu,Ruihan Sun,Hengjie Yang,Zipeng Wu,Zhaohan Chen,Xiaofan Zhang,Yang Xu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LiveMem augments LLMs with a persistent, fixed-size memory state to maintain useful information across context windows, enabling state continuity even after original tokens leave the active context.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-running LLM agents interact over streams that exceed the model’s context window, causing loss of earlier but still-relevant information. Existing methods like summarization and retrieval can surface past content but do not give the model a continuous, intrinsic computational state spanning its full lifecycle as the working context turns over.

Method: The authors formalize “state continuity under context turnover” and propose LiveMem, an intrinsic memory mechanism that attaches a persistent, fixed-capacity memory state to a pretrained full-attention LLM. The main attention path operates with a bounded key-value (KV) cache window, while LiveMem maintains a separate memory state whose lifetime is decoupled from the active context. They design procedures for (1) context turnover and memory maintenance, (2) memory-oriented post-training so the model learns to write to and read from this memory, and (3) state-aware serving so the memory remains load-bearing after originating tokens are dropped.

Result: On benchmarks including LongMemEval, LiveMem outperforms other evaluated systems and intrinsic memory baselines. It can correctly answer questions using only the learned memory state, even after the explicit evidence tokens have been removed from the current context. Evidence-distance analyses indicate that information remains useful well beyond the active KV window.

Conclusion: LiveMem demonstrates that a persistent, intrinsic memory state can provide state continuity independent of the current context window, enabling continual inference over long interaction lifecycles. This establishes state continuity as a distinct and complementary abstraction to traditional context-based methods for long-horizon LLM applications.

Abstract: Long-running assistants and agents consume interaction streams that eventually outgrow the context. Existing context retention, summarization, and retrieval preserve access to selected history, but do not provide a persistent state over the full lifecycle when working context changes. We formulate this missing inference capability as \emph{state continuity under context turnover}: carrying computation forward through a fixed-capacity memory state whose lifetime is independent of the active context. We introduce an intrinsic memory method, \textbf{LiveMem}, which augments a pretrained full-attention LLM with a memory state that preserves the historical information over the whole lifecycle while the main attention path retains a bounded KV window. Context turnover and memory state maintaining, memory-oriented post-training, and state-aware serving jointly make this memory state load bearing after its originating tokens are released. Our experiments show that LiveMem achieves leading overall performance among evaluated systems and other intrinsic memory methods. Experiments on LongMemEval show that LiveMem is able to answer the question based on the memory state, even when the supporting evidence has been removed from the current context, and evidence-distance analysis shows that useful information persists beyond the active window. LiveMem thus establishes state continuity as a distinct and complementary abstraction for continual LLM inference.

</details>


### [126] [MedPRESS: A Multi-turn Benchmark for Patient-Pressure-Induced Medical Sycophancy in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02520)
*Saman Sarker Joy,Niloy Farhan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces MedPRESS, a benchmark to test how LLMs handle patient pressure in medical conversations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM safety evaluations use static questions and fail to capture how models behave in realistic, pressured, multi-turn patient interactions, where users may push for unsafe or desired answers.

Method: The authors build MedPRESS, a dataset of 600 five-turn, medically grounded dialogues in three health-related scenario families, each escalating patient pressure. They test 20 LLMs from various categories using structured judging and safety metrics, and also test anti-sycophancy prompting strategies.

Result: LLMs often become more sycophantic and agree with unsafe medical suggestions when subjected to repeated patient pressure, with performance differing notably by model family, size, and prompting strategy. Anti-sycophancy prompts help some models but fail to fully prevent unsafe agreement.

Conclusion: Current evaluations overestimate LLM medical safety because they ignore conversational pressure; maintaining safe behavior under pressure is a distinct challenge, and MedPRESS exposes this gap and provides a benchmark for more realistic safety testing.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for health-related advice. Existing research measures their safety with static questions rather than pressured patient-facing conversations. We introduce MedPRESS, a multi-turn benchmark for measuring patient-pressure-induced sycophancy in LLMs. MedPRESS contains 600 medically grounded five-turn dialogues across three scenario families: medication and treatment demand, personal health self-care, and symptom triage and care resistance. Each dialogue begins with a health query and escalates through personal experience, social proof, external evidence claims, and direct adversarial challenge. We evaluate 20 LLMs across general, medical-domain, lightweight, large, open-weight, and proprietary families using structured judging and safety-focused metrics. Results show that models frequently shift toward unsafe agreement under repeated patient pressure, with substantial variation across model families, model scale, and prompt type. Anti-sycophancy prompting improves robustness for several models, but does not eliminate unsafe agreement. MedPRESS highlights a critical gap in medical LLM evaluation: safe medical knowledge is not enough unless models can maintain it under conversational pressure.

</details>


### [127] [Romanized Arabic Across Dialects: Views, Usage Patterns, and Linguistic Variation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02555)
*Amr Keleg,Ahmed Amine Ben Abdallah,Taha Yassine,Chadi Helwe,Imane Guellil,Nedjma Ousidhoum*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates Arabizi (Arabic in Latin script) as a stable socio-technical writing practice rather than a temporary workaround, providing new cross-dialectal resources and analyses of its norms and perceptions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most NLP work treats Arabizi as a transient artifact of insufficient Arabic-script support and often ignores its social and dialectal dimensions. However, Arabizi use varies by region, age, and dialect, and it exhibits its own norms. There is a lack of large, human-centered, cross-dialectal studies and publicly available resources that systematically characterize Arabizi’s variation and users’ perceptions, limiting robust modeling and understanding.

Method: The authors conduct a human-centered study involving speakers of five Arabic dialects: Algerian, Egyptian, Lebanese, Moroccan, and Tunisian. Through surveys, they collect transliterations of Arabic-script words into Arabizi. They then (1) create a character-level alignment between Arabic-script words and their Arabizi forms to quantitatively analyze intra- and inter-dialectal variation; and (2) construct a manually curated parallel corpus of sentences where each sentence in Arabic script has multiple Arabizi transliterations produced by speakers of each dialect. They also analyze how speakers perceive and recognize dialectal and stylistic variation in Arabizi at sentence level.

Result: The character-level alignment reveals systematic regularities in how individual dialect communities transliterate into Arabizi (intra-dialectal regularity) and clear differences in these transliteration patterns across dialects (inter-dialectal variation). The sentence-level corpus demonstrates that speakers can both produce and recognize dialect-specific and stylistic cues in Arabizi. The authors release both the alignment resource and the parallel corpus as new datasets for the community.

Conclusion: Arabizi is not merely a temporary or noisy artifact but a structured, dialect-sensitive writing practice with consistent internal norms. The study provides the largest human-centered, cross-dialectal analysis of Arabizi to date and introduces two datasets that enable more accurate, socially aware NLP research on Arabic written in Latin script.

Abstract: Arabizi refers to Arabic written in Latin script. Although previous studies have shown that the prevalence and usage of Arabizi vary by factors such as region and age group, most NLP research on Arabic texts treats it as a temporary phenomenon resulting from limited technological support for the Arabic script. In this work, we engage with Arabic speakers to collect insights on their perceptions and usage of Arabizi. We further examine writing norms among speakers of different dialects, focusing on Algerian, Egyptian, Lebanese, Moroccan, and Tunisian Arabic. To this end, we release two resources. First, a character-level alignment of Arabic words to study inter- and intra-dialectal variation across these five dialects, based on words transliterated by survey participants, finding systematic intra-dialectal regularity and inter-dialectal variation. Second, to study Arabic speakers' ability to identify this stylistic variation at the sentence-level, we build a manually curated parallel corpus of sentences written in Arabic script alongside multiple Arabizi transliterations, collected from speakers of the same five dialects. Our study presents the largest human-centered, cross-dialectal study of Arabizi's perceptions and practices to date.

</details>


### [128] [AURORA-LM: Autoencoding Unified Representation for Continuous-Latent Diffusion Language Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02602)
*Jiajun Liang,Yucheng Liao,Yukang Cao,Jiazhe Wei,Ken Li,Wende Tan,Jiankun Zhang,ZY Cui,Jingkang Yang,Liucheng Guo,Shiqi Yang,B. Yang,Caifeng Shan,Ziwei Liu,Chenyang Si*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes AURORA-LM, a diffusion-based continuous latent language model that preserves a high-capacity decodable text representation while tailoring the diffusion process to model its distribution effectively, achieving state-of-the-art results among continuous/diffusion LMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unlike images, video, and audio, language generation still mainly uses discrete tokens. Existing continuous language models either use embedding spaces not designed for joint generation and decoding, or compress latents to make diffusion easier, which harms token-level fidelity. The authors aim to build a continuous generative model for language that keeps a rich, decodable latent space without sacrificing generation quality, and to close the performance gap between diffusion-based and standard autoregressive LMs.

Method: They introduce AURORA-LM, which separates representation and generative modeling. First, a Query-based Encoder-Decoder converts text into a high-capacity, prefix-aligned latent sequence that is directly decodable to text. Second, a Block-causal Diffusion Transformer, trained via flow matching, learns the distribution of these latents: it generates latent blocks left-to-right, while denoising all positions inside each block in parallel. To handle the difficulty of modeling a wide latent, they restrict only the noisy-input pathway while keeping the full clean-latent prediction target, allowing full-width latents without shrinking decoder capacity. They also adjust the noise-level distribution to match latent width and introduce self-trajectory consistency to better align training (single-step noise) with inference (iterative denoising).

Result: On OpenWebText free generation and XSum summarization, AURORA-LM outperforms prior continuous and diffusion-based language models. When scaled to 1B parameters with about 1500 EFLOPs of compute, it further improves and surpasses a larger released latent-diffusion LM under the same evaluation setup. All experiments are run on Ascend NPUs, demonstrating scalability and hardware compatibility.

Conclusion: AURORA-LM shows that a diffusion model can directly learn the distribution of a high-capacity, fully decodable text latent without compressing it for convenience, and that architectural and training adjustments (block-causal diffusion, restricted noisy path, noise calibration, and self-trajectory consistency) make such modeling effective. This approach narrows the gap between continuous-latent diffusion LMs and strong autoregressive baselines, suggesting a viable path for continuous generative modeling of language.

Abstract: Language remains an outlier in generative modeling: while images, video, and audio are increasingly modeled in continuous latent spaces, text generation still relies predominantly on discrete tokens. Existing continuous language models either inherit embedding spaces not designed for joint generation and decoding, or compress autoencoded latents to ease diffusion, sacrificing token-level fidelity. Instead of simplifying the representation to suit the generative model, we preserve a high-capacity, decodable text latent and design the diffusion model to learn its distribution directly.
  We introduce AURORA-LM, a continuous-latent diffusion language model that separates the construction of a decodable text representation from the modeling of its distribution. A Query-based Encoder-Decoder organizes text into a high-capacity, prefix-aligned latent sequence, and a Block-causal Diffusion Transformer learns its distribution through flow matching, generating blocks left to right while denoising positions within each block in parallel. Because such a latent is harder for diffusion to model, AURORA-LM restricts only the noisy-input pathway while retaining the full clean-latent prediction target, accommodating full-width latents without reducing decoder-facing capacity. We further calibrate the noise-level distribution to the latent width, and introduce self-trajectory consistency to bridge independently sampled training noise and iterative denoising at inference.
  AURORA-LM achieves the strongest performance among evaluated continuous and diffusion-based language models on OpenWebText free generation and XSum summarization. Scaling to 1B parameters with about 1500 EFLOPs of total compute yields further gains, surpassing a larger publicly released latent-diffusion language model under a matched evaluation protocol. All experiments are conducted on Ascend NPUs.

</details>


### [129] [Amplitude-Only FFN Intervention for Tool-Structured LLM Inference Method: Gated Evaluation Protocol, and Cross-Model Empirical Results](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11183)
*Sheng Xu,Junhua Wang,Boyuan Huang,Ke Jia,Jiadun Zhu,Zhen Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes an inference-time method, Amplitude Gating (AG), to improve the reliability of structured outputs (like tool calls and JSON) in large language models by adjusting FFN activations without retraining model weights, showing consistent gains on tool-structured benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models acting as tool-using agents often fail due to small formatting or function-call errors that break otherwise good responses. Fixing these issues via retraining is costly and risky. The authors want an inference-time, weight-preserving way to repair structured outputs by intervening in the model’s feed-forward networks, improving tool and JSON reliability while keeping the base model intact.

Method: They first explore Orthogonal Residual Projection (ORP), which alters the direction of FFN activations, discovering sensitive intervention sites in SwiGLU FFNs but also frequent degradation. They then introduce Amplitude Gating (AG), which keeps FFN weight directions fixed and only modulates activation magnitudes at specific layers/branches (P1/P2/P3 and P1s/P2a/P2b). They design an evaluation protocol distinguishing oracle headroom (best possible combinations of intervention sites) from fixed and learned gating configurations, enforce per-sample accounting, and apply task-aware metrics for binary and partial-credit structured-output datasets. They compare different AG variants, including entropy-based AG and Newton–Schulz-windowed AG, across several Qwen model families and task categories.

Result: Across Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, AG yields small but generally positive gains, especially on tool-structured tasks. On Qwen3.5-9B, a learned category-level gate raises tool/structured/agentic accuracy from 38.66% to 42.92% (+4.27 points), with Hermes function-call tasks gaining about +7.6 points. On Qwen3-8B, Hermes JSON mode improves by +11.36 points. Qwen2.5-7B shows that substantial oracle headroom exists but current learned gates cannot fully exploit it, indicating routing and configuration must be model- and category-specific. Comparisons show entropy-based and Newton–Schulz-windowed AG trade off, with no universally best variant.

Conclusion: Inference-time FFN-level interventions, when designed to preserve weight directions and only gate activation amplitudes, can measurably improve structured, tool-oriented outputs of LLMs without retraining. Amplitude Gating is particularly promising for tool-structured inference, but effective deployment requires careful, model- and task-specific routing choices. Further work is needed for online validation and comprehensive cross-model evaluation, and ORP-like direction-changing interventions appear more hazardous than amplitude-only approaches for safe optimization.

Abstract: Large language models increasingly operate as tool-using agents, where small format, argument, or function-call errors can invalidate otherwise plausible responses. We study inference-time feed-forward network (FFN) intervention for improving structured outputs without retraining model weights. Our project began with Orthogonal Residual Projection (ORP), a direction-changing repair attempt that revealed sensitive SwiGLU FFN intervention sites but often caused more harm than fixes. We therefore propose Amplitude Gating (AG), a non-destructive alternative that preserves pretrained FFN weight directions and modulates only activation magnitudes during generation. We define a fine-grained intervention system spanning P1/P2/P3 and branch-specific P1s/P2a/P2b sites, and introduce an evaluation protocol that separates combination-oracle headroom from fixed configurations and learned gates, enforces sample-level accounting, and uses task-aware metrics for binary and partial-credit datasets. Across Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, AG is weakly positive in aggregate but strongest on tool-structured tasks. On Qwen3.5-9B, a category-level learned gate improves tool/structured/agentic performance from 38.66% to 42.92% (+4.27 percentage points), with Hermes function-call tasks reaching about +7.6 points. On Qwen3-8B, Hermes JSON mode improves by +11.36 points. Qwen2.5-7B retains oracle headroom but current learned gates fail to capture it, showing that deployment requires model- and category-specific routing. Comparisons of entropy AG with Newton-Schulz-windowed AG show that neither family is uniformly dominant. These results identify tool-structured inference as the most credible first target for safe FFN-level inference optimization, while prospective online validation and broader cross-model evaluation remain necessary.

</details>


<div id='cs.AI'></div>

# cs.AI [[Back]](#toc)

### [130] [Revisiting Classic Thought Experiments to Measure Consciousness for Artificial Intelligence Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00001)
*Peter David Fagan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a formal toy framework (CCE) to distinguish between behavioural performance and the efficiency of internal structure, using it to reinterpret classic thought experiments on machine understanding and highlight implications for AI safety.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classic debates (Leibniz’s mill, Turing test, Chinese Room) often conflate outward behaviour with inner understanding. The authors want a precise way to separate what a system does from how its internal organisation supports what it does, in order to clarify what is really at stake in these debates and to inform later AI safety work.

Method: They define a symbolic toy model within the Conservation-Congruent Encoding (CCE) framework. In this model, they specify: (1) a measure of task performance, W_{causal,T}, capturing behavioural success on tasks; and (2) a measure of “operational consciousness,” κ_T, quantifying how efficiently preserved internal structure is reused to support that behaviour. They then compare two types of systems in this formalism: an uncompressed lookup table that stores unreused input-output mappings, and a compact generative system that reuses a small set of structural rules to generate outputs.

Result: In this setting, both the lookup system and the generative system can reach similar levels of task performance W_{causal,T}. However, they differ significantly in κ_T: the lookup system requires an ever-growing store of independent mappings with little structural reuse, whereas the generative system reuses compact internal representations, yielding higher κ_T. This shows that matching behaviour does not imply similar internal organisation or “operational consciousness.”

Conclusion: The framework makes explicit a distinction between outward behavioural performance and the efficiency/structure of the internal mechanisms that produce it. This allows classic arguments about understanding (Leibniz, Turing, Searle) to be reframed in terms of differences in κ_T rather than mere behavioural equivalence, and it suggests that for AI safety, we should care not only about what systems do but how compactly and systematically their internal structures support their behaviour.

Abstract: This research note revisits Leibniz's mill, Turing's imitation game, and Searle's Chinese Room through the Conservation-Congruent Encoding (CCE) framework. It formalises a toy symbolic setting in which successful behaviour is measured by task performance ($W_{causal,T}$), while the efficiency with which preserved internal structure supports that behaviour is measured by operational consciousness ($κ_T$). Within this setup, an uncompressed lookup system and a compact generative system can in principle achieve comparable behavioural success, yet diverge sharply in $κ_T$: the former relies on an expanding standing store of unreused mappings, whereas the latter reuses compact internal structure. The note therefore reframes classic disputes about understanding by separating outward performance from the organisation that sustains it, and motivates why this distinction may matter for later AI-safety analysis.

</details>


### [131] [AutoFOAM: The Self-Refining Autonomous OpenFOAM Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00003)
*Arun Govind Neelan,A Seshaditya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce AutoFOAM, an LLM-based agent that automatically sets up and iteratively improves OpenFOAM CFD simulations from natural-language instructions, using a self-evolution loop with safeguards against model collapse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CFD with open-source tools like OpenFOAM is powerful but hard to use, requiring deep expertise and time-consuming setup of configuration files. There is a need to make advanced CFD more accessible and faster to prototype without demanding extensive user knowledge.

Method: They build AutoFOAM, a large language model agent based on Qwen-coder 2.5-14B, fine-tuned on 252 prompts that cover multiple OpenFOAM solvers, mesh templates, and a y+-aware numerical policy. The core is a 7-stage evolution loop where the agent autonomously creates, evaluates, runs, and refines simulations. To avoid degradation from repeated self-training, they introduce three anti-collapse mechanisms: RAG-augmented retry context, fine-grained dictionary-level patching, and paraphrasing for prompt diversity.

Result: AutoFOAM can autonomously generate and refine OpenFOAM simulations from natural language, handling solver selection, meshing, and numerical setup while maintaining stability during self-evolution through its anti-collapse mechanisms. It accelerates prototyping and reduces the need for manual CFD configuration. (Specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.)

Conclusion: By combining generative LLM capabilities with CFD solvers, AutoFOAM lowers the barrier to using OpenFOAM, enabling rapid, automated, and robust CFD workflows from natural language instructions. The self-evolving design and anti-collapse strategies keep the agent effective over time, helping to democratize advanced CFD for a broader range of users.

Abstract: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) plays an important role in modern engineering, but using open-source solvers such as OpenFOAM requires considerable knowledge and skills, as well as time-consuming configuration file setup. To reduce this burden, we propose AutoFOAM - a self-evolving large language model (LLM) agent that creates, evaluates, runs, and evolves its own OpenFOAM simulations based solely on natural-language instructions. Our model is pre-trained on the Qwen-coder 2.5-14B, which is then fine-tuned on 252 text prompts targeting 7 OpenFOAM solvers, 13 parametrized mesh templates, and a y plus-aware numerical policy. The crucial element of the algorithm is a sophisticated evolution loop composed of 7 stages. To prevent model degeneration under repeated self-training, the agent employs three complementary anti-collapse streams: RAG-augmented retry context, surgical dictionary-level patching, and prompt-diversity paraphrasing. By bridging generative artificial intelligence with rigorous fluid simulations, AutoFOAM accelerates rapid prototyping and democratizes advanced CFD workflows.

</details>


### [132] [Enhancing LLMs with Context-Specific Knowledge for Mitigating Misinformation in SMEs: A RAG-based Modeling and Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00006)
*Md. Samiul Islam,Iqbal H. Sarker,Chadni Islam,Ahmad Mohsin,Ahmed Ibrahim,Helge Janicke*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how to reduce hallucinations in LLM-based question answering for SMEs using RAG methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SMEs increasingly use LLMs for Q&A and decision support, but hallucinations create misinformation risks and undermine trust, so better methods are needed to make outputs reliable and context-aware.

Method: The authors design and implement two Retrieval-Augmented Generation approaches, VectorRAG and GraphRAG, that inject external knowledge into LLMs (LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen). They run experiments in SME-like settings and evaluate responses on usefulness, hallucination risk, contextual relevance, and human interpretability.

Result: Across multiple state-of-the-art LLMs, the RAG-enhanced setups (VectorRAG and GraphRAG) produce more useful, contextually relevant answers with fewer hallucinations and lower misinformation risk, and are rated better by human evaluators.

Conclusion: Using RAG architectures such as VectorRAG and GraphRAG substantially improves the reliability, trustworthiness, and contextual awareness of LLM outputs for SMEs, making them more suitable for decision-making workflows.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), a part of artificial intelligence (AI), are increasingly being adopted by Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) to enhance question-answering capabilities and support business decision-making processes. However, hallucinations in LLM-generated outputs can serve as a source of misinformation, reducing user confidence in their reliability and trustworthiness within SMEs. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a promising approach to address this challenge by incorporating external knowledge sources into the modeling process. In this paper, we present VectorRAG and GraphRAG modeling approaches to mitigate hallucinations and misinformation risks and evaluate their effectiveness in SME environments. Our experimental evaluation is conducted on multiple state-of-the-art LLMs, including LLaMA, Mistral, and Qwen, to assess performance in terms of useful response generation, risk of hallucination, contextual relevance, as well as human-interpretation. The results demonstrate that RAG-enhanced LLMs can significantly improve response quality by reducing hallucinations and misinformation, thereby supporting more reliable, trustworthy, and context-aware decision-making in SME environments.

</details>


### [133] [Energy Efficiency of Locally Deployed LLMs: A Preliminary Quantitative GPU Power Benchmark on Consumer Hardware](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00008)
*Philipp M. Zähl,Anika Hennig*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper benchmarks the energy consumption of several open-source LLMs on a consumer GPU, showing that architecture and quantization matter more than just parameter count for energy efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most LLM benchmarks focus on accuracy or latency, leaving energy consumption on consumer hardware underexplored despite growing interest in local, privacy-preserving deployment. Understanding energy cost per prompt and per token is critical for practical on-premise use and sustainable AI.

Method: Run nine open-source LLMs (1B–7B parameters) locally on a single RTX 4060Ti 16GB using the Ollama engine. For a fixed prompt set, sample GPU power at 2 Hz via nvidia-smi. Compute mean/peak power, total energy per prompt (J/prompt), energy per output token (J/token), and throughput (tokens/s), then compare models and configurations (architectures, quantization).

Result: Small 1B models (gemma3:1b and llama3.2:1b) achieve the best energy efficiency (0.56 and 0.65 J/token) and highest throughput (>170 tok/s). Larger models, especially a 7B Mistral variant, use up to 4.4× more energy per token. One model, qwen3.5:2b, shows unusually high per-prompt energy because of prolonged internal reasoning, inflating energy per prompt relative to per-token measures.

Conclusion: Energy efficiency of LLM inference on consumer GPUs is strongly influenced by architectural and behavioral factors, not just parameter count. Efficient small models can deliver much lower energy per token and higher throughput. Internal reasoning behaviors can distort per-prompt energy metrics, so future evaluations should separate different token generation modes and consider both energy and throughput when selecting models for local deployment.

Abstract: The local deployment of large language models (LLMs) is gaining traction due to privacy concerns and the desire for on-premise inference. However, the energy costs on consumer hardware remain poorly characterized, as most benchmarks focus solely on accuracy. This paper presents a reproducible, hardware-level energy benchmark of nine open-source LLMs (1B to 7B parameters) executed on a single consumer GPU (RTX 4060Ti 16GB). Using the Ollama inference engine, GPU power draw was sampled at 2Hz via nvidia-smi across a fixed prompt set. We evaluate mean/peak power, total energy per prompt (J/prompt), energy per output token (J/token), and throughput (tok/s). Our findings suggest that factors beyond raw parameter count, including model architecture and quantization strategy, drive energy efficiency. Specifically, gemma3:1b and llama3.2:1b achieve the lowest energy cost (0.56 J/token and 0.65 J/token) and the highest throughput (>170 tok/s). In contrast, the 7B-Mistral model consumes up to 4.4x more energy per token than the most efficient model. Notably, qwen3.5:2b exhibits anomalously high per-prompt energy due to extended internal reasoning, highlighting the need to distinguish between token generation modes in efficiency metrics.

</details>


### [134] [CoT-Core: Accelerating LLM Evaluation via CoT-Aware Coreset Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00014)
*Qihua Pan,Zhenheng Tang,Peijie Dong,Xiang Liu,Huacan Wang,Bo Li,Xiaowen Chu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CoT-Core is a training-free framework that selects a small, representative set of evaluation questions by clustering LLM chain-of-thought trajectories, cutting evaluation cost while preserving score accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating LLMs continuously is computationally expensive. Existing coreset selection methods either need large historical interaction logs (cold start problem) or rely on surface text similarity, which fails to capture deeper reasoning patterns. There is a need for an evaluation subset selection method that is both training-free and reasoning-aware, so that we can cheaply yet accurately estimate model performance during development.

Method: The authors introduce CoT-Core, a training-free core question selection framework. For each candidate question, they prompt an LLM to generate a zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning trajectory. They then embed or project these reasoning paths into a latent space where questions are grouped by the similarity of their underlying logical reasoning rather than their lexical form. From these clusters, a small set of representative core questions is selected as an evaluation coreset. This allows pruning many redundant questions whose reasoning patterns are already covered by the selected core set.

Result: On benchmarks including GSM8K, MMLU, MMLU-Pro, and GPQA, CoT-Core significantly reduces the number of questions needed for evaluation while still providing accurate estimates of full-benchmark scores. The experiments also investigate when reasoning-aware pruning works well and when it degrades, tying its success to properties such as task and reasoning complexity.

Conclusion: CoT-Core offers an effective, training-free way to build reasoning-aware evaluation coresets by clustering CoT trajectories, thus cutting LLM evaluation costs without sacrificing fidelity. However, its benefits are bounded by task complexity: for highly complex tasks, pruning too aggressively may harm the reliability of evaluation, revealing intrinsic limits of reasoning-based subset selection.

Abstract: Evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) incurs prohibitive computational overhead during continuous development processes. While coreset selection accelerates evaluation, existing methods either suffer from a severe ``cold start'' bottleneck requiring massive historical logs (e.g., Item Response Theory) or exhibit a surface lexical bias that misses the underlying reasoning manifold of tasks. We propose CoT-Core, a novel training-free core question selection framework. Recognizing that lexically disparate questions can share equivalent underlying logic, CoT-Core prompts LLMs to unroll zero-shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning trajectories. Projecting these paths into a latent space effectively clusters questions by intrinsic logical equivalence rather than superficial text similarity. Extensive experiments on GSM8K, MMLU, MMLU-Pro, and GPQA demonstrate that CoT-Core drastically reduces evaluation costs while maintaining high-fidelity score estimation, and delineate the boundary conditions of reasoning-aware pruning, revealing that its efficacy is intrinsically gated by task complexity.

</details>


### [135] [Optimization and Constraint Modeling using LLMs with a Retrieval Augmented Generation Process](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00015)
*Prateek Roy,Akash Singirikonda*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper shows that adding retrieval-augmented synthetic examples to LLM prompts significantly improves the correctness and structure of optimization models generated from natural language, offering an alternative to fine-tuning for decision-support applications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Building correct optimization and constraint models from natural language is difficult and usually requires experts. Current LLMs often generate incomplete or structurally invalid optimization formulations, especially for combinatorial problems. Organizations in domains like logistics and healthcare need reliable automated modeling without the expense and complexity of fine-tuning large models. The authors want to test whether retrieval-augmented generation over a dedicated optimization corpus can bridge this gap.

Method: The authors construct a synthetic dataset of 500 optimization problems. They start from Text2Zinc seed descriptions and expand them with LLM-generated professional personas, encoding each problem in JSON and pairing it with validated Python solver scripts. These problems are embedded into a Chroma vector database. At inference time, for a new optimization task, semantically similar problems are retrieved and provided as context to a LangChain-based LLM agent using the Qwen 3 30B Instruct model. The pipeline’s performance is evaluated on three benchmark suites: NL4OPT, MAMO Easy, and MAMO Complex, comparing baseline LLM performance versus the retrieval-augmented setup.

Result: With the retrieval-augmented synthetic dataset, modeling accuracy improves substantially across all benchmarks. On NL4OPT, accuracy increases from 40% to 72%; on MAMO Easy, from 40% to 56%; and on MAMO Complex, from 32% to 56%. In addition to higher accuracy, the generated optimization models exhibit better structural validity and completeness compared to the baseline Qwen 3 30B Instruct model without retrieval augmentation.

Conclusion: Curated synthetic optimization problems, when used in a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline, can substantially enhance LLM performance in optimization modeling without the need for fine-tuning. The approach improves both correctness and structural quality of generated formulations and appears to be a viable, cost-effective path for deploying LLM-based optimization tools in real-world decision-support settings. This suggests that domain-specific synthetic corpora plus retrieval are a practical alternative to retraining large models for specialized tasks like mathematical optimization modeling.

Abstract: Both optimization modeling and constraint modeling are non-trivial problems requiring deep domain expertise and proficiency in modeling formalism languages. Despite their importance across logistics, healthcare, and supply chain management, current large language models regularly produce structurally inconsistent or incomplete optimization formulations, particularly in combinatorial settings. This paper evaluates whether a Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline built on a curated synthetic dataset can meaningfully improve LLM optimization modeling performance. A total of 500 optimization problems were synthesized using seed descriptions from the Text2Zinc dataset and professional personas created using an LLM, specified in JSON and associated with validated Python solver scripts. These problems were encoded in a Chroma vector database. For each inference problem, semantically similar problems were retrieved and used as contextual guidance for a LangChain LLM agent. Three benchmark testbeds were used to evaluate the proposed pipeline under the Qwen 3 30B Instruct model. Accuracy rose from 40% to 72% on NL4OPT, 40% to 56% on MAMO Easy, and 32% to 56% on MAMO Complex. The use of semantically validated synthetic examples greatly improves both solution accuracy and structure. The combination of synthetic dataset generation with retrieval augmentation provides an effective alternative to fine-tuning, suggesting that domain-specific synthetic corpora paired with retrieval augmentation can serve as a practical pathway for deploying LLM-based optimization tools in real-world decision-support contexts without costly model retraining.

</details>


### [136] [Memory Reward Inflation in Self-Improving LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00017)
*Mohammad Asadolahi,Amir Amini,Samira Talebi,Amirfarhad Farhadi,Azadeh Zamanifar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies failure modes in self-improving LLM agents that learn via external memory and proposes a theory and algorithm (LUCID) to correct reward inflation and improve reliability, demonstrated on text-to-SQL.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-improving LLM agents store and reuse past episodes with self-assigned scores instead of updating weights, but in deployment they lack ground-truth rewards and must rely on LLM self-judgment. This causes systematic overvaluation of confident mistakes, which can then be preferentially retrieved, compounding errors over time. There is a need to understand this failure mode formally and to design methods that can correct it without access to labels.

Method: The authors reinterpret memory-based agents as implementing an implicit non-parametric policy whose ‘reward’ is the stored episode score. They analyze theoretically how self-assessed scores introduce a failure mode they call the Echo Gap, and formalize a necessary Error-Independence Assumption (EIA) that any corrective signal must satisfy: its error must both correlate with truth and be decorrelated from the memory’s bias. They derive a closed-form characterization of the recoverable payoff as a function of these properties. They then design LUCID, an answer-free de-inflation algorithm that adjusts stored rewards to counteract inflation, applicable both when retrieval is score-based and when it is similarity-based.

Result: They prove that without EIA, no verifier can systematically correct the inflated rewards caused by biased self-assessment, and that error inflation persists even when memory retrieval is based solely on similarity rather than scores. Empirically, they evaluate on the BIRD text-to-SQL benchmark and show that LUCID consistently improves performance: execution accuracy reaches 56.9%, outperforming a Memento-style self-graded memory agent (54.0%, a +2.9 point mean gain across seeds) and a memory-less baseline with the same architecture (52.4%).

Conclusion: Self-improving LLM agents that rely on self-graded memory are vulnerable to an Echo Gap where confident mistakes are reinforced, and simply adding a judge model is insufficient unless its errors are independent of the memory’s bias. The Error-Independence Assumption is a necessary requirement for reward correction, and exploiting it enables practical, answer-free de-inflation of memory scores. The proposed LUCID method mitigates reward inflation and yields consistent end-to-end gains on text-to-SQL, indicating that principled memory calibration is key to reliable self-improvement in LLM agents.

Abstract: Self-improving LLM agents increasingly learn from experience without updating any weights. Each episode is stored in an external memory, scored, and retrieved for similar future tasks to shape later behavior. Viewed through a reward lens, the stored score is a proxy reward for an implicit, non-parametric policy. Each retrieved episode then becomes a policy-improvement step whose reliability hinges on how that score is produced. In deployment, ground-truth labels are unavailable, so the stored reward is at best an LLM assessment. This substitution creates a failure mode, the *Echo Gap*, across the memory-based self-improving agents and model families studied. Incorrect episodes receive inflated rewards; thus, the agent preferentially reuses the very mistakes it has most confident in. Because the error compounds through memory rather than averaging out and the confirming judge's errors remain correlated with the original self-grading bias, so it cannot identify which memories are overvalued. The missing property is formalized as the *Error-Independence Assumption* (EIA), which we prove is a *necessary* condition for correcting the inflation, not merely a description of a good verifier: a usable signal must track truth *and* decorrelate its error from the memory bias, and the recoverable payoff is a closed-form function of exactly those two quantities. We further show the inflation compounds not only when retrieval ranks by the stored score but also under plain similarity retrieval which is the regime the deployed agent uses. Finally, the answer-free de-inflation algorithm LUCID delivers a consistent end-to-end gain on the BIRD text-to-SQL benchmark. It raises execution accuracy to $56.9\%$, above both a Memento-style self-graded agent ($54.0\%$, a $+2.9$-point mean gain across seeds) and a memory-less agent of identical architecture ($52.4\%$).

</details>


### [137] [Request-Level Energy Attribution for Batched LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00026)
*Qi Luo,Kunlin Li,Ziwen Wang,Dongsheng Wang,Yun Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces JouleShare, a framework to fairly attribute GPU energy usage to individual LLM requests under batched serving, using Shapley-based ground truth and a learned calibration model for online use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Batched serving of large language models improves throughput but makes it hard to assign energy costs fairly to individual requests because GPU power measurements are only available at aggregate level. Organizations need accurate per-request energy attribution for sustainability reporting, internal chargeback, and workload analysis. Existing approaches only measure energy at coarse levels (model, phase, or token) and assume simple rules like token-proportional allocation, and while Shapley-value-based fairness has been discussed conceptually, there has been no measured request-level ground truth to validate or correct these rules.

Method: The authors propose JouleShare, consisting of two main components. First, an offline harness replays selected subsets of requests under vLLM with a standardized, reproducible protocol. It collects GPU power telemetry and uses it to compute exact Shapley-value energy allocations for each request in a batch, yielding ground-truth marginal energy shares. Second, they train a lightweight calibration model called JCalib that learns to predict each request’s Shapley energy share from inexpensive request-level features, enabling practical deployment during online serving without expensive per-subset replays. They evaluate JouleShare across different batching regimes (static and continuous), workloads, models, and three data-center GPUs, and also use sampled Shapley techniques to extend results to larger group sizes.

Result: The study finds that the common heuristic of assigning energy in proportion to token counts deviates substantially from exact Shapley allocations: average normalized L1 error is 0.440 under static batching and 0.458 under continuous batching, and this discrepancy is consistent across three different data-center GPUs. JCalib, trained on the Shapley ground truth, sharply reduces attribution error to 0.116 for static batching and 0.177 for continuous batching, outperforming even a standalone-measurement baseline that cannot be applied in online settings. The framework maintains exact batch-level energy conservation, and sampled Shapley analyses for larger groups confirm that the token-based rule remains inaccurate while a single offline-trained calibration model continues to give the most accurate deployable estimates.

Conclusion: Token-count-based energy attribution is an unreliable stand-in for marginal per-request energy usage in batched LLM inference. By generating measured Shapley-value ground truth offline and learning a compact calibration model, JouleShare enables substantially fairer and more accurate request-level energy accounting that is still efficient enough for deployment. This demonstrates that principled cooperative-game-theoretic attribution, combined with measurement-driven calibration, can significantly improve sustainability and chargeback metrics for batched LLM serving systems.

Abstract: Batched LLM serving improves throughput but complicates energy accounting. GPU power telemetry is aggregate, whereas sustainability reporting, chargeback, and workload analysis often require request-level energy charges. Existing inference-energy benchmarks report model-, phase-, or token-level energy, and recent carbon-accounting work motivates Shapley fairness conceptually. Neither provides measured request-level ground truth, so how far the accounting rules used in practice deviate from a fair allocation has remained unknown. We present JouleShare, an attribution framework with two components. An offline harness establishes this ground truth by replaying request subsets under vLLM with a reproducible protocol, integrating GPU power telemetry, and computing exact Shapley energy for each request. A lightweight calibration model, JCalib, then learns to predict Shapley shares from cheap request features for use at serving time. Across 16 model/workload runs, token-proportional attribution differs from exact Shapley by 0.440 normalized L1 on average under static batching and by 0.458 under continuous batching, a gap that reproduces across three data-center GPUs. JCalib reduces this error to 0.116 under static batching and 0.177 under continuous batching, below even a standalone-measurement baseline that is unavailable online, while preserving exact batch-energy efficiency. Sampled Shapley extends the measured reference to larger group sizes, where the gap persists and a single offline calibration remains the most accurate deployable rule. The results show that token attribution is not a reliable proxy for marginal energy under batched execution, and that measured Shapley ground truth can calibrate low-cost request features toward fairer attribution.
