</details>


### [138] [Motif-Mamba: network motif improved mamba for long-range sequence modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00027)
*Chonghe Hao,Yue Sun,Jian Zhang,Yansong Wang,Wangzi Yao,Yunjie Yao,Tielin Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Motif-Mamba augments the Mamba architecture with a motif-guided low-rank recurrent pathway to improve long-sequence modeling while keeping linear-time complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard self-attention in large language models scales quadratically with sequence length, making efficient long-sequence modeling challenging. Mamba addresses this with linear-time selective state space recurrence, but its mainly diagonal state transitions limit explicit interactions between different state dimensions, potentially reducing modeling capacity for complex long-range dependencies.

Method: The paper introduces Motif-Mamba, a structured state space model that adds a motif-constrained low-rank recurrent pathway on top of the original Mamba architecture. Drawing inspiration from three-node network motifs, the model: (1) projects hidden states into a smaller dynamical subspace, (2) applies motif-guided interactions within that subspace using structured low-rank dynamics, and (3) maps the transformed dynamics back to the original state space. This preserves Mamba’s linear-time recurrent computation while enriching cross-dimensional communication.

Result: Across tasks including long-sequence extrapolation, standard language modeling benchmarks, and brain–computer interface decoding, Motif-Mamba consistently outperforms baseline Mamba models that lack the motif-guided low-rank pathway.

Conclusion: Motif-guided low-rank recurrent dynamics act as an effective structural prior for modeling long-range dependencies, enhancing cross-dimensional communication without sacrificing Mamba’s linear-time complexity. Motif-Mamba therefore offers a stronger and still efficient alternative for long-sequence modeling compared with plain Mamba backbones.

Abstract: Efficient long-sequence modeling remains a central challenge for large language models, as self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length. Mamba offers a linear-time alternative through selective state space recurrence, but its predominantly diagonal state transitions restrict explicit interactions among state dimensions. We propose Motif-Mamba, a structured state space model that augments Mamba with a motif-constrained low-rank recurrent pathway. Inspired by the dynamics of three-node network motifs, the proposed pathway projects hidden states into a compact dynamical subspace, imposes motif-guided interactions, and maps the resulting dynamics back to the original state space. This design enhances cross-dimensional communication while preserving the linear-time recurrent structure of Mamba. Experiments on long-sequence extrapolation, language modeling benchmarks, and brain--computer interface decoding show consistent improvements over Mamba backbones, suggesting that motif-guided low-rank dynamics provide an effective structural prior for long-range sequence modeling.

</details>


### [139] [Nova: An End-to-End MLIR Compiler for Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00029)
*Adwaid Suresh,Aparna A,Harshini V M,Jona Delcy C A,Killi Uma Maheswara Rao,Ram Charan Golla,Surendra Vendra*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Nova is an end-to-end JIT compiler that optimizes deep learning workloads by tightly mapping high-level tensor operations to hardware, surpassing or matching existing systems while reducing memory usage and enabling larger models on the same GPU.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Eager execution in popular tensor frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow lacks whole-graph visibility and low-level hardware control, leading to suboptimal utilization of compute and memory resources. Existing compilers and libraries (e.g., cuBLAS, XLA) are strong but still constrained by fixed kernels, limited fusion, or search-based tuning overhead. There is a need for a system that can automatically capture eager workloads, perform global graph optimizations, and synthesize fine-grained kernels that exploit hardware and memory hierarchies more completely, all while avoiding expensive autotuning.

Method: The authors design Nova, an automated end-to-end JIT compiler that: (1) captures eager tensor executions and converts both forward and backward passes into a unified value-semantic intermediate dialect; (2) performs aggressive whole-graph optimizations, including cross-op fusion and memory hierarchy optimizations; (3) uses an Analytic Configurator to deterministically compute optimal execution schedules based on arithmetic intensity, eliminating search-based tuning; and (4) employs a structural hashing runtime to synthesize fine-grained kernels directly from computation structure, with optimizations down to the register level.

Result: On an RTX 3060 GPU, Nova matches or slightly outperforms cuBLAS and XLA for TF32 matrix multiplications across most shapes while keeping relative numerical error below 5e-4. At the end-to-end model level on a 42M-parameter model, Nova improves training throughput by up to 10.6% over PyTorch and 4.4% over XLA. Nova also reduces memory footprint by up to 29% compared to PyTorch, which allows training a 144M-parameter model at 17,900 tokens/s on a 12 GB GPU where PyTorch runs out of memory.

Conclusion: Nova demonstrates that an end-to-end JIT compiler with whole-graph visibility, analytic scheduling, and structure-driven kernel synthesis can rival and sometimes exceed highly optimized libraries and compilers in both speed and memory efficiency. By significantly reducing memory usage and eliminating autotuning overhead, Nova enables larger models and higher throughput on commodity hardware, suggesting a promising direction for future ML compilation and runtime systems.

Abstract: The performance of deep learning models at scale relies heavily on how effectively high-level mathematical operations are mapped to underlying physical hardware. While high-level tensor frameworks provide flexible abstractions for model design, their eager execution models inherently lack the whole-graph visibility and granular control over hardware and memory required to maximize physical hardware utilization natively. To bridge this gap, we designed Nova, an automated end-to-end JIT compiler whose defining purpose is to achieve absolute control over this hardware mapping: fusing operations across operation boundaries, optimizing complex memory hierarchies, and tuning execution down to the register level. By capturing eager executions and unifying forward and backward passes into a single value-semantic dialect, Nova unlocks aggressive whole-graph optimizations. It then utilizes an Analytic Configurator to deterministically derive optimal execution schedules based on arithmetic intensity, dropping search time to zero. Backed by a structural hashing runtime, Nova synthesizes fine-grained kernels directly from the computation's structure. In our evaluations on an RTX 3060, Nova matches or modestly exceeds cuBLAS and XLA on TF32 matmuls on most shapes, maintaining a stringent < 5e-4 relative error. At the model level, Nova achieves up to 10.6% greater throughput than PyTorch and 4.4% greater than XLA on a 42-million parameter model, without compromising on numerical fidelity. Crucially, by reducing the memory footprint by up to 29% relative to PyTorch, Nova successfully trains a 144-million parameter model at 17,900 tokens/s where PyTorch encounters Out-Of-Memory (OOM) failures on the same 12 GB consumer GPU.

</details>


### [140] [SIRIN: A Unified Toolkit for Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented and Memory-Grounded LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00033)
*Julia Belikova,Rauf Parchiev,Mikhail Filimonov,Konstantin Polev,Andrey Savchenko,Maksim Makarenko*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SIRIN is a unified toolkit and web UI for detecting and inspecting hallucinations in retrieval-augmented and memory-grounded LLM systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models often generate contextual hallucinations—fluent but unsupported content—especially in retrieval-augmented, agentic, and memory-grounded settings, and current hallucination detectors are fragmented, hard to compare, and difficult to integrate into real systems.

Method: The authors build SIRIN, a unified framework that integrates three major hallucination detection paradigms (representation probing, uncertainty estimation, and judge-style verification) along with a query answerability checker, all under a single configuration, interface, and evaluation pipeline that supports both white-box and black-box models at response and span level. They also provide an interactive web UI for live analysis of context-query-answer triples with visualization of hallucination scores, highlighted unsupported spans, and pluggable detectors.

Result: SIRIN successfully supports multiple hallucination-detection tasks (hallucination detection, query answerability estimation, and faithfulness gating in long-term memory systems) and allows side-by-side comparison of different detectors through a unified interface and evaluation pipeline, demonstrating its flexibility and extensibility.

Conclusion: A unified, extensible toolkit like SIRIN makes it easier to detect, inspect, and compare contextual hallucinations in modern LLM systems, facilitating practical deployment of hallucination detection methods and enabling their use as components such as faithfulness gates in memory-augmented applications.

Abstract: SIRIN (Semantic Inconsistency Recognition and Inspection Nexus) is a unified toolkit and interactive web UI for detecting contextual hallucinations (fluent, plausible responses unsupported by the provided evidence) in retrieval-augmented, agentic, and memory-grounded LLM systems. SIRIN unifies three detector paradigms (representation probing, uncertainty estimation, and judge-style verification) and the complementary task of pre-generation query answerability under one interface, configuration system, and evaluation pipeline, supporting response- and span-level inspection in both white-box and black-box settings. The web UI enables live analysis of user-supplied context-query-answer triples through hallucination scores, unsupported-span highlighting, and side-by-side detector comparison, with a lightweight plug-in design for adding new detectors. We demonstrate SIRIN on hallucination detection, query answerability, and as a faithfulness gate within long-term memory systems.
  The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/sb-ai-lab/SIRIN.

</details>


### [141] [Linguistic Context Recodes Visual Representations in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00035)
*Brian Song,Michael A. Lepori,Ellie Pavlick*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper shows that in vision-language models, language prompts dynamically reshape visual representations, rather than just querying fixed visual features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human vision flexibly adapts to task goals expressed in language, focusing on relevant objects and attributes. Existing work on VLMs mostly assumes that visual tokens are static feature banks that language reads from, without clarifying if or how language actually recodes these visual representations for specific goals. Understanding this is crucial both for cognitive plausibility and for better controlling and interpreting VLM behavior.

Method: The authors analyze internal representations of VLMs under different natural language prompts. (1) They identify “reference representations” that encode which objects are goal-relevant for a given prompt, and derive contrastive steering vectors that separate goal-relevant from irrelevant objects. They use causal interventions (e.g., adding these vectors) to test their influence on predictions and assess generalization across objects, tasks, and synthetic vs. natural images. (2) They study attribute modulation by inspecting later-layer visual representations under prompts emphasizing particular attributes, measuring selective amplification of goal-relevant attributes and testing its robustness across many prompts. They further conduct causal interventions to demonstrate that changing attribute modulation alters the model’s output distribution.

Result: (1) They find abstract reference representations that robustly encode goal-relevance induced by language prompts. The associated steering vectors are causally involved: intervening along these vectors systematically changes model predictions, and these effects generalize across object types, task variations, and from synthetic to real images. (2) They show that language prompts induce attribute-specific modulation in later visual layers: features corresponding to prompted attributes are selectively amplified for relevant objects across diverse prompts. Causal interventions confirm that this modulation materially shifts the model’s response distribution, indicating a mechanistic role in goal-directed behavior.

Conclusion: Vision tokens in VLMs are not static visual feature stores. Instead, language prompts dynamically recode and modulate these visual representations via abstract reference representations and attribute-specific amplification, thereby supporting goal-directed tasks. This supports a more dynamic, interactive view of cross-modal processing in VLMs and suggests that task goals expressed in language reshape internal vision pathways rather than merely reading out from them.

Abstract: Goal-directed visual processing is a hallmark of human visual intelligence, resulting in representations that support downstream tasks such as categorization or search. Though vision-language models (VLMs) are often faced with these same tasks, their ability to recode visual representations when presented with goal-directed language remains poorly characterized. Indeed, prior work largely treats visual representations in VLMs as static repositories of visual information that are manipulated by language representations. In the present work, we provide evidence for two concrete instances of language-induced recoding of visual representations. First, we identify an abstract reference representation that denotes which objects are goal-relevant under a natural language prompt. We extract contrastive steering vectors corresponding to this reference representation and demonstrate that they are causally implicated in model predictions. These reference representations are abstract in that they generalize to different objects, different task contexts, and even from synthetic to naturalistic images. Second, we demonstrate language-induced attribute modulation: later layers selectively amplify goal-relevant attributes in visual representations of objects. We demonstrate this phenomenon across a range of different prompts. Finally, we provide a causal intervention that demonstrates that attribute modulation mediates a VLM's response distribution. Together, our results support a more dynamic account of cross-modality processing in VLMs -- rather than vision tokens serving as static repositories of information, they are modulated to support queries articulated in language.

</details>


### [142] [RAG-TESTER: Automated End-to-End Testing of Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00054)
*Ange Maiztegi,Jon Ayerdi,Miren Illarramendi,Aitor Arrieta*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces RagTester, an automated, end-to-end testing framework that systematically evaluates Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, revealing failure modes across retrieval, generation, and their interaction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG systems allow LLMs to use external knowledge, but their reliability is fragile and depends on complex interactions between the retriever, embedding model, LLM, and prompts. Existing evaluations often miss subtle or interaction-driven failures, and there is a need for a systematic, automated way to test RAG pipelines before deployment, especially on complex or unsupported queries and diverse document conditions.

Method: The authors design RagTester, an automated test framework that (1) synthesizes retrieval corpora, queries, and ground-truth answers; (2) runs the complete RAG pipeline under different combinations of LLMs, embedding models, and retrieval mechanisms; and (3) uses an LLM-as-a-judge to score answers. Their test generation emphasizes coverage of challenging passage types, queries with no support in the corpus, and criteria that ensure various documents and parts of documents are exercised. They compare RagTester’s coverage-oriented test generation against a baseline generator across many model configurations.

Result: Using RagTester on 24 RAG configurations (8 LLMs × 6 embedding models) and running 72,000 tests, the framework identified 21,633 failures—6.6% more than a baseline input generator—and performed better in 20 out of 24 configurations. The observed failures span bad retrieval, hallucinated or unsupported answers, incomplete utilization of retrieved context, and problems handling complex passages, demonstrating the richness of failure modes RagTester uncovers.

Conclusion: Coverage-driven, automated test generation can more effectively surface interaction-related failures in RAG systems than simpler baselines. RagTester provides a practical way to evaluate and compare RAG configurations prior to deployment, helping practitioners identify weaknesses in retrieval, generation, and their interplay and thereby improve the robustness of RAG-based applications.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to use external and domain-specific knowledge, but its reliability depends on the interaction between the generative model, embedding model, retrieval mechanism, and prompt construction strategy. We present RagTester, an automated end-to-end testing approach for RAG systems. RagTester generates retrieval documents, test inputs, and expected outputs; executes the tests; and evaluates the resulting answers using an LLM as a judge. Its test-generation strategy targets complex passages, unsupported queries, and document-coverage criteria. We evaluate RagTester using eight LLMs and six embedding models, yielding 24 compatible configurations, and compare it with a baseline test-input generator. Across 72,000 test executions, RagTester detected 21,633 failures, 6.6% more than the baseline, and outperformed it in 20 of the 24 configurations. The detected failures include inaccurate retrieval, unsupported answers, incomplete use of retrieved context, and difficulties interpreting complex passages. These results show that coverage-oriented test generation can effectively expose failures caused by the interaction between retrieval and generation components and support the assessment of RAG configurations before deployment.

</details>


### [143] [H+ Embedding: Harmonizing Global and Token-Level Retrieval with Context-Dependent Phrases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00065)
*Shusen Zhang,Junyi Hu,Ye Feng,Ziteng Wang,Zhaoyuan Pan,Guosheng Dong,Xiaojun Yuan,Jiangshou Hong,Xiangzhi Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes H+ Embedding, a multi-granularity retrieval model that uses context-dependent phrases as an intermediate unit between global vectors and tokens, improving medical and scientific information retrieval efficiency and effectiveness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing retrieval methods either compress entire documents into single vectors, losing fine-grained term relevance, or use token-level late interaction, which is accurate but costly in indexing, storage, and scoring—especially problematic in terminology-heavy domains like medicine where multi-word entities, abbreviations, and numeric constraints matter.

Method: They design H+ Embedding, a unified retriever that: (1) predicts variable-length, context-dependent phrase partitions over text; (2) keeps tokens that are not in phrases as singletons; and (3) selects important units via an importance-guided mechanism and performs weighted MaxSim interaction between query and document units. This yields a multi-granularity representation spanning phrases and tokens under a controlled vector budget.

Result: On 16 scientific, medical, and bilingual retrieval tasks, the phrase-level retrieval branch outperforms the global (single-vector) branch by 6.91 macro nDCG@10, nearly matches a full token-level interaction model while requiring 13.7% fewer document vectors, and beats simple, content-independent grouping heuristics when vectors are limited.

Conclusion: Context-dependent phrase units with weighted MaxSim provide an effective middle ground between global document compression and full token-level interaction, offering a better quality–cost tradeoff for practical terminology-intensive retrieval systems such as those in medicine and scientific search.

Abstract: Terminology-intensive retrieval, especially in medical settings, depends on preserving multi-word entities, abbreviations, numerical constraints, and compositional concepts. However, existing representations lie at two extremes: single-vector retrievers often over-compress local relevance signals, while token-level late interaction retains every tokenizer subword at substantial indexing, storage, and scoring cost. This mismatch raises a natural question: can context-dependent phrases provide a useful retrieval unit between global vectors and tokens? We introduce H+ Embedding, a unified multi-granularity retriever that predicts variable-length phrase partitions, preserves uncovered tokens as singletons, and applies importance-guided unit selection with weighted MaxSim interaction. Across 16 scientific, medical, and bilingual tasks, its phrase retrieval branch exceeds the global retrieval branch by 6.91 macro nDCG@10. It also nearly matches Token while using 13.7% fewer document vectors and outperforms content-independent grouping rules under moderate vector budgets. Context-dependent phrase interaction therefore provides an intermediate quality-cost point between global compression and token-level interaction for practical retrieval systems.

</details>


### [144] [Agentic Coding in the Wild: Characterizing GitHub Copilot Traces at Production Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00101)
*Banruo Liu,Haoran Qiu,Íñigo Goiri,Rodrigo Fonseca,Ricardo Bianchini,Esha Choukse*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Characterization of production-scale AI coding agent workloads using GitHub Copilot traces to inform agent-native infrastructure design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM serving systems are optimized for chatbot-style interactions, but AI coding agents exhibit different workload patterns involving multi-step inference and tool use. There is little empirical data about these real-world agent workloads, hindering effective system and infrastructure design.

Method: Analyze large-scale operational traces from GitHub Copilot (June 2026): 3.2M users, 13M sessions, 761M LLM calls, and 95T tokens. Measure interaction patterns, KV cache behavior within and across user turns, token and session distributions, tool usage, and idle times. Build and evaluate an idle-time predictor based on observed patterns.

Result: Found that coding sessions have sparse user turns, each expanding into autonomous agent loops with many LLM+tool calls; KV cache hits are high within a turn (~90%) but drop across turns (~55%) and after events like model switches or context compaction. Workloads have diverse, long-tailed distributions in tokens, duration, and tool calls. User idle times between turns are minutes-long, while agentic loops are fast. A lightweight predictor captures 86–90% of idle time, enabling proactive resource orchestration.

Conclusion: AI coding agents generate workloads very different from chatbots, invalidating some assumptions of current LLM-serving designs. Understanding cache dynamics, tool-coupled agent loops, and long idle intervals is crucial. The empirical insights and idle-time prediction mechanism provide groundwork for building more efficient, agent-native serving infrastructure.

Abstract: AI coding agents like GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and Codex interleave multi-step LLM inference with tool execution, creating a workload different from chatbots. We present the first production-scale characterization of this workload using sampled GitHub Copilot traces from June 2026, comprising 3.2M users, 13M sessions, 761M LLM calls, and 95T tokens.
  Our analysis reveals distinctive workload properties with important systems implications. For example, agentic coding sessions consist of sparse user-initiated turns, each unfolding into an autonomous agent loop of LLM calls almost always coupled with tool execution. This structure yields KV cache hit rates averaging 90% within a turn, but falling to 55\% across turn boundaries and drastically invalidated after events like model switches or context compaction. Diverse workflows and user behaviors are observed with variable and long-tailed token consumption, time span, and tool calls. We highlight the difference between quick agentic turnaround times and the minutes-long user idle periods at turn boundaries, and design a lightweight idle-time predictor that captures 86-90\% of total idle time, enabling proactive decisions for efficient resource orchestration. These findings challenge assumptions underlying current LLM-serving systems and provide an empirical foundation for agent-native infrastructure.

</details>


### [145] [Can LLM Agents Price Competitively? A Dynamic Multi-Attribute Auction Benchmark for Agentic Commerce](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00102)
*Shimaa Ahmed,Yiwei Cai,Mohsen Minaei,Rahul Rachuri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how well modern LLM-based agents can set prices and bid in realistic, dynamic market environments using a new benchmark called Bazaar.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents begin to transact autonomously in real-world commerce, it is unclear whether current LLMs can make competent pricing decisions when facing hidden customer preferences, adaptive competitors, and sudden demand changes. There is a need for a standardized, analytically-tractable benchmark to test and compare different LLMs under such realistic market dynamics.

Method: The authors design Bazaar, a dynamic sealed-bid multi-attribute auction environment with closed-form customer utility functions. This setup allows precise, ground-truth evaluation while still capturing realistic dynamics like competition, hidden information, and demand shocks. They then benchmark 11 state-of-the-art LLMs from four providers as pricing/bidding agents, comparing performance on customer acquisition, profit generation, learning speed, and adaptation to demand shocks.

Result: The study finds that LLMs that excel at winning customers are often not the ones that maximize profit; for example, Gemini 3.1 Pro leads in customer acquisition, while Opus 4.6 leads in profit. Rankings of models change again when the environment experiences demand shocks: models that learned fastest before the shock tend to adapt the slowest afterward, whereas Gemini 3.1 Pro recovers fastest from shocks despite not being the most profitable overall. Even the best-performing model achieves less than one-third of the profit that could be obtained with perfect hindsight.

Conclusion: Current frontier LLMs show meaningful but limited competence at dynamic pricing in realistic agentic commerce settings. There are clear trade-offs between customer acquisition, profit maximization, and adaptability to shocks, and no single model dominates on all metrics. Substantial room remains for improving LLM architectures, training, or agent designs if they are to be relied upon for autonomous commercial decision-making.

Abstract: Agentic commerce is moving from concept to deployed infrastructure: payment networks, retailers, and AI platforms are setting the stage for agents to transact on behalf of merchants and consumers. Yet whether the LLMs behind these agents can price competently in real markets, where customer preferences are hidden, competitors adapt in real time, and demand can shift without warning, has not been systematically tested. We introduce Bazaar, a dynamic sealed-bid benchmark for multi-attribute auction under these conditions. Despite its dynamics, the benchmark is grounded in closed-form customer utilities, enabling exact evaluation. Across 11 frontier LLMs from four providers, the leading agents on customer acquisition (e.g. Gemini 3.1 Pro) are often not the leading agents on profit (e.g. Opus 4.6). The ranking shifts again under demand shocks: agents that learned fastest pre-shock are typically the slowest to revise their beliefs afterwards, while Gemini 3.1 Pro recovers fastest despite not leading on profit. However, even the strongest agent captures less than a third of hindsight-optimal profit, suggesting current LLMs are progressing in agentic commerce but leave substantial headroom.

</details>


### [146] [Shared Organizational Memory for Enterprise Coding Agents: System Design and Deployment Snapshot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00122)
*Harsh Rao Dhanyamraju,Leonidas Raghav*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper describes an in-production organizational memory system that automatically captures and reuses task-adjacent coding experience for enterprise coding agents, with security/privacy gating and retrieval support.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise coding agents need access to organization-specific knowledge—like internal DSLs, proprietary platforms, and local conventions—that is not present in public training data or formal documentation. Existing knowledge interfaces (e.g., wikis, knowledge bases, retrieval systems) expose stored resources but rely on developers to consciously record lessons and best practices, often outside the natural coding workflow. This leads to repeated rediscovery of the same solutions and under-utilization of prior experience.

Method: The authors deploy a platform-level organizational memory system integrated into the coding workflow. It automatically collects task-adjacent experience from coding activities, subject to contributor approval, and transforms this raw experience into curated, reusable question-answer style memories. The system incorporates security and privacy filters to block obvious risky content and provides retrieval mechanisms so that future coding agents can leverage these memories when solving similar tasks. The paper focuses on describing the lifecycle of memory capture, curation, gating, and retrieval, along with an operational snapshot of the live deployment.

Result: The primary result is an operational, in-production deployment of the organizational memory system within an enterprise environment. The paper offers an empirical snapshot of how the lifecycle functions in practice (capture, approval, curation, gating, retrieval), but it does not yet present formal quantitative evaluations of performance impact. Effects on retrieval quality and coding task outcomes are still being evaluated and are not reported as finalized results.

Conclusion: Integrating organizational memory capture directly into the coding platform, instead of relying on separate documentation practices, makes it possible to systematically collect, secure, and reuse task-adjacent developer experience for enterprise coding agents. While the deployment appears operationally viable, the paper notes that rigorous assessment of its impact on retrieval effectiveness and coding productivity is ongoing, indicating that the work is an early report on a promising but still-evaluated system.

Abstract: Enterprise coding agents rely on tools and retrieval, yet enterprise knowledge often remains outside public training data and formal documentation: internal DSLs, proprietary platforms, local conventions, recent fixes, and tacit workflows. Existing knowledge interfaces expose stored resources but still depend on agents recognizing and explicitly recording lessons worth reusing, disconnecting capture from the coding workflow and leaving development experience repeatedly rediscovered. We report an ongoing production deployment of a shared organizational memory system that makes capture a platform-level part of coding work: it collects task-adjacent experience with contributor approval, curates it into reusable question-answer memories, gates obvious security and privacy risks, and retrieves memories for future agents. This short paper describes the deployed lifecycle and an operational snapshot. Effects on retrieval and coding tasks remain under evaluation.

</details>


### [147] [AgentStream: How Well Do Self-Evolving LLM Agents Perform Under Streaming Tasks?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00155)
*Dong Yan,Jian Liang,Dapeng Hu,Ran He,Nicholas Jing Yuan,Qi Zhang,Tieniu Tan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces AgentStream, a unified evaluation framework that tests how self-evolving LLM agents learn over realistic, streaming task sequences instead of isolated tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most work on self-evolving LLM agents evaluates them on isolated tasks, ignoring realistic streaming settings where tasks arrive over time, span multiple domains, and can recur or interleave. This leaves an incomplete understanding of how these agents actually behave and improve in practice when facing complex, non-stationary task streams.

Method: The authors propose AgentStream, which organizes existing agentic benchmarks into configurable task streams and defines three streaming scenarios—Isolated, Sequential, and Interleaved—that differ in scope and domain composition. They then systematically evaluate five representative self-evolving methods combined with three strong foundation models across these scenarios, enabling a combinatorial study of how model capability, method architecture, and streaming conditions interact to affect self-evolution.

Result: Empirical results show that (1) the reliability and effectiveness of self-evolution vary substantially across the different streaming scenarios; (2) the gains from self-evolution depend strongly on base model capability and are non-monotonic with model strength—stronger models do not always benefit more; and (3) no single self-evolving method consistently outperforms others across all models and streaming settings.

Conclusion: Self-evolving LLM agents should be evaluated on realistic, streaming task setups rather than isolated single-task benchmarks. AgentStream reveals important interactions between model strength, method design, and streaming scenario, and offers practical guidance on which self-evolving methods to use under different model and task-stream conditions.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can self-evolve by continually improving from their own accumulated experience. However, existing studies predominantly adopt independent evaluation. Consequently, the behavior of self-evolving agents in realistic streaming settings, where agents adapt to diverse and complex task streams, remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we introduce AgentStream, a unified framework that evaluates self-evolving agents spanning diverse evolution components by organizing agentic benchmarks into a configurable task stream and instantiating the \texttt{Isolated}, \texttt{Sequential}, and \texttt{Interleaved} streaming scenarios at test time, which progressively vary the scope and domain composition of the stream. Over these scenarios, we combinatorially evaluate five representative self-evolving methods across three frontier foundation models, disentangling how model capability, method architecture, and streaming scenario jointly shape self-evolution. Our results show that self-evolution reliability varies across streaming scenarios, the benefit of self-evolution is gated by model capability and non-monotonic in model strength, and no single method dominates across models and scenarios. These findings offer concrete guidance for selecting self-evolving methods across models and streaming scenarios. Overall, we advocate that self-evolving agents should be evaluated under realistic task streams rather than isolated single-task settings.

</details>


### [148] [TRACE-TS: Attribution-Grounded and Traceable Sensor-Language Reasoning for Human Activity Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00200)
*Sparsh Rastogi,Tanmay Kumar,Baiyu Chen,Jatin Bedi,Zechen Li,Flora D. Salim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TRACE-TS is a framework for generating traceable, signal-grounded reasoning over wearable sensor time series, improving both activity recognition performance and explanation fidelity compared to prior LM-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most wearable-sensor methods collapse rich motion signals into coarse activity labels, losing behavioral detail. New LM-based explanation methods can describe sensor data in natural language, but their reasoning is often weakly grounded in the actual sensor signal, leading to fluent but unverifiable or hallucinated explanations. There is a need for models that both classify activities and provide faithful, evidence-linked reasoning traces grounded in the original time-series data.

Method: TRACE-TS first uses attribution from an expert classifier to find salient spatio-temporal regions in wearable time-series signals. It then constructs directed acyclic graph (DAG) reasoning traces whose nodes are observations and inferences explicitly linked to these salient regions as evidence. A compact language model is trained to generate these reasoning traces using gated cross-attention over sensor memory tokens that encode the time-series input. During training, the model is supervised with the expert’s attributions and reasoning traces; at inference, it directly outputs both the activity prediction and its reasoning trace in one forward pass, without recomputing attributions or relying on a large teacher model. The authors also propose Semantic Node Match (SNM), an LLM-as-judge evaluation metric that checks reasoning fidelity at multiple levels (observation, inference, synthesis) and identifies hallucinated observations and broken evidence chains that standard NLG metrics fail to capture.

Result: On seven wearable-sensor benchmarks, TRACE-TS attains the highest average accuracy (84.43%) and F1 score (81.24%) among all compared methods, improving F1 by 17.96% over the strongest LLM-based baseline. The SNM metric successfully exposes reasoning issues—such as hallucinated sensor observations and invalid evidence chains—that are not captured by conventional text-generation metrics.

Conclusion: TRACE-TS demonstrates that attribution-guided, structured reasoning grounded in time-series sensor evidence can simultaneously improve activity recognition performance and the faithfulness of natural-language explanations. The framework’s DAG-based traces, gated cross-attention over sensor memories, and the SNM evaluation metric collectively provide more transparent and diagnostically useful explanations for wearable-sensor models than prior LM-based approaches.

Abstract: Wearable sensors capture fine-grained motion patterns that support rich behavioral understanding, yet most existing methods reduce these signals to activity labels. Recent LM-based approaches generate natural-language explanations for sensor data, but their reasoning is weakly grounded in the underlying signal, leading to fluent yet unverifiable explanations. We introduce TRACE-TS (Traceable Reasoning with Attribution-Grounded Evidence), a framework for structured and signal-grounded reasoning over wearable time series. TRACE-TS uses attribution from an expert classifier to identify salient spatio-temporal sensor regions, uses them to construct DAG reasoning traces with explicit evidence provenance, and trains a compact language model to generate these traces through gated cross-attention over sensor memory tokens. At inference, the adapted model jointly outputs the activity prediction and its reasoning trace, without requiring attribution computation or teacher guidance. We introduce Semantic Node Match(SNM), an LLM-as-judge metric that diagnoses reasoning fidelity at the observation, inference, and synthesis levels, localizing hallucinated observations and broken evidence chains missed by standard NLG metrics. Across seven wearable benchmarks, TRACE-TS achieves the best average accuracy and F1 among all evaluated methods (84.43%/81.24%), and outperforms the best LLM-based baseline by 17.96% in F1. Our code is available at https://github.com/SparshRastogi/TRACE-TS.

</details>


### [149] [Personalizing Large Language Model Agents with Small Policy Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00215)
*Dian Jin,Zhi Zhang,Huichao Li,Yihe Pan,Rundong Huang,Doudou Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce FABLE, a lightweight layer that personalizes how a frozen LLM agent uses memory, tools, and response styles based on per-user feedback.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM agents struggle to adapt how they act (e.g., tool calling, clarification, style) to individual users, especially when the base model is proprietary or hard to fine-tune. Existing approaches mainly inject user info via prompts or memory, which doesn’t directly learn a user-specific execution policy from feedback.

Method: They cast personalization as online learning of a per-user execution policy using bandit feedback: only the chosen action gets a scalar reward. They propose FABLE, a factorized policy layer that sits outside a possibly black-box host agent. FABLE decomposes decisions (memory use, information acquisition, response choice), filters them through a feasible-action set, and then applies Bayesian contextual Thompson sampling to learn user-specific residual preferences over a default-and-cost baseline, under a linear residual-reward model. They also develop a calibrated variant with regret guarantees, analyze which preferences are unidentifiable under feasibility constraints, and design anytime-valid false-promotion control.

Result: In evaluations that test personalized reasoning, controlled feedback, and executable tool use, FABLE improves preference-sensitive behaviors compared to using only rule-based control, while preserving competitive overall task performance.

Conclusion: A separate, bandit-based policy layer like FABLE can effectively personalize execution decisions of frozen LLM agents, even when the base model is black-box, yielding better alignment with user preferences without sacrificing task performance and with theoretical guarantees on regret and error control.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can retrieve memory, call tools, ask clarifying questions, and vary response style, yet adapting these execution decisions to an individual user remains difficult. Fine-tuning a separate LLM is costly or impossible for proprietary systems, while prompts and memory primarily expose user information to the agent rather than adapt its execution decisions from feedback. We formulate personalization of a frozen agent as online learning of a per-user execution policy from scalar feedback observed only for the executed action. We propose FABLE (Factorized Adaptive Bandit Layer for Execution), a lightweight policy layer outside a potentially black-box host agent. FABLE factorizes memory, information-acquisition, and response decisions so feedback updates related choices; filters actions through an externally specified feasible set before exploration; and learns user-specific residual preferences relative to a fixed default-and-cost score via Bayesian contextual Thompson sampling. Under a linear residual-reward model, a calibrated variant inherits an expected-regret bound against the best feasible action. We also characterize preferences unidentifiable under persistent feasibility constraints and provide anytime-valid false-promotion control. Across personalized-reasoning, controlled-feedback, and executable tool-use evaluations, FABLE improves several preference-sensitive behaviors relative to rule-only control while remaining competitive on end-to-end task performance.

</details>


### [150] [More Debate, Same Evidence: Structural Limits of Homogeneous Multi-Agent Groundedness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00243)
*Yuelyu Ji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper examines whether organizing large language models into multi-agent panels with critique exchange actually improves accuracy in groundedness verification tasks, finding mixed results across benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent LLM ‘jury’ or ‘panel’ systems are becoming popular under the belief that agents debating and critiquing each other will yield better, more reliable judgments, especially for tasks requiring verification of factual support. However, this assumption has not been rigorously tested for groundedness verification, where models must decide if a claim is backed by given evidence. The paper aims to empirically test whether such multi-agent panels indeed outperform a strong single LLM judge.

Method: The authors construct a homogeneous three-agent LLM panel, where the agents exchange critiques to arrive at a final judgment, and compare it against a fixed single-agent LLM baseline. They evaluate both settings on six public benchmarks related to fact verification and hallucination detection. Performance is measured in terms of system-level accuracy, and results are analyzed for statistical reliability of gains or losses, noting that the two systems use different model variants so the comparison is at the level of full systems rather than isolating the effect of debate alone.

Result: Across six benchmarks, the three-agent panel’s accuracy relative to the single-agent reference ranges from an improvement of +8.5 percentage points to a decline of -4.4 percentage points. Two datasets show statistically reliable improvements, one shows a statistically reliable decrease in accuracy, and three datasets produce results that are statistically inconclusive. Thus, benefits of multi-agent critique are not consistent across tasks.

Conclusion: The assumption that multi-agent LLM panels with critique exchange uniformly improve groundedness verification performance is not supported by the evidence presented. While panel-based judging can yield substantial gains on some datasets, it can also harm performance or yield inconclusive advantages on others. Moreover, because the panel and baseline rely on different model variants, the reported differences reflect overall system design rather than an isolated, causal benefit of the debate mechanism itself.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) judges are increasingly organized as multi-agent panels under the assumption that exchanging critiques improves judgment quality. We test this assumption for \emph{groundedness verification}, where a judge must determine whether a claim is supported by the supplied evidence. We evaluate a homogeneous three-agent panel on six public fact-verification and hallucination-detection benchmarks. Relative to a fixed single-agent reference, the panel's system-level accuracy difference ranges from $+8.5$ to $-4.4$ percentage points: two datasets show reliable gains, one shows a reliable loss, and three are statistically inconclusive. Because the reference and panel use different model variants, these differences characterize the complete systems rather than isolate a causal debate effect.

</details>


### [151] [Geometric Self-Supervised Pre-training for Neural Combinatorial Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00270)
*David Aguado,Daniel Fuertes,Carlos R. del-Blanco,Fernando Jaureguizar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a geometric self-supervised pre-training approach to improve neural combinatorial optimization models for large-scale TSP, achieving better solution quality and much faster inference than exact solvers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement learning-based Neural Combinatorial Optimization methods perform well on routing problems like TSP but fail to generalize to larger, high-dimensional instances. Other fields have improved model generalization via self-supervised pre-training, but this is difficult to apply directly to routing graphs because they mainly contain simple 2D coordinates rather than rich graph attributes. The authors aim to design a pre-training scheme tailored to spatial geometric structures so that NCO models can scale and generalize better.

Method: They propose a geometric self-supervised pre-training framework where the model is trained, before policy optimization, to learn invariances and global distance patterns in TSP instances. This is done by applying isometric transformations (rotations, axial reflections) to the 2D coordinates of nodes and using these transformed views to enforce consistency and capture spatial invariance and global relative distance distributions. After this pre-training, the model is fine-tuned via reinforcement learning for TSP solving.

Result: Empirically, the pre-trained model outperforms the same architecture trained from scratch. On large-scale zero-shot extrapolation to TSP with 1,000 nodes, it yields an average 7.23% improvement in tour length over the baseline RL model. In addition, the method is highly efficient at inference time, achieving speedups of up to 100x compared to the exact Concorde solver on massive instances.

Conclusion: Geometric self-supervised pre-training focused on spatial invariances and distance structure can significantly enhance the generalization and scalability of neural combinatorial optimization models for routing problems. The proposed framework not only improves solution quality in large-scale TSP settings but also offers substantial computational speed advantages over exact solvers. The authors release code and pre-trained models to encourage further work in this direction.

Abstract: Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) techniques have emerged as a highly efficient alternative to traditional exact algorithms for solving routing problems such as the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP). However, the generalization capabilities of these Reinforcement Learning-based models are severely hindered when scaling to high-dimensional instances. This issue has been mitigated in other domains, like computer vision and natural language processing, by adopting a self-supervised pre-training strategy. Nevertheless, its application to routing graphs, which lack complex topological attributes beyond 2D spatial coordinates, remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose a geometric self-supervised pre-training framework specifically designed to capture spatial invariance and global relative distance distributions. By applying isometric transformations, such as rotations and axial reflections, the model learns robust structural representations prior to the policy optimization phase. Empirical results demonstrate that this strategy consistently outperforms models trained from scratch (baselines), achieving a 7.23\% improvement in tour length for massive zero-shot extrapolation scenarios (TSP1,000). Furthermore, the proposed model exhibits remarkable computational efficiency, delivering speedups of up to two orders of magnitude over the exact solver Concorde at massive scales.
  The source code and pre-trained models are publicly available at https://github.com/davidaguadocosano/TSP-GeoPretrain.git.

</details>


### [152] [RF-HOI: Recognize Human-Object Interaction with Radio Frequency Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00289)
*Lihao Wang,Linlu Gao,Jiacan Yu,Yanyu Lin,Yifan Yin,Jianxin Wang,Tianmin Shu,Renjie Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents RF-HOI, the first framework for recognizing human-object interactions using only RF signals, achieving near-vision performance while preserving privacy and robustness to lighting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing HOI recognition methods rely mainly on vision, which raises privacy concerns and fails in poor lighting. There is a need for a privacy-preserving, lighting-invariant approach that can still recognize both the human action and the specific object being interacted with.

Method: RF-HOI fuses two RF modalities—mmWave radar for capturing human motion and RFID for identifying objects—through a novel modality fusion framework. The authors also build a simulator to synthesize large-scale multimodal RF data covering diverse HOIs and environments, then fine-tune models on a small amount of real-world data to improve generalization.

Result: Experiments show RF-HOI outperforms RF-only baselines and approaches the performance of vision-based HOI models. The synthetic RF data significantly improves real-world performance and generalization across different setups.

Conclusion: Multimodal RF sensing (mmWave + RFID) is a viable and effective alternative to vision for HOI recognition, offering robustness to lighting and improved privacy. Synthetic RF data generation is an effective way to address data scarcity and enhance system performance in real-world scenarios.

Abstract: Recognizing Human-Object Interactions (HOI) is essential for intelligent systems, underpinning applications in virtual and augmented reality, embodied AI, and assistive robotics. However, vision-based HOI methods face challenges in privacy concerns and poor light conditions. In this work, we introduce RF-HOI, the first framework that only uses radio frequency (RF) signals for HOI recognition. A key challenge of RF-HOI is that single-modality RF sensing is insufficient to recognize both actions and the objects being interacted with. RF-HOI addresses this through a novel modality fusion that combines mmWave radar and RFID, enabling simultaneous action recognition and target identification. Another challenge is limited training data across diverse setups, which impairs the generalizability of the recognition model. To overcome this, we develop a simulator that synthesizes multimodal RF data for diverse HOIs at scale, allowing us to fine-tune with only a small amount of real-world data. Experiment results show that RF-HOI outperforms all baselines, approaching vision model performance, and that our diverse synthetic training data can significantly boost our system's performance on real-world scenarios. These results highlight the potential of multimodal RF sensing for robust and privacy-preserving HOI recognition as well as the effectiveness of our RF data synthesis.

</details>


### [153] [WM-Cov: Test Adequacy for Interactive World-Model-Style Autonomous Driving Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00298)
*Jianxun Cui,Ping Wu,Stanisa Peric,Marko Milojkovic,Vladan Devedzic*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes WM-Cov, an evaluation framework for interactive world-model-based testing of autonomous driving systems, focusing on what constitutes sufficient and valid test evidence rather than just counting generated failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing world models and generative simulators can create reactive, counterfactual, and rare driving scenarios, but current evaluation focuses mainly on whether they can generate dangerous or rare events, not on whether the produced evidence is valid, non-duplicated, and adequate to support a testing goal and stopping criterion.

Method: The authors formalize the notion of testing adequacy for interactive, world-model-style simulation and introduce WM-Cov, a provider-agnostic evaluation layer. WM-Cov processes raw outputs from different world-model or simulator providers and classifies them into requested, realized, and valid evidence. It then measures coverage growth, valid-failure discovery, diversity of failure modes, realism, suppression of artifacts, duplicate accounting, and precision of valid evidence. They run WM-Cov on several datasets and setups, including TeraSim/SUMO simulations, mixed trace pools that mimic world models, and a real deployment combining DriveArena TrafficManager with the WorldDreamer world model, across multiple planners, horizons, prompts, and ego-route requests.

Result: Empirical studies show that many dangerous-looking events are not straightforward evidence: they may be invalid ADS failures, duplicates, partial realizations of the request, or artifacts. In the DriveArena–WorldDreamer matrix, out of 360 requested ego routes, 304 become fully realized valid evidence while 56 are only partially realized; a separate 80-request slice results in 74 fully realized and 6 partial attempts. These analyses demonstrate different facets of adequacy such as convergence of valid evidence, diversity of failure modes, and the impact of duplicates and artifacts on perceived failure counts.

Conclusion: World-model-style testing for autonomous driving should be evaluated by the convergence and quality of valid interactive evidence under a given testing budget, rather than by raw counts of generated failures or prompt coverage. WM-Cov provides a systematic, provider-agnostic way to translate raw simulator/world-model output into meaningful adequacy metrics, helping define sound stopping criteria and interpretability for such interactive testing campaigns.

Abstract: World models and generative simulators are emerging as interactive testing infrastructure for autonomous driving because they can react to the ego planner and produce counterfactual, rare, and safety-critical rollouts. This changes a test scenario from a fixed replayed trajectory into an interactive scenario family whose realized evolution depends on the planner under test. The unresolved question is therefore not only whether dangerous rollouts can be generated, but what valid closed-loop evidence is enough to support a specified testing intent and stopping decision. This paper formulates interactive world-model-style testing adequacy and introduces WM-Cov, a provider-agnostic evaluation layer that converts raw provider outputs into requested, realized, and valid evidence. WM-Cov reports adequacy through coverage growth, valid-failure discovery, failure-mode diversity, realism, artifact suppression, duplicate accounting, and valid-evidence precision. Studies on executed TeraSim/SUMO events, WM-like mixed trace pools, and a real DriveArena TrafficManager--WorldDreamer matrix show that dangerous-looking events can include valid ADS failures, duplicates, partial realizations, and artifacts. The DriveArena matrix evaluates two planners, two horizons, six prompt conditions, and 360 ego-route requests; 304 attempts become fully realized evidence and 56 remain partial. A disjoint 80-request route-slice check yields 74 fully realized and 6 partial attempts. The results support evaluating world-model-style testing by convergence of valid interactive evidence under budget, rather than by raw generated failures or prompt coverage alone.

</details>


### [154] [CrystalMem: Elastic Memory for Self-Evolving LLM Agents via Knowledge Crystallization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00303)
*Beining Wu,Jun Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies and addresses "memory hysteresis" in LLM agents: when memory budgets are squeezed and then restored, agents fail to fully recover capability. It introduces CrystalMem, a multi-fidelity, elastic memory system that mitigates this by gradually degrading and later reconstructing memory, achieving superior restored performance under dynamic memory budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents deployed in the cloud face fluctuating memory quotas due to cost and load management. Existing memory management assumes monotonically growing memory and uses policies that only keep or delete entries or apply lossy compression. When memory is reduced and later restored, agents do not regain their original performance—creating a persistent capability gap (memory hysteresis). The authors aim to understand this phenomenon theoretically and practically, and to design a memory system that preserves or recovers capability despite dynamic memory budgets.

Method: 1) Formally define "memory hysteresis" and prove that any policy limited to keep/drop decisions (and one-way compression) inevitably leaves a residual performance deficit after a squeeze-and-recover cycle. 2) Design CrystalMem, a sidecar memory architecture with four fidelity states for entries, controlled by a "crystallization-energy" schedule that progressively demotes information at varying levels of detail. 3) Rank entries for demotion by advantage-weighted influence while considering dependencies among entries, so that more influential and dependency-critical memories are retained at higher fidelity. 4) Enable capability recovery via "verified recrystallization" procedures that selectively reconstruct higher-fidelity representations of stored information within explicit compute and byte constraints. 5) Empirically evaluate CrystalMem across seven environments, 17 baselines, six LLM backbones, including multi-tenant and edge-cloud settings, focusing on restored capability after budget fluctuations.

Result: Theoretical results show that pure keep/drop or one-way compressed memory policies cannot avoid a residual performance deficit following a reduction and restoration of memory capacity. Empirical experiments demonstrate that CrystalMem consistently provides the highest restored capability across all tested environments, backbones, and deployment conditions. From a 50% memory budget, CrystalMem matches or surpasses the best competing method operating at full memory provision in every environment. Under equal memory budgets, CrystalMem outperforms the strongest baseline by an average of +4.6 percentage points in restored capability metrics. It also successfully operates in realistic multi-tenant and edge-cloud scenarios, demonstrating robustness and practicality.

Conclusion: Memory hysteresis is an inherent structural issue for LLM agents under dynamic memory budgets when using conventional keep/drop or one-way compression policies. To overcome this, memory systems must support graded fidelity and reversible transformations that preserve reconstructible information across budget changes. CrystalMem implements such an elastic, multi-fidelity memory with principled demotion and reconstruction strategies, closing the capability gap left by prior approaches. The framework offers a practical solution for cloud and edge deployments with fluctuating resource constraints, enabling LLM agents to maintain or recover high performance even under aggressive memory squeezing.

Abstract: Memory for self-evolving large language model (LLM) agents is often provisioned as if its byte budget only grows. Cloud platforms, however, adjust quotas with load and cost, and we show that capability does not follow the budget back up: after a squeeze-and-recover cycle, the agent settles below its pre-squeeze level, a gap we call memory hysteresis. The cause is structural. Deletion and one-way compression discard the material needed for later rebuilding, and we prove that any policy that only keeps or drops entries carries a residual-deficit floor. We propose CrystalMem (Crystallized Memory), an elastic memory sidecar that demotes entries across four fidelity states under a crystallization-energy schedule, orders demotions by advantage-weighted influence with dependency coupling, and recovers capability through verified recrystallization under explicit compute and byte caps. Across seven environments, seventeen methods, and six backbones, with multi-tenant serving and a physical edge-cloud deployment, CrystalMem achieves the highest restored capability in every setting and closes the loop left open by every baseline. From a 50% byte budget, CrystalMem matches the strongest budgeted baseline at full provision on every environment; at equal budgets, it leads by +4.6 pp on average.

</details>


### [155] [Trust and Its Betrayal under Three Representational Strategies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00321)
*Mihnea C. Moldoveanu,Joel A. C. Baum*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper formalizes interpersonal trust as a special kind of subjunctive epistemic state and compares three formal representations of it, analyzing how each handles common trust and reacts to betrayal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand what trust is, how it differs from mere prediction, and how it can be formally modeled in epistemic/game-theoretic frameworks, especially in relation to the Brandenburger–Keisler impossibility result about common belief and rationality.

Method: Trust is defined as subjunctive attitudes about another’s knowledge (competence) and willingness to disclose (integrity). The authors then construct three formal models of this state: (1) as lexicographic assumptions, (2) as ordinal closeness in Lewis–Stalnaker sphere systems, and (3) as strong belief in conditional probability systems. For each, they examine whether replacing rationality with trustworthiness avoids the Brandenburger–Keisler impossibility and analyze how a specific act of betrayal affects each representation.

Result: All three models agree that any finite level of common trust can be represented, but achieving full common trust (the fixed point) remains problematic. However, the nature of the problem and the response to betrayal differ across the models: betrayal breaks the level ordering in the lexicographic model, proportionally distorts closeness orderings in the sphere model depending on deliberateness, and only changes the operative conditioning hypothesis—without global incoherence—in the strong-belief model.

Conclusion: Trust can be rigorously represented as a subjunctive epistemic state, but different formal frameworks capture different structural and dynamic aspects of trust and betrayal. While finite hierarchies of common trust are feasible in all three, full common trust is structurally fragile. The most robust under betrayal is the strong-belief/conditional-probability representation, which preserves overall coherence while updating the conditions under which trust is operative.

Abstract: Trust is a propositional attitude of a distinctive kind: to trust is to rely on another under conditions where reliance could be disappointed, and the disappointment of trust---betrayal---differs qualitatively from the disappointment of a prediction. We treat trust as a \emph{subjunctive} epistemic state: $A$ trusts $B$'s competence when $A$ believes that \emph{were $P$ true, $B$ would know it}, and $B$'s integrity when $A$ believes that \emph{were $B$ to know $P$, he would disclose it to $A$}. We develop three representations of this state---as lexicographic \emph{assumption} as \emph{ordinal closeness} in a Lewis--Stalnaker sphere system , and as \emph{strong belief} in a conditional probability system and for each we ask whether the Brandenburger--Keisler impossibility on common belief survives when the assumption of rationality is replaced by an assumption of trustworthiness. The three representations agree that every \emph{finite} depth of common trust is realizable while the \emph{completed} common-trust fixed point is the locus of difficulty, but they differ sharply in \emph{how} the difficulty manifests, and---our organizing finding---in how each survives a concrete betrayal. W show that the same betrayal refutes an agent's \emph{level ordering} under the lexicographic representation, contaminates her \emph{closeness ordering} in proportion to the betrayer's deliberateness under the ordinal representation, and merely \emph{shifts her operative conditioning hypothesis} while leaving her belief structure coherent under the strong-belief representation.

</details>


### [156] [Learning to Coordinate Symbolic Tools: LLM Agents for Verified Sum-of-Squares Certificates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00326)
*Bohan Chen,Shivam N. Patel,Richard Hoffmann,Sam Looi,Tony Yue Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper builds a tool-using LLM agent that proves polynomial inequalities via weighted sum-of-squares decompositions, using supervised training plus reinforcement learning with verifier feedback and symbolic tools, achieving strong performance on synthetic benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tool-calling LLMs can in principle handle complex symbolic tasks like proving polynomial nonnegativity, but existing models struggle with the combinatorial search over algebraic transformations needed for weighted sum-of-squares (SOS) decompositions. Since SOS proofs are exactly checkable, they offer a clean testbed for studying how to combine domain-specific training, external tools, and verifier-based optimization in AI for mathematics.

Method: The authors construct a 1.35M-example synthetic training set spanning eight auxiliary polynomial manipulation tasks plus weighted SOS decomposition. They first apply supervised fine-tuning on direct algebra problems and simulated symbolic traces, without exposing the model to native tool calls. They then apply Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a reinforcement learning method, using task-specific symbolic rewards grounded in an exact SOS verifier. At evaluation time, the agent is allowed to call SymPy tools for expansion, collection, reordering, factorization, and its final SOS outputs are verified by exact expansion and coefficient comparison. They compare multiple configurations: base model, SFT only, SFT+GRPO, and SFT+GRPO+tools.

Result: On held-out synthetic problems from the same generators, the full system (SFT+GRPO+tools) attains 78.96% verified success on weighted SOS tasks, significantly outperforming the base model with tools (44.73%). Across nine polynomial tasks (the eight auxiliaries plus SOS), it achieves 91.75% macro accuracy, making it the strongest of the four considered configurations in this controlled setting.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that combining domain-focused supervised training, symbolic tool use, and verifier-grounded reinforcement learning can substantially improve an LLM agent's performance on a complex, exactly checkable mathematical reasoning task like weighted SOS decomposition. This structured setup serves as a useful case study and suggests principles for building tool-using LLM agents in other domains where outputs can be mechanically verified.

Abstract: Tool calling allows large language models (LLMs) to invoke external computation during problem solving, a useful capability in various fields including AI for mathematics. We study this setting through weighted sum-of-squares (SOS) decomposition, a machine-checkable route to proving polynomial nonnegativity and hence polynomial inequalities. A candidate decomposition can be checked exactly, but finding one requires choosing among non-unique regroupings and coordinating multiple symbolic transformations. We develop an agent that combines algebraic task training, symbolic tools, and verifier-grounded optimization for this task. Rather than training only on the composite SOS task, we construct 1.35 million synthetic examples covering eight supporting polynomial tasks together with weighted-SOS decomposition. We first apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to direct algebra problems and simulated symbolic traces, and then use Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with task-specific symbolic rewards. The SFT corpus contains no native tool-calling messages; at evaluation, the agent uses native SymPy calls for expansion, collection, reordering, and factorization. Every final SOS answer is checked by exact expansion and coefficient comparison. On held-out, same-generator synthetic problems, the full SFT+GRPO+tools system is the strongest of four evaluated configurations, reaching 78.96% verified success on weighted SOS, compared with 44.73% for the base model with the same tools, and 91.75% macro accuracy across nine polynomial tasks. Within this controlled setting, our work provides a case study of combining domain-specific skill training, executable tools, and verifier feedback, and may inform the design of tool-calling agents in other domains with exactly checkable outputs.

</details>


### [157] [RMSWeb: Reflection, Failure-Mode Mining, and Salvage-DS for Web Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00335)
*Chengbo Liu,Lifang Zhou,Ruijie Yan,Pei Tan,Ao Sun,Haojun Huang,Guichun Hua,Sining Wei,Yining Chen,Yingying He,Yutao Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces RMSWeb, a three-part recipe to more efficiently train compact web agent models, improving data collection efficiency and post-SFT RL to achieve better accuracy with fewer interaction steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training compact web agents is costly and inefficient: successful trajectories are hard to collect and often contain unnecessary detours, SFT datasets are dominated by uninformative routine states, and existing group-relative RL on web actions suffers from weak or misleading rewards and no fallback signal when groups are rejected.

Method: The authors propose RMSWeb, consisting of: (1) reflection-conditioned retries to boost the yield of successful trajectories and shorten them; (2) failure-mode mining to focus offline RL on critical, error-prone states surfaced by the SFT policy; and (3) Salvage-DS, which integrates an action-semantic polarized reward, dynamic sampling gated by contrast and competence, and an action-only anchor that still extracts learning signal from groups deemed unsuitable for standard group-relative RL updates.

Result: Using reflection-collected data leads to policies that solve tasks with up to 19.7% fewer action steps. Across three benchmarks (WebVoyager, Online-Mind2Web, WebTailBench), RMSWeb-trained policies improve over SFT baselines by 2.4–7.0 points for the 8B model and 1.2–7.7 points for the 32B model. The 8B model attains the strongest reported Online-Mind2Web performance among similarly sized open-weight models considered, and offers a leading accuracy-cost trade-off on WebVoyager and WebTailBench, acknowledging cross-paper evaluation differences.

Conclusion: RMSWeb effectively addresses data efficiency and RL signal quality issues in training compact web agents, producing models that are more accurate and require fewer interaction steps, and that achieve competitive or state-of-the-art results among similar-sized open-weight models on several web benchmarks, albeit with some caveats about evaluation comparability.

Abstract: Compact web agents can reduce deployment cost, but training them poses challenges in both data collection and post-SFT reinforcement learning (RL). Successful trajectories are expensive to collect and often contain inefficient detours. After supervised fine-tuning (SFT), full trajectory corpora are dominated by routine states; moreover, when group-relative RL is applied to web actions, inadequately designed action-level rewards can yield weak or misleading relative updates, while groups rejected as unsuitable for such updates receive no fallback learning signal. We present RMSWeb, a three-part recipe for Qwen3-VL-Instruct at 8B and 32B. Reflection-conditioned retries increase collection yield and shorten successful trajectories; failure-mode mining concentrates offline RL on critical states exposed by the SFT policy; and Salvage-DS combines an action-semantic polarized reward, contrast-and-competence-gated dynamic sampling, and an action-only anchor for rejected groups. Policies trained with reflection-collected data use up to 19.7% fewer action steps on solved tasks. On WebVoyager, Online-Mind2Web, and WebTailBench, RMSWeb improves over SFT by 2.4-7.0 points at 8B and 1.2-7.7 points at 32B. Our 8B model also achieves the strongest reported Online-Mind2Web result among similarly sized open-weight models in our comparison and a leading reported accuracy-cost trade-off on WebVoyager and WebTailBench, with the caveat that external evaluation protocols differ.

</details>


### [158] [Bayesian and Motivated Reasoning in AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00339)
*Eddie Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper shows that AI agents' conclusions depend heavily on how identical numerical data are framed, revealing susceptibility to prior-belief-driven framing effects in high-stakes domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents are increasingly used to support or automate consequential decisions, it is critical to understand whether they robustly interpret evidence or are vulnerable to context and framing. Human decision-makers are known to exhibit framing effects and confirmation bias, and similar vulnerabilities in AI agents could pose significant risks, especially when their internal priors and reasoning are opaque.

Method: The authors run controlled experiments in several high-stakes domains (medicine, election forensics, geopolitical forecasting) where they hold the underlying numerical evidence constant but systematically vary the substantive scenario or framing in which that evidence is embedded. They compare multiple AI agents across twelve agent-domain combinations, measuring how conclusions change with framing and how internal processes such as search behavior, choice of analytical specifications, and evaluation of evidence differ depending on the prior-consistent or prior-inconsistent framing.

Result: Across all twelve agent-domain settings, AI agents' final conclusions are significantly influenced by their prior beliefs and the associated framing. Agents are more likely to endorse propositions they already consider likely when the same data are framed as supporting those propositions, and are correspondingly more skeptical when the framing conflicts with their priors. The framing also alters the agents' intermediate behavior, including how extensively they search for additional information, which analytical methods they select, and how they interpret the same numerical evidence.

Conclusion: AI agents exhibit framing- and prior-dependent reasoning analogous to human confirmation bias: their conclusions on identical evidence can shift with scenario framing, and their internal workflows also change. This creates a hidden risk in delegating consequential decisions to AI, because important determinants of decisions—implicit priors and framing-sensitive reasoning—are not explicitly specified in the task and may not appear in the recorded decision process, undermining transparency, reliability, and auditability.

Abstract: AI agents increasingly perform open-ended tasks in settings where their conclusions can guide consequential decisions. We provide evidence that AI agents draw different conclusions from identical numerical data when the substantive framing changes. We demonstrate this behavior in high-stakes domains in medicine, election forensics, and geopolitical forecasting by holding the evidence fixed while changing the scenario in which the evidence appears. Across twelve agent-domain comparisons, agents' conclusions are strongly influenced by their prior beliefs.
