They are more likely to reach an affirmative conclusion when it is framed around a proposition they already regard as likely, while the reverse holds when the framing conflicts with their prior. The framing also changes how some agents work: they search more extensively, choose different analytical specifications, and evaluate the same evidence differently. These results identify a particular risk of delegating decision-making to AI agents, as their decisions may depend on prior beliefs that are neither specified in the task nor visible in the decision record.

</details>


### [159] [Gene Ontology-Guided Hierarchical Spatial Gene Expression Prediction from Histopathology Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00405)
*Zhiwen Xu,Xiaoming Yan,Chengkun Wu,Juan Chen,Haoang Chi,Liyang Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents MSGR, a method that uses Gene Ontology hierarchy as a structural prior to predict spatial gene expression from histopathology images, improving over flat decoding and random hierarchies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current models predict gene expression from images by treating genes as an unstructured vector, neglecting known biological relationships and hierarchies among genes. This wastes valuable prior knowledge and forces models to learn inter-gene dependencies purely from data, which is limited and harms prediction accuracy. The authors aim to leverage the curated Gene Ontology hierarchy to explicitly guide gene expression prediction and improve performance and biological plausibility without changing image encoders.

Method: MSGR (Multi-Scale Gene Refiner) introduces a GO-guided decoder that organizes target genes into a four-level tree based on Gene Ontology. Starting from coarse functional groups and refining to individual genes, the decoder applies residual corrections at each level, with scale-weighted supervision to enforce consistency across hierarchy levels. The module operates only on the gene decoding side, making it a plug-in replacement for existing flat decoders without altering the image-side architecture. Comparisons include flat decoders, hierarchical decoders with random trees, and state-of-the-art generative methods.

Result: On nine datasets from the HEST-1k benchmark, MSGR consistently outperforms flat decoding approaches and even a strong generative baseline. Furthermore, when compared to a decoder using a random but structurally identical hierarchy, MSGR achieves an additional +0.027 performance gain, demonstrating that the improvement stems from the biological structure encoded in GO rather than from hierarchical prediction alone.

Conclusion: Incorporating Gene Ontology as a structural prior for decoding gene expression from histopathology images yields systematically better predictions compared with unstructured, flat decoding. The gains cannot be explained merely by using any hierarchy; they specifically arise from the biologically meaningful ontology. MSGR is modular and compatible with existing architectures, suggesting that biologically informed structured decoders are a promising direction for large-scale spatial transcriptomics prediction.

Abstract: Predicting spatial gene expression from histopathology images enables large-scale transcriptomic profiling without the cost of direct measurement. Existing methods decode the target gene set as a flat, unstructured vector, ignoring the inter-gene dependencies arising from shared biological pathways and regulatory programs. Without explicit structural guidance, models must infer these dependencies entirely from limited paired data, constraining prediction quality. We propose MSGR (Multi-Scale Gene Refiner), which bridges this gap by incorporating the Gene Ontology (GO), a curated functional hierarchy of genes, as an explicit structural prior. MSGR organizes target genes into a four-level GO tree. Its GO-guided decoder then progressively refines predictions from coarse functional domains to fine individual genes via residual corrections under scale-weighted supervision. Operating solely on the gene side, the GO-guided decoder serves as a seamless plug-in replacement that consistently improves existing architectures without requiring any image-side modifications. Extensive experiments on nine datasets from the HEST-1k benchmark provide empirical evidence for two central claims: GO-structured decoding consistently outperforms flat decoding, even against a state-of-the-art generative baseline, and the gain is attributable to biological ontology structure rather than hierarchical decomposition per se, as confirmed by a +0.027 margin over a structurally equivalent random hierarchy.

</details>


### [160] [Where did the ambiguity go? Examining how multimodal models interpret polysemous words](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00410)
*Jasin Cekinmez,Addison J. Wu,Raja Marjieh,Thomas L. Griffiths*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how polysemous word meanings (like 'bank' or 'palm') are expressed differently in text vs. images by large models, and finds that images cover far fewer senses than text and humans, revealing a multimodal gap in meaning expression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs show strong understanding of multiple word senses in text, it is unclear how this polysemy is expressed in other modalities such as text-to-image generation. Understanding whether and how this semantic richness transfers across modalities is important for building truly multimodal foundation models and for diagnosing where current systems fall short of human-like understanding and imagination.

Method: The authors evaluate 17 text-to-image and 15 text-generation models using isolated polysemous words without disambiguating context. For each word, they collect many generated samples and categorize which word sense each sample represents. They then compute the distribution over senses and measure its diversity with normalized entropy. They also prompt models in a meta way—asking them to estimate how often they would generate outputs corresponding to each meaning—and compare these self-reported distributions to the empirical ones and to human imagination distributions.

Result: Generated images consistently realize far fewer senses of polysemous words than generated text does, leading to much lower sense diversity (normalized entropy ~0.10 for images vs. ~0.25 for text). Both modalities underrepresent the diversity of meanings that humans associate with the same words (normalized entropy ~0.47). When models are explicitly asked to report sense frequencies, their predicted sense distributions are more diverse than what is observed in their actual generations, suggesting a mismatch between their internal semantic knowledge and expressed outputs, especially in the visual modality.

Conclusion: There is a systematic multimodal gap in how foundation models express polysemous meanings: visual generations collapse onto a limited subset of senses compared to text and to human imagination, and models’ explicit meta-reports about their own sense distributions overstate their actual expressive diversity. This implies that semantic understanding does not transfer equally or faithfully across modalities, highlighting the need for better multimodal alignment and generation mechanisms that more fully reflect the rich, polysemous structure of human language and thought.

Abstract: Human language is highly polysemous. Many common words (e.g., 'bank' or 'palm') carry several distinct meanings that shape what humans communicate and imagine. Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to understand this multiplicity of meaning, but much less is known about how polysemy surfaces in other modalities such as images. We study this across 17 text-to-image and 15 text-generation models by giving each a polysemous word with no context to fix its meaning and measuring which senses are produced over many samples. We find a clear multimodal gap, where within every model family, generated images settle on far fewer senses than generated sentences (normalized entropy 0.10 vs. 0.25), and both are far less varied than what people imagine for the same words (normalized entropy 0.47). However, when we instead ask a model to list how often it would generate outputs corresponding to each possible meaning of a word, it predicts distributions that are more diverse than the actual space of outputs. These results reveal a multimodal gap in how foundation models express meaning, and how their understanding may not transfer faithfully nor equally across modalities.

</details>


### [161] [SymboUQ: Symbolic Uncertainty Quantification for Spatial Reasoning in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00417)
*Dahai Yu,Lin Jiang,Rongchao Xu,Guang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SymboUQ is a framework to estimate the reliability of LLM spatial reasoning answers by leveraging symbolic verification signals beyond token-level confidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can produce plausible step-by-step spatial reasoning, but those steps may not truly support the final answer, and formal verifiers only partially apply, often returning inconclusive results. There is a need for a principled way to assess when and how verifier feedback can be used to quantify answer reliability.

Method: The authors propose SymboUQ, which separates two aspects: symbolizability (whether a textual claim can be expressed in a formal language) and semantic determinacy (whether executing that formal representation yields a clear entailment or contradiction). SymboUQ includes (i) a Layout Auditor that symbolically executes ordered spatial claims and extracts feasibility, conflicts, and possible repairs; (ii) a label-free Determinacy Profile that summarizes how much of the reasoning trace is both symbolizable and determinately checkable; and (iii) a Determinacy-Aware Reliability Composer that adaptively combines constraint-based, representation-based, and decoding-based confidence scores depending on where the verifier is applicable.

Result: On five spatial reasoning benchmarks using four frozen LLM backbones, SymboUQ improves AUROC for uncertainty estimation by about 8% relatively and reduces class-balanced Brier loss by about 7% compared to the strongest prior baseline, indicating more accurate reliability estimation of final answers.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling when formal verification is applicable (symbolizability) and when it gives decisive semantic judgments (determinacy), and composing multiple signals accordingly, leads to significantly better uncertainty quantification for LLM-based spatial reasoning than relying on token-level confidence or naively using verifier outputs.

Abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) can produce fluent spatial reasoning traces, their intermediate relations may fail to support the final conclusion, making token-level confidence insufficient for final-answer reliability estimation. Existing formal verifiers provide stronger semantic evidence, but their applicability is partial: a parsed claim need not yield a definite semantic verdict. To address this issue, we introduce SymboUQ, a symbolic uncertainty quantification framework that estimates final-answer reliability from reasoning traces by distinguishing symbolizability, whether a claim can be represented in the verifier's formal language, from semantic determinacy, whether its execution yields an entailed or contradicted verdict rather than an unknown or not-evaluable outcome. SymboUQ comprises (i) a Layout Auditor that executes ordered spatial claims and extracts feasibility, conflict, and repair evidence; (ii) a label-free Determinacy Profile that characterizes effective executable coverage; and (iii) a Determinacy-Aware Reliability Composer that integrates constraint-based, representation-based, and decoding-based scores according to verifier applicability. Extensive experiments on five spatial reasoning benchmarks with four frozen LLM backbones show that SymboUQ achieves approximately an 8% relative improvement in AUROC and a 7% relative reduction in class-balanced Brier loss over the strongest baseline.

</details>


### [162] [Mask-Based Priors Are More Persistent than Query-Key Initializations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00418)
*Mingze Ma,Hemanth Saratchandran,Cameron Gordon,Simon Lucey*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper shows that standard Transformers systematically extrapolate incorrectly on Boolean tasks and proposes a simple, persistent structural prior implemented as a learnable attention mask, which fixes this failure and also helps in other domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work found that Transformers, while fitting training data on Boolean extrapolation tasks, generalize using a default, simpler interpolating rule instead of the true function, revealing a problematic inductive bias. Existing attempts to inject structure via query-key (QK) initialization do not reliably persist through training. The authors want a more direct and robust way to encode structural priors into attention so that Transformers extrapolate correctly, especially on controlled reasoning tasks that probe inductive bias.

Method: They compare two ways of encoding structural priors into Transformers’ attention: (1) existing QK-based structured initializations, where query and key projections are chosen so that their similarity induces a desired attention pattern, and (2) a new mask-based initialization that directly initializes the additive attention mask. Their mask is a finite, learnable bias on the attention logits, initialized from the known interaction structure of the task (e.g., which tokens should interact). Unlike fixed causal or local masks, this mask is trainable and separated from content-based scores, so the structural prior can survive optimization. They evaluate these approaches on Boolean reasoning extrapolation tasks, low-data arithmetic, and standard vision and language benchmarks.

Result: On Boolean extrapolation tasks, standard Transformers and those with QK-based priors both converge to the default, incorrect extrapolation rule, failing to fix the inductive bias. In contrast, the proposed mask-based initialization yields near-perfect extrapolation, indicating that the intended structural prior persists and governs generalization. Beyond Boolean tasks, the same mechanism improves performance in low-data arithmetic settings and remains competitive on vision and language benchmarks, suggesting that the approach is broadly useful and does not harm performance on more standard tasks.

Conclusion: Directly initializing a learnable additive attention mask from task-level structure provides a simple and robust way to encode persistent inductive bias in Transformers. Unlike QK-based structured initialization, mask-based priors are not easily overwritten during training and can correct systematic extrapolation failures on Boolean reasoning tasks while also benefiting other domains. Attention masks should be viewed not only as hard architectural constraints but also as a flexible substrate for embedding enduring structural priors into Transformer models.

Abstract: Transformers do not merely lack data on some Boolean extrapolation tasks; they generalize in a systematically wrong way. Recent work on generalization on the unseen has shown that, despite fitting the observed domain, Transformers often extrapolate according to a simpler minimum-degree interpolator rather than the true target function. These Boolean tasks are not practical applications, but controlled stress tests for understanding Transformer inductive bias. We ask whether this failure mode can be corrected by injecting explicit structural priors into attention. Existing structured-initialization methods alter Transformer inductive bias indirectly, by choosing query and key projections whose similarity scores approximate a desired attention pattern. However, we find that when applied to Boolean extrapolation, these QK-based priors can be rapidly overwritten during training and fail to change the learned extrapolation rule. We propose a simpler alternative: initialize the additive attention mask directly. Unlike standard hard masks used for causality or locality attention, our mask is a finite, learnable attention-logit bias initialized from task-level interaction structure. This separates the structural prior from content-dependent attention scores, allowing it to persist throughout optimization. On Boolean reasoning tasks, mask-based initialization achieves near-perfect extrapolation where vanilla and QK-initialized Transformers remain trapped by the default inductive bias. The same mechanism also improves low-data arithmetic performance and remains competitive on vision and language benchmarks. These results show that attention masks can serve not only as architectural constraints, but as a simple substrate for encoding persistent inductive bias in Transformers.

</details>


### [163] [TrAC: Trace-Conditioned Answer Consistency for Efficient Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00422)
*Dahai Yu,Lin Jiang,Rongchao Xu,Guang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes TrAC, a new framework to estimate how likely an LLM’s final answer is correct by analyzing a single full reasoning trace plus a short, conditioned re-elicited answer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs often produce plausible reasoning that still yields wrong answers, so we need accurate response-level uncertainty measures to decide when to abstain, trigger human review, or allocate more computation. Existing methods either rely on token-level confidence of a single trace, compare multiple sampled traces (expensive), or probe partial prefixes, but none explicitly checks how well a completed reasoning trace actually supports the final answer.

Method: The authors introduce Trace-Conditioned Answer Consistency (TrAC), which operates on one completed reasoning trace. Its active component, Prefix-Conditioned Elicitation (PCE), re-elicits a short answer conditioned on the full trace and encodes both the agreement with the original answer and the token-level probability of that re-elicited answer. Its passive component, Trace Uncertainty Profile (TUP), summarizes how token-level uncertainty evolves over the tokens of the original reasoning trace. A small learned head then combines the PCE and TUP representations into a single score estimating whether the response is correct.

Result: On five math reasoning benchmarks and three different LLM families, TrAC outperforms an eight-sample self-consistency baseline while using only one full trace plus a short cached probe. Specifically, it improves macro AUROC by 1.8% and reduces AURC by 3.4%. When eight samples are already available, adding TrAC-style re-elicitation on top of sample consensus further boosts macro AUROC by 4.3% and lowers AURC by 8.3%, without requiring extra long generations.

Conclusion: Re-eliciting answers conditioned on a completed reasoning trace, together with profiling token-level uncertainty along that trace, provides a more sample-efficient and accurate way to estimate response-level correctness. TrAC can either replace more expensive multi-sample methods or augment them to significantly improve uncertainty quantification for LLM reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent reasoning traces that nevertheless lead to incorrect answers, making response-level uncertainty estimation important for abstention, human review, and adaptive compute allocation. Existing approaches generally fall into three categories: passive single-trace methods use token-level confidence signals, sampling-based methods compare multiple complete traces at higher generation cost, and active prefix-based methods probe partial traces to study answer stabilization or preference transitions. However, none actively re-elicits an answer from a completed reasoning trace to measure its consistency with and support for the original answer. To address this gap, we introduce Trace-Conditioned Answer Consistency (TrAC), a correctness-supervised uncertainty quantification framework that combines active and passive signals anchored to one completed reasoning trace. Its active component, Prefix-Conditioned Elicitation (PCE), re-elicits a short answer conditioned on the completed trace and represents both its consistency with the original answer and its token-level probabilistic support. Its passive component, Trace Uncertainty Profile (TUP), summarizes how token-level uncertainty evolves throughout the original generation without additional decoding. A lightweight head then integrates the two representations into a response-correctness score. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three LLM families, TrAC improves macro AUROC by 1.8% and reduces AURC by 3.4% relative to eight-sample self-consistency, while using one complete reasoning trace and a short cached answer probe. When eight samples are already available, augmenting sample consensus with re-elicitation further improves macro AUROC by 4.3% and reduces AURC by 8.3%, without additional full-trace generation.

</details>


### [164] [Diagnose Before You Compress: Prediction-Independent Bottleneck Witness Refinement for LLM Serving Traces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00423)
*Liming Liu,Chao Hu,Mingfei Lu,Cong Tan,Yiwei Ge,Chijin Zhou,Yongjun Xie,Runzhe Wang,Xiaohai Shi,Heyuan Shi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce BPW, a framework to build small yet diagnostically reliable replay workloads for LLM serving, ensuring every bottleneck type is evidenced without relying on workload representativeness or bottleneck predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Full trace replay of production LLM traffic is too expensive, and existing trace reduction focuses on representing typical workloads rather than ensuring that all potential bottlenecks (scheduler, prefill, decode, KV-cache) are exposed. Rare, non-representative workloads may be exactly those that reveal bottlenecks, and using predicted bottlenecks as ground truth leads to circular evaluation.

Method: BPW is a three-stage framework. (1) Workload Candidate Nomination uses response-blind features and closed source-side measurements to select traffic subsets likely to expose specific bottlenecks (scheduler, prefill, decode, KV-cache). (2) Coverage-Priority Sequence Construction treats multi-component bottleneck proposals as hyperedges, then builds a prioritized sequence of workloads that maximizes coverage of weak and uncovered components. (3) Bottleneck Truth Verification uses only direct measurements on the target system (no prediction models) to label which components are actually bottlenecks, and finds the shortest workload prefix that satisfies a two-witness requirement for every component.

Result: On three LLM-serving benchmarks (BurstGPT, ServeGen, Mooncake), BPW achieves the diagnostic coverage goal with a compact replay suite and outperforms 16 baseline policies. It improves Mean prefix Macro-F1 by 2.3% and WBRC-AUC by 16.3%, and ablation/sensitivity studies show each stage contributes distinctly and the overall method is locally stable.

Conclusion: BPW provides a principled way to construct small, bottleneck-preserving replay workloads for LLM serving, avoiding circular evaluation and ensuring each bottleneck type has independent evidence. It yields better diagnostic performance than prior trace reduction methods while remaining compact and robust across configurations.

Abstract: Production LLM serving generates millions of diverse requests, making full-trace replay across serving configurations increasingly expensive. Existing trace reduction methods mainly preserve workload distributions or representative requests, but bottleneck-revealing workloads may be rare and non-representative. Moreover, evidence for one component cannot compensate for missing evidence in another, while using predicted bottlenecks as target truth creates circular evaluation. These limitations make it necessary to preserve evidence for every bottleneck component rather than rely on workload representativeness alone. We propose Bottleneck-Preserving Witnessing (BPW), a quality-constrained framework for compact and diagnostically reliable LLM serving replay suites. BPW first performs Workload Candidate Nomination using response-blind workload features and closed source-side measurements. This stage identifies workloads that may expose scheduler, prefill, decode, or KV-cache bottlenecks. Coverage-Priority Sequence Construction then organizes multi-component proposals as reusable hyperedges and prioritizes weak and uncovered dimensions. Finally, Bottleneck Truth Verification derives prediction-independent labels solely from direct target-system measurements. The verified results determine the earliest prefix satisfying the direct two-witness requirement for every component. Experiments on BurstGPT, ServeGen, and Mooncake show that BPW reaches the verified gate with a compact workload set and outperforms 16 policies, achieving relative improvements of 2.3% and 16.3% in Mean prefix Macro-F1 and WBRC-AUC, respectively. Stage-resolved and sensitivity analyses confirm the distinct contributions and local stability of its three stages. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/llmllmllm/BPW

</details>


### [165] [Ekova: A Personality-Support Agent for Self-Discovery Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00478)
*Yuyan Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a new paradigm, Personality Support (PS), distinct from traditional Emotional Support systems, and implements it via a new dataset, a multi-persona PS system, and a unified long-term PS agent that outperforms prompt-based baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Emotional Support systems focus mainly on short-term distress relief and miss a complementary need: helping users gain cognitive clarity and better articulate their own personalities, values, and patterns. The authors want to formalize and support this broader, reflective use case.

Method: They (1) design and collect DSD, a Chinese self-discovery dataset with 8,590 longitudinal interaction samples across five support styles/personas (Coach, Warm, Tsukkomi, Real, Gonzo); (2) propose DeepSupport, a multi-persona PS system trained with OrthoTune, which uses style-specific adapters and a style-consistency regularizer so each persona maintains a distinct style; and (3) integrate these personas into Ekova, a unified PS agent with a cross-session memory layer enabling adaptive persona routing and explicit user persona choice.

Result: Models trained with OrthoTune on DSD significantly outperform a range of baselines, including the strongest prompt-based baseline, achieving an average relative performance gain of 16.3% across all evaluation metrics. This shows that the proposed PS-specific training and architecture better capture and deliver personality-supportive behaviors.

Conclusion: Personality Support is a distinct and practically useful paradigm from standard Emotional Support. Purpose-built data, training methods (OrthoTune), and system design (Ekova with multi-persona and cross-session memory) lead to measurably better PS behavior than prompt-based approaches, suggesting future support systems should explicitly model and optimize for self-discovery and cognitive clarity, not just immediate distress reduction.

Abstract: Emotional Support (ES) systems have long optimized a single objective: alleviating the user's emotional distress in the moment. We argue that a complementary need, helping users see themselves more clearly, defines a distinct paradigm we call Personality Support (PS). PS is not counseling or clinical intervention: it targets cognitive clarity and self-articulation, not symptom relief or diagnosis. We instantiate this paradigm in three layers. First, we present DSD, a Chinese self-discovery PS Dataset of 8,590 samples collected through real longitudinal interaction across five minimal units, Coach, Warm, Tsukkomi, Real, and Gonzo. Second, we build DeepSupport, a multi-persona PS system trained with OrthoTune, a PS-tailored framework with style-specific adapters and a style-consistency regularizer. Third, we unify the five DeepSupport personas into Ekova, a persistent personality-support agent with a unified cross-session memory layer, supporting both adaptive routing and user-customized persona selection. Experiments show that OrthoTune-trained models outperform all baselines with an average relative gain of 16.3% across all metrics over the strongest prompt-based baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/Yukyin/Ekova.

</details>


### [166] [F-WANDA: Fisher-Reweighted Post-Training Pruning for Sustainable Deployment of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00481)
*Himanshu Mishra*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes F-WANDA, a more efficient one-shot post-training pruning method for large language models that improves accuracy at a similar or lower computational cost compared to prior methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing one-shot pruning methods for LLMs either significantly hurt model quality (e.g., WANDA) or require expensive computation and energy (e.g., SPARSEGPT). There is a need for a pruning approach that maintains or improves performance while keeping the pruning process cheap and sustainable.

Method: F-WANDA modifies the WANDA pruning scheme by reallocating the per-row keep budget across output neurons based on the empirical Fisher information of their pre-activations. It gathers the Fisher signal using a single additional backward pass over the same calibration dataset used by WANDA, without updating any weights, and then uses this information to guide which weights to keep at a given sparsity level.

Result: On LLaMA-2-7B with 50% unstructured sparsity, F-WANDA achieves a WikiText-2 perplexity of 6.85, matches WANDA in fluency, and improves 5-shot MMLU scores by 1.6 percentage points over WANDA and 1.1 percentage points over SPARSEGPT. It also reduces pruning wall-clock time and energy to about one-third of that required by SPARSEGPT.

Conclusion: F-WANDA achieves a better trade-off between model quality and pruning cost than existing one-shot pruning methods, without requiring extra calibration data or any fine-tuning. This positions F-WANDA on the Pareto frontier of quality versus pruning cost, making it a strong and sustainable option for compressing large language models.

Abstract: One-shot post-training pruning is the most energy-frugal compression strategy for largelanguage models (LLMs), yet existing approaches trade either quality (WANDA) or compute cost (SPARSEGPT). We introduce F-WANDA, a drop-in modification of WANDA that reallocates the per-row keep budget across output neurons in proportion to the empirical Fisher information of the pre-activation. The Fisher signal is collected in a single additional backward pass over the same calibration corpus WANDA already uses; no weights are updated. On LLAMA-2-7B at 50 % unstructured sparsity, F-WANDA attains WikiText-2 perplexity of 6.85, matches WANDA fluency, and improves 5-shot MMLU by +1.6 pp over WANDA and +1.1 pp over SPARSEGPT, while incurring only one-third of SPARSEGPT pruning wall-clock and energy. The headline trade-off is achieved without extra calibration data or fine-tuning, placing F-WANDA on the Pareto frontier of quality versus pruning cost for sustainable LLM compression.

</details>


### [167] [The Bayesian Reflex: A Predictive Coding Engine for Artificial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00492)
*Sourabh Bhattacharya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes the 'Bayesian reflex', a scalable, brain-inspired predictive coding framework for AI built on recent Bayesian and probabilistic advances.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Predictive coding is a compelling theory of how the cortex computes, but current AI lacks a scalable, algorithmic realization that preserves its probabilistic rigor and brain-inspired properties. The authors want to close this gap and provide a practical framework for continual learning, perception, and decision-making.

Method: They define the Bayesian reflex around three pillars: (1) hierarchical generative models for representing and maintaining beliefs; (2) sequential Bayesian updating implemented as prediction-error minimization (a formalization of predictive coding); and (3) active inference to drive actions based on uncertainty. They operationalize this using three modern techniques: ellipsoidal decomposition for exact i.i.d. sampling from complex posteriors, recursive Gaussian processes for deep hierarchical inference, and derivative-aware Bayesian optimization for efficient exploratory decision-making.

Result: They build a unified computational framework that is mathematically principled, scalable, and directly aligned with predictive coding and active inference principles. They demonstrate its versatility via applications including climate model evaluation and discovering patterns in prime numbers, showing that it can handle diverse continual-learning and decision-making tasks.

Conclusion: The Bayesian reflex provides a concrete, scalable instantiation of predictive coding and active inference for AI, acting as a blueprint for adaptive, brain-inspired systems that integrate perception, learning, and decision-making under uncertainty across domains.

Abstract: Predictive coding offers a powerful theory of cortical computation, but corresponding scalable algorithmic implementations for artificial intelligence have remained elusive. This paper introduces the Bayesian reflex, a computational framework that directly instantiates predictive coding through three pillars: belief maintenance via hierarchical generative models, sequential Bayesian updating via prediction-error minimization, and uncertainty-driven action via active inference. We show that recent breakthroughs---ellipsoidal decomposition for exact $i.i.d.$ sampling, recursive Gaussian processes for deep hierarchical inference, and derivative-aware Bayesian optimization---provide the missing algorithmic ingredients. The resulting framework enables mathematically principled, scalable, and brain-inspired continual learning, perception, and decision-making. We illustrate its versatility through applications ranging from climate model evaluation to prime number discovery, offering a blueprint for truly adaptive artificial intelligence.

</details>


### [168] [TaPR: Test-Aware Policy Refinement for Feedback-Conditioned Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00494)
*Aofan Liu,Jingxiang Meng,Fangxin Liu,Yongbiao Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TaPR introduces a test-aware, per-turn reward and evaluation framework for multi-turn code agents, aligning training and metrics with feedback-driven code repair.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-turn code agents are trained and evaluated with single-shot, outcome-only rewards, which conflate initial code generation with subsequent repair steps and discard fine-grained execution feedback, making it unclear whether models truly learn self-repair capabilities.

Method: TaPR defines a consistent multi-turn interaction protocol and converts execution feedback (test results) into a dense, per-turn test-pass-ratio reward signal. Policies are optimized using this turn-level reward, and performance is evaluated with metrics that separately capture first-shot success and multi-turn improvement. Experiments are run on six models across 219 LiveCodeBench problems, including targeted slices and ablations (e.g., Qwen3-8B) to compare against outcome-only GRPO training.

Result: Using TaPR, pooled three-turn Pass@3 improves by 2.44 percentage points across six models. In a 7B/8B model subset, pooled accuracy rises from 30.25% to 33.56%, with 42 tasks improving and 13 regressing. For Qwen3-8B, TaPR’s dense reward offers informative feedback in all of the first ten steps and achieves a higher performance peak on a harder subset than GRPO under the same budget, while GRPO approaches TaPR’s pooled Pass@3 only after 300 steps.

Conclusion: TaPR’s reward-decomposition and turn-aware evaluation protocol better aligns training and evaluation with the desired behavior of multi-turn code agents, successfully separating initial code quality from repair ability and leveraging dense test-based rewards to improve multi-turn performance over outcome-only methods like GRPO.

Abstract: Multi-turn code agents rely on execution feedback to repair incorrect programs, yet standard reinforcement learning paradigms optimize and evaluate policy performance primarily using single-shot outcome rewards. This misalignment conflates initial code generation with feedback-driven refinement, discards granular execution signals across intermediate turns, and fails to evaluate whether the policy actually acquires self-repair capabilities. We propose Test-aware Policy Refinement (TaPR), a framework that transforms execution feedback into a dense per-turn test-pass-ratio reward under a consistent multi-turn interaction protocol. Across six models on 219 code-generation problems from LiveCodeBench, TaPR improves the pooled three-turn success rate (Pass@3) by 2.44 percentage points. In the predefined 7B/8B high-headroom slice, pooled accuracy increases from 30.25% to 33.56% (+3.31 pp), with 42 improvements and 13 regressions in paired trials. On a matched Qwen3-8B ablation, the dense reward supplies nonzero feedback in all of the first ten steps and reaches a higher Hard-subset peak than outcome-only GRPO within the tested budget, although GRPO nearly matches pooled Pass@3 by step 300. Our primary contribution is a reward-decomposition framework and a turn-aware evaluation protocol that decouple first-shot generation quality from multi-turn repair competence.

</details>


### [169] [BayesSeg: A Bayesian Optimization Framework for State Segmentation of Electricity Consumption Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00513)
*Zhenya Zhang,Wendi Zhu,Ping Wang,Hongmei Cheng,Shuguang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BayesSeg is a Bayesian-optimized, unified NILM segmentation framework that automatically tunes parameters and jointly evaluates event-level and global structure quality to produce accurate, scalable steady/transition-state segmentation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing NILM segmentation methods suffer from heuristic, manual parameter tuning, high sensitivity to exact segment boundaries, and saturated or weakly discriminative evaluation metrics (often point-wise), making robust, scalable segmentation difficult. There is a need for an automated, principled way to segment time series into steady and transition states while fairly evaluating both local switching events and global sequence structure, and to efficiently optimize segmentation parameters without exhaustive search.

Method: The paper proposes BayesSeg, a three-layer framework: (1) Segmentation layer: uses a dual steady-state criterion based on tail value and mean of preceding subsequences, plus sequential extraction and complement-set parsing, to produce unsupervised segmentation into steady and transition states. (2) Evaluation layer: converts segments into binary state sequences and defines a composite metric combining event-level F1 (event_F1, via tolerance-based event matching) and Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) to jointly assess event detection and global structural consistency, mitigating boundary sensitivity and metric saturation. (3) Optimization layer: formulates the composite score as an objective for Bayesian optimization using a TPE surrogate model to efficiently search the parameter space for near-optimal segmentation configurations with far fewer evaluations than grid search.

Result: On the SustDataED2 dataset, Bayesian optimization with BayesSeg finds parameter regions within 0.35% of the exhaustive grid-search optimum using only ~100 objective function evaluations. The best configuration achieves a weighted composite score of 0.7149 and an event_F1 of 0.9340, while reducing optimization time from about 5300 seconds (grid search) to under 1 second, corresponding to a speedup of more than 5700x.

Conclusion: BayesSeg delivers a scalable, efficient, and largely automated solution for NILM time-series segmentation by unifying segmentation, robust multidimensional evaluation, and Bayesian parameter optimization. It overcomes the limitations of heuristic tuning and boundary-sensitive, weakly discriminative metrics, enabling accurate, high-speed configuration of steady/transition-state segmentation for NILM and potentially other time-series analysis tasks.

Abstract: In Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM), adaptive segmentation of electricity consumption time series is critical for appliance recognition. However, prevailing methods face challenges including heuristic parameter tuning, boundary sensitivity, and metric saturation. This paper proposes BayesSeg, a unified framework integrating time-series segmentation, multidimensional evaluation, and automatic parameter optimization. The segmentation layer employs a dual steady-state criterion based on the tail value and mean of preceding subsequences, combined with a sequential extraction and complement-set parsing strategy, to achieve precise unsupervised partitioning of steady-state and transition-state segments. The evaluation layer maps segmentation results to binary state sequences and formulates a composite metric integrating an event-level F1 score (event_F1) with Normalized Mutual Information (NMI). The event_F1 quantifies switching-event precision and recall via tolerance matching, while NMI captures global structural consistency, jointly overcoming the boundary sensitivity and limited discriminability of point-wise metrics. In the optimization layer, the composite score serves as the objective function for Bayesian optimization, which constructs a TPE surrogate model for efficient global parameter-space exploration. Experiments on the SustDataED2 dataset demonstrate that Bayesian optimization requires only ~100 objective evaluations to locate a parameter region within 0.35% deviation of the exhaustive grid-search optimum. The framework achieves a weighted composite score of 0.7149 and an event_F1 of 0.9340 while reducing optimization latency from ~5300 seconds to under 1 second, a speedup exceeding 5700x. BayesSeg automates segmentation configuration and provides a scalable, efficient solution for time-series analysis in NILM and related domains.

</details>


### [170] [CURE: Local Uncertainty Repair for Block-Parallel Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00531)
*Aofan Liu,Jingxiang Meng,Fangxin Liu,Yongbiao Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes CURE, a dynamic repair tree mechanism for speculative decoding that selectively fixes high-uncertainty token errors to improve acceptance rate and speedup in autoregressive LLM decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speculative decoding reduces latency in autoregressive LLMs by drafting and then verifying outputs, but current parallel drafting backends suffer from high rejection rates over long sequences because errors cluster around uncertain tokens and propagate forward, hurting both accuracy and speedup. There is a need for a method that improves draft acceptance rates without incurring large verification overheads.

Method: The authors introduce CURE, a budget-aware dynamic repair tree that operates on block-parallel drafts. It uses predictive confidence margins to detect likely error tokens (uncertainty focal points), selectively expands bounded repair paths only at these fragile locations, and then applies a repair resynchronization mechanism so that, after verification, the draft can be efficiently realigned with the target model’s trajectory. The system is designed as a plug-and-play module compatible with standard parallel drafting frameworks and includes controls to manage the trade-off between drafting computation and verification efficiency.

Result: On code-generation benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench-lite) and a math reasoning benchmark (GSM8K), CURE increases the average accepted length by 4.2–7.5% compared to parallel speculative decoding baselines without repair. This yields end-to-end speedups of 2.66–3.49× relative to target-only decoding, demonstrating better use of speculative drafts. The authors also empirically analyze how varying the repair budget affects both drafting and verification efficiency.

Conclusion: CURE effectively addresses localized error patterns in speculative decoding by selectively repairing high-uncertainty tokens, improving both acceptance length and overall decoding speed. It integrates seamlessly with existing parallel drafting frameworks and offers tunable trade-offs between extra draft computation and verification cost, providing a practical way to obtain higher wall-clock speedups without sacrificing correctness.

Abstract: Speculative decoding mitigates the latency of sequential generation in autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) by interleaving draft generation with target verification. However, existing parallel drafting backends often suffer from rapid accuracy degradation over long horizons, leading to high rejection rates during verification and suboptimal wall-clock speedups. We observe that drafting errors are not uniformly distributed but typically stem from localized high-uncertainty tokens that destabilize downstream generation trajectories. Motivated by this token error pattern, we propose CURE, a budget-aware dynamic repair tree designed to repair errors at uncertainty focal points without incurring prohibitive tree-verification overheads. Specifically, our method uses predictive confidence margins to dynamically locate candidate error tokens within a block-parallel draft, expands bounded repair paths only at these fragile nodes, and employs a novel repair resynchronization mechanism to realign draft states post-verification. Evaluations on code-generation benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, and LiveCodeBench-lite) and mathematical reasoning benchmark (GSM8K) demonstrate that CURE increases the average accepted length by 4.2-7.5% over parallel baselines without repair, translating to an end-to-end speedup of $2.66-3.49\times$ over target-only decoding. Furthermore, we provide a plug-and-play repair module compatible with standard parallel drafting frameworks. We also characterize the trade-off between draft compute and verification efficiency.

</details>


### [171] [Through the LENS: Local Geometric Decomposition of Vision-Language Model Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00561)
*Shalom Kachko,Raz Lapid,Margarita Vald,Almog Dubin,Moshe Sipper*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes LENS, a method using Mixture of Factor Analyzers to locally approximate the geometry of activations in vision-language models, revealing how modalities fuse across layers and enabling effective causal interventions and improved retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Global linear interpretability methods may miss structure in vision-language models where representations are globally high-dimensional but locally low-dimensional, leaving local cross-modal fusion mechanisms poorly understood and hard to steer.

Method: They introduce LENS, which fits a Mixture of Factor Analyzers to VLM activations to decompose them into local low-rank Gaussian neighborhoods. They apply this to LLaVA-1.5-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B, build an automated multimodal labeling pipeline for the neighborhoods, and test causal interventions by interpolating activations toward neighborhood centroids, comparing against difference-in-means and VL-SAE. They also evaluate the effect of using MFA coefficient space on image-to-rendered-text retrieval and run ablations on model and MFA hyperparameters.

Result: LENS reveals distinct, stable depth-dependent fusion trajectories in the two VLMs (late progressive fusion in LLaVA; early fusion, partial re-segregation, and late recombination in Qwen3-VL). MFA-based steering reliably redirects generation across modalities and outperforms baselines (e.g., 5.7x VL-SAE score in one LLaVA vision-to-vision task), is rated by humans as competitive with prompting and stronger than other interventions, and boosts Qwen3-VL retrieval R@1 from 14.9% to 48.6% at the deepest evaluated layer.

Conclusion: Local low-rank geometric neighborhoods, as modeled by a Mixture of Factor Analyzers, act as meaningful, interpretable, and causally effective units of representation in vision-language models, enabling finer-grained analysis of cross-modal fusion and improved control and retrieval performance.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) process image patches and text tokens in a shared residual stream, but the local geometry through which the two modalities interact remains poorly understood. Most interpretability methods identify global linear directions, which may miss representations that are globally high-dimensional but locally low-dimensional. We introduce LENS (Local Explanation of Neighborhood Subspaces), a method that decomposes VLM activations into local low-rank Gaussian neighborhoods using a Mixture of Factor Analyzers. Applied to LLaVA-1.5-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B, LENS reveals distinct depth-dependent fusion trajectories consistent with each model's fusion mechanism: LLaVA progressively mixes modalities at later layers, whereas Qwen3-VL mixes them early, partially re-segregates them, and recombines them near the output. An automated multimodal labeling pipeline assigns concise semantic descriptions to these neighborhoods. Interpolating activations toward neighborhood centroids causally redirects generation within and across modalities and outperforms difference-in-means and VL-SAE in most evaluated conditions; in one LLaVA vision-to-vision setting, MFA achieves 5.7 times the VL-SAE score. Human evaluation finds MFA steering competitive with prompting and substantially stronger than the other intervention baselines. Finally, the MFA coefficient space improves Qwen3-VL image-to-rendered-text retrieval at the deepest evaluated layer from 14.9% to 48.6% R@1. Ablations show that the reported fusion trajectories are stable across component counts, local ranks, and modality-purity thresholds. These results support local geometric neighborhoods as useful interpretable and causal units for analyzing cross-modal representations in the evaluated VLMs.

</details>


### [172] [Why Does the Future Branch? Identifiable Closure Tests for Stochastic Physical World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00591)
*Yibin Dong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces ClosurePairs, an evaluation protocol for stochastic world models that distinguishes between uncertainty due to state aliasing and process noise, which traditional accuracy and calibration metrics cannot do.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluation metrics for stochastic world models focus on predictive accuracy and calibration but cannot tell whether uncertainty in predictions comes from aliasing of underlying states or inherent randomness in the dynamics. This ambiguity is decision-relevant and theoretically unidentifiable from standard transition data, prompting the need for a new evaluation method that can attribute the sources of uncertainty.

Method: The authors propose ClosurePairs, an interventional evaluation protocol that constructs pairs of compatible microstates and applies repeated exogenous disturbances to them. They perform a two-way variance decomposition to separate contributions from state aliasing, process noise, and their interaction. They also develop an independent-repeat variant for cases where the same disturbances cannot be reused. The method is applied to Gaussian systems, nonlinear Langevin dynamics, and a pixel-conditioned recurrent model, and evaluated via alias-fraction error, attribution MAE, sensing regret, routing accuracy, and NLL.

Result: On Gaussian systems with likelihood-equivalent models, ClosurePairs reduces alias-fraction error by a factor of 15.96 while keeping test NLL unchanged. Across 18 nonlinear Langevin settings, the method reduces attribution MAE from 0.372 to 0.051 and sensing regret from 0.0138 to 0.0003, again without affecting NLL. For a pixel-conditioned recurrent model, using a shared-state probe guided by ClosurePairs reduces alias-fraction MAE vs. a deep ensemble from 0.584 to 0.130 in-distribution and from 0.630 to 0.170 out-of-distribution. In a matched-total-variance REFINE/BRANCH test, a baseline total-variance router achieves about 66.5% accuracy, whereas ClosurePairs reaches 99.99% accuracy and improves selected NLL from -2.087 to -2.717.

Conclusion: ClosurePairs provides a principled way to attribute predictive uncertainty in stochastic world models to state aliasing versus process noise, something that conventional forecasting scores and likelihood metrics cannot disentangle. This attribution significantly improves understanding and utilization of learned models without sacrificing standard predictive performance, offering a powerful tool for diagnosing and improving world models used in decision-making tasks.

Abstract: Stochastic world models are usually evaluated by the accuracy and calibration of their predicted futures. These criteria leave a decision-relevant ambiguity: the same conditional future distribution can arise because an observation aliases different physical states, or because the dynamics remain random after the declared full state is fixed. We prove that this attribution is not identifiable from ordinary transition data, even with an optimal probabilistic predictor. We introduce ClosurePairs, an interventional evaluation protocol that crosses compatible microstates with repeated exogenous disturbances. A two-way variance decomposition identifies state aliasing, process noise, and their nonlinear interaction; an independent-repeat variant applies when disturbances cannot be reused. On likelihood-equivalent Gaussian systems, paired supervision reduces alias-fraction error 15.96-fold at identical test NLL. Across 18 nonlinear Langevin conditions, it reduces attribution MAE from 0.372 to 0.051 and sensing regret from 0.0138 to 0.0003 without changing NLL. On a pixel-conditioned recurrent model, a frozen shared-state probe reduces alias-fraction MAE against a deep ensemble from 0.584 to 0.130 in distribution and from 0.630 to 0.170 out of distribution over ten seeds. Finally, in a matched-total-variance REFINE/BRANCH test, a total-variance router reaches 66.48 percent plus or minus 1.06 percent accuracy, whereas ClosurePairs reaches 99.99 percent plus or minus 0.02 percent and improves selected NLL from -2.087 to -2.717 over five seeds. ClosurePairs therefore measures why futures branch, information that proper forecast scores cannot identify.

</details>


### [173] [Escaping Confidence Trap: Evolutionary Decoding for Mathematical Reasoning in Diffusion LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00605)
*Zhenhong Sun,Hanqing Zhao,Yatao Bian,Rongcheng Tu,Liuyue Xie,Xu Zhang,Jue Wang,Davide Modolo,Daoyi Dong,Dacheng Tao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies a key failure mode in diffusion-based large language models for math reasoning and proposes an evolutionary-style decoding strategy to improve reliability without extra training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion LLMs are attractive due to efficient block-wise generation, but their good general performance does not carry over to mathematical reasoning, which needs globally coherent numerical-symbolic trajectories. The authors observe that standard confidence-based decoding in dLLMs often gets trapped: tokens can have high local confidence while the overall reasoning path is wrong. This misalignment motivates a deeper analysis of diffusion decoding dynamics and a new decoding method tailored for reasoning tasks.

Method: The authors analyze LLaDA 2.0’s decoding trajectories and uncover a recurring “diffusion confidence trap,” distinguishing two failure types: (1) sampling-sensitive failures, where correct solutions exist but are unstable across samples, and (2) sampling-consistent failures, where multiple samples converge to the same confident but wrong pattern. To address this, they introduce Evolutionary Decoding, a test-time, training-free framework that interprets diffusion decoding as an evolutionary process over candidate reasoning states. It uses step-wise selection to keep promising numerical-symbolic signals and suppress repetitive patterns, and block-wise mutation to generate structured alternative reasoning paths, helping the model escape high-confidence but incorrect basins.

Result: On several mathematical reasoning benchmarks, Evolutionary Decoding applied to LLaDA 2.0 outperforms standard confidence-based diffusion decoding. The method reduces both types of confidence traps, improves stability of correct reasoning trajectories, and increases overall accuracy in math problem solving without modifying the underlying model parameters.

Conclusion: Diffusion LLMs suffer from systematic misalignment between local token confidence and global reasoning correctness, leading to characteristic failure modes in math reasoning. Viewing diffusion decoding as an evolutionary process and applying step-wise selection plus block-wise mutation at test time can substantially mitigate these issues, making diffusion-based LLMs more reliable for mathematical reasoning tasks without additional training.

Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, offering efficient generation through block-wise progressive unmasking. However, their strong general-purpose performance does not necessarily translate into reliable mathematical reasoning, where correctness depends on preserving coherent numerical-symbolic reasoning trajectories. In this work, we analyze the decoding trajectories of LLaDA 2.0 and identify a recurring diffusion confidence trap: local token confidence can become misaligned with global reasoning correctness during progressive block decoding. Our analysis reveals two representative failure regimes: sampling-sensitive failures, where correct paths exist but are unstable, and sampling-consistent failures, where repeated sampling converges to repetitive high-confidence but incorrect continuations. Motivated by this observation, we propose Evolutionary Decoding, a training-free test-time scaling framework that views diffusion decoding as an evolutionary process over candidate reasoning states. The framework combines step-wise selection, which preserves useful numerical-symbolic signals and suppresses repetitive patterns, with block-wise mutation, which introduces structured alternatives to escape incorrect high-confidence basins. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that Evolutionary Decoding improves LLaDA 2.0 over confidence-based decoding, leading to more reliable mathematical reasoning.

</details>


### [174] [Slides2MindMap: Reconstructing Cognitively Efficient Knowledge Hierarchies from Lecture Slides](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00610)
*Yuzhi Wang,Rongjun Ye,Shengyuan Chen,Huachi Zhou,Jiaqi Bai,Chuang Zhou,Zhicong Hong,Xiao Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper defines a new task, Slides2MindMap, and a benchmark S2M-Bench for automatically generating mind maps from lecture slides, and proposes AutoMindMap, an agent-based framework that generates cognitively efficient knowledge hierarchies outperforming baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learners often receive fragmented knowledge through large, heterogeneous slide decks, making it hard to build a coherent mental model of a course. Mind maps are effective for organizing and assimilating such knowledge but generating them manually is time-consuming and requires expertise. There is a lack of automatic methods and systematic evaluation frameworks for converting entire slide collections into cognitively efficient mind maps, especially methods that balance global course structure with local slide-level details.

Method: The authors first formalize the Slides2MindMap (S2M) task: reconstructing knowledge hierarchies (mind maps) from a full course’s slide deck. They build S2M-Bench, a benchmark with 12,774 slide pages and expert-annotated mind maps for 24 courses, plus an evaluation framework grounded in cognitive science that combines (1) comparison to ground-truth mind maps, (2) structure conformity analysis, and (3) evaluation via vision-language models as judges. To solve the task, they introduce AutoMindMap, an agentic framework inspired by the Structure Building Framework, composed of three main stages: (1) Skeleton Laying, which establishes a global scaffold or top-level structure of the mind map; (2) Iterative Knowledge Integration, where slide content is integrated into the scaffold using context-aware summarization; and (3) Dual-Stage Refinement, which decouples local refinement of subtrees from global structural coherence to balance faithfulness to slide details with overall clarity and organization, while adapting to varied slide formats.

Result: On the S2M-Bench benchmark, AutoMindMap is empirically evaluated against various baseline methods. It consistently achieves better scores across the proposed evaluation dimensions, including closer alignment with expert-annotated ground truths, better structural conformity, and higher ratings from VLM-as-a-Judge. The approach also shows robustness across different backbone models and scenarios, indicating that the framework generalizes and does not rely on a specific model configuration.

Conclusion: The study shows that (1) the Slides2MindMap task is feasible and meaningful for intelligent education, (2) S2M-Bench provides a solid and cognitively grounded way to evaluate mind map generation from slides, and (3) the proposed AutoMindMap framework effectively balances global course structure and local slide details, outperforming baselines and displaying robustness. These results highlight the potential of automated mind map generation as a pedagogically valuable tool for helping students build coherent knowledge structures from large slide collections.

Abstract: Generating mind maps from lecture slides can help learners efficiently assimilate fragmented knowledge, promising substantial benefits for intelligent education. However, dedicated automatic generation and evaluation frameworks remain underexplored and challenging, requiring a global-local knowledge focus balance and handling large-scale, heterogeneous slides. We formulate the Slides2MindMap task, which aims to reconstruct cognitively efficient knowledge hierarchies from a course's slide deck collection. For systematic evaluation, we introduce S2M-Bench, a benchmark comprising 12,774 slide pages with expert-annotated mind maps spanning 24 university courses. S2M-Bench includes a cognitive-science-grounded evaluation framework that integrates ground-truth-based comparison, structure conformity analysis, and VLM-as-a-Judge. To address this task, we propose AutoMindMap, an agentic framework inspired by the Structure Building Framework. AutoMindMap comprises Skeleton Laying for global scaffold anchoring, Iterative Knowledge Integration augmented by context-aware summarization, and Dual-Stage Refinement with a local-global decoupling mechanism. The framework reconciles local knowledge faithfulness with global coherence, and adapts to slide-specific features. Experiments on S2M-Bench demonstrate that AutoMindMap outperforms baselines and achieves superior robustness across different models and scenarios, underscoring its pedagogical application value.

</details>


### [175] [DASH: Decoupled Adaptive Surrogate - Acquisition Harness for Automated Bayesian Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00641)
*Changquan Zhao,Yuxiang Sun,Ruihao Zhu,Cheng Hua,Yulian He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces DASH, a framework that decouples and adaptively tunes both the surrogate model and acquisition function in Bayesian optimization, leveraging LLMs to make AutoBO more reliable and effective across tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Automated Bayesian Optimization approaches either adapt only the surrogate or only the acquisition function, or they choose fixed surrogate–acquisition pairs with a single shared criterion. This ignores that surrogates and acquisitions have different roles and requirements, leading to mismatches and performance bottlenecks, especially as optimization progresses or across diverse tasks such as chemical optimization.

Method: DASH (Decoupled Adaptive Surrogate–Acquisition Harness) independently adapts surrogates and acquisition functions. Surrogates are selected based on predictive reliability, uncertainty calibration, and ranking consistency. Acquisitions are managed by a two-stage controller that periodically reallocates evaluation quotas among acquisition functions, builds a shortlist of candidate suggestions, and then uses an LLM to select the final query. An integrated harness provides knowledge-guided warm starts and structured memory to inject domain knowledge and past feedback into the optimization loop. The whole system is evaluated in LLM-enhanced AutoBO settings.

Result: On four chemical optimization benchmarks, DASH improves over the strongest AutoBO baseline by 12.51% in trajectory-level Acceleration Factor and 5.00% in endpoint Enhancement Factor. The improvements hold across different LLM backbones, and ablation studies show that each component of DASH (decoupled surrogate selection, acquisition controller, and integrated harness) contributes complementary gains. Additional checks reveal no evidence that the performance comes from benchmark memorization or leakage from source implementations.

Conclusion: Decoupling and adaptively controlling surrogate and acquisition components in AutoBO, while leveraging LLMs for final decision making and domain-informed guidance, significantly improves Bayesian optimization performance in challenging domains like chemical optimization. DASH offers a robust and general framework for LLM-enhanced AutoBO, with validated gains that are not attributable to contamination or memorization.

Abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) relies on a surrogate model and an acquisition function, yet the most suitable choices vary across tasks and optimization stages. Automated Bayesian optimization (AutoBO) addresses this variability by adapting BO components online. However, existing AutoBO methods either adapt one component, leaving the other mismatched and creating a bottleneck, or jointly select surrogate--acquisition pairs under a shared criterion, overlooking their distinct roles: surrogate selection depends on predictive reliability, whereas acquisition adaptation should respond to campaign context.In this paper, we propose DASH, a Decoupled Adaptive Surrogate--Acquisition Harness for large-language- model (LLM)-enhanced AutoBO. DASH selects surrogates by predictive reliability, uncertainty calibration, and ranking consistency; its two-stage acquisition controller periodically reallocates quotas across acquisition functions, builds a BO shortlist accordingly, and delegates final selection to an LLM. DASH also incorporates an integrated harness, consisting of knowledge-guided warm start and structured memory, to ground optimization in domain knowledge and accumulated feedback. Across four chemical optimization tasks, DASH outperforms the best AutoBO baseline by 12.51% in trajectory-level Acceleration Factor and 5.00% in endpoint Enhancement Factor. Results remain strong across LLM backbones, and ablations verify the complementary contributions of all components. Full-table and behavioral contamination checks find no detectable evidence that direct benchmark memorization or source-cell leakage explains these gains.

</details>


### [176] [HetGPS: Scalable Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Physics-Anchored Adaptive Safety for EV Charging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00679)
*Xiangwei Wang,Nanduni Nimalsiri,Yu Xia,Peng Wang,Saman Halgamuge*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HetGPS is a hybrid graph-control framework that uses learned risk on a graph plus a physics-based correction model to safely control large networks of agents, demonstrated on large-scale EV charging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safe control of many network-coupled agents (like EV chargers on power grids) must enforce shared safety constraints (e.g., voltage limits) without overly restricting the agents’ ability to pursue their tasks (e.g., achieving desired charge levels), and existing methods often struggle to scale or to balance safety with performance.

Method: Propose HetGPS, which separates how much to intervene (magnitude) from how to intervene (direction). A learned, action-conditioned graph residual model predicts risk and schedules state-dependent intervention authority over agents, while a physics-based network model defines the safety-preserving corrective direction. They integrate this with a heterogeneous graph Soft Actor-Critic policy that shares parameters across agents for scalable, topology-aware coordination in EV charging networks.

Result: On five distribution networks sized from 200 to 3,218 EVs over 100 evaluation days, the adaptive authority mechanism substantially lowers voltage violation rates (from roughly 4–8% to about 0.5–3.5%) while keeping 99–100% of EVs meeting departure charge targets. Compared to a baseline that uses the same physics-based projection but with fixed intervention authority, HetGPS improves average reward in all networks and reduces a safety score in most. The deployed model uses about 3.8e5 parameters regardless of scale, whereas an equivalent centralized SAC policy would be about 170× larger at the largest scale. Policies trained on a smaller network transfer zero-shot to larger networks with similarly low violation rates and very high departure success.

Conclusion: Learned graph-based risk estimation can effectively determine when and how strongly to override agents’ actions, while physics-based models anchor the actual corrections, enabling scalable, safe, and high-performance control of large heterogeneous networks such as EV charging systems, with strong generalization across grid topologies and sizes.

Abstract: Safety interventions for large populations of network-coupled agents must protect shared constraints without unnecessarily overriding task-oriented policy decisions. We present HetGPS, a hybrid graph-control framework synergizing learned graph risk with physics-anchored correction by separating intervention magnitude from corrective direction. An action-conditioned graph residual model schedules state-dependent intervention authority, while a physics model determines its direction. For electric vehicle (EV) charging, we couple this filter with a parameter-shared heterogeneous graph soft actor-critic policy, enabling topology-aware coordination with a learned model size independent of fleet size. Across five nested distribution networks with 200--3,218 EVs and 100 evaluation days, Adaptive Authority reduces bus--step voltage violations from 3.93--7.74\% without filtering to 0.52--3.44\%, while maintaining 99.06--100\% departure success. Relative to the same physics-directed projection with fixed authority, it improves mean reward on all five networks and lowers the mean safety score on four. The deployed policy-and-risk model contains 383,702 learned parameters at every scale; at 3,218 EVs, a matched centralized SAC actor is about $170\times$ larger. A policy trained on the eight-transformer system transfers zero-shot to the 16- and 32-transformer systems, attaining 0.57--0.75\% violation rates and at least 99.99\% departure success. These results show that learned graph risk can allocate intervention authority at scale while feeder physics anchors corrective action.

</details>


### [177] [Multi-Dimensional Assessment for AI Cognition (MAAC): A Theoretical Framework for Process-Oriented Cognitive Evaluation of Text-Based AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00680)
*Abdalla Doleh,Ratna Babu Chinnam*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes MAAC, a framework to evaluate AI systems by examining their internal cognitive-like processes rather than only their outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional AI evaluation benchmarks focus on outcomes such as accuracy, robustness, and fairness, but they do not reveal how AI systems achieve these results. This leaves gaps in understanding AI reasoning, memory use, complexity management, and hallucination control, which are crucial for diagnosing and improving AI behavior.

Method: The authors develop MAAC, a theoretically grounded framework defining nine cognitively inspired assessment dimensions: Cognitive Load, Tool Execution, Content Quality, Memory Integration, Complexity Handling, Hallucination Control, Knowledge Transfer, Processing Efficiency, and Process-Outcome Alignment. They anchor these dimensions in established cognitive science theories and conduct five theoretical analyses: mapping each dimension to theory, constructing a coverage matrix to test breadth and redundancy, performing a gap analysis versus current practices, providing a worked diagnostic example, and proposing interdependency predictions among dimensions for future empirical validation.

Result: The theoretical analyses indicate that MAAC’s nine dimensions are coherent, non-redundant, and well-grounded in cognitive science. The framework highlights systematic gaps in current outcome-based evaluations and shows, through an illustrative diagnostic, how MAAC can reveal process-level strengths and weaknesses in AI systems. It also generates testable predictions about how different cognitive dimensions should interact in practice.

Conclusion: MAAC offers a structured, cognitively motivated way to evaluate how text-based AI systems think, not just what they output. It complements existing benchmarks by enabling principled, process-level diagnosis along multiple dimensions, and it sets the stage for future empirical work to operationalize and validate these assessments in practice.

Abstract: Evaluating artificial intelligence systems has historically relied on outcome-based benchmarks that measure task accuracy, robustness, or fairness. While indispensable, these benchmarks provide limited diagnostic insight into the underlying cognitive processes that generate performance-leaving critical questions unanswered about how AI systems reason, integrate memory, manage complexity, or avoid generating false information. This paper introduces the Multi-Dimensional Assessment for AI Cognition (MAAC), a theoretically grounded framework for shifting evaluation from what text-based AI systems produce to how they think. MAAC defines nine cognitively motivated dimensions: Cognitive Load, Tool Execution, Content Quality, Memory Integration, Complexity Handling, Hallucination Control, Knowledge Transfer, Processing Efficiency, and Process-Outcome Alignment. Each dimension is grounded in established cognitive science theory-drawing on Marr's tri-level hypothesis, Baddeley's working memory model, Sweller's cognitive load theory, and unified theories of cognition. Five theoretical analyses provide initial support for the framework's coherence and empirical testability: dimension-to-theory mapping; a coverage matrix assessing breadth and non-redundancy; a formal gap analysis relative to current evaluation practice; a worked diagnostic illustration; and a set of a priori interdependency predictions for future empirical testing. MAAC provides a theoretical and operational framework for principled process-level cognitive assessment of text-based AI systems, complementing existing outcome-based benchmarks with cognitively grounded, multi-dimensional evaluation.

</details>


### [178] [When Does LLM Orchestration Pay Off? A Controlled Evaluation of Accuracy, Cost, and Task Difficulty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00685)
*Nicolas Leins,Nico Pelleriti,Jana Gonnermann-Müller,Sebastian Pokutta*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how much LLM orchestration methods (Self-Refine, Best-of-N, Debate) actually help over single-call baselines when all methods receive equal optimization effort, finding only moderate accuracy gains that come at 2–4x token cost and depend strongly on the base model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many believe that orchestration techniques—using multiple LLM calls, self-refinement loops, or multi-agent debate—significantly improve reasoning by adding inference-time compute. However, reported gains may partly come from unequal hyperparameter tuning and optimization effort, and from cherry-picked settings. There is a need for a fair, controlled comparison across models and domains to understand the true value and cost-effectiveness of orchestration, rather than assuming extra inference-time structure is always beneficial.

Method: The authors perform a controlled empirical study comparing three orchestration methods (Self-Refine, Best-of-N sampling, and Debate) against two single-call baselines: direct task-only prompting and chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting. They run experiments on five different LLM backbones across three challenging domains: competitive programming, chess puzzles, and mathematics. To ensure fairness, they use GEPA to optimize the hyperparameters of each method under the same optimization budget, and they evaluate all methods on shared, difficulty-stratified benchmark items. They also conduct within-benchmark analyses and exploratory mixed-effects modeling to study interactions between orchestration methods, backbone models, and item difficulty.

Result: Across benchmarks, orchestration gives only moderate and benchmark-dependent improvements. When averaging across backbones within each benchmark, the largest gains are roughly 4.6 percentage points over optimized CoT and 4.5 percentage points over task-only inference. These gains require about 2–4x more total tokens than task-only inference, implying higher inference cost. Human-labeled difficulty correlates with lower absolute accuracy for all methods, but within each benchmark, orchestration does not become relatively more beneficial at higher difficulty levels. Mixed-effects analyses show strong interactions between orchestration method and backbone model: different models respond differently to the same orchestration, indicating that effectiveness is highly model-dependent.

Conclusion: LLM orchestration is not a universally large win: it yields modest accuracy improvements that may or may not be worth the extra inference cost, and its benefits vary substantially by base model and benchmark. Thus, orchestration choices should be tailored to the specific backbone model and should weigh accuracy gains against increased token usage.
