The study argues that future evaluations of orchestration must tightly control for optimization effort and report model-specific accuracy–cost trade-offs, instead of presuming that adding complex inference-time structures (like self-refinement or debate) is inherently and uniformly advantageous.

Abstract: LLM orchestration is often assumed to improve reasoning by allocating additional inference-time computation, yet its gains may not justify its cost. Existing comparisons also frequently overlook differences in optimization effort, making it difficult to isolate the value of orchestration itself. We conduct a controlled evaluation of Self-Refine, Best-of-$N$, and Debate against task-only and chain-of-thought (CoT) single-call baselines across five LLM backbones and three domains: competitive programming, chess puzzles, and mathematics. For comparability, we optimize each method with GEPA under the same optimization budget and evaluate all methods on the same difficulty-stratified benchmark items. Orchestration yields moderate but benchmark-dependent gains: averaged across backbones within each benchmark, the largest improvement is 4.6 percentage points over optimized CoT inference and 4.5 points over task-only inference, while requiring approximately 2 to 4 times the mean total tokens of task-only inference. Human-derived difficulty is associated with lower absolute accuracy in all three benchmarks, but within-benchmark analyses do not indicate that orchestration effects increase with task difficulty. By contrast, exploratory mixed-effects analyses reveal strong interactions between orchestration method and backbone model across all three benchmarks, showing that orchestration effectiveness depends substantially on the underlying model. Our results suggest that orchestration decisions should be model-specific and account for whether moderate accuracy gains justify the additional inference cost. More broadly, evaluations of LLM orchestrations should control optimization effort and report model-specific accuracy--cost trade-offs rather than treating additional inference-time structure as uniformly beneficial.

</details>


### [179] [Evolutionary Curriculum Learning Improves Biological Sequence Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00697)
*Richard Zhu,Kento Nishi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce Evolutionary Curriculum Learning (ECL), a way to train VAEs on biological sequences by gradually adding more evolutionarily distant sequences, leading to better performance on protein variant prediction and RNA sequence generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard VAEs on MSAs ignore the evolutionary relationships among sequences, treating them as exchangeable. Yet homologous sequences are organized by evolutionary distance, which could guide learning. The authors aim to exploit this structure to improve generative modeling and downstream tasks like disease variant prediction and RNA design.

Method: They propose ECL, a curriculum learning strategy for VAEs on MSAs. Training is organized around anchor sequences, and the model is progressively exposed to sequences at increasing evolutionary distances from these anchors, according to a power-law expansion schedule. They apply ECL to two different VAE architectures and tasks: EVE for protein variant effect prediction (p53, PTEN) and RfamGen for RNA family sequence generation, and compare against baselines like uniform random sampling and fixed-size neighborhood sampling. They also run ablation studies to isolate the effect of the evolutionary-distance-based curriculum.

Result: On protein variant effect prediction, ECL improves ClinVar classification AUROC: for p53 from 0.981 to 0.989, and for PTEN it stabilizes and maximizes performance (AUROC 1.000 in every seed versus a baseline mean of 0.905 with strong instability). For RNA, ECL increases mean covariance-model bit scores on three tested families and beats seed-matched baselines in 12/15 runs, though the small number of families prevents claiming significance at the family level. Ablations show evolutionary-distance-based progressive expansion outperforms fixed-size neighborhood and uniform random sampling.

Conclusion: Ordering training data by evolutionary distance provides a beneficial inductive bias for VAEs trained on MSAs. Evolutionary Curriculum Learning improves downstream performance and stability across proteins and RNAs, and evolutionary distance is a principled way to structure the training curriculum for biological sequence models.

Abstract: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) trained on multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) have emerged as powerful generative models for biological sequences, with applications ranging from disease variant prediction to functional RNA design. However, standard biological VAE training treats all sequences as exchangeable, ignoring the rich evolutionary structure that organizes homologous sequences from evolutionarily close to highly divergent. We propose Evolutionary Curriculum Learning (ECL), a training strategy that exploits this structure by progressively exposing the model to sequences of increasing evolutionary distance from sampled anchors, following a power-law expansion schedule. Applied to two architecturally distinct VAE models and two biological domains--protein variant effect prediction with EVE and RNA family sequence generation with RfamGen--ECL improves downstream task performance across five random seeds per configuration. Mean ClinVar classification AUROC rises from 0.981 to 0.989 for p53; for PTEN, ECL attains 1.000 in every seed whereas the baseline is unstable (mean 0.905, falling as low as 0.54). For RNA, ECL raises mean covariance-model bit scores on all three families tested and exceeds its seed-matched baseline in 12 of 15 training runs, though with only three families the effect cannot be established as significant at the family level. Ablation experiments show that progressively expanding the sampled sequences by evolutionary distance outperforms fixed-size neighborhood sampling in addition to uniform random sampling. Evolutionary distance is therefore a useful inductive bias for ordering the training curriculum in biological sequence modeling.

</details>


### [180] [DGA$_2$D: Directed Graph-Guided Automated Algorithm Design with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00700)
*Jiale Zhao,Zimu Chen,Sirui Mao,Wentao Yang,Yuxiang Bai,Liyuanjun Lai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces DGA2D, a directed-graph-based framework that uses LLMs to automatically design full algorithms for NP-hard combinatorial optimization, achieving better solution quality than prior LLM-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based automated heuristic design methods are constrained by rigid solver templates and focus on tuning isolated modules, which limits their ability to autonomously design full algorithms. Moreover, moving to system-level design faces key challenges: unreliable generated operators, vast program search spaces, and poor credit assignment for assessing components in different contexts. A new framework is needed to structure the search space and reliably evaluate algorithmic components.

Method: The authors propose DGA2D, which models the algorithm design space as a directed graph where nodes are functional operators and edges describe possible compositions. Each node can be instantiated with multiple candidate code implementations generated by LLMs. Complete algorithms correspond to directed walks through this graph. They introduce a first-order, path-dependent credit assignment mechanism that evaluates each code variant based on its performance within specific topological (pipeline) contexts, guiding the search over implementations and walks.

Result: On 12 different combinatorial optimization problems, including various scheduling and routing tasks, DGA2D consistently outperforms state-of-the-art LLM-driven AHD baselines. It achieves up to a 10.96 percentage-point improvement in average normalized optimality gap, indicating notably better solution quality across diverse COPs.

Conclusion: Structuring the algorithm design space as a directed graph and using path-dependent credit assignment enables more reliable, autonomous system-level algorithm design with LLMs. DGA2D effectively handles large program spaces and context-sensitive evaluation of operators, delivering superior performance over existing LLM-based heuristic design approaches on a broad set of NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems.

Abstract: The rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs) has opened new avenues for Automated Heuristic Design (AHD) for solving NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems (COPs). However, existing LLM-driven AHD methods are largely confined to rigid solver templates, relegating the search process to isolated module tuning. Transitioning to fully autonomous, system-level algorithm design is essential but fraught with low reliability of generated operators, extremely large search spaces, and ineffective credit assignment. To overcome these drawbacks, this paper proposes a Directed Graph-Guided Automated Algorithm Design framework, termed DGA$_2$D. It structures the open-ended program space as a directed graph, where each node represents a functional operator that can be instantiated using one of multiple candidate code implementations, while directed walks constitute complete algorithmic pipelines. A first-order path-dependent credit assignment mechanism is introduced to evaluate code variations strictly based on their topological context. Extensive experiments across 12 distinct COPs, ranging from complex scheduling to routing, demonstrate the consistent empirical advantages of DGA$_2$D. It reduces the average normalized gap by up to 10.96 percentage points compared to state-of-the-art LLM baselines.

</details>


### [181] [Tracing the Cascade: A Topology-Aware Evaluation Framework for Scientific Agent Hallucinations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00711)
*Xinshun Feng,Ziqi Miao,Lijun Li,Jing Shao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SCHEMA is a topology-aware evaluation framework to assess and analyze hallucinations in scientific LLM agents, focusing on how errors propagate through interconnected scientific concepts rather than on isolated facts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In scientific research settings, LLM agents must be highly reliable, but hallucinations can be especially harmful because scientific knowledge is densely interconnected. A single wrong foundational claim can cascade through multi-step reasoning and corrupt entire solution trajectories. Existing hallucination benchmarks treat facts in isolation and use uniform accuracy metrics, ignoring the structure of scientific knowledge and the process by which agents reason. There is a need for an evaluation framework that accounts for knowledge topology and provides mechanism-level insight into hallucinations in scientific agents.

Method: The authors propose SCHEMA, an evaluation framework that (1) automatically constructs scientific concept graphs from benchmark seeds and literature evidence; (2) uses these graphs to synthesize a diverse set of tasks (claim verification, multi-hop reasoning, open-ended explanation, and experimental code generation); and (3) evaluates LLM agents with two diagnostics. The first is a trajectory hallucination pipeline that audits intermediate reasoning steps and assigns a topology-weighted severity score to hallucinations, reflecting their position and importance in the concept graph. The second is a multi-agent counterfactual attribution module that analyzes selected failures to identify the causal mechanisms behind hallucinations by exploring counterfactual reasoning paths. Together, these components give a topology-aware, process-level view of hallucinations in scientific agents.

Result: Using SCHEMA, the authors find that hallucinations tend to concentrate on a small set of highly connected nodes (knowledge hubs) in the scientific concept graph. They also show that models can achieve correct final answers while relying on flawed internal reasoning trajectories, demonstrating a decoupling between final-answer accuracy and the honesty or faithfulness of the reasoning process. This highlights that current accuracy-based benchmarks can miss severe underlying hallucinations, especially at critical knowledge hubs.

Conclusion: The study concludes that in high-stakes scientific applications, relying on terminal accuracy alone is inadequate for judging the reliability of LLM agents. Because hallucinations cluster at influential knowledge hubs and can corrupt entire reasoning trajectories, evaluation must instead be mechanism-level and grounded in the topology of scientific knowledge. SCHEMA provides such a framework and shows how topology-aware diagnostics can better reveal where and how hallucinations arise in scientific LLM agents.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in scientific research, where reliability is critical and the underlying knowledge is densely interconnected. In such settings, hallucinations are particularly damaging: a single erroneous claim on a foundational concept can propagate through multi-step reasoning and corrupt entire trajectories. Existing hallucination benchmarks largely operate at the surface level, treating facts in isolation and relying on uniform accuracy metrics that ignore this topological structure. We address this gap with SCHEMA, the first evidence-grounded, topology-aware evaluation framework for hallucinations in scientific agents. SCHEMA automatically constructs scientific concept graphs from benchmark seeds and literature evidence, synthesizes graph-grounded tasks spanning claim verification, multi-hop reasoning, open-ended explanation, and experimental code generation, and evaluates agents with two complementary diagnostics. A trajectory hallucination pipeline audits intermediate reasoning at scale via a topology-weighted severity score, while a multi-agent counterfactual attribution module pinpoints the causal mechanism behind selected failures. SCHEMA reveals that hallucinations concentrate at a small set of highly connected knowledge hubs, and that final-answer accuracy decouples from trajectory honesty; models often reach correct conclusions through structurally flawed reasoning. These results indicate that for high-stakes scientific applications, terminal accuracy alone is an insufficient signal of agent reliability, motivating mechanism-level evaluation grounded in knowledge topology. Code is available at https://github.com/circles-post/SCHEMA.

</details>


### [182] [AI-Based Thesis Assessment: An Empirical Study of Human Evaluation Priorities and Their Impact on Automated Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00717)
*Garv Vikram Gursahaney,Baskhad Idrisov,Thorsten Fröhlich,Tim Schlippe*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how thesis supervisors weight assessment criteria, compares these weights to those built into an AI rubric system, and tests whether adjusting the AI’s weights to match supervisors meaningfully improves AI–human agreement. It finds only a very small, non-significant improvement and much higher agreement among human supervisors than between AI and humans.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rubric-based AI systems for thesis assessment typically rely on criterion weights defined by experts or developers, with little empirical evidence that these weights match how real thesis supervisors prioritize criteria. Misaligned weights may cause AI assessments to diverge from human judgments in ways that are hard to justify or explain. The study aims to empirically determine how supervisors weight criteria, compare these weights to those used in an existing AI system (RubiSCoT), and test whether aligning AI weights with supervisor-derived weights improves agreement between AI and human evaluations.

Method: The authors surveyed 84 thesis supervisors from four academic disciplines and asked them to assign importance weights to 35 thesis assessment criteria. They then compared these supervisor-derived weights with the default weights in the AI assessment system RubiSCoT, identifying divergences. To assess practical effects, they integrated the supervisor-derived weights into several calibration configurations of RubiSCoT and evaluated them using a corpus of 80 German-language theses. They quantified differences between AI-generated scores and supervisor-assigned evaluations using mean relative deviation and tested for statistical significance. Inter-supervisor agreement was also measured using the same deviation metric.

Result: There were substantial differences between the criterion weights provided by supervisors and the default weights in RubiSCoT. When the supervisor-derived weights were incorporated into multiple AI calibration setups and tested on 80 theses, the best-performing configuration only slightly reduced the mean relative deviation between AI and human evaluations—from 11.18% to 10.85—and this improvement was not statistically significant. In contrast, human supervisors showed much stronger mutual agreement, with a mean inter-supervisor relative deviation of 4.44%, substantially lower than any AI–human deviation observed.

Conclusion: The study concludes that simply calibrating criterion weights in an AI rubric-based assessment system to match supervisor-derived weights does not meaningfully improve alignment between AI-generated and human thesis evaluations. The modest, statistically non-significant performance gains suggest that other factors—such as how criteria are operationalized, feature extraction quality, model design, or the nature of thesis evaluation itself—play a larger role in AI–human discrepancies. Therefore, improving AI-based thesis assessment requires more than adjusting criterion weights; broader methodological and model-level changes are needed to approach human-level agreement.

Abstract: Rubric-based AI systems for thesis assessment use criterion weights to assign different levels of importance to evaluation criteria. These weights are typically defined through expert judgment, although little empirical evidence exists regarding how thesis supervisors actually prioritize evaluation criteria. Consequently, this study investigates supervisor-derived criterion weights in thesis assessment and evaluates their impact on AI-based assessment. We surveyed 84 thesis supervisors across four academic disciplines and collected weighting data for 35 thesis assessment criteria. Comparison with the default criterion weights of the AI assessment system RubiSCoT [1] revealed substantial divergences between supervisor-derived and default criterion weights. To evaluate the practical implications of these differences, the supervisor-derived weights were integrated into multiple calibration configurations and evaluated on a corpus of 80 German-language theses. The best-performing configuration reduced the mean relative deviation between AI-generated and supervisor-assigned evaluations from 11.18% to 10.85%, although the improvement was not statistically significant. Human supervisors showed substantially stronger agreement with each other, exhibiting a mean inter-supervisor relative deviation of 4.44%. The findings indicate that criterion-weight calibration alone does not substantially improve alignment between AI-generated and human assessments.

</details>


### [183] [Behavioral Grammar: Detecting Adaptive Malware via Tiny Language Model Priors and Second-Order Temporal Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00745)
*Zihan Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a compact Transformer-based behavioral grammar model for endpoint security that models host events as a language, enabling self-supervised anomaly detection and robust adversarial resistance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Signature-based endpoint detection is easily bypassed by polymorphic/adaptive threats, while large deep-learning models are hard to audit and deploy at scale; there is a need for an interpretable, lightweight, and robust behavior-based detection method that remains effective against adaptive adversaries.

Method: Model host runtime behavior as a structured language by encoding each system event into 8 discrete tokens (event type, process, argument skeleton, path category, parent process, user, destination, inter-event timing). Train a small (0.88M-parameter) causal Transformer, TinyGPT, in a self-supervised way to learn the conditional distribution of normal behavior. Compute per-slot negative log-likelihoods to obtain anomaly scores with bounded false-positive rate. Enhance this with prototype learning for attribution of known attacks, second-order temporal analysis focusing on inter-event interval statistics (e.g., coefficient of variation), self-learning pattern extraction, and fuse outputs from five networks for final detection.

Result: When evaluated against an Adaptive Adversarial Agent that actively learns evasion strategies, mimics benign behavior, and matches host event rates, the system detects 93% of attacks at a 3.84% onboarding false-positive rate. Analysis shows the most powerful discriminative feature is the coefficient of variation of inter-event timing: the adversary’s stepping cadence (CV=0.310) differs by about 30x from benign sleep intervals (CV=9.786), indicating a strong temporal-structure signal.

Conclusion: Behavioral Grammar detection using a small Transformer effectively detects sophisticated adaptive threats with low false positives by modeling the distribution of normal behavior and exploiting temporal cadence patterns. This approach increases the adversary’s cost by forcing distribution-level behavior matching rather than simple rule circumvention, creating a structural, economic asymmetry that favors defenders in the long run.

Abstract: Modern endpoint detection systems face a fundamental tension: signature-based approaches are trivially evaded by polymorphic or adaptive threats, while heavy deep-learning models resist auditability and deployment at scale. This paper presents Behavioral Grammar, a detection architecture that treats host runtime behavior as a structured language and learns its grammar with a compact 0.88M-parameter causal Transformer (TinyGPT). Each system event is discretized into an 8-token representation spanning event type, process, argument skeleton, path category, parent process, user, destination, and inter-event timing. The model learns the conditional distribution of normal behavior in a purely self-supervised manner, and anomaly scores are derived from per-slot negative log-likelihood (NLL) statistics, yielding a mathematically bounded false-positive rate. We augment this prior with prototype learning for known-attack attribution, second-order temporal analysis for cadence-based detection, self-learning pattern extraction, and a five-network fusion pipeline. Against an Adaptive Adversarial Agent (AAA)--a threat that learns survival strategies under defensive pressure, performs behavioral mimicry, and matches host event rates--our system achieves 93% detection at 3.84% onboarding false-positive rate. The strongest discriminative signal arises not from any single event but from the coefficient of variation of inter-event intervals: the AAA stepping cadence exhibits CV=0.310 versus 9.786 for benign sleep intervals, a 30x separation reflecting a fundamental stealth-functionality trade-off. We frame these findings within a coevolutionary economics model, arguing that behavior-grammar detection shifts the evasion cost from rule circumvention (cheap) to distribution matching (expensive), establishing a structural asymmetry favoring the defender.

</details>


### [184] [FinDeepIndicator: Benchmarking Deep Research Agents in End-to-End Financial Indicator Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00764)
*Chaoqun Yang,Fengbin Zhu,Xinyu Lin,Long Bai,Xiaoluan Liu,Ke-Wei Huang,Roger Zimmermann,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces FinDeepIndicator, a benchmark to evaluate Deep Research agents on end-to-end financial indicator construction, revealing weaknesses in data retrieval and numerical execution despite good formula specification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing financial AI benchmarks largely evaluate only final answer accuracy and usually presuppose that the relevant data have already been collected. This ignores the critical intermediate stages of constructing financial indicators in realistic workflows, such as specifying formulas, gathering data, and performing calculations. The authors want to systematically assess and improve Deep Research agents’ capabilities in these full, end-to-end processes used in real financial analysis tasks.

Method: The authors design FinDeepIndicator, a benchmark focused on end-to-end construction of financial indicators. It decomposes the task into four stages—formula specification, data collection, indicator calculation, and answer generation—and spans fundamental, technical, and macroeconomic indicators, organized into 21 sub-categories. The benchmark consists of 3,350 curated QA pairs covering both U.S. and Chinese markets, with 10 years of historical financial data for 800 listed companies. They run extensive experiments comparing search-equipped LLMs and Deep Research agents on each stage of the pipeline to measure performance gaps and error patterns.

Result: Experiments show that search-equipped LLMs perform relatively well at identifying and specifying the correct financial indicator formulas but suffer substantial performance drops in the data retrieval and numerical computation stages. Deep Research agents, which more actively plan and search, outperform the search-equipped LLM baselines across stages, yet still exhibit notable failures and instability when applied to realistic financial analysis tasks.

Conclusion: FinDeepIndicator reveals that the bottlenecks in current financial AI systems lie less in conceptual knowledge of indicators and more in executing data-intensive, multi-step workflows involving retrieval and calculation. While Deep Research agents represent a step forward over vanilla search-equipped LLMs, they are not yet dependable for real-world financial analysis. The benchmark provides a structured way to diagnose these weaknesses and a foundation for developing more robust, trustworthy Deep Research agents for finance-related applications.

Abstract: Financial indicators are essential tools for transforming raw financial data into interpretable measures for various downstream tasks, such as valuation, risk assessment, and economic analysis. However, existing financial benchmarks largely focus on answer-level accuracy and often assume that relevant data are already provided, leaving the assessment of the intermediate process of indicator construction underexplored. In this work, we propose FinDeepIndicator, the first benchmark dedicated to evaluating Deep Research (DR) agents in end-to-end financial indicator construction. Specifically, FinDeepIndicator evaluates DR agents across four stages in indicator construction: formula specification, data collection, indicator calculation, and answer generation, and covers fundamental, technical, and macroeconomic indicators organized into 21 fine-grained sub-categories. It contains 3,350 curated question-answer (QA) pairs derived from both U.S. and Chinese markets, 10 years of historical financial data, and 800 listed companies. Extensive experiments on search-equipped Large Language Models (LLMs) and DR agents show that, while LLMs generally perform well in formula specification, their accuracy drops substantially during data retrieval and numerical execution. DR agents consistently outperform search-equipped LLMs, yet remain unreliable in realistic financial analysis settings. These findings provide insights for developing more capable and trustworthy DR agents in finance.

</details>


### [185] [Measurement Without Validity: The Compounding Reliability Problem in Agentic AI Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00794)
*William Caban*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Paper argues current automated benchmarks for agentic AI (using LLM-written tasks, LLM simulators, and weak IRR practices) are far less trustworthy than commonly assumed, and proposes psychometric standards to fix this.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic AI systems are increasingly evaluated and certified using benchmark scores. These scores inform deployment, safety, and regulatory decisions, yet the community largely assumes they are valid without rigorously checking measurement quality. As LLMs start generating tasks and simulating users, new failure modes appear that may systematically distort benchmark outcomes, especially for certain user groups. The paper aims to quantify how bad these problems are and how they interact, because poor measurement can invalidate downstream claims about system capability and safety.

Method: The authors conduct: (1) audits of ten popular LLM-based or LLM-augmented benchmarks, inspecting task-generation pipelines and documentation for validity flaws and reporting gaps; (2) calibration studies comparing multiple LLM simulators to real human users, measuring inter-simulator variance and directional biases, particularly across language varieties; (3) a structured literature review of 55 papers to analyze how they apply inter-rater reliability (IRR) metrics, and whether these match their evaluation designs. They then develop a simple multiplicative validity model formalizing how validity losses at three layers—task generation, simulation, and judgment—compound across the pipeline, and instantiate it with empirical ranges estimated from their audits and review.

Result: Empirically, 7 of 10 benchmarks generated or curated via LLMs exhibit clear validity flaws, and all 10 have missing or inadequate reporting. LLM simulators show up to 9 percentage points variance between simulators and systematic miscalibration relative to humans, with especially poor calibration for users who do not speak Standard American English. In the literature review, about 82% of papers misapply IRR: they use mismatched statistics for their design, apply incomplete reliability reporting, or omit IRR entirely. Theoretical analysis shows that even moderately good components (e.g., 70% valid tasks, 80% valid simulation, 65% valid judgments) together yield at most about 36% overall validity, with realistic empirical ranges implying 0.22–0.54 validity, and this upper bound tightens further when the same model family is used at multiple stages, due to correlated errors.

Conclusion: Current practice in LLM benchmarking, especially for agentic systems, substantially overstates the validity of measurement pipelines. Because validity losses at task generation, user simulation, and judgment stages multiply rather than merely add, seemingly acceptable weaknesses at each stage can together render benchmark scores poorly aligned with the constructs they claim to measure. The authors formalize this compounding effect and argue that proper psychometric practices are both available and necessary. They propose concrete standards—minimum simulator calibration (ICC(A,1) ≥ 0.70), reliability thresholds tailored to decision consequences, principled selection of IRR metrics for each pipeline design, and mandatory IRR reporting—to make benchmark-based claims about capability, safety, and compliance defensible.

Abstract: Agentic AI systems are evaluated using automated benchmarks whose scores justify deployment decisions, safety certifications, and regulatory compliance claims. We present an empirical analysis demonstrating that these scores are systematically less trustworthy than current practice acknowledges.
  The problem operates at three compounding layers. First, tasks are increasingly generated by language models: audits of ten popular benchmarks found validity flaws in seven and reporting gaps in all ten. Second, human users are replaced by LLM simulators, but calibration studies document inter-simulator variance up to 9 percentage points and systematic directional miscalibration, particularly for non-Standard American English speakers. Third, our structured survey of 55 papers finds that approximately 82% apply structurally mismatched, incomplete, or absent inter-rater reliability (IRR) metrics.
  These failures compound multiplicatively rather than additively. Under independence, a pipeline retaining 70% of valid signal at task generation, 80% at simulation, and 65% at judgment is at most 36% valid against the intended construct; the bound spans 0.22--0.54 across the empirical estimate range. We formalize this as $V_{\text{total}} \leq V_1 \times V_2 \times V_3$ and show it tightens further under correlated failures when the same model family operates across all three layers.
  We derive eight prescriptions grounded in psychometric science: a simulation calibration floor of $\text{ICC}(A,1) \geq 0.70$; domain-stratified reliability thresholds ($α\geq 0.67$ / $0.70$ / $0.80$ by consequence level); structured IRR metric selection rules based on pipeline design; and IRR as a mandatory reporting field. The measurement tools exist; the field's task is to apply them.

</details>


### [186] [AgentSLABench: Evaluating and Benchmarking Agentic Systems Under Resource Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00805)
*Meher Bhaskar Madiraju,Meher Sai Preetam Madiraju*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgentSLABench is a benchmark and framework to evaluate autonomous AI agents not only on correctness but also on detailed resource usage under explicit budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for autonomous AI agents focus mainly on task accuracy or success rate and largely ignore practical system constraints like latency, cost, CPU, memory, and network usage. In real deployments, however, agents must respect strict resource budgets while still being correct and reliable. The authors want a way to systematically, reproducibly compare agents along these multiple axes so that research and deployment decisions are grounded in production-like constraints rather than accuracy alone.

Method: They design AgentSLABench, a resource-aware evaluation framework with 16 task environments across 6 categories, emphasizing 5 core task types: multi-hop question answering, retail substitution, code generation, web shopping, and travel planning. Each environment runs agents inside isolated Docker containers with declared CPU/memory/time/network budgets. Test sets are sealed and integrity-protected with SHA256 hashes. A standardized profiling protocol measures correctness (task success) together with latency, monetary cost, compute, memory, and network usage. They implement and evaluate 5 general-purpose baseline agents (ReAct, PlanAndSolve, Reflexion, Chain-of-Thought, and a Random agent) plus 4 agents specialized for particular tasks. They define a new aggregate metric, Efficiency-Adjusted Success Rate (EASR), that weights success by how efficiently an agent uses resources relative to the specified budgets.

Result: Specialized agents perform much better on domain-specific tasks: they reach 100% success on 3 of the 5 core tasks (fact_qa, web_shopping, travel_planning) and between 66.7% and 83.3% success on retail substitution and code generation. In contrast, the general-purpose baseline agents fail completely on 4 of the 5 domain tasks. When using the EASR metric, they observe that some agents can achieve high accuracy only by consuming excessive resources, making them impractical for real-world deployment under budget constraints. The collected profiling results show diverse trade-offs between correctness and resource usage across agents and tasks.

Conclusion: AgentSLABench enables multi-dimensional, resource-aware evaluation of autonomous AI agents that better reflects real-world constraints than accuracy-only benchmarks. By providing infrastructure, sealed test sets, explicit resource budgets, and a standardized profiling protocol, it supports reproducible comparisons of agents along both correctness and efficiency axes. The Efficiency-Adjusted Success Rate metric highlights that unbounded resource consumption is not acceptable in production, encouraging the development of agents that are both accurate and resource-efficient. The authors release the full framework and results to catalyze research on practical, deployable AI agents.

Abstract: We present AgentSLABench, a resource-aware evaluation framework for autonomous AI agents that measures correctness alongside latency, cost, compute, memory, and network usage under declared resource budgets. Unlike standard benchmarks that report only accuracy, AgentSLABench produces a multi-dimensional profile per agent per task - the same way systems profilers (perf, pprof, cProfile) measure resource consumption of code, but extended with task correctness as a first-class dimension. AgentSLABench provides 16 task environments across 6 categories (5 core: multi-hop QA, retail substitution, code generation, web shopping, travel planning; 11 extended) with isolated Docker containers, declared CPU/memory/time/network budgets, sealed test sets with SHA256 hashes, and a standardized profiling protocol. We profile 5 general-purpose baseline agents (ReAct, PlanAndSolve, Reflexion, CoT, Random) plus 4 task-specialized agents, finding that specialized agents achieve 100% success on 3/5 core tasks (fact_qa, web_shopping, travel_planning) and 66.7-83.3% on retail and code_gen, while general baselines fail entirely on 4/5 domain tasks. Crucially, we report the Efficiency-Adjusted Success Rate (EASR) - success weighted by resource consumption relative to declared budgets - revealing that high accuracy at unbounded cost is not production-viable. We release the full infrastructure, sealed test sets, and profiling results to enable reproducible, resource-aware agent evaluation.

</details>


### [187] [Large language models improve physician accuracy but lead to false reliance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00817)
*Tirtha Chanda,Christoph Wies,Franziska Schramm,Carina Nogueira Garcia,Nicolas B. Merl,Martin J. Hetz,Jochen S. Utikal,Phillip Tschandl,Cristian Navarrete-Dechent,Alexander Thiem,Jakob N. Kather,Consortium,Titus J. Brinker*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces CORA, a retrieval-augmented LLM for clinical decision support, and evaluates how citation-linked answers affect physician accuracy and reliance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand whether and how retrieval-augmented, source-linked LLMs truly help clinicians make better decisions, and to characterize any new safety risks they introduce, especially overreliance on citation-backed but incorrect answers.

Method: The authors built CORA, an agentic retrieval-augmented LLM that surfaces supporting citations, tested its benchmark performance including on post-training-cutoff cases, and ran a study with 46 physicians comparing unaided decisions versus decisions with CORA, analyzing accuracy and how physicians reacted to correct vs incorrect, citation-supported vs unsupported answers.

Result: CORA preserved benchmark performance and improved most on newer cases. In a 46-physician study, accuracy rose from 70.8% unaided to 82.6% with CORA. Answers with supporting citations were more likely to be correct (87.7% vs 65.5%), and citations increased adoption of correct advice (from 34% to 76.9%) but also reduced resistance to incorrect advice when it appeared citation-supported (from 92% to 34.8%).

Conclusion: Source-linked, retrieval-augmented LLM assistance can meaningfully improve physician diagnostic accuracy but also introduces a safety concern: clinicians are more likely to accept incorrect advice when it appears to be supported by citations, making system grounding and citation reliability critical for safe deployment.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented large language models (LLMs) promise source-linked clinical support, but their value depends on whether displayed evidence guides rather than distorts physician reliance. We developed CORA, an agentic retrieval-augmented LLM, to investigate how source-linked assistance affects physician decision-making. CORA maintained benchmark performance and achieved larger gains on cases published after the models' training-data cutoffs. In a study of 46 physicians, accuracy increased from 70.8% unaided to 82.6% with CORA. Supporting citations predicted correct answers (87.7% vs 65.5%), but citations created an important asymmetry: perceived support increased adoption of correct advice from 34% to 76.9% but when an incorrect LLM answer appeared citation-supported, physician resistance to it fell from 92% to 34.8%. These findings show that source-linked LLM assistance can improve physician accuracy while introducing a grounding-dependent safety risk.

</details>


### [188] [The Scaling Paradox in Human-AI Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00818)
*Anyan Qi,Mengxin Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI scaling laws don’t automatically translate into better human-AI team performance; outcomes depend critically on how humans perceive and use the AI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Empirical scaling laws show that larger AI models predictably improve in capability, leading many organizations to assume that “bigger is better.” However, AI is usually deployed in settings where humans remain in the decision loop. There is limited understanding of whether and how the benefits of scaling AI systems carry over to human-AI collaborations, particularly when humans may misjudge AI capabilities. This paper addresses this gap by analyzing the interaction between AI scale, human perception, and operational performance.

Method: The authors build an analytical (theoretical) model of a human-AI decision system. In the model, the AI’s standalone performance improves with scale according to scaling laws, while the human’s behavior is governed by their perception—possibly biased—of the AI’s capabilities. They formally characterize system performance under accurate perception, over-perception, and under-perception of AI capability. They then analyze how different firm-level operational policies, such as internalizing AI costs and implementing perception-alignment mechanisms, can mitigate or exacerbate misperception effects, given economic parameters of AI deployment.

Result: The model shows that when humans accurately perceive AI capabilities, human-AI joint performance scales positively with AI size, mirroring empirical scaling laws. With over-perception, a “scaling paradox” can emerge: increasing AI scale worsens overall performance and magnifies firm profit losses because humans over-rely on the AI. With under-perception, performance still improves as AI scales but at a slower, suboptimal rate due to under-utilization. The analysis further finds that firm policies like cost internalization and perception alignment can partially correct these distortions, and their effectiveness depends on both the cost-benefit structure of AI and whether humans over- or under-perceive the AI.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that the value created by scaling AI depends not only on technological advances but also on human beliefs and operational design. Organizations cannot assume that larger or more powerful AI models will automatically yield better outcomes; misperceptions of AI capability can either negate or blunt scaling benefits. Effective management of the human-AI interface—through aligning perceptions and designing appropriate incentives and policies—may yield greater gains than simply investing in bigger AI systems. AI scaling is therefore as much a behavioral and operational challenge as it is a technological one.

Abstract: The discovery of scaling laws has highlighted the extraordinary potential of AI systems with a striking empirical pattern: as AI systems scale, their capabilities tend to improve predictably. Yet, in real-world applications, AI rarely operates in isolation; instead, it often works alongside humans, raising the question of whether these gains persist in human-AI collaboration. In this work, we develop an analytical model to examine when the empirical scaling benefits of AI translate into improved human-AI joint system performance. We demonstrate that the performance of a human-AI system can scale positively as the AI scales up-provided that humans have an accurate perception of the AI's capabilities. Human misperception, however, can fundamentally alter this relationship: i) when humans over-perceive the AI's capabilities, a scaling paradox may arise, in which greater AI scale reduces overall system performance and amplifies firm-level profit losses, and (ii) when humans under-perceive the AI's capabilities, performance still improves with scale but at a substantially slower rate. We further show that firms can actively manage these distortions through operational policies such as cost internalization and perception alignment, whose effectiveness depends on the economics of AI deployment and the direction of human misperception. These findings suggest that organizations may benefit more from managing the human-AI interface than from simply investing in larger, more expensive AI systems. More broadly, our results suggest that AI scaling should be viewed not only as a technological challenge, but also as a behavioral and operational one, and caution against the view that larger AI systems will automatically lead to better operational outcomes. Whether AI scaling creates value ultimately depends on how increased AI capabilities shape human beliefs and collaborative efforts.

</details>


### [189] [Isotropy Cliffs: The Geometric Signature of Decision-Making in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00828)
*Okan S. Coskun,Florian Rottach,Carsten Eickhoff,William Rudman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how multiple-choice QA models geometrically change their internal representations when making decisions, focusing on isotropy, and finds key transition layers whose geometric behavior strongly correlates with task accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To better understand the internal decision-making process of MCQA models beyond just input-output behavior, especially by characterizing how representation geometry and isotropy relate to model accuracy and robustness.

Method: Analyze five open-weight language models on various MCQA datasets; measure isotropy across layers; identify layers where there is a sharp change in isotropy; examine representation structure and clustering at those layers; correlate geometric transition metrics with downstream accuracy; test robustness of the identified transitions to different prompt formats.

Result: They find specific transition layers where isotropy changes markedly; these layers coincide with major representation changes and the emergence of task-relevant clusters. The strength and clarity of this geometric transition is strongly correlated with MCQA accuracy (correlation coefficient about 0.84), and the phenomenon persists under prompt variations.

Conclusion: MCQA models exhibit synchronized geometric transitions in specific layers—marked by isotropy shifts and clustering—that are tightly linked to accurate decision-making. This transition appears to be a general, prompt-robust mechanism of model behavior, suggesting that geometric metrics like isotropy can serve as indicators of model competence on MCQA tasks.

Abstract: We investigate the geometry of decision-making in Multiple Choice Question Answering (MCQA) through the lens of isotropy. Analyzing five open-weight models across diverse datasets, we identify decision-critical transition layers characterized by a shift in isotropy, coinciding with a major representational change and the emergence of task-relevant clusters. We demonstrate that this synchronized geometric behavior is strongly correlated with downstream accuracy ($r\approx0.84$), displaying its relevance for successful decision-making. Furthermore, we show that this transition is robust to prompt variations, suggesting that it reflects a general mechanism of model behavior.

</details>


### [190] [Similarity Weighted Aggregation with Global Differential Privacy for Federated Brain Lesion Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00872)
*Muhammad Irfan Khan,Eero Lehtonen,Joni Obradovic,Elina Kontio,Esa Alhoniemi,Suleiman A. Khan,Mojtaba Jafaritadi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DP-SimAgg is a federated learning framework that combines similarity-weighted aggregation with server-side differential privacy to enable privacy-preserving brain tumor segmentation across institutions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated learning in medical imaging must handle heterogeneous (non-IID) data across institutions and prevent information leakage through shared model updates, challenges that limit its safe deployment in practice.

Method: The authors propose DP-SimAgg, which (1) clips client model updates with an L2 norm bound, (2) computes similarity-based weights for aggregating client updates to reduce the impact of non-IID data, and (3) adds calibrated Gaussian noise at the central server based on the sensitivity bound to provide per-round (epsilon, delta)-differential privacy guarantees. They implement this framework on Intel's OpenFL and train segmentation models on the FeTS 2022 multi-modal brain MRI dataset.

Result: On the FeTS 2022 brain tumor segmentation dataset, DP-SimAgg achieves competitive Dice scores for enhancing tumor (ET), tumor core (TC), and whole tumor (WT) regions, even under strict privacy constraints (e.g., epsilon = 1 per round, cumulative epsilon_total = 20 over 20 rounds). With a more relaxed privacy budget (epsilon = 10 per round, epsilon_total = 200), performance approaches that of a non-private baseline while still providing formal DP guarantees.

Conclusion: DP-SimAgg effectively balances privacy and utility in federated medical image segmentation by combining similarity-aware aggregation with server-side differential privacy, making it a promising approach for privacy-preserving collaborative learning in healthcare settings.

Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training of machine learning models across multiple institutions without sharing sensitive data, making it particularly suitable for medical imaging applications. However, heterogeneous data distributions across institutions and potential information leakage through model updates remain important challenges. In this work, we propose DP-SimAgg, a privacy-preserving federated learning framework that integrates similarity-weighted aggregation with a server-side differential privacy mechanism. The proposed method applies L2 clipping to bound collaborator updates, computes similarity-based aggregation weights to mitigate the effects of non-IID data distributions, and injects calibrated Gaussian noise at the central server, providing per-round privacy guarantees under the assumed sensitivity bound. The framework is implemented using Intel's OpenFL platform and evaluated on the FeTS 2022 dataset consisting of 1251 multi-modal MRI scans for brain tumor segmentation. Experimental results demonstrate that DP-SimAgg maintains competitive segmentation performance while providing privacy protection. Under a strict per-round privacy budget (epsilon = 1, cumulative epsilon_total = 20 over 20 rounds), the method achieves Dice scores of 0.6357, 0.5305, and 0.5274 for the enhancing tumor (ET), tumor core (TC), and whole tumor (WT) regions, respectively. With a more relaxed per-round budget (epsilon = 10, cumulative epsilon_total = 200), performance approaches that of the non-private baseline while incorporating a central Gaussian mechanism with per-round (epsilon, delta)-DP accounting under the assumed sensitivity bound. These results highlight the potential of DP-SimAgg for enabling privacy-preserving collaborative learning in medical imaging applications.

</details>


### [191] [Assuming You Knew: Fixing an Epistemic Semantics for Flow Policies Using Agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00882)
*David A. Naumann*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper revisits and corrects a prior framework for specifying high‑level information‑flow security policies using epistemic semantics, providing a fully machine‑checked formalization that is simpler and more general.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-level security policies often describe what information about secret data may become known to observers, involving tricky notions of selective downgrading. Existing formalisms, including the earlier CSF 2018 paper, either lack precision, generality, or fully checked formalizations. A robust, unifying epistemic-logic-based framework is needed to precisely capture and compare expressive information‑flow policies and support their enforcement.

Method: The authors take the epistemic semantics idea from the CSF 2018 paper (relating program runs and observers’ knowledge) and reconstruct it carefully in the Rocq proof assistant. They correct the previously sketchy parts, fix an error acknowledged at the original presentation, and provide a clean, general formalization of the framework, phrased in terms of relational annotations and epistemic notions of knowledge. The entire framework is mechanized to validate definitions, lemmas, and theorems.

Result: They obtain a corrected, fully mechanized formal framework that accurately captures expressive information-flow policies involving selective downgrading. The resulting theory is both simpler and more general than before, and its soundness has been machine-checked in Rocq. This shows that the core ideas of the 2018 framework can be made precise and internally consistent.

Conclusion: A robust epistemic semantics framework for relational annotations and expressive flow policies can be stated cleanly and verified mechanically. This corrected, machine‑checked theory provides a solid foundation for comparing diverse policy specification styles and for leveraging existing enforcement techniques, potentially improving the reliability of high‑level information‑flow security tools and analyses.

Abstract: Many high-level security requirements are about the allowed flow of information in programs and are difficult to make precise because they involve selective downgrading. Notions from epistemic logic have emerged as a good approach to policy semantics but a robust general framework remains elusive. A paper appearing in CSF 2018, entitled ``Assuming You Know: Epistemic Semantics of Relational Annotations for Expressive Flow Policies'', attempted to provide a unifying framework---but the formalization was sketchy and a correction was announced during the conference presentation. With aid from an agentic AI coding assistant, a corrected formalization has been machine checked in the Rocq proof assistant. The simplicity and generality of the framework may help compare different policy specification styles and enforce them by leveraging existing techniques.

</details>


### [192] [Neuro-Evolved Heuristics for Variable Gapped Common Subsequence Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00888)
*Marko Djukanović,Christian Blum,Aleksandar Kartelj,Saso Dzeroski,Ziga Zebec*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They tackle a constrained variant of longest common subsequence (VGLCSP) and replace hand-crafted beam-search heuristics with a neuro-evolved neural heuristic that significantly improves search performance on synthetic and real data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-sequence VGLCSP with gap constraints is important for sequence alignment and time-series analysis. Existing dynamic programming works mainly for two sequences; the multi-sequence case relies on beam-search heuristics that are manually designed and often brittle or suboptimal. There is a need for robust, data-driven heuristics that adapt better to problem structure.

Method: They represent the search heuristic as a neural network with a fixed architecture whose weights are optimized via a genetic algorithm (neuro-evolution). The network does not construct solutions but assigns scores to partial states to guide an iterative multi-source beam search, which is the underlying solver. Training alternates between evolutionary weight optimization and evaluation within the beam-search process. They also build an ensemble heuristic by combining the learned heuristic’s scores with those from the best hand-crafted heuristic.

Result: The neuro-evolved heuristic, embedded in iterative multi-source beam search, yields better solutions than prior hand-crafted heuristics on standard synthetic benchmarks of VGLCSP. On new real-world instances with empirically derived gap constraints, the hybrid ensemble approach further improves performance, achieving state-of-the-art results in both domains.

Conclusion: Automatically learned, neuro-evolved neural heuristics can robustly guide beam search for complex combinatorial problems like multi-sequence VGLCSP, outperforming carefully engineered heuristics. Combining learned and hand-crafted heuristics in an ensemble within the beam-search framework provides additional gains, suggesting a promising general strategy for data-driven heuristic design in sequence alignment and related optimization tasks.

Abstract: This study addresses the Variable Gapped Longest Common Subsequence Problem (VGLCSP), a variant of the classical longest common subsequence problem with additional gap constraints and applications in sequence alignment and time-series analysis. While the two-sequence version has been widely studied using dynamic programming, the generalized multi-sequence form is usually solved with beam search-based heuristics, whose hand-crafted designs often lack robustness.
  To overcome this limitation, we propose a learning-based approach for automatically designing more effective data-driven heuristics. The heuristics are represented by a neural network with predefined architecture, whose weights are optimized by a genetic algorithm within a neuro-evolutionary framework. The learning process alternates between weight optimization and evaluation within an iterative multi-source beam search procedure, a state-of-the-art method for the problem. Rather than constructing solutions directly, the neural network learns to guide the search process, producing a neuro-evolved heuristic. We further introduce an ensemble heuristic that combines the scores of learned and the best-performing hand-crafted heuristic. Integrated into the iterative multi-source beam search framework, the resulting hybrid approach outperforms existing methods on both synthetic benchmark instances and newly introduced real-world instances with data-driven gap constraints.

</details>


### [193] [CADIR: A Cross-Backend Editable Intermediate Representation for Agentic CAD Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00891)
*Yu Liu,Jingzhe Ni,Yiming Chen,Junqi Huang,Ruofeng Tong,Min Tang,Peng Du*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CADIR is a new intermediate representation and retrieval framework that enables robust, editable CAD generation and cross-backend reconstruction from language or images.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CAD generation approaches either rely on backend-specific sequential scripts with implicit dependencies or on static geometry, which fails to preserve construction history, stable topology references, and feature-level editability across different CAD systems. This limits reliable editing, transfer, and agent-based manipulation of CAD models.

Method: The authors design CADIR, an executable intermediate representation built on the OCCT geometry kernel via OCP, which exposes explicit compositional modeling operations and detailed execution diagnostics. CADIR logs operations, parameter dependencies, constraints, and topology selections into a construction graph during execution. They introduce Geometric Signature Matching to map corresponding edges and faces across parameter changes and CAD backends, and implement adapters to reconstruct native editable feature histories in FreeCAD, SolidWorks, and Fusion 360. They also develop a construction-graph retrieval mechanism for text and image queries that supports both full-graph and subgraph retrieval, enabling agents to reuse whole models or substructures. Extensive experiments compare CADIR to existing CAD representations on geometric fidelity, execution reliability, generation quality, and cross-backend editing robustness.

Result: CADIR achieves higher geometric fidelity and more reliable execution than prior CAD representations. The proposed construction-graph retrieval further improves the quality of generated models. Cross-backend editing using CADIR allows reliable reconstruction of models and subsequent editable operations in multiple CAD environments (FreeCAD, SolidWorks, Fusion 360), demonstrating robust transfer of construction history and topology mappings.

Conclusion: CADIR provides an effective intermediate representation and retrieval framework for CAD that preserves construction history, supports robust topology mapping across backends, and enables feature-level editability in multiple CAD systems. Its design facilitates agent-based CAD generation from language or images and improves reliability and quality over existing CAD program or geometry-only approaches.

Abstract: Large language models have made it possible to generate executable computer-aided design (CAD) programs from natural-language descriptions or images. However, existing methods represent modeling processes as backend-specific sequential scripts with implicit dependencies or as static geometry, making it difficult to simultaneously preserve construction history, stable topological references, and feature-level editability across different CAD systems. We present CADIR, an agent-friendly executable intermediate representation for CAD generation and cross-backend editing. Built on the OCCT geometry kernel via OCP, CADIR provides explicit, compositional modeling operations and fine-grained execution diagnostics. During program execution, CADIR records modeling operations, parameter dependencies, constraints, and topology selections in a construction graph. To enable reliable cross-backend reconstruction, we introduce Geometric Signature Matching, which identifies corresponding edges and faces despite parameter changes and backend differences, allowing adapters to reconstruct native editable feature histories in FreeCAD, SolidWorks, and Fusion 360. Building on this representation, we further propose a construction-graph retrieval method for text and image queries that supports both full-graph and subgraph retrieval, enabling agents to leverage complete models and modeling substructures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CADIR achieves higher geometric fidelity and execution reliability than existing CAD representations, that construction-graph retrieval further improves model generation quality, and that cross-backend editing enables reliable model reconstruction and post-reconstruction editing across multiple CAD environments.

</details>


### [194] [Modeling Social Dynamics with an LLM-Enabled Agent Based Network-Dynamic (LAND) Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00929)
*Lynnette Hui Xian Ng,Kathleen M. Carley*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents a large-scale social simulation using a hybrid LLM-enabled agent-based network model to study how online interactions give rise to collective influence and coordinated behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To better understand how individual-level online interactions in complex social networks give rise to emergent phenomena such as narrative dominance, coordination, and influence, and to test whether LLM-driven agent-based simulations can meaningfully reproduce such social dynamics.

Method: They use the GhostField architecture, a hybrid LLM-enabled Agent Based Network-Dynamic (LAND) model, to construct the AuraSight scenario. In this scenario, over 300k heterogeneous cyber-social agents and human actors interact for 30 simulated days around a fictional international songwriting contest, exchanging over half a million messages. The analysis examines emergent dynamics along four layers: ego-network topology (who connects to whom), semantic network evolution (how narratives and meanings evolve), coordination dynamics (patterns of organized behavior), and influence dynamics (which actors or narratives gain dominance).

Result: The simulation yields rich social dynamics where network structures, evolving semantics, coordination, and influence patterns can be quantitatively examined. The observed coordination and influence patterns do not simply follow from any single agent’s behavior but from the interplay between the changing network topology and ongoing narrative exchanges among agents.

Conclusion: LLM-driven social simulations can generate realistic-looking emergent social dynamics. Coordination and influence are shown to emerge from recursive feedback between network structure and narrative exchange rather than being reducible to individual agent properties, supporting the utility of hybrid LAND models like GhostField for studying complex online social phenomena.

Abstract: Social dynamics encode the process in which individual network and discourse interactions aggregate into collective influence, narrative dominance and coordinate behavior. This paper uses the the GhostField architecture, a hybrid LLM-Enabled Agent Based Network-Dynamic (LAND) model as a social simulation framework to build the AuraSight scenario. In the AuraSight scenario, 314,244 heterogeneous cyber social agents and human actors exchange 529,327 messages over 30 days surrounding a fictional international song-writing contest. We methodologically examine emergent social dynamics across four analytical layers: ego-network topology, semantic network evolution, coordination dynamics and influence dynamics. Our results show how generated social simulations do also produce social dynamics, and how the dynamics of coordination and influence emerge not from individual agents but from the recursive interaction between network topology and narrative exchange.

</details>


### [195] [PMMC: Prospective Multimodal Memory Compilation for Long-Term LVLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00962)
*Jingyu Sun,Yan Lin,Yuyang Xue,Yifan Wang,Zhengtao Yao,Rui Qian,Zefeng Xu,Jiachen Li,Xianyang Liu,Jiancheng Pan,Jingyuan Sun,Syed Murtuza Baker,Hongpeng Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A new memory framework for LVLM agents that pre-compiles multimodal memories via predicted questions and validated evidence paths, improving long-term visual-text reasoning efficiency and quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LVLM agents need robust long-term multimodal memory to maintain consistency and reason over extended image-text interactions. Existing systems either compress visual experiences into lossy textual summaries or depend on heavy retrieve-then-reason pipelines at query time, which are inefficient and fragile when tasks require precise image-text alignment, temporal updates, or detailed visual recall. A better approach is needed to handle complex multimodal queries while reducing latency and token usage.

Method: The paper introduces Prospective Multimodal Memory Compilation. From accumulated multimodal dialogues, a Questioner module predicts likely future questions. A Planner then builds question-conditioned "multimodal memory programs"—structured evidence paths specifying which stored visual and textual elements are relevant. A Doubter module verifies that each planned path can indeed support the predicted answer. Only verified question–program pairs are stored as a structured question bank. At query time, the agent routes incoming questions via this bank to quickly retrieve relevant evidence, instead of doing full retrieval and reasoning from scratch.

Result: On multimodal long-term memory benchmarks, this framework yields better answer accuracy and higher-quality visual evidence recall compared to baselines. It also reduces token consumption and latency at query time, demonstrating more efficient use of LVLM compute. Ablation studies dissect contributions from self-feedback mechanisms, dynamic planning strategies, access to raw images, and the coverage/size of the constructed question bank.

Conclusion: Shifting part of memory reasoning from query time to a prospective consolidation phase—through predicted questions, planned evidence programs, and verification—enables LVLM agents to handle long-term multimodal memory more effectively and efficiently. Structured question banks built in this way improve both reasoning quality and system efficiency, suggesting a promising direction for scalable multimodal agents that operate over extended interactions.

Abstract: Long-term memory is essential for LVLM agents to maintain consistency and integrate information across extended multimodal interactions. Existing agent memory systems, however, often reduce visual experiences into textual summaries or rely on static retrieve-then-reason pipelines, which are inefficient at query time and brittle when questions require image-text binding, temporal updates, or visual details. We propose Prospective Multimodal Memory Compilation, a framework that shifts part of the memory reasoning process from query time to memory consolidation time. Given accumulated multimodal interactions, a Questioner predicts future question candidates, a Planner compiles question-conditioned multimodal memory programs, and a Doubter verifies whether the planned evidence path can support the predicted answer. The verified question-program pairs form a structured question bank for efficient query-time routing and evidence retrieval. Experiments on multimodal long-term memory benchmarks show that our method improves answer quality and visual evidence recall while reducing query-time token and latency costs. Extensive ablations analyze the effects of self-feedback, dynamic planning, raw-image access, and question bank coverage.

</details>


### [196] [TrajWiki: Source-Grounded Memory Trajectories for Long-Horizon Dialogue Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00967)
*Jingyu Sun,Yuyang Xue,Mingyang Li,Zhengtao Yao,Jiachen Li,Yang Cui,Wenhao Cai,Haozhe Liu,Fangying Wang,Magdalene Katharina Montgomery,Syed Murtuza Baker,Hongpeng Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TrajWiki is a trajectory-based memory framework that enables long-horizon, interpretable dialogue for LLM agents by representing memories as evolving trajectories and organizing them into a structured Memory Wiki for efficient, evidence-grounded retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM agents struggle with robust long-horizon dialogue because their external memories are not traceable, updatable, or transparent. Existing memory mechanisms store information as isolated records or mutable states, making it hard to track how knowledge originates, changes, conflicts, or becomes outdated, and limiting interpretability and diagnostic analysis.

Method: The paper introduces TrajWiki, where each memory is modeled as a source-grounded evolution trajectory composed of immutable episodic snapshots. Claim-level operations (ADD, REVISE, DEPRECATE) update these trajectories without overwriting history. On top of this, the authors build a Memory Wiki: a persistent, structured layer that incrementally summarizes dialogue history into interlinked wiki pages keyed by entities, events, quantities, topics, and conflicts. At inference, a hierarchical retrieval process routes from relevant wiki pages to linked trajectories, then to specific snapshots and source messages to support answer generation.

Result: On the LoCoMo and MedMT benchmarks, TrajWiki improves long-horizon dialogue performance for both open-source and closed-source LLM backbones compared to existing baselines. It also yields more interpretable behavior by exposing memory evolution, retrieval paths, and where failures in memory or reasoning occur.

Conclusion: Trajectory-based, source-grounded memory combined with a structured Memory Wiki enables LLM agents to conduct more reliable long-horizon conversations, while offering transparent, diagnosable memory operations. This design addresses fragmentation and opacity in prior memory systems and provides a general framework for interpretable, persistent conversational memory.

Abstract: Large language model agents have shown strong capabilities in generating coherent and contextually appropriate responses, yet robust long-horizon dialogue remains limited by the lack of external memory that is traceable, updatable, and diagnostically transparent. Existing memory-augmented agents often store memories as isolated records or overwritable states, making it difficult to preserve how information originates, evolves, conflicts, or becomes obsolete over time. We propose TrajWiki, a trajectory-based memory framework for long-horizon conversational agents. Instead of treating memory as static entries, TrajWiki represents each memory as a source-grounded evolution trajectory, maintained through immutable episodic snapshots and claim-level operations such as ADD, REVISE, and DEPRECATE. To reduce fragmentation and retrieval cost, TrajWiki further introduces Memory Wiki, a persistent intermediate layer that incrementally compiles dialogue history into structured and interlinked wiki pages capturing salient entities, events, quantities, topics, and conflicts. At inference time, queries are routed hierarchically from relevant wiki pages to linked memory trajectories, then to corresponding snapshots and source messages for evidence-grounded answer synthesis. Experiments on LoCoMo and MedMT show that TrajWiki improves long-horizon dialogue performance across both open-source and closed-source LLM backbones, while providing greater interpretability and diagnostic visibility into memory evolution, retrieval failures, and answer generation.

</details>


### [197] [PROGRESS: Coverage-guided RL to Train Search-augmented LLM Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00969)
*Sudipta Paul,Vijay Srinivasan,Vivek Kulkarni,Aounon Kumar,Yashas Malur Saidutta,Wenbo Li,Srinivas Chappidi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces PROGRESS, a method that improves search-augmented LLM agents by explicitly rewarding good query decomposition using teacher guidance, leading to better reasoning and task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current search-augmented LLM agents mostly use RL with outcome-level rewards, which do not directly supervise how the agent searches or decomposes complex queries into effective sub-queries. This lack of fine-grained guidance can result in suboptimal search strategies and poor handling of complex information needs. The authors aim to provide more targeted supervision over the query decomposition process to improve reasoning and search behavior without incurring the cost of dense process-level annotation.

Method: The authors propose PROGRESS, an RL framework that adds a teacher-guided coverage reward on top of an R1-style training setup. Frozen teacher models first decompose complex user queries into essential search queries. These teacher-generated essential queries act as a target set that the policy model should cover when it decomposes the original query during search. During RL training, the policy’s decomposed queries are compared to the teacher’s essential queries, and a coverage-based reward is computed to explicitly encourage the policy to generate similar, high-coverage sub-queries. This works as a lightweight supervision signal that shapes search behavior without requiring step-by-step process labels.

Result: Experiments show that integrating the coverage-based reward into RL training improves the overall task performance of search-augmented LLM agents compared to baselines that only use outcome-level rewards. The results indicate that the policy learns better query decomposition strategies and more effective search behavior when guided by teacher-derived essential queries.

Conclusion: Explicitly supervising the query decomposition and search strategy of LLM agents via teacher-guided coverage rewards leads to better performance than relying solely on outcome-level rewards. PROGRESS demonstrates that lightweight, teacher-based guidance can significantly improve agentic LLMs’ ability to handle complex queries and perform effective search, without the overhead of dense process-level supervision.

Abstract: Existing search-augmented LLM agents are trained using Reinforcement Learning to boost its reasoning capabilities. However, these approaches primarily rely on outcome-level rewards, which provide little supervision over search behavior and overlook agent's ability to decompose complex queries properly. To mitigate this issue, we propose PROGRESS which utilizes teacher-guided coverage reward to explicitly shape decomposed query generation of the policy model. During training, frozen teacher models are used to decompose complex queries into essential search queries. These essential search queries are utilized to guide the search behavior of the policy model. Integrated into an R1-style training framework, our approach provides lightweight guidance over query decomposition decisions without dense process-level supervision. Experiments show that coverage-guided RL improves overall task performance, highlighting the importance of explicitly supervising search strategies in agentic LLMs.

</details>


### [198] [Search-GRT: Guided Retrieval Training of Search Agents to Optimize for Complex Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00974)
*Aounon Kumar,Sudipta Paul,Vivek Kulkarni,Vijay Srinivasan,Srinivas Chappidi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Guided Retrieval Training (GRT), an RL-based method that constrains document retrieval using ground-truth signals to improve large language models’ performance on complex, multi-hop QA, yielding large accuracy gains and more efficient training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs struggle with complex, multi-hop QA because they must decompose questions, issue subqueries, retrieve multiple documents, and synthesize answers. Errors in early retrieval steps cascade, and existing RL-based search agents suffer from sparse rewards, making it hard to learn good retrieval and query decomposition strategies. The authors aim to provide a stronger, more informative learning signal during training to make search-augmented LLMs more reliable and efficient, especially on MHQA tasks.

Method: They propose Guided Retrieval Training (GRT), where during RL training the search agent’s retrieval is restricted to a curated set of documents that are known to be relevant based on ground truth. This guided retrieval space reduces noise and exposes the agent mostly to useful documents, thereby densifying the reward signal. Within this constrained setting, the agent learns to generate better subqueries and to combine information from retrieved documents.
