This mismatch means feedback is dense but credit is not, limiting how well policies can be optimized over multi-step refinement processes. The paper aims to bridge this gap with a principled way to turn verifier scores into meaningful per-turn credit signals.

Method: The authors propose TCPO, a score-to-credit conversion framework that produces turn-level advantages for multi-turn RL. TCPO uses reference-based comparisons to decompose credit into: (1) retrospective credit, which evaluates each turn by how much it improves or worsens relative to the best previous state; (2) hindsight delayed credit, which assigns credit to earlier non-improving turns that later lead to better outcomes; and (3) selective fixed-history counterfactual estimation, which re-evaluates high-surprisal turns under the same history to better estimate their contribution. These components are integrated into a policy optimization procedure for verifier-guided multi-turn generation.

Result: Across math reasoning, code generation, and AppWorld agent tasks, TCPO consistently matches or outperforms strong baselines over various model sizes and verifier configurations. It achieves best or tied-best best-turn Pass@8 for Qwen3-4B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, reduces the average number of turns needed to reach success, and yields better performance for multi-turn agents, indicating more effective use of verifier feedback.

Conclusion: TCPO demonstrates that carefully designed score-to-credit conversion is crucial for effective verifier-guided multi-turn RL in LLMs. By converting dense per-turn scores into accurate turn-level credit assignments, TCPO enables more sample-efficient and performant policy optimization, improving reasoning quality, solution rates, and interaction efficiency across diverse tasks and models.

Abstract: Verifier-guided reinforcement learning has become a powerful paradigm for improving LLM reasoning. In multi-turn settings, models receive a verifier score after each turn and iteratively refine their outputs. Although such scores provide dense feedback, they do not directly provide dense credit: a score measures the quality of the current output, while credit should measure how the current turn changes the refinement trajectory. We propose TCPO, a turn-level credit assignment method for verifier-guided multi-turn RL. TCPO casts credit assignment as score-to-credit conversion and constructs turn-level advantages through reference-based comparisons: retrospective credit captures immediate progress and regression relative to the best prior state; hindsight delayed credit identifies non-improving turns with later payoff; and selective fixed-history counterfactual estimation refines high-surprisal turns under the same history. Experiments on math reasoning, code generation, and AppWorld agent tasks show that TCPO improves or matches the strongest baselines across model scales, task domains, and verifier types. TCPO achieves the best or tied-best best-turn Pass@8 on Qwen3-4B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, reduces turns to success, and improves multi-turn agent performance. These results highlight score-to-credit conversion as a central ingredient for verifier-guided multi-turn policy optimization.

</details>


### [253] [When Memory Becomes Authority: Benchmarking Authority Collapse at the Memory Consolidation Boundary](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01679)
*Qiuyang Zhan,Rui Zhang,Sheng Guo,Lepeng Zhao,Zhuotao Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how long-term memory in LLM agents can mis-handle the *authority* behind stored information, leading to unsafe behavior, and proposes a benchmark plus an authority-labeling method to detect and prevent this issue.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents increasingly use persistent memory to store and reuse information from past interactions as facts, preferences, or rules. However, the way these memories are consolidated often loses critical information about *who said what under which permissions* (the source authority). When this happens, stored memories can be used more broadly or more powerfully than originally authorized, causing security, safety, and privacy risks. The authors are motivated to systematically characterize and measure this problem—called authority collapse—and to explore whether automatic methods can preserve or restore authority information.

Method: 1) Conceptualize and define the problem of authority collapse in the context of LLM agent memory consolidation.
2) Build AuthMem-Bench, a paired benchmark where each memory item has variants that differ only in the authority level of the source (e.g., user fact vs. untrusted statement vs. revocable preference), while keeping the core claim and downstream task fixed.
3) Implement seven different consolidators modeled after common agent-memory systems, and evaluate them with seven different LLM backbones.
4) Measure (a) write-time collapse, i.e., whether consolidation strips away authority information; (b) downstream authorization errors, i.e., whether agents take actions they should not when relying on collapsed memory; and (c) the effectiveness of automatically predicting and persisting authority labels as part of the memory.
5) Conduct both controlled, action-grounded experiments (explicitly testing whether the agent performs unauthorized actions) and end-to-end evaluations of agents performing tasks with and without authority-aware memory.

Result: 1) Authority collapse is pervasive: 48 out of 49 combinations of memory-consolidation schemes and LLM backbones exhibit authority collapse.
2) When memories lack authority metadata, agents frequently misuse them: in controlled action-grounded tests, collapsed memories yield an average unauthorized-action rate of 50.3%.
3) Introducing automatically predicted and stored authority labels on memories dramatically reduces misuse: in end-to-end evaluations, the unauthorized-action rate drops from 16.9% to 0.0%, while performance on benign tasks is essentially unaffected.

Conclusion: Persistent-memory LLM agents are vulnerable to authority collapse, where memory consolidation preserves content but loses the constraints on how it may be used, leading to frequent unauthorized actions. This problem is widespread across current systems. However, explicitly modeling and preserving authority—e.g., via automatic authority labeling and storage—can eliminate observed unauthorized actions without degrading normal task performance. Therefore, robust agent memory systems must track and enforce not only *what* is remembered, but also *under what authority* it was learned and may be reused.

Abstract: Persistent memory allows (self-evolving) LLM agents to adapt across tasks by consolidating heterogeneous interaction histories into reusable facts, preferences, observations, and rules. Yet consolidation also imposes an implicit authorization boundary: it determines whether stored information may later be consumed as a user fact, an attested observation, or a standing instruction. We identify authority collapse, in which consolidation preserves a claim while erasing the source constraints governing its authorized use, causing the stored memory to imply greater authority than its source permits. We introduce AuthMem-Bench, a controlled paired benchmark that holds the focal claim and downstream task fixed while varying only source authority. It evaluates write-time collapse, downstream authorization errors, and automatic authority preservation. Across seven consolidators based on widely used agent-memory systems and seven LLM backbones, we observe authority collapse in 48 of 49 evaluated configurations. In a controlled action-grounded evaluation, collapsed memories without authority metadata yield a mean unauthorized-action rate of 50.3%. In an end-to-end evaluation, automatically predicted and persisted authority labels reduce the observed unauthorized-action rate from 16.9% to 0.0%, while benign task success remains essentially unchanged. These findings show that memory-driven adaptation must preserve not only what was
  learned, but also the authority under which it may be reused.

</details>


### [254] [GABench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Agents on Graph Analysis Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01684)
*Jiarui Tan,Zhongjian Zhang,YaBo Guo,Jiawei Liu,Yujie Xing,Muhan Zhang,Cheng Yang,Chuan Shi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GABench is a comprehensive benchmark to evaluate large language model (LLM) agents on realistic, tool-based graph analysis tasks across multiple graph types and task categories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph benchmarks for LLMs are narrow in both task coverage and graph types, and they usually convert graph problems into pure text question answering where the graph is embedded in the prompt. This avoids evaluating core agentic abilities such as planning, multi-step tool use, and interacting with external graph environments, making it hard to systematically study how well LLM agents perform end-to-end graph analysis.

Method: The authors design GABench, a benchmark that (1) spans three different types of graphs, (2) covers four categories of graph analysis tasks—graph retrieval, graph theory, graph machine learning, and open-ended graph QA, and (3) exposes 84 executable tools for graph data access and operations. They build an agentic task-generation pipeline that uses these tools to synthesize 10,400 graph analysis tasks with verifiable ground truth, and then use the benchmark to systematically evaluate multiple frontier LLMs and different agent harnesses (controller frameworks) under a tool-using agent setup.

Result: Across the 10,400 tasks, the evaluated LLM agents underperform on complex graph analysis, with substantial error rates. Performance varies substantially with the chosen agent harness, indicating that current orchestration frameworks are a major bottleneck. Analyses also show that successful graph analysis is more strongly tied to the quality (appropriateness and correctness) of tool calls than to the sheer number of tool invocations.

Conclusion: GABench exposes clear limitations of current LLM agents and harnesses in conducting complex, tool-based graph analysis. It demonstrates that better harness design and improved tool-use reasoning are crucial for progress, and provides a broad, standardized testbed for developing and rigorously evaluating future LLM agents in graph-centric environments.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of planning, using tools, and interacting with external environments. They are typically supported by harnesses, which manage state and coordinate multi-step execution. Graph analysis provides a promising setting for evaluating their agentic capabilities, because it requires agents to access data and execute operations in a graph environment. However, existing graph benchmarks for LLMs provide limited coverage of graph tasks and graph types, making it difficult to comprehensively evaluate LLM agents. Moreover, they typically formulate graph analysis as text-based question answering, where graph information is directly provided in the prompt, limiting the evaluation of end-to-end agentic capabilities. To address these limitations, we introduce GABench, a comprehensive benchmark for agentic graph analysis. GABench spans three graph types and covers four graph analysis task categories: graph retrieval, graph theory, graph machine learning, and graph open-ended question answering. GABench also provides 84 executable tools for accessing graph data and performing diverse graph operations. Building on these tools, we develop an agentic graph analysis task generation pipeline and construct 10,400 tasks with verifiable ground truth.Using GABench, we evaluate a range of frontier LLMs and agent harnesses. Our experiments reveal three key findings: (1) Existing LLM agents still struggle with complex graph analysis tasks. (2) Harness choice significantly affects performance, yet existing harnesses remain limited on complex graph tasks. (3) Graph analysis depends more on tool-call quality than quantity. Our findings provide practical insights into the development and evaluation of LLM agents for graph analysis.

</details>


### [255] [Beyond Single-Use Tokens: Durable Authorization State for Replay-Resistant LLM Agent Actions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01710)
*Jinghan Xu,Longze Fan,Zeyuan Wang,Xinjin Li,Hankai Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies and addresses 'semantic replay', where LLM agent behaviors (retries, replans, crash recovery) cause the same user-approved action to be executed multiple times despite single-use tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tool-using LLM agents often need to perform complex, stateful actions under user authorization. Because they frequently retry, replan, delegate, and recover from failures, naive token-based authorization schemes can unintentionally allow the same logical action to be executed multiple times, leading to overspending, duplicated side effects, or policy violations. Existing mechanisms focus on preventing reuse of token identifiers, but do not prevent fresh reissuance of authorizations representing the same user approval.

Method: The authors formally define 'semantic replay' and analyze why identifier-local token consumption is insufficient without durable, monotonic state about the authorized action, confirmation, and remaining execution budget. They design CapLease, an authorization-consumption layer that binds authenticated user confirmations to canonical actions and enforces transactional Issue-Prepare-Commit phases. They compare CapLease with simpler identifier-local token schemes and a Server Ledger across various realistic LLM-agent scenarios, such as replanning, retries, delegation, concurrency, confirmation replay, and crash recovery.

Result: The study shows that in all evaluated LLM-agent scenarios, schemes that only consume tokens by identifier allow fresh semantic reissuance of authorizations, enabling repeated execution of the same user-approved action. In contrast, both CapLease and a similarly stateful Server Ledger prevent duplicate admission of the same logical action and, when combined with an idempotent backend (sink), also prevent duplicated external effects. This empirically validates that durable authorization state is required for replay resistance.

Conclusion: The work concludes that robust replay resistance for LLM agents cannot be achieved by token design alone. Instead, systems must maintain durable, monotonic authorization state that tracks canonical actions, confirmations, and execution budgets, enforcing transactional transitions. CapLease embodies this requirement and successfully prevents semantic replay across challenging LLM-agent behaviors, providing a systems-level foundation for safer agentic tool use and authorization handling.

Abstract: Tool-using large language model agents frequently replan, retry failed operations, delegate tasks, and resume after crashes. These behaviors can cause one user authorization to be requested and executed multiple times under freshly issued token identifiers, even when each individual token is single-use. We call this failure semantic replay: exceeding the execution budget of a token-independent authorization instance rather than merely reusing an old token identifier. We show that identifier-local token consumption cannot prevent fresh reissuance unless the issuer retains monotonic durable state over the authorized action, confirmation event, and remaining execution budget. We introduce CapLease, an authorization-consumption layer that follows proposal- and authority-level defenses, binds an authenticated user confirmation to a canonical action, and enforces transactional Issue-Prepare-Commit transitions. Across LLM-agent replanning, retry, delegation, concurrency, confirmation-replay, and crash-recovery scenarios, identifier-local tokens permit fresh semantic reissuance, whereas CapLease and an equally stateful Server Ledger prevent duplicate admission and, with an idempotent sink, duplicate external effects. Our results identify durable authorization state, rather than token representation alone, as the systems requirement for replay-resistant agent execution.

</details>


### [256] [Constructing Executable Analytical Knowledge Representations for Meta-Analysis Synthesis Using an Agentic Harness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01711)
*Lingbo Li,Anuradha Mathrani,Teo Susnjak*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Executable Analytical Knowledge Representation (EAKR) and the MetaSynDec system to turn structured evidence into fully specified, machine-executable meta-analyses, showing higher fidelity and methodological agreement than direct LLM-based generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Meta-analyses need more than structured evidence; they require explicit specification of analytical decisions (e.g., effect-size choice, outcome mapping, admissibility criteria) that are typically implicit, opaque, or buried in code and model outputs. Existing automated or LLM-based methods fail to represent these decisions as independently checkable knowledge, limiting validation, reuse, and trustworthy automation. The authors aim to create a representation and workflow in which all analytical knowledge needed for computation is explicit, machine-actionable, and verifiable.

Method: The authors design Executable Analytical Knowledge Representation (EAKR), a schema for capturing all knowledge required for a meta-analysis (evidence, relations, numerical inputs, constraints, provenance, unresolved issues). They implement this in MetaSynDec, an agentic framework where LLMs propose structured changes and deterministic services perform schema validation, contract checking, and statistical execution. They test MetaSynDec on 58 synthesis units (discrete meta-analytic problems), construct EAKRs for each, and compare the resulting analyses and evidence sets to reference (published) analyses and to analyses produced by direct LLM generation without EAKR.

Result: MetaSynDec successfully constructed EAKRs for all 58 synthesis units, and 57 of these advanced to statistical execution. Among 56 units with enough information to form a reference analysis object, 38 (67.9%) exactly matched the reference objects and 42 (75.0%) had exact agreement on the included evidence sets, with an average Jaccard similarity of 0.909 between evidence sets. Confidence intervals from MetaSynDec and the published meta-analyses overlapped in 54 of 55 units (98.2%). Compared with direct LLM generation, MetaSynDec achieved higher agreement with reference synthesis structures (57/58 vs. 23/58; p<0.001) and, in 23 units where both methods produced analyses, perfect agreement on reference formulations (23/23 vs. 1/23; p<0.001).

Conclusion: Explicit, machine-actionable representations of analytical knowledge—via EAKR and the MetaSynDec framework—make it feasible to automate meta-analyses while preserving formal validation, traceability, and methodological transparency. This structured, contract-based approach yields higher fidelity to reference analyses and more reliable methodological decisions than directly asking LLMs to generate meta-analyses, suggesting a promising path for trustworthy, semi-automated evidence synthesis workflows.

Abstract: Meta-analysis synthesis highlights a fundamental challenge in knowledge-based scientific analysis: structured evidence does not by itself represent the analytical knowledge required for executable computation. Decisions about evidence assignment, analytical contrasts, outcome and time-point alignment, effect-size formulation, and methodological admissibility must be explicit before statistical execution. Existing automated approaches often embed these decisions in model outputs, generated code, or workflow traces rather than representing them as independently verifiable knowledge. We introduce the Executable Analytical Knowledge Representation (EAKR), a machine-actionable representation of the knowledge required to transform structured evidence into executable meta-analysis. An EAKR represents evidence, relations, numerical inputs, constraints, provenance, and unresolved issues. We operationalise EAKR in MetaSynDec, an agentic harness in which large language models propose structured updates and deterministic services govern schema- and contract-based validation and execution. Across 58 synthesis units, MetaSynDec constructed all EAKRs, with 57 proceeding to statistical execution. Of 56 units with sufficient information to define a reference analysis object, 38 (67.9%) achieved complete object fidelity and 42 (75.0%) exact evidence-set agreement, with a mean Jaccard similarity of 0.909. Generated and published confidence intervals overlapped in 54 of 55 units (98.2%). MetaSynDec outperformed direct LLM generation in reference synthesis-structure agreement (57/58 versus 23/58; p<0.001) and among 23 jointly completed units, exact reference-formulation agreement (23/23 versus 1/23; p<0.001). These findings provide feasibility evidence that EAKR supports formal validation, traceability, statistical execution, and improved methodological agreement relative to direct LLM generation.

</details>


### [257] [LaCache: Robust Semantic Caching for LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01718)
*Jiacheng Liang,Yuhui Wang,Tanqiu Jiang,Ting Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces LaCache, a secure and efficient semantic caching scheme for LLMs that mitigates cache-collision attacks by additionally caching and checking the first k decoded tokens of responses, improving both robustness and retrieval quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing semantic caching for LLM serving speeds up inference and reduces cost by reusing responses to semantically similar queries via embeddings, but is vulnerable to cache-collision attacks where adversaries poison the cache with crafted queries that later cause incorrect results for benign users. There is a need for a theoretically grounded, practical design that preserves the benefits of semantic caching while providing formal security guarantees against such poisoning attacks.

Method: The authors redesign semantic caching into LaCache, where a cache entry is indexed not just by the query embedding (as in prior work) but also by the semantics of the initial model output. Specifically, when a new query arrives, LaCache not only checks for embedding-based cache hits on the query but also speculatively decodes the first k tokens of the response and checks for cache hits on those tokens as well. The scheme relies on the fact that an adversary can control the query but not the resulting response tokens, which are constrained by multiple semantic factors. The authors develop a formal model of cache-collision attacks, prove that under this scheme an adversary cannot construct a query that both collides with benign queries and yields malicious responses, and implement LaCache in LLM serving pipelines. They then empirically evaluate performance, security, and relevance across different LLMs and benchmarks.

Result: LaCache achieves provable resistance to cache-collision attacks: the authors show that no adversarial query can be constructed that both triggers a malicious response and collides with benign queries in the cache under their model. Experimentally, LaCache maintains or improves latency and cost benefits of semantic caching while preventing cache pollution attacks. The enriched index that includes the first k decoded tokens also improves the semantic relevance of cache hits in practical workloads, leading to higher-quality reused responses in addition to security gains.

Conclusion: LaCache demonstrates that semantic caching for LLMs can be made robust to cache-collision attacks through a simple but principled modification: augmenting query-based indexing with checks on the initial output tokens. This dual-side semantic matching both thwarts adversarial cache poisoning with formal security guarantees and enhances retrieval quality. The empirical results across models and datasets suggest LaCache is an effective and efficient direction for deploying secure semantic caching in real-world LLM serving systems.

Abstract: Semantic caching, which reuses responses to semantically similar requests via their embeddings, has seen growing adoption in LLM serving, offering faster responses and reduced costs. Yet existing schemes are fundamentally vulnerable to cache-collision attacks, wherein an adversary pollutes the cache by injecting crafted queries, corrupting responses to subsequent legitimate requests. We present LaCache, a novel semantic caching scheme that addresses this vulnerability through a conceptually simple yet principled redesign. The key insight is that while the adversary has full control over the adversarial query, it has far less control over its response, which must simultaneously satisfy multiple semantic constraints. Rather than checking only the cache hit of a query, LaCache additionally checks the cache hit of its first k (speculatively) decoded tokens. This design yields two concrete benefits. First, it provides formally guaranteed resilience against cache-collision attacks: we prove that it is impossible to craft adversarial queries that simultaneously elicit malicious responses and collide with benign queries. Second, the enriched index supplies additional semantic context for cache retrieval, improving response relevance. Empirical evaluation across diverse LLMs and benchmarks validates both LaCache's security guarantees and efficiency gains, pointing to a promising direction for robust semantic caching.

</details>


### [258] [DAPD: Dual-Anchored Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01735)
*Jianyu Wu,Yizhou Wang,Encheng Su,Chen Tang,Shixiang Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies a failure mode of on-policy self-distillation for LLMs, called privilege illusion, caused by information asymmetry between a privileged teacher and a student at inference, and proposes Dual-Anchored Policy Distillation (DAPD) to fix it, improving performance across model scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy self-distillation is widely used to improve language models by having a stronger or privileged teacher guide a student. However, when the teacher has access to privileged information (e.g., extra context, tools, or signals) that the student does not have at inference, the student can learn behaviors that implicitly depend on this unavailable information. This creates a privilege illusion: the student acts as if it still has access to privileged signals, which can hurt real-world performance. The authors aim to understand this failure mode and design a distillation method that avoids transferring privilege-dependent behavior while still gaining the benefits of teacher guidance.

Method: The authors first analyze on-policy self-distillation and identify information asymmetry between the privileged teacher (during training) and the student (during inference) as the core issue. They then propose Dual-Anchored Policy Distillation (DAPD), which has two anchoring mechanisms. Dual-Path Anchoring (DPA) creates a self-conditioned bridge that aligns both the reference-policy behavior and the rollout-policy behavior along information-matched paths, so that what is distilled can be reproduced by the student at inference time. Dual-Source Anchoring (DSA) uses these aligned paths in both directions—reference-to-rollout and rollout-to-reference—to reduce over-reliance on privileged reference guidance while still supervising correctness. Together, these mechanisms form a unified training framework meant to keep the student grounded in its actual inference-time information set.

Result: Through extensive experiments on Qwen3-4B and its scaled variants, DAPD is shown to substantially reduce the privilege illusion problem compared to standard on-policy self-distillation. Quantitatively, DAPD improves average task performance by about +2.00 points over OPSD on Qwen3-4B, with gains that persist and even slightly increase as model size grows: +2.69 at 4B parameters and +2.78 at 32B parameters. These empirical results suggest that DAPD yields more reliable inference-time behavior while preserving or enhancing the benefits of distillation.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that information asymmetry between a privileged teacher and a student is a key failure mode in on-policy self-distillation, leading to privilege illusion where the student depends on information it will not have at inference. By introducing Dual-Anchored Policy Distillation, with Dual-Path and Dual-Source Anchoring, the authors provide a principled way to align training-time and inference-time information. This approach effectively mitigates privilege illusion and consistently outperforms conventional OPSD across tasks and model scales, indicating it is a more robust strategy for post-training language models under privileged-teacher settings.

Abstract: On-policy (self) distillation (OPSD) is increasingly adopted for language-model post-training. It strengthens the teacher with privileged information but can induce a privilege illusion: the student learns privilege-dependent behavior it cannot reproduce from its inference-time context, yet behaves as if the training-time privileged information remained available, ultimately degrading performance. In this paper, we identify information asymmetry between the privileged teacher and the student at inference as the root cause of this failure in OPSD. To resolve this asymmetry, we propose Dual-Anchored Policy Distillation (DAPD), a unified framework with two levels of anchoring. Dual-Path Anchoring (DPA) introduces a self-conditioned bridge and aligns reference and rollout behavior along two matched-information paths, preventing privilege-dependent behavior from being transferred to the inference-time student. Dual-Source Anchoring (DSA) applies these paths in both reference-to-rollout and rollout-to-reference directions, reducing reliance on privileged reference guidance while preserving correctness supervision. Extensive experiments show that DAPD significantly alleviates privilege illusion, outperforming OPSD on Qwen3-4B by +2.00 points on average across tasks. Notably, its gains persist across scales, reaching +2.69 at 4B and +2.78 at 32B.

</details>


### [259] [CoEvo-Mem: Co-Evolving Retrieval Policy and Memory Bank for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01739)
*Bowen Ye,Yongchao Xu,Zhijian Li,Xiang Yin,Junkai Ma,Wenzhao Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CoEvo-Mem is a closed-loop framework where the retrieval policy and memory bank of long-term LLM agents are jointly and alternately optimized, leading to state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-term LLM agents must manage growing memories across tasks and sessions, where performance depends on both accurate retrieval for each query and continual refinement of the memory store. Existing approaches typically focus on either better retrieval (query refinement, adaptive policies) or better memory evolution (structural updates) in isolation. This separation ignores the feedback loop where retrieval determines which memories are used and updated, while memory updates in turn change future retrieval behavior. The paper aims to explicitly model and exploit this co-dependence to improve long-term performance.

Method: The authors propose CoEvo-Mem, a closed-loop framework that co-evolves the retrieval policy and the memory bank. For each query, a frozen LLM produces route-specific query rewrites and a routing prior. A small residual router then adjusts this prior online to decide which memories to retrieve. Retrieved context forms the interface between two learning processes: (1) task outcomes provide credit assignment signals to train the router, and (2) trajectory-conditioned feedback updates memory values and graph relations in the memory bank. To reduce instability from mutual adaptation, the system alternates phases: first updating the router while freezing the memory bank, then updating the memory bank while freezing the retrieval policy.

Result: On seven diverse benchmarks, CoEvo-Mem outperforms prior methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance for long-term LLM agents that rely on external memory. The experiments validate that explicitly co-evolving retrieval and memory yields better results than optimizing either component alone.

Conclusion: Jointly optimizing retrieval policy and memory evolution in a closed-loop manner is crucial for long-term LLM agents. By coupling them via retrieved context and alternating their updates to stabilize learning, CoEvo-Mem effectively exploits the feedback between memory usage and memory refinement, leading to superior performance across varied tasks.

Abstract: As memories accumulate across tasks and sessions, the performance of long-term LLM agents depends jointly on query-specific retrieval and continual memory refinement. However, existing methods typically optimize either memory access, through iterative query refinement or adaptive retrieval policies, or memory evolution such as structural update. This separation overlooks a fundamental feedback loop: retrieval determines which memories receive usage signals, while updated memory bank reshape future retrieval. We propose \textbf{CoEvo-Mem}, a closed-loop framework for co-evolving the retrieval policy and memory bank. For each query, a frozen LLM generates route-specific query rewrites and a routing prior, which a lightweight residual router corrects online. The retrieved context serves as the coupling interface between the two learning processes: task outcomes assign credit to routing decisions, while trajectory-conditioned feedback updates memory values and graph relations. These updates alter how memories are ranked and selected for subsequent queries, thereby closing the feedback loop. To mitigate coupling induced non-stationarity, CoEvo-Mem alternates between updating the router with the memory bank fixed and evolving the memory bank with the retrieval policy fixed. Across seven diverse benchmarks, \textbf{CoEvo-Mem} achieves state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating the importance of retrieval-memory coevolution.

</details>


### [260] [MemSIF: From Structured Interactions to Dual-Track Fact Memory for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01742)
*YuFei Luo,Xiucheng Xu,Zhen Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces MemSIF, a structured memory framework for LLM agents that improves long-term interaction performance by addressing two misalignment issues in existing memory systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-term memory systems for LLM agents struggle in long-horizon interactions due to two key misalignments: (1) Temporal-Structural Misalignment (TSM), where temporal closeness of information does not match topical or event-level relatedness; and (2) Delayed Utility Manifestation (DUM), where information that seems salient when stored does not necessarily turn out to be useful for future queries. These issues reduce retrieval quality and overall agent effectiveness.

Method: The authors propose MemSIF, which consists of two main components. (1) Structured Interaction Memory: This organizes raw interaction logs into Topical Segments that maintain local topical coherence and Event Trajectories that track events across time, ensuring structurally and semantically meaningful groupings beyond simple recency. (2) Dual-Track Fact Memory: This has two coordinated tracks—CoreFact memory, which stores stable, schema-guided facts at write time, and ActiveFact memory, which dynamically forms and updates facts on demand, promoting those supported by multiple historical sources and frequent query use, thus adapting to delayed utility. The system is evaluated on long-context benchmarks with multiple backbone LLMs.

Result: On the LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S benchmarks across five different backbone LLMs, MemSIF achieves the best Total ACC in all experimental settings. It surpasses the strongest baseline methods by 2.29%-8.79% accuracy improvement on LoCoMo and 2.87%-6.15% on LongMemEval-S, demonstrating its effectiveness in long-term interaction tasks.

Conclusion: Combining Structured Interaction Memory with a Dual-Track Fact Memory effectively mitigates Temporal-Structural Misalignment and Delayed Utility Manifestation in long-term memory for LLM agents. This leads to consistently better performance across benchmarks and models, suggesting MemSIF is a robust approach for enhancing long-horizon interaction capabilities in LLM-based agents.

Abstract: Long-term memory is critical for LLM agents operating over long-horizon interactions. However, several persistent limitations of existing memory systems can be traced to two recurring misalignment patterns in long-term interaction settings: Temporal-Structural Misalignment (TSM) and Delayed Utility Manifestation (DUM). TSM arises when temporal proximity does not reliably align with topical or event-level relatedness, whereas DUM arises when write-time salience does not reliably predict future query utility. To mitigate these misalignment patterns, we propose MemSIF (Memory with Structured Interactions and Facts), a structured interaction-to-fact memory framework. Structured Interaction Memory organizes raw interactions into Topical Segments that preserve local topical coherence and Event Trajectories that maintain cross-time event continuity. Dual-Track Fact Memory uses two complementary tracks: CoreFact memory consolidates stable, schema-guided information at write time, whereas ActiveFact memory forms facts on demand and promotes those supported by multiple historical sources and recurring query demand for reuse. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S across five backbone LLMs show that MemSIF achieves the highest Total ACC in all settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by 2.29%-8.79% on LoCoMo and 2.87%-6.15% on LongMemEval-S. These results support the effectiveness of combining Structured Interaction Memory with Dual-Track Fact Memory to mitigate TSM and DUM. Code is available at https://github.com/luoyufeihaha/MemSIF.

</details>


### [261] [RL-Lock: Reinforcement Learning for Generating Interlocking Assemblies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01744)
*Xuyang Ma,Chaewoon Kim,Haonan Zhang,Rulin Chen,Ziqi Wang,Peng Song*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce RL-Lock, a reinforcement-learning-based method to automatically decompose 3D voxel objects into interlocking assemblies, outperforming heuristic approaches especially on difficult cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Interlocking assemblies are valued for structural stability and are widely used, but existing automatic generation methods treat it as a pure search/shape decomposition problem and rely heavily on handcrafted heuristics, which struggle or fail on complex shapes due to the huge combinatorial search space.

Method: Formulate interlocking assembly generation as a sequential decision-making problem where an agent assigns each voxel to a piece step by step. Use a reinforcement learning framework (RL-Lock) that combines structured action chunking to reduce the effective action space with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-guided policy-value learning to explore the large combinatorial space efficiently.

Result: Experiments show that RL-Lock can successfully produce valid interlocking assemblies for a range of 3D voxel models and performs particularly well on challenging instances where heuristic-based methods are too slow or fail to find valid decompositions.

Conclusion: Treating interlocking assembly generation as an RL problem and solving it with RL-Lock, which integrates structured action chunking and MCTS-guided learning, is an effective alternative to heuristic search, enabling robust and efficient generation of complex interlocking decompositions.

Abstract: An interlocking assembly is an assembly in which component parts are connected purely through their geometric arrangement, without relying on external connectors such as glue and nails. Such assemblies have been widely used in a variety of real-world applications due to their structural stability. The problem of generating interlocking assemblies is generally formulated as a shape decomposition problem, where a target 3D object represented as a voxel grid is partitioned into a prescribed number of interlocking pieces. We observe that generating interlocking assemblies is inherently a sequential decision-making problem, where an agent repeatedly decides which piece each voxel should be assigned to. Inspired by the observation, we propose the first reinforcement learning framework RL-Lock for generating interlocking assemblies, without relying on handcrafted search heuristics as existing works did. RL-Lock combines structured action chunking with MCTS-guided policy-value learning to efficiently navigate the large combinatorial search space for interlocking assembly generation. We demonstrate through experiments that RL-Lock allows effective generation of interlocking assemblies, especially for challenging cases in which existing approaches take too long or even fail to find a valid solution.

</details>


### [262] [Deferred Exposure of Future Trajectories for Verifiable Reasoning in Autonomous Driving VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01755)
*Zixuan Huang,Yang Zhou,Kaixuan Wang,Guli Zhang,Hongyan Xie,Yakun Zhu,Hao Geng,Yikun Ban,Deqing Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies a trajectory anchoring bias in current chain-of-thought supervision for driving VLAs and proposes a multiple-choice trajectory selection framework (AD-MCQ) and a training method (DEFT-RLVR) that uses future trajectories only for post-decision verification, leading to more causally faithful reasoning and better autonomous-driving decision quality without harming general visual capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing autonomous driving Vision-Language-Action models use chain-of-thought supervision where teacher models see the ground-truth future trajectory while generating explanations. This setup causes models to explain a known outcome instead of reasoning from visual evidence, introducing trajectory anchoring bias and hallucinations, particularly in causally complex scenes. The authors are motivated to design a supervision and evaluation framework that forces models to make verifiable driving decisions based on scene understanding, not hindsight, and avoids the difficulty of fully open-ended trajectory generation.

Method: 1) They define trajectory anchoring bias and empirically demonstrate it by comparing CoTs and hallucination rates when the teacher has or does not have access to ground-truth future trajectories. 2) They introduce AD-MCQ, a framework that formulates planning as a multiple-choice problem over a set of explicit candidate trajectories, so that the model selects rather than synthesizes trajectories. 3) They propose DEFT-RLVR (Deferred Exposure of Future Trajectories for RLVR), where future trajectories are hidden during decision making and only revealed afterward for verification, converting them from anchors (that bias reasoning) into evaluation targets. 4) They train and evaluate VLA/VLM systems under this new scheme, controlling task difficulty via the design of candidate trajectories.

Result: Empirical studies show that when teacher models see the ground-truth future trajectory during CoT generation, their reasoning becomes less causally grounded and more hallucinatory, especially in challenging causal scenarios. Using AD-MCQ with DEFT-RLVR reduces these issues, improves autonomous driving reasoning performance, and maintains or improves general visual-language capabilities. The multiple-choice formulation also enables controllable difficulty and verifiable evaluation of planning decisions.

Conclusion: Revealing ground-truth future trajectories during CoT supervision introduces a harmful anchoring bias in autonomous driving VLAs. By reframing trajectory planning as a multiple-choice selection problem (AD-MCQ) and deferring exposure to future trajectories until after decisions are made (DEFT-RLVR), models can be trained to reason more causally from scene evidence while retaining strong general visual-language abilities. This framework provides a scalable, controllable basis for future research on verifiable reasoning in autonomous driving.

Abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for autonomous driving (AD) increasingly utilize chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision to enhance the reasoning capabilities of their Vision-Language Model (VLM) components, yet existing annotation pipelines commonly expose the teacher model to the logged ground-truth (GT) future trajectory. We empirically show that this induces trajectory anchoring bias: teacher models rationalize the revealed outcome rather than infer a decision from scene evidence, producing less causally faithful CoTs and substantially more severe hallucinations, especially in causally challenging scenes. Removing the GT trajectory eliminates this shortcut, but open-ended trajectory generation entangles high-level decision-making with precise geometric synthesis and low-level dynamics. To make trajectory-level driving decisions verifiable without requiring open-ended trajectory synthesis, we introduce Autonomous-Driving Multiple-Choice Question (AD-MCQ), which casts planning as selection among explicit trajectory candidates. Taking this a step further, we propose Deferred Exposure of Future Trajectories for RLVR (DEFT-RLVR) to transform future trajectories from pre-decision anchors into post-decision verification targets. Experimental results show that DEFT-RLVR improves AD reasoning while preserving or even enhancing general visual capabilities. With VLM-only inference and controllable difficulty through candidate construction, AD-MCQ provides a flexible, scalable, and extensible foundation for future research on verifiable AD reasoning.

</details>


### [263] [Leveraging AI for fine-grained food safety risk forecasting in sparse data conditions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01767)
*Dongqi Wang,Weiwei Chen,Han Zhou,Weihua Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A Transformer-based model predicts city-level food safety risks by combining over 11 million inspection records with demographic and environmental data, using a three-stage pretraining with Wilson interval-based partial supervision to improve risk forecasting and inspection planning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Food safety oversight is constrained by limited inspection resources and sparse, uneven sampling data across regions. Traditional risk assessment methods struggle to produce accurate, fine-grained forecasts when local sample sizes are small. The paper aims to build a scalable, data-driven framework that can leverage massive historical inspection records and auxiliary indicators to proactively identify high-risk areas and optimize inspection resource allocation.

Method: The authors design a Transformer-based framework that integrates more than 11 million historical food inspection records with demographic, economic, and environmental indicators from a Statistical Yearbook to predict city-level food safety risk scores. They introduce a three-stage pretraining scheme: (1) use Wilson interval estimates to provide partially supervised labels that encode both safety and risk rankings while handling uncertainty due to small samples; (2) apply semi-supervised label refinement to improve label quality when explicit supervision is weak or missing; and (3) fine-tune the model end-to-end for risk prediction. They evaluate performance on 2022 data and run a real-world field experiment with a provincial market regulation authority to compare against manually designed inspection plans.

Result: On 2022 food safety data, the proposed model significantly outperforms baseline methods in predicting city-level food safety risks. In a field deployment with the Zhejiang Provincial Administration for Market Regulation, using the model’s risk scores to guide inspections leads to higher detection rates of food safety problems and a more efficient allocation of limited inspection resources than a manually crafted inspection schedule. Analysis of inspectors’ behavior reveals that they often apply a threshold-based heuristic when acting on risk scores.

Conclusion: The study concludes that combining large-scale public inspection data with Wilson interval-based confidence modeling and Transformer-based deep learning enables earlier and more granular prediction of food safety risks, even in regions with sparse sampling. The framework improves real-world inspection efficiency and detection rates, and its impact could be further enhanced by training regulators or designing decision-support interfaces that align with their threshold-based decision patterns. Overall, the approach supports a shift from reactive to proactive, data-driven food safety regulation, with potential implications for global food supply oversight.

Abstract: Ensuring food safety represents a critical public health challenge, particularly when inspection resources are limited and regional sampling data are sparse. This study proposes a Transformer-based framework capable of forecasting fine-grained, city-level food safety risks by unifying over 11 million inspection records with supplemental demographic, economic, and environmental indicators extracted from the Statistical Yearbook. A three-stage pretraining design leverages partial supervision from the Wilson interval (capturing both safety and risk rankings), together with semi-supervised label refinement, to effectively utilize historical records even when local sample sizes are insufficient. Experimental evaluations on data from 2022 show that the proposed approach outperforms baselines significantly. A subsequent field experiment in collaboration with the Zhejiang Provincial Administration for Market Regulation further demonstrates improved detection rates and more efficient allocation of inspection resources compared to a manually developed plan. Observations of regulatory decision-making reveal a threshold-based heuristic employed by inspectors, hinting that additional training or decision-support interfaces could further enhance the impact of AI-generated risk scores. Overall, these findings underscore that a rigorous integration of large-scale public inspection data, Wilson interval-based confidence modeling, and advanced deep learning can facilitate earlier and more granular identification of food safety threats. By reducing reliance on reactive measures alone, the proposed framework has the potential to advance proactive, data-driven oversight of the global food supply.

</details>


### [264] [FRAMES: Guarded and Dual-Objective Skill Evolution for Agents in Policy-Governed Enterprise Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01772)
*Xuhui Wang,Ruoqi Shu,Chen Dan,Tianhua Xu,Mengxi Luo,Yanming Mai,Bo Wan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces FRAMES, a framework for improving LLM-based enterprise agents under cost, accuracy, and auditability constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise LLM agents must follow strict policies, provide grounded and auditable decisions, and operate cost-efficiently, but improving them is difficult due to sparse feedback, risk of regressions when updating rules, and the need to maintain or reduce inference costs.

Method: FRAMES is a closed-loop system that initializes skills from existing enterprise assets, then iteratively refines them using consensus-based mutation of agent policies, Pareto-based selection balancing accuracy and cost, and mechanisms that guarantee no regression on previously solved cases, while keeping detailed audit trails.

Result: Deployed in an internal production system, FRAMES achieves a superior accuracy-cost trade-off compared to baselines, and these improvements generalize to the public tau-bench benchmark.

Conclusion: FRAMES provides a practical and auditable way to evolve LLM agents for policy-bound workflows, improving accuracy without unacceptable cost increases or regressions, and its effectiveness is demonstrated both in production and on standard benchmarks.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly run policy-bound enterprise workflows such as document auditing, where they must apply rules consistently, ground every value, and stay auditable. Improving these agents is hard: operational feedback is sparse and unlabeled, edits to one rule can regress unrelated cases, and accuracy must improve without inflating inference cost or losing auditability. We present FRAMES, a closed-loop framework that cold-starts deployable skills from existing assets and then evolves them through consensus-based mutation, Pareto selection over accuracy and cost, and an anti-regression guarantee, all while preserving auditability. Deployed on our internal production system, FRAMES attains the best accuracy-cost trade-off among baselines, with the same gains reproduced on tau-bench.

</details>


### [265] [REFLEX: Rethinking MoE Inference as Refinement-Aware Compute Allocation in Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01784)
*Xiang Xia,Cheng Yan,Yiming Zhang,Jiazheng Liu,Hongyu Zhang,Wuyang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces REFLEX, a training-free, refinement-aware expert allocation method for Mixture-of-Experts diffusion language models that cuts expert compute ~15% while maintaining or improving generation quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In diffusion language models, every denoising step processes all tokens equally, even though different tokens are at different refinement stages and thus need different amounts of expert computation. Existing MoE routing in this setting is static and token-position agnostic, leading to a mismatch between where computation is spent and where it is actually needed. The authors want to allocate MoE compute according to each token block's refinement state to improve efficiency without hurting quality.

Method: The authors propose REFLEX, a training-free method that keeps the original MoE router but reorganizes expert computation based on refinement dynamics. They introduce a coarse-to-fine hierarchy to allocate expert budgets at the level of token blocks, aligning compute with block-relative refinement roles, and define a Frontier-Progress Score to rank and prioritize active blocks during the denoising process. This allows the model to flexibly concentrate more experts on parts of the sequence that need more refinement while reducing experts on already-refined regions, all without retraining.

Result: On multiple benchmarks and two MoE-based diffusion language models (LLaDA-MoE and LLaDA2.0-mini), REFLEX reduces the amount of expert computation by about 15% on average. Despite lower compute, it preserves or improves generation quality on most tasks when compared to default, fixed routing, and exhibits a smoother and more predictable trade-off between computation and quality than autoregressive-style variable-expert routing baselines.

Conclusion: Viewing MoE inference in diffusion language models as refinement-aware compute allocation across heterogeneous token states enables more efficient expert use. REFLEX demonstrates that reorganizing expert budgets around the evolving refinement process, without changing the router or retraining, can substantially cut expert compute while maintaining or improving output quality, and yields more consistent quality–compute trade-offs than prior variable-expert routing approaches.

Abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models increase parameter capacity by activating only a small subset of experts for each token. This conditional-computation paradigm has enabled autoregressive language models to scale model capacity without a proportional increase in per-token computation. In diffusion language models (DLMs), however, each denoising forward jointly revisits all token positions despite their sharply different refinement demands, while the default fixed token-choice routing assigns them a uniform expert budget, creating a mismatch between expert computation and refinement demand. We argue that MoE inference in DLMs should therefore be viewed as refinement-aware compute allocation across heterogeneous token refinement states. We propose REFLEX (\textbf{RE}finement-aware \textbf{FLEX}ible expert allocation), a training-free method that keeps the default router unchanged while reorganizing expert computation around the evolving refinement process. Specifically, REFLEX introduces a coarse-to-fine hierarchy for expert-budget allocation that aligns computation with block-relative refinement roles while using the Frontier-Progress Score to resolve active-block priorities. Across multiple widely used benchmarks on two representative MoE-based DLMs, LLaDA-MoE and LLaDA2.0-mini, REFLEX reduces allocated expert computation by 15\% on average while preserving or even improving generation quality on most benchmarks relative to default routing. Compared with autoregressive-style variable-expert routing methods, REFLEX also yields a more consistent quality--computation trade-off, further supporting the importance of allocating expert computation according to the heterogeneous refinement demands exposed within each denoising forward.

</details>


### [266] [Can You Trust the Confidence? ConfBench for Vision-Language Models on Document Extraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01792)
*Priyashree Roy,Sujitha Martin,Mohammad Rostami,Spencer Romo,Renhao Xue,Bob Strahan,Diego A. Socolinsky,Boyi Xie,Md Mofijul Islam*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents ConfBench, a calibration-focused benchmark for confidence estimation in key information extraction from documents, using systematically degraded documents to cover the full accuracy spectrum.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing document AI and IDP benchmarks contain mostly clean, high-quality samples, so models appear accurate and well-calibrated, but there is little data in low-accuracy, difficult conditions where reliable confidence scores matter most for routing tasks between automation and human review.

Method: The authors construct ConfBench by applying 20 controlled degradation pipelines (e.g., noise, blur, artifacts) to a diverse set of source documents, producing 1,346 document variants and over 70K entity-level labels for key information extraction. They evaluate four proprietary and three open-weight vision-language models under different confidence estimation strategies (verbalized confidence vs. log-probabilities), three input modalities (image-only, OCR-only, OCR+image), and multiple log-probability aggregation schemes (first-token, mean-token, margin). They also develop ECARB, an evaluation metric that maps improvements in discriminative confidence quality to expected savings in human review budget.

Result: (i) Using both OCR and image as input leads to more accurate confidence estimates than other modalities; (ii) within a given model family (Claude), better base capability leads to better confidence calibration, but across different model families, larger parameter counts do not reliably predict calibration quality; (iii) models differ sharply in calibration, with some nearly perfectly calibrated and others highly overconfident, but post-hoc calibration can rescale confidences to improve absolute thresholds while preserving ranking-based metrics; and (iv) for log-probability-based confidence, aggregating using the first token gives consistently better calibration than mean-token or margin-based aggregation.

Conclusion: ConfBench enables systematic, calibration-focused evaluation of confidence estimation methods for key information extraction in intelligent document processing, particularly under challenging, degraded conditions. The authors show concrete design choices that improve calibration (OCR+image modality, first-token log-prob aggregation, better base models, post-hoc rescaling) and provide ECARB as a way to connect calibration gains to real-world reductions in human review costs, supporting more trustworthy deployment of IDP systems.

Abstract: Intelligent document processing (IDP) with vision-language models (VLMs) hinges on confidence scores trustworthy enough to route extractions between automation and human review. Existing document benchmarks are dominated by clean, high-quality samples, leaving low accuracy regions too sparse for calibration assessment. We introduce ConfBench, the first calibration-specific benchmark for key information extraction (KIE), built by applying 20 controlled degradation pipelines to a diverse document set, yielding 1,346 variants and 70K+ entity-level evaluations spanning the full accuracy spectrum. We evaluate four proprietary and three open-weight VLMs under verbalized and log-probability confidence estimation methods across three input modalities, and find: (i) OCR+Image modality results in more accurate confidence estimates; (ii) model capability is the dominant factor: within the Claude family confidence quality scales monotonically with capability, while across families parameter count is a poor predictor; (iii) calibration quality varies widely across models, from near-perfect to severely overconfident, and per-model post-hoc correction rescales these absolute confidence values for threshold-based routing without altering ranking-based operational metrics; and (iv) log-probability with first-token aggregation consistently outperforms mean-token and margin aggregations. We also introduce ECARB, a review-budget metric translating discriminative gains into operational savings. We release ConfBench publicly to enable systematic study of confidence estimators and calibration methods for trustworthy IDP application deployment.

</details>


### [267] [CoNav-UAV: Cooperative Dual-Altitude Aerial Navigation via Stackelberg Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01802)
*Junru Song,Wenhao Zhang,Yang Yang,Xuekai Qiu,Feifei Wang,Weien Zhou,Tingsong Jiang,Ying Wen,Yang Li,Wen Yao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes CoNav-UAV, a cooperative two-UAV system for target-oriented vision-and-language navigation, modeled as a Stackelberg game between a high-altitude leader and low-altitude follower, achieving significantly better performance and data efficiency than prior single- or dual-agent baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing UAV vision-and-language navigation methods struggle to jointly handle efficient large-scale exploration and precise collision-free close-range control, often requiring privileged information, external assistance, or independently-trained agents that cannot mutually adapt. There is a need for a fully onboard, cooperative multi-agent framework that can efficiently explore, ground language-described targets, and approach them safely without relying on extra information.

Method: The authors formulate the cooperative navigation problem as a Stackelberg game between a high-altitude leader UAV and a low-altitude follower UAV. They propose Iterative Stackelberg Learning, where the leader performs high-level vision-language reasoning refined via memory-based in-context learning, and the follower performs fine-grained motion control learned via DAgger-style expert distillation. The two agents are alternately updated so that their policies converge toward a Stackelberg equilibrium, using only onboard visual and linguistic inputs.

Result: On the AerialVLN benchmark with three high-fidelity urban scenes, CoNav-UAV outperforms both single-agent and prior dual-agent baselines. It achieves up to a 30.8 percentage point improvement in success rate on the training/learning scene and a 9.0 point improvement in cross-scene transfer, while requiring about three times less adaptation data. Ablation and analysis show that both leader and follower updates contribute complementary performance gains, and that the approach provides robust improvements across different vision-language model backbones, albeit with varying learning dynamics.

Conclusion: Modeling cooperative aerial vision-and-language navigation as a Stackelberg game between a leader and follower UAV and solving it with Iterative Stackelberg Learning yields more effective, data-efficient, and robust target-oriented navigation using only onboard visual and language inputs. The leader-follower decomposition with alternating updates enables mutual adaptation and complementary strengths in global exploration and local control, surpassing existing paradigms and generalizing better across scenes and VLM backbones.

Abstract: Target-oriented vision-and-language navigation (VLN) on aerial platforms is attracting growing attention for missions such as disaster rescue, infrastructure inspection, and security patrol. In this task, an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) needs to locate targets given only a concise description of their appearance and surroundings. This requires global exploration and grounding as well as collision-free close-range approach, two interleaved processes difficult to reconcile within a single agent. Most existing methods transfer the ground VLN paradigm to a low-altitude UAV and compensate for its inefficient exploration with external assistance. A recent attempt deploys two UAVs at complementary altitudes yet still relies on privileged information and trains its two agents independently, precluding any mutual adaptation essential for cooperation. Here we propose CoNav-UAV, which explicitly models the task as a Stackelberg game between a high-altitude leader and a low-altitude follower, with the system operating on onboard visual and linguistic inputs alone. To solve this game, we introduce Iterative Stackelberg Learning. The leader's high-level vision-language reasoning is refined via memory-based in-context learning, while the follower's precise motion control is updated via DAgger-style expert distillation. The alternation drives both agents toward a Stackelberg equilibrium. CoNav-UAV consistently outperforms single- and dual-agent baselines across three high-fidelity urban scenes from the AerialVLN benchmark. Success rate improves by up to 30.8 points on the learning scene, and 9.0 points under cross-scene transfer while using about 3x less adaptation data. Further analyses validate the complementary gains of the leader and follower updates and reveal robust gains yet distinct learning dynamics across VLM backbones.

</details>


### [268] [CockpitHAT: Dependency-Graph-Driven Hierarchical Attribution for Embodied Multi-Agent Cockpits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01805)
*Wei Wang,Shuanghe Liu,Zhu Zhuo,Jiaqi Zhong,Xiaozhao Zhao,Xiaojie Zuo,Jie Su*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes CockpitHAT, a dependency-aware, multi-channel, safety-weighted attribution framework and CockpitBench benchmark to diagnose failures in embodied LLM multi-agent systems, achieving substantially better attribution accuracy than prior text-only methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems in embodied, safety-critical domains (like automotive cockpits) can exhibit Correctness Collapse: overall task success hides serious process-level errors that may still trigger dangerous physical actions. Existing error-attribution methods look only at text logs, ignoring the underlying dependency structure between actions, non-text channels (e.g., environment, memory, vehicle state), and safety severity. This makes it hard to reliably identify which agent decisions actually caused failures and which ones are safety-critical.

Method: The authors introduce CockpitHAT, a hierarchical attribution method that: (1) models interactions as directed acyclic graphs and replaces simple positional windows with dependency-distance thresholds to better capture causal influence; (2) fuses evidence from multiple channels (dialogue, vehicle state, environment, memory) via an embodied adapter; and (3) applies a safety-uplift that upweights high-risk (ISO 26262 ASIL) failures when aggregating attributions via confidence-weighted analyst consensus. They also construct CockpitBench, a dataset of 212 failure traces labeled across channels, each with ASIL severity obtained from three expert annotators.

Result: On the existing Who&When benchmark, CockpitHAT achieves agent-level / step-exact attribution accuracies of 77.9% / 37.8% on a Hand-Crafted split and 86.5% / 46.0% on an Algorithm-Generated split, improving over the prior state-of-the-art, the text-only ECHO method, by up to 17.6 and 16.7 accuracy points respectively. On the newly released CockpitBench benchmark, it reaches 78.3% agent-level and 38.2% step-exact accuracy, demonstrating strong performance in the targeted embodied cockpit setting.

Conclusion: Dependency-aware, multi-channel, and risk-calibrated attribution significantly improves the diagnosis of failures in embodied LLM multi-agent systems. CockpitHAT, together with the CockpitBench benchmark, provides an effective framework and evaluation suite for identifying which agents and steps are responsible for failures, especially in safety-critical contexts like automotive cockpits.

Abstract: LLM multi-agent systems suffer from Correctness Collapse, where high task-level accuracy conceals severe process-level failures. This is especially hazardous in safety-critical embodied settings such as automotive cockpits, where lexically correct utterances may trigger dangerous physical operations. Existing attribution methods rely on text traces alone, missing dependency structure, multi-channel evidence, and safety-aware evaluation. We introduce CockpitHAT, a hierarchical attribution framework that replaces positional windows with dependency-distance thresholds from interaction DAGs, integrates multi-channel evidence via an embodied adapter, and applies a safety-uplift to high-risk failures during confidence-weighted analyst consensus. We further release CockpitBench, a benchmark of 212 annotated failure traces spanning dialogue, vehicle-state, environmental, and memory channels, each labeled with ISO 26262 ASIL severity via three-expert consensus. On the public Who&When benchmark, CockpitHAT achieves agent-level / step-exact accuracies of 77.9% / 37.8% on the Hand-Crafted split and 86.5% / 46.0% on the Algorithm-Generated split, surpassing the text-only SOTA ECHO by up to 17.6 / 16.7 points. On CockpitBench, it attains 78.3% agent-level and 38.2% step-exact accuracy. These results establish dependency-aware, multi-channel, risk-calibrated attribution as an effective paradigm for reliable failure diagnosis in real-world embodied LLM multi-agent systems.

</details>


### [269] [SearchMaster: Grounded and Regulated Self-Play for Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01822)
*Wentao Tan,Qiong Cao,Jiaqi Wang,Nan Duan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SearchMaster is a self-play framework that lets a single LLM generate, solve, and verify its own search tasks to train itself as a search agent, using explicit controls to ensure tasks truly require deep multi-hop retrieval and efficient tool use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training LLM-based search agents usually needs expensive, high-quality supervision such as human-written tasks, expert trajectories, or stronger teacher models. Moreover, naïve self-play can create low-quality data: questions that only appear multi-hop, shallow search trajectories that succeed without real depth, and inefficient tool use that opens many documents without targeted evidence collection. The authors want a way to automatically create challenging, genuinely multi-hop search data and effective search trajectories without human labels or teacher models.

Method: They propose SearchMaster, a self-play framework running in a local search environment where a single LLM generates tasks, solves them with search tools, and verifies outcomes. To counter typical self-play failure modes, they introduce three core mechanisms: (1) Evidence-Chain Generator (ECG), which first constructs explicit cross-document evidence chains and then generates questions grounded in those chains, making tasks truly multi-hop instead of pseudo multi-hop; (2) Search-Depth Reward (SDR), which measures task difficulty based on the depth of search in successful rollouts rather than raw success rate, so only search-intensive tasks are retained; (3) Over-Opening Penalty (OOP), which penalizes trajectories that open too many documents, promoting concise, targeted retrieval instead of shallow browsing. They then jointly optimize the Proposer and Solver agents’ verified trajectories using GRPO (a policy-optimization method).

Result: On six deep-search benchmarks, applying SearchMaster to a Qwen3.5-9B model increases its average accuracy from 38.19% to 51.52%. The framework yields especially large improvements on BrowseComp-Plus, with a 30.1-point accuracy gain. These empirical results indicate that the generated tasks and trajectories are effective training signals for improving search-agent capabilities.

Conclusion: Grounded and regulated self-play, as implemented in SearchMaster, can produce high-quality training data for LLM-based search agents without relying on human-labeled QA pairs or expert demonstrations. Explicit evidence chains, depth-aware difficulty scoring, and penalties for inefficient tool use help ensure that the learned policies perform genuine multi-hop retrieval and targeted document acquisition, substantially boosting performance on deep-search benchmarks.

Abstract: Training LLM-based search agents requires high-quality search data: tasks that demand genuine multi-hop retrieval and trajectories that use search tools effectively. Existing pipelines often depend on human-written tasks, expert demonstrations, or stronger teacher models. We present SearchMaster, a self-play framework that trains a single LLM from search tasks it generates, solves, and verifies in a local search environment. The key challenge is that self-generated tasks and rollouts can yield misleading signals: pseudo multi-hop questions, success-rate difficulty estimates that ignore search depth, and rollouts with excessive opening but little targeted evidence acquisition. SearchMaster addresses these failure modes with three controls. An Evidence-Chain Generator (ECG) grounds task generation in explicit cross-document evidence chains to reduce pseudo multi-hop questions. A Search-Depth Reward (SDR) scores task difficulty by the search depth of successful rollouts rather than success rate alone, keeping retained tasks search-intensive. An Over-Opening Penalty (OOP) regulates tool use by discouraging excessive document opening, avoiding long but shallow browsing. Verified Proposer and Solver rollouts are then jointly optimized with GRPO. Across six deep-search benchmarks, SearchMaster improves a Qwen3.5-9B backbone from 38.19% to 51.52% average accuracy, with a 30.1-point gain on BrowseComp-Plus. These results show that grounded and regulated self-play can provide effective search-agent training data without human-labeled QA pairs or expert demonstrations. The code is available at https://github.com/WentaoTan/SearchMaster.

</details>


### [270] [Rewriting or Reweighting? A Geometric Account in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01835)
*Juntong Wang,Shengkun Yang,Xiyuan Wang,Muhan Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a geometric framework (behavioral manifold analysis) to understand how post-training methods like supervised fine-tuning and reward optimization change specific behaviors (like repetition and sycophancy) in language models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-training clearly changes language model behaviors, but aggregate behavior metrics cannot tell whether these changes come from modifying existing internal mechanisms, creating new ones, or just reusing them differently. The authors want a mechanistic, geometry-based way to track how particular failure modes are represented inside models and how different post-training objectives affect those internal structures.

Method: They identify two distinct failure modes—repetition (a decoding attractor) and sycophancy (a preference/alignment failure)—and introduce behavioral manifold analysis to study them. The method first isolates sparse, behavior-associated coordinates in model representations, then lifts them into low-dimensional local charts (manifolds) that capture the geometry of these behaviors. They construct such charts in two spaces: (1) ACT, based on runtime activation states; and (2) NOC, based on how strongly the model routes functional information flow through the shared behavior-associated subspace (a contribution-space perspective). They then compare these geometric charts across multiple architectures and track how they move or deform under different post-training procedures (supervised fine-tuning vs reward optimization).

Result: For several model families, the behavior-specific manifolds are highly compressed and can be partially aligned across architectures. Charts in contribution space (NOC) reveal a more architecture-invariant shared core of the behavior, while charts in activation space (ACT) retain model-family-specific structure. When post-training is applied, they observe that supervised fine-tuning significantly reshapes the inherited behavioral geometry, whereas reward optimization mainly alters model behavior while leaving the underlying geometric chart largely intact.

Conclusion: Behavioral manifold analysis offers a unified geometric framework for mechanistically analyzing how specific behaviors are represented and transformed by post-training. The key distinction is that supervised fine-tuning tends to rewrite behavioral geometry (changing the internal mechanisms), while reward optimization primarily reweights existing geometry (changing how often or how strongly mechanisms are used without fundamentally altering them).

Abstract: Post-training can substantially alter language-model behavior, yet aggregate behavior rates do not reveal whether training removes an existing mechanism, creates a new one, or changes how an inherited mechanism is used. We study this question through two mechanistically distinct failures, repetition as a decoding-attractor pathology and sycophancy as a preference-related alignment failure. We introduce behavioral manifold analysis, which isolates behavior-specific geometry by selecting sparse behavior-associated coordinates and lifting them into low-dimensional local charts. We construct these charts in two complementary spaces. ACT captures runtime activation states, while NOC quantifies how strongly the model routes functional information flow through the shared behavior-associated subspace. Across multiple model families, the resulting charts are highly compressed and partially alignable across architectures. Contribution-space charts expose a more architecture-robust shared core, whereas activation-space charts retain stronger family-specific structure.
