Tracking these charts through controlled post-training reveals a consistent asymmetry. Supervised fine-tuning substantially alters the inherited behavioral geometry, whereas reward optimization changes behavior while largely preserving the underlying chart. This geometric perspective provides a unified framework for understanding the mechanistic distinction between the two objectives. SFT tends to rewrite behavioral geometry, whereas reward optimization primarily reweights it. Code is available at https://github.com/ronglingze/Manifold-Analysis

</details>


### [271] [Diagnosing Search Behavior and Failure Modes in Long-Horizon Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01913)
*Qi Liu,Jiaxin Mao,Fengbin Zhu,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper analyzes how long-horizon, deep search agents actually use web search over multiple steps, showing that more search does not necessarily mean better answers; instead, answer quality is mainly driven by the quality and recall of retrieved evidence and by how well agents use that evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep search agents can issue many iterative queries to answer complex information-seeking questions, but it is unclear whether increasing search effort—more queries, more pages, more context—actually improves answer quality, and where these agents fail: in finding the right evidence or in using it. The paper aims to open this black box with a detailed, trajectory-level analysis.

Method: The authors collect long search trajectories from various long-horizon search agents and obtain human relevance judgments for documents at each search step. With the retrieval model and evaluation setup held fixed, they analyze, step-by-step, what evidence is retrieved and how it is used to generate answers. They define and quantify retrieval gaps (necessary evidence never retrieved) and utilization gaps (relevant evidence retrieved but misused), and compare six agents on BrowseComp-Plus, validating with an open-web API on BrowseComp. They examine metrics such as cumulative retrieval recall, number of searches, and amount of consumed context, and inspect query reformulations, redundancy, and the timing of useful evidence in trajectories.

Result: They find that search effort (e.g., more queries, longer trajectories, more context) is only weakly correlated with answer quality. Instead, answer accuracy correlates strongly with the quality of retrieved evidence, particularly cumulative retrieval recall. Many trajectories retrieve useful evidence early, but agents continue searching, adding many low-yield steps. Exploratory query reformulations help, but high-performing agents avoid redundant queries and retrieve high-value evidence more efficiently. Both retrieval and utilization gaps are prevalent and distinguish types of failures across agents.

Conclusion: The study concludes that simply scaling search effort is inefficient for deep search agents; what matters is retrieving high-quality, sufficient evidence early and using it effectively. Practical improvements should focus on better query formulation, smarter evidence selection and context management, and principled stopping criteria that detect when enough supporting evidence has been gathered. These directions can reduce unnecessary search, mitigate both retrieval and utilization gaps, and lead to more reliable deep research systems.

Abstract: Deep search agents answer difficult information-seeking questions by iteratively issuing search queries to gather supporting evidence, but it remains unclear whether and how greater search effort leads to better answers. We study these questions through a trajectory-level diagnosis of long-horizon search agents. Using human-annotated document-level relevance judgments, we evaluate the evidence retrieved at each search step and separate two stages of agent behavior: what evidence an agent retrieves and how effectively it uses that evidence. This distinction further allows us to decompose failures into retrieval gaps, where the necessary evidence is never found, and utilization gaps, where relevant evidence is retrieved but not used correctly. With the retrieval model and evaluation harness held fixed, we compare six agents on BrowseComp-Plus and further validate our findings on BrowseComp with an open-web search API. Across settings, we find that search effort and answer quality are only weakly aligned. Answer accuracy is better correlated with the quality of retrieved evidence, especially cumulative retrieval recall, than with the number of searches or the amount of context consumed. Useful evidence often appears early in the trajectory, yet agents tend to continue searching, producing a long tail of low-yield retrieval steps. At the query level, exploratory reformulations remain useful, but the best-performing agents issue far fewer redundant queries. Overall, by systematically characterizing the search behavior and failure modes of long-horizon search agents, this work points to practical directions for building better deep research systems, including stronger query formulation, more effective evidence selection and context management, and stopping criteria based on whether sufficient supporting evidence has been retrieved.

</details>


### [272] [PCSD: Persistent Consistency for Self-Distillation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01837)
*Chunji Lv,Yangguang Wei,Junlin Liu,Yang Gao,Ming Liu,Xinming Wang,Jinyang Wu,Guoren Wang,Changsheng Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces PCSD, a self-distillation method that assigns token-level weights based on persistent teacher-student consistency signals, improving RL fine-tuning of LLM agents under sparse rewards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL training of LLM agents in interactive environments suffers from sparse, trajectory-level rewards. On-policy self-distillation can provide dense token-level guidance from a teacher, but existing approaches either treat token discrepancies independently (noisy and unstable) or apply uniform step-level weights (ignoring positional variation). A more robust way is needed to exploit the teacher’s guidance while being resilient to unreliable positions and noise.

Method: They propose Persistent Consistency Self-Distillation (PCSD), which computes token-level distillation weights according to how persistently the teacher favors certain tokens relative to the student. PCSD uses adaptive temporal windows combined with exponentially decayed aggregation to measure persistent teacher support, incorporates trend-aware modulation to downweight tokens where support is locally declining, and then converts these signals into continuous weights using a sigmoid gating function. This weighted distillation loss is jointly optimized with GRPO-based RL, blending dense teacher supervision with sparse environment rewards.

Result: PCSD is evaluated on LLM agents in ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks. On ALFWorld, across two backbone models, it outperforms pure GRPO by 15.6 and 13.3 Overall points, and a strong self-distillation baseline SDAR by 6.2 and 5.5 points, respectively. It also stays competitive on WebShop and yields a 15.8-point gain over GRPO on an unseen ALFWorld split, all without relying on extra inference-time skills or tools.

Conclusion: Persistently consistent teacher signals can be leveraged to derive reliable token-level distillation weights, yielding better integration of self-distillation with RL. By focusing on local persistence and trend-aware weighting rather than isolated discrepancies or uniform step weights, PCSD provides more stable and informative supervision, significantly improving the performance and generalization of LLM agents in sparse-reward interactive environments.

Abstract: Large language model agents have shown strong potential in complex interactive tasks, yet their reinforcement learning (RL) is often hindered by sparse rewards, as a long multi-turn trajectory may receive only a single outcome-level signal. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) provides dense token-level supervision from a privileged teacher, but the teacher may not be reliable at every position. Existing methods commonly rely on isolated token-level discrepancies, which can be sensitive to noise, or assign a shared step-level weight that may overlook positional variation. We propose Persistent Consistency Self-Distillation (PCSD), which derives token-level distillation weights from the local persistence of teacher-favoring signals. PCSD combines adaptive windows with exponentially decayed aggregation to capture persistent relative teacher support, applies trend-aware modulation to attenuate locally declining support, and produces continuous weights through sigmoid gating. The resulting objective is jointly optimized with GRPO, combining dense teacher guidance with sparse environmental feedback. Without inference-time skills, PCSD achieves the best ALFWorld Overall results among all baselines on both backbones, exceeding GRPO by 15.6 and 13.3 points and SDAR by 6.2 and 5.5 points, while remaining competitive on WebShop and gaining 15.8 points over GRPO on unseen ALFWorld split.

</details>


### [273] [Instruction-Conditioned Exploration with Asymmetric Reinforcement Learning and Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02087)
*Jim Dilkes,Vahid Yazdanpanah,Sebastian Stein*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce a new exploration strategy (ICE) and a combined RL + self-distillation objective (Asymmetric-RL/SD) to better fine-tune LLMs with RL, achieving better math reasoning performance than a strong baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical RL exploration methods don’t directly fit LLMs because their action spaces (tokens, long sequences, rich prior knowledge) differ from typical RL settings. Existing RL post-training methods under-utilize the pre-trained model’s capacity to generate diverse behaviors during training, which can limit learning signal and performance on complex tasks like math reasoning.

Method: 1) Instruction-Conditioned Exploration (ICE): during RL training, every task prompt is augmented with one of several explicit exploration instructions (e.g., "think in multiple ways" / "try unusual approaches"), which encourages the model to generate more varied trajectories.
2) Asymmetric-RL/SD objective: train two policies—an instruction-conditioned exploration policy and a standard unconditioned policy—and use a joint objective that combines standard RL (to learn from rewards) with self-distillation (to transfer the beneficial behaviors discovered under instruction-conditioning back into the base, instruction-free policy used at test time).
3) Evaluate on Qwen3-1.7B for math reasoning at different context lengths (4K, 8K), comparing against DAPO, a strong RL post-training baseline.

Result: On mathematical reasoning benchmarks at 4K response length, applying ICE with the Asymmetric-RL/SD objective improves held-out pass@1 by 5.0% over DAPO, and the gains remain when extending to an 8K context window, showing that the method scales to longer contexts without losing its advantage.

Conclusion: Explicitly conditioning LLMs with exploration-oriented instructions during RL training, and then distilling those behaviors back into the standard deployment-time policy via a combined RL + self-distillation objective, yields more effective exploration and better downstream performance than prior RL post-training methods, at least on mathematical reasoning tasks for Qwen3-1.7B and up to 8K context length.

Abstract: Post-training Large Language Models (LLMs) with Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become an important tool for improving model capabilities, but the LLM action-space structure introduces challenges distinct from classical RL, with implications for inducing exploration. New methods are required that leverage the broad knowledge and flexibility of pre-trained LLMs to deliberately generate diverse experience at training time. We propose Instruction-Conditioned Exploration (ICE), which supplements task prompts during training with one of several distinct instructions, increasing the coverage of behaviours attempted. To facilitate ICE, we propose Asymmetric-RL/SD, a combined Reinforcement Learning and Self-Distillation training objective, to transfer explored behaviours to the unconditioned test-time policy. ICE with the Asymmetric-RL/SD objective improves Qwen3-1.7B held-out pass@1 performance at $4$K response length on mathematical reasoning tasks by $5.0\%$ relative to training with DAPO, with improvement persisting at a longer 8K context.

</details>


### [274] [FOCUS: FP4 Optimization via Coupled-Relaxation and Dual-Granularity Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01847)
*Xianglong Yan,Hong Liu,Chengzhu Bao,Tianao Zhang,Guanghua Yu,Jianchen Zhu,Yulun Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FOCUS is a post-training FP4 quantization framework for LLMs that learns quantization/dequantization scales end-to-end to preserve accuracy while staying hardware-compliant and adding no inference overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are large and expensive to deploy; FP4 formats like MXFP4 and NVFP4 are hardware-efficient but severely hurt accuracy, mainly because current methods force both quantization and dequantization scales to follow the same low-precision hardware format even though the quantization scale is never stored, wasting optimization potential.

Method: Introduce FOCUS, which performs post-training quantization with two key techniques: (1) Coupled-Relaxation Scaling (CRS), which decouples quantization and dequantization scales via a learnable full-precision coefficient so quantization scales can be optimized in full precision while dequantization scales remain hardware-compliant; (2) Dual-Granularity Scaling (DGS), which assigns scales at both block and finer sub-block levels to adapt more precisely to local weight distributions, all trained end-to-end on calibration data.

Result: On multiple LLM families and benchmarks, FOCUS achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among FP4 quantization methods under both MXFP4 and NVFP4 formats, matching or closely approaching higher-precision baselines without adding inference-time computational or memory overhead.

Conclusion: By relaxing unnecessary constraints on quantization scales and using finer-grained scaling, FOCUS significantly improves FP4 post-training quantization for LLMs, delivering better accuracy at the same hardware cost and demonstrating that careful scale design unlocks much of FP4’s potential for efficient LLM deployment.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve remarkable performance but are expensive to deploy due to their enormous size. FP4 quantization, with formats such as MXFP4 and NVFP4, offers an appealing solution with native hardware support on modern accelerators. However, maintaining accuracy under FP4 precision remains difficult. A key bottleneck lies in scale optimization: existing methods tightly couple the quantization and dequantization scales, forcing both to conform to the discrete low-precision format required by hardware, such as E8M0 in MXFP4. Yet the quantization scale is never stored and need not obey this constraint, suggesting a significant untapped optimization space. In this work, we propose FOCUS, a post-training quantization framework with end-to-end scale learning for FP4 Optimization via Coupled-Relaxation and Dual-Granularity Scaling. Coupled-Relaxation Scaling (CRS) relaxes the tight coupling between quantization and dequantization scales with a learnable full-precision coefficient, enabling more effective optimization without breaking hardware compliance. Dual-Granularity Scaling (DGS) further refines the quantization scale at a finer sub-block granularity, allowing more precise adaptation to local weight distributions. Experiments across multiple LLM families and benchmarks show that FOCUS achieves state-of-the-art FP4 accuracy under both MXFP4 and NVFP4 formats, while introducing no additional inference overhead. Code and quantized models will be released at https://github.com/tencent/AngelSlim.

</details>


### [275] [Right Answer, Wrong Method: Shortcut Hacking Misleads the Evaluation of LLM Reasoning on Frontier Science Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02442)
*Xuan Ren,Weiqi Zhai,Tianle Pu,Yihua Zhu,Yihua Zhu,Hu Wei,Bing Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper shows that current scientific reasoning benchmarks overestimate large language models’ reasoning abilities because models often “solution hack” – reaching correct answers via invalid shortcuts rather than genuine reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Benchmarks for scientific reasoning usually score models only by whether the final answer is correct. This ignores how the answer was obtained. As LLMs get stronger, they may exploit shortcuts like guessing or brute-force search to get right answers without performing the intended reasoning, leading to a misleading picture of their true scientific reasoning capabilities.

Method: The authors define and characterize “Solution Hacking,” where an LLM produces the right answer using shortcuts such as numerical search, enumeration, guessing, or answer-first verification instead of a valid, task-targeted derivation. They then systematically measure how often this occurs across different difficulty levels, domains, and across multiple frontier LLMs. They also design expert-inspired anti-hacking strategies: (1) an automatic judge that detects hacked solutions and (2) a test-time instruction intended to suppress shortcut behavior, and they evaluate how these affect reported accuracies.

Result: They find that solution hacking is rare on easy problems (2.2% on common problems) but rises sharply with difficulty (28.3% on Olympiad-level problems and 37.4% on HLE). Across frontier models, between 8.2% and 44.1% of answers that would normally be marked as correct are actually hacked solutions. When they apply anti-hacking strategies, overall reported accuracy drops substantially, while the subset of correct, non-hacked answers is much less affected.

Conclusion: Answer-only evaluation significantly overestimates the scientific reasoning capabilities of frontier LLMs because many “correct” answers are obtained via solution hacking rather than genuine reasoning. Incorporating process-aware evaluation and anti-hacking strategies is necessary to more accurately assess and foster true scientific reasoning in large language models.

Abstract: Scientific reasoning benchmarks typically evaluate large language models (LLMs) using final-answer accuracy. However, a correct answer does not necessarily demonstrate the reasoning capability targeted by the problem. We identify Solution Hacking, a failure mode in which an LLM reaches the correct answer through invalid shortcuts, such as numerical search, enumeration, guessing, or answer-first verification, without providing a valid task-targeted derivation. We systematically analyze this phenomenon across difficulty levels, scientific domains, and frontier models. Solution hacking increases sharply with benchmark difficulty, from 2.2\% on common problems to 28.3\% on Olympiad-level problems and 37.4\% on HLE. Moreover, 8.2\%-44.1\% of answers credited as correct across frontier models are identified as hacked solutions. We further develop expert-inspired anti-hacking strategies, including an automatic judge and a test-time instruction. The results show that suppressing shortcut behavior substantially reduces reported accuracy while having a smaller effect on correct and non-hacked accuracy. These findings reveal that answer-only evaluation can overestimate the scientific reasoning capabilities of frontier LLMs.

</details>


### [276] [Exploring and Bridging Knowledge Holes in Unlearned Multimodal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01849)
*Junxiang You,Junkai Chen,Yuhao He,Ruiqi Liu,Zhetao Guo,Shu Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies and addresses a key weakness in current machine unlearning for multimodal LLMs: unintentional degradation (knowledge holes) on benign, pattern-related inputs. It introduces a new benchmark to measure these effects and a method, SPAR, that preserves useful generic patterns while still reliably forgetting unsafe content.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing unlearning methods for multimodal LLMs focus on removing unsafe content but overlook nearby benign knowledge that shares similar patterns with the forget set. Current evaluations mostly test on unrelated utility benchmarks, thereby missing serious performance drops on benign, adjacent inputs (knowledge holes). This paper is motivated by the need to systematically detect and mitigate these unintended harms, so that unlearning is both safe and precise.

Method: (1) Construct a benchmark that contains benign inputs which share generic patterns (e.g., structures, entities abstracted away) with unsafe data in the forget set, allowing direct probing of "knowledge holes". (2) Empirically show that standard unlearning methods systematically cause large performance degradation on this benchmark while seemingly maintaining performance on distant benchmarks. (3) Propose SPAR (Selective Protection with Anchored Regularization), which (a) uses anchored activation filtering to protect generic patterns from being erased during unlearning, and (b) reinforces these patterns with entity-abstracted enhancement so that only specific unsafe instances are forgotten, not the underlying benign capabilities.

Result: On the SafeEraser benchmark, SPAR recovers over 98% of the original (vanilla) model’s response quality on benign data, whereas standard unlearning baselines recover less than 50%. At the same time, SPAR achieves a 0.00% attack success rate on the unsafe content it is supposed to forget and maintains competitive overall model utility on standard benchmarks.

Conclusion: Conventional evaluation of machine unlearning for MLLMs is too coarse and misses critical "knowledge holes" around the forget set. By introducing a dedicated benchmark and the SPAR method, the paper shows that it is possible to achieve both strong forgetting guarantees and high-fidelity retention of benign, pattern-related knowledge. This highlights the importance of fine-grained, pattern-aware evaluation and design of unlearning methods for trustworthy deployment of MLLMs.

Abstract: Machine unlearning offers a promising approach to remove unsafe content from Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), yet ensuring the precision of unlearning remains a persistent challenge. One reason is that current MLLM unlearning evaluation paradigms suffer from a critical blind spot: they assess model utility through benchmarks whose representations are distant from the forget set, failing to capture knowledge holes---severe degradation on benign adjacent inputs. To probe knowledge holes in unlearned MLLMs, we construct a benchmark that captures unintended degradation on benign inputs sharing generic patterns with the forget set, and confirm through controlled experiments that they are a systematic consequence of commonly used approaches. Furthermore, to bridge this gap, we propose Selective Protection with Anchored Regularization, which protects generic patterns via anchored activation filtering while reinforcing them through entity-abstracted enhancement. Our experiments on SafeEraser demonstrate that SPAR recovers over 98% of vanilla response quality compared to below 50% for standard baselines---while achieving 0.00% attack success rate and competitive model utility. These results underscore the necessity of more fine-grained evaluation for trustworthy MLLM unlearning.

</details>


### [277] [Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Complex Eigenfrequency Identification and Mode Structure Reconstruction of the Ground-State ITG Branch](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01850)
*Dengdi Sun,Bingbing Zhang,Xiao Wang,Zikang Yan,Yuqiang Tao,Qingquan Yang,Guosheng Xu,Jin Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper develops a specialized physics-informed neural network framework to recover complex eigenfrequencies and 2D complex mode structures of ion-temperature-gradient drift waves in the tokamak pedestal from sparse data and physical constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding and modeling ion-temperature-gradient (ITG) drift waves in the steep-gradient pedestal of H-mode tokamaks is crucial because these modes are tightly connected to plasma confinement and edge transport. However, analyzing these modes requires simultaneously identifying complex eigenfrequencies and reconstructing two-dimensional complex-valued mode fields, which is difficult with standard PINNs due to localized high-frequency oscillations, strong coupling between real and imaginary parts, and nonlinear coupling between the eigenfrequency and the mode field. There is thus a need for a more expressive and stable PINN framework capable of representing and jointly optimizing these coupled complex quantities from sparse observations.

Method: The authors propose a physics-informed neural framework that integrates three key components: (1) Fourier feature encoding to better represent localized high-frequency structures; (2) complex-valued feature propagation to naturally handle complex-valued mode fields and their real–imaginary coupling; and (3) a three-stage training strategy designed to stabilize and improve the joint optimization of the complex eigenfrequency and the mode field under sparse data and governing physical equations. The framework is applied to a representative ground-state ITG branch in the pedestal region, where the governing physics is embedded as constraints in the loss function while the network learns both the eigenfrequency and the spatial mode structure.

Result: In numerical experiments on a representative pedestal ITG problem, the proposed framework successfully and accurately recovers the target complex eigenfrequency and the two-dimensional complex-valued mode field. Quantitative comparisons show that it outperforms baseline physics-informed neural network approaches in both eigenfrequency identification and mode reconstruction quality, particularly in capturing localized high-frequency oscillations and the coupled real–imaginary structures.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that the proposed physics-informed neural framework is effective for jointly inferring complex eigenfrequencies and 2D complex mode fields of ITG drift waves in tokamak pedestals from sparse observations and physical laws. Its improved representation of high-frequency, complex-valued structures and stabilized training make it superior to standard PINNs, and it establishes a foundation for future extensions to higher-order and multi-branch drift-wave modes in more realistic plasma scenarios.

Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) combine sparse observations with physical equations, providing an important approach for modeling complex plasma processes and inferring unknown physical quantities. The steep-gradient pedestal of high-confinement-mode tokamaks is closely linked to plasma confinement and edge transport. Analyzing ion-temperature-gradient (ITG) drift waves in this region requires jointly identifying complex eigenfrequencies and reconstructing two-dimensional complex-valued mode fields. Localized high-frequency oscillations, strong real-imaginary coupling, and nonlinear coupling between the mode field and eigenfrequency challenge PINN representation and joint optimization. To address these challenges, we propose a physics-informed neural framework combining Fourier feature encoding, complex-valued feature propagation, and three-stage training. Under sparse observations and physical constraints, it jointly solves for the complex eigenfrequency and mode field of a representative ground-state ITG branch. Experiments show that the framework accurately recovers the target complex eigenfrequency and two-dimensional complex-valued mode field and outperforms representative PINN baselines. It also provides a basis for analyzing higher-order and multiple-branch drift-wave modes.

</details>


### [278] [EchoChange: A Diffusion Language Model with Dual Pass Remasking for Factual Remote Sensing Disaster Change Captioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01856)
*Dongwei Sun,Bowen Yao,Yujie Zhang,Pei Liu,Jing Yao,Xiangyong Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EchoChange is a multimodal discrete diffusion language model that improves bi-temporal remote-sensing disaster change captioning by iteratively refining whole captions instead of generating them left-to-right.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing remote-sensing change captioning models use autoregressive decoding, so an early misinterpretation of objects, events, or spatial relations becomes an irreversible premise that propagates and amplifies errors throughout the generated description. There is a need for a captioning framework that can revise earlier decisions in light of global context to reduce cascading factual errors, especially for sparse, localized changes in large-scale disaster imagery.

Method: The paper proposes EchoChange, which treats change captioning as an iterative masked-token denoising process using a multimodal discrete diffusion language model. Instead of left-to-right generation, it repeatedly revises the entire caption conditioned on the pre- and post-event image pair. The authors design three key training strategies to better match inference: (1) draft-aware dual-pass training to explicitly model revision from an initial draft to a refined caption, (2) a progressive masking curriculum that gradually increases the difficulty of denoising, and (3) confidence-guided remasking that focuses refinement on low-confidence tokens during iterative inference.

Result: On the RSCC benchmark, EchoChange significantly outperforms both general-purpose vision–language models and specialized remote-sensing change captioning baselines, achieving gains across both lexical metrics (e.g., BLEU, CIDEr) and semantic metrics that better capture factual correctness of change descriptions.

Conclusion: Formulating change captioning as iterative masked-token denoising via a multimodal discrete diffusion language model allows the system to reconsider and correct earlier caption tokens, reducing cascaded factual errors inherent to autoregressive decoding. EchoChange, enhanced with draft-aware dual-pass training, progressive masking, and confidence-guided remasking, delivers more accurate and semantically faithful disaster change descriptions from bi-temporal remote-sensing imagery, establishing a new state of the art on the RSCC benchmark.

Abstract: Bi-temporal remote-sensing disaster change captioning often needs to identify sparse and spatially localized changes across large pre- and post-event scenes and then translate them into coherent, factual descriptions. However, existing change captioning methods always follow an autoregressive decoding paradigm to generate the change description and thus an early misinterpretation of the changed object, event, or spatial relation becomes an irreversible premise for subsequent text, amplifying visual ambiguity into cascading factual errors. To address this limitation, we propose EchoChange, a multimodal discrete diffusion language model that formulates change captioning as iterative masked-token denoising rather than left-to-right generation. By repeatedly revising the entire caption while conditioning on the image pair, EchoChange can reconsider uncertain content and correct imperfect intermediate predictions. We further introduce draft-aware dual-pass training, a progressive masking curriculum, and confidence-guided remasking to align training with iterative inference. Extensive experiments on the RSCC benchmark show that EchoChange substantially outperforms both general-purpose and remote-sensing-specific baselines across lexical and semantic metrics. The EchoChange Project is at https://github.com/sundongwei/EchoChange_Project

</details>


### [279] [Wnuan: Staged Post-Training for Question Answering over Proprietary Enterprise Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01862)
*Xiaofeng Shi,Xiaosong Qiu,Wenxin Ma,Qian Kou,Yiming Pan,Longbin Yu,Ying Liu,Haiping Wang,Hua Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Wnuan, a three-stage pipeline to adapt large language models for enterprise question answering while measuring the trade-off with general capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise QA systems must incorporate proprietary, domain-specific knowledge without severely degrading their general abilities. Existing adaptation methods often either underfit to enterprise data or overfit, harming general performance. The paper aims to design and quantify a principled adaptation process that efficiently leverages limited labeled QA data from documents and characterizes the resulting trade-offs.

Method: The authors propose Wnuan, a three-stage adaptation pipeline for a 32B-parameter model: (1) constructing task-oriented supervision from enterprise documents to create a domain QA benchmark (WnuanBench with 707 questions), (2) performing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on this supervision while replaying general data to preserve broad capabilities, and (3) applying reinforcement learning (RL) targeted at residual errors—examples the model still gets wrong after SFT. They compare residual-error-based sampling against full-pool and size-matched random sampling under a fixed 100-update budget. They also develop an automatic evaluation ensemble and validate it against a domain expert on a stratified response sample. General capabilities are monitored using an aggregate of standard benchmarks, with attention to specific skill areas such as instruction following.

Result: On WnuanBench, the base 32B model’s acceptable-answer rate (AAR) improves from 52.76% pre-adaptation to 80.06% after SFT and 91.51% after RL, showing substantial gains from each stage. Under a matched 100-update RL protocol, residual-error sampling outperforms full-pool sampling by 3.11 AAR points and size-matched random sampling by 2.97 points; bootstrap confidence intervals based on source clusters remain above zero, and a same-domain validation set confirms the superiority of residual-error sampling. However, general benchmark performance drops by an average of 5.17 points along the adaptation route, with most of the degradation in instruction-following tasks. The automatic evaluation ensemble aligns with judgments from an authoritative domain expert on 90.5% of a stratified sample from Wnuan-Inst, supporting its reliability for large-scale evaluation.

Conclusion: A staged enterprise adaptation pipeline combining SFT with general-data replay and RL focused on residual errors can markedly improve domain-specific QA performance (AAR 52.76%→91.51%) on proprietary-document questions. Targeting residual errors yields more efficient RL improvements than random or full-pool sampling under equal update budgets. Nonetheless, the approach incurs a measurable cost to general capabilities, especially in instruction following, quantifying a trade-off practitioners must consider. The validated automatic evaluation ensemble enables scalable measurement of both enterprise-task gains and general-performance degradation, offering a practical framework to tune and monitor enterprise QA adaptation strategies.

Abstract: Enterprise question answering requires models to acquire proprietary knowledge without discarding general capabilities. We present Wnuan, a three-stage pipeline that constructs task-oriented supervision from documents, performs supervised fine-tuning with general-data replay, and applies reinforcement learning to residual errors. On the 707-question WnuanBench, the primary 32B route raises acceptable-answer rate (AAR) from 52.76% before adaptation to 80.06% after SFT and 91.51% after RL. Under a matched 100-update protocol, residual-error sampling outperforms full-pool and size-matched random sampling by 3.11 and 2.97 points, respectively. Source-cluster bootstrap intervals remain above zero for both contrasts, and a same-domain validation set preserves the ordering. The general-benchmark average decreases by 5.17 points across the route, concentrated in instruction following. The automatic evaluation ensemble agrees with an authoritative domain expert on 90.5% of a stratified Wnuan-Inst response sample. These results characterize both the gains and the general-capability cost of staged enterprise adaptation.

</details>


### [280] [ReasonCast: Towards Explainable Time Series Forecasting with Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01875)
*Seunghan Lee,Jun Seo,Jaehoon Lee,Junhyeok Kang,Sangjun Han,Sungdong Yoo,Minjae Kim,Tae Yoon Lim,Dongwan Kang,Hwanil Choi,Soonyoung Lee,Wonbin Ahn*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a task-fused approach for time series that jointly performs forecasting and natural-language reasoning about the forecast in a single response, along with a benchmark (ReasonTS-Bench) and a fine-tuning recipe (ReasonCast) that improves both accuracy and interpretability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing time series models typically specialize in either numerical forecasting or textual understanding/explanation, and even recent unified models still treat these as separate output paths. This separation prevents models from simultaneously generating predictions and coherent explanations that are causally linked to those predictions. The authors want a single model that can both forecast a time series and explain the reasons for its forecast in one integrated process, allowing systematic study and evaluation of this joint capability.

Method: The authors propose a task-fused framework and provide two main components: (1) ReasonTS-Bench, a benchmark designed around five fundamental time-series patterns to jointly evaluate forecasting performance and reasoning quality; and (2) ReasonCast, a fine-tuning recipe that can be applied to any large language model so it can generate a chain-of-thought explanation and a numerical forecast together in a single autoregressive pass. They train and evaluate ReasonCast on time series data annotated with both target forecasts and explanatory reasoning, and compare it against both traditional TS models and LLM-based approaches.

Result: Models trained with the ReasonCast recipe outperform both standard time series forecasting models and large language models on prediction accuracy across the benchmark tasks. In addition, the generated explanations are verifiable and exhibit causal reasoning that is aligned with the underlying time series patterns defined in ReasonTS-Bench.

Conclusion: Jointly modeling time series forecasting and natural-language reasoning in a task-fused architecture is both feasible and beneficial. The proposed ReasonTS-Bench enables rigorous assessment of this capability, and the ReasonCast fine-tuning recipe produces models that not only achieve superior forecasting accuracy but also provide interpretable, causally grounded explanations in a single coherent response.

Abstract: Most time series (TS) models are specialized for a single task, either understanding (i.e., returning text answers about a TS) or generation (i.e., returning a numeric forecast). Only recently have unified models begun to handle the two within a single architecture. Even these models, however, produce the two outputs as task-separated paths and cannot predict a series and explain why that prediction arises within a single coherent response. In this paper, we argue for a task-fused model that jointly produces 1) prediction (generation) and 2) selfexplanation (understanding), thereby integrating 1) numerical TS forecasting and 2) interpretable text reasoning within a single response. To enable the systematic study of this capability, we present both a benchmark and a recipe that jointly address the two tasks. The benchmark, ReasonTS-Bench, identifies five fundamental patterns underlying TS and enables the joint evaluation of both tasks. ReasonCast, our recipe for finetuning any LLM to perform both tasks jointly, yields a model that generates a reasoning chain and a forecast together in a single autoregressive pass. Extensive experiments show that ReasonCast outperforms both LLMs and TS models on prediction accuracy while producing verifiable, causal reasoning. Code is available at: https://github.com/seunghan96/reasoncast.

</details>


### [281] [CoEvoKG: Co-Evolving Knowledge Graphs with Self-Evolving Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01904)
*Zhaoyang Li,Zenghuang Fu,Qiuyuan Ai,Ping Jiang,Haoyu Wu,Minghui Wu,Chenxu Zhao,Jie Song,Guannan He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CoEvoKG is a co-evolution framework that uses a knowledge graph both to generate verifiable multi-hop QA tasks and to store verified evidence, enabling reinforcement learning-based search agents to improve over time while accumulating structured knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing self-play reinforcement learning frameworks for search agents repeatedly generate tasks but discard the evidence and knowledge from successful searches, missing a chance to build a persistent, verifiable memory that can in turn improve future training and task quality.

Method: CoEvoKG converts a knowledge graph into two coupled components: (1) a task generator that samples entity chains from the KG to form multi-hop questions, and (2) a search agent trained with reinforcement learning using rewards for correct answers and for trajectories whose entity paths align with KG evidence. When the agent successfully answers a question, the framework verifies, deduplicates, and writes the retrieved evidence back into the KG nodes and edges, enriching the graph. Subsequent training rounds reuse this enriched KG for both generating harder or more diverse tasks and computing more accurate rewards, creating a closed-loop co-evolution of agent and knowledge graph.

Result: On six QA benchmarks (NQ, TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, Bamboogle) and three backbone LLMs (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), CoEvoKG yields substantial macro-average accuracy gains of +11.2, +10.1, and +11.6 points over the corresponding base models. When compared under matched training budgets to strong self-play and RL baselines for search agents, CoEvoKG further improves performance by +2.6 to +3.7 macro-average points across all three backbones.

Conclusion: Using a knowledge graph as both a generator of verifiable multi-hop QA tasks and a persistent evidence memory enables a co-evolution process between the search agent and the KG, leading to more sample-efficient training and better QA performance than existing self-play and RL baselines. CoEvoKG demonstrates that closing the loop between model learning and structured knowledge accumulation can significantly boost the capabilities of LLM-based search agents.

Abstract: Large language models can improve with reinforcement learning for search agents, yet existing self play agents repeatedly generate tasks while discarding the knowledge gained during successful searches. We introduce CoEvoKG, a framework that turns a
  knowledge graph into both a source of verifiable training tasks and a persistent evidence memory for agent evolution. CoEvoKG jointly trains a task generator and a search agent: the generator creates multihop questions from entity chains sampled
  from the knowledge graph, while the agent learns from rewards for answer correctness and search trajectories whose entity paths are supported by graph evidence. When a search succeeds, CoEvoKG verifies and deduplicates the retrieved evidence, then
  writes it back to the corresponding graph nodes and edges. Future rounds reuse this enriched graph for task generation and reward computation, closing the loop between model self evolution and knowledge accumulation. Experiments on six QA benchmarks
  (NQ, TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and Bamboogle) with three backbone models show that CoEvoKG improves macro average accuracy over the corresponding base models by +11.2, +10.1, and +11.6 points on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct,
  Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, respectively. Under matched training budgets, CoEvoKG further improves over competitive self play baselines and RL baselines for search agents by +2.6 to +3.7 macro average points across the three
  backbones. Code is available at https://github.com/lazzy1225/CoEvoKG.

</details>


### [282] [ProWorld: Progress-Aware Hyperbolic World Models for Long-Horizon Visual Goal Reaching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01926)
*Zihan Liu,Yuzhe Zhuang,Yuanzu Li,Wanshuang Gou,Jiahong Liu,Min Zhou,Menglin Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes ProWorld, a progress-aware hyperbolic visual world model for long-horizon visual goal planning, improving success rates over prior JEPA-style models by modeling goal-conditioned progress order in latent space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing JEPA-style visual world models focus on accurate next-step latent prediction, which does not guarantee sustained progress toward a goal in long-horizon tasks. Multi-step rollouts can stay locally plausible yet drift from goal-relevant trajectories, and locally similar future states may represent very different long-term progress, which current locally consistent latent spaces cannot distinguish well. The authors aim to build a world model that explicitly encodes directional, goal-oriented progress for better planning.

Method: The authors introduce the concept of goal-conditioned progress order, a relative ordering of states by how much they advance toward a given goal, which has an asymmetric coarse-to-fine structure. They argue this structure fits hyperbolic geometry and design ProWorld, a hyperbolic visual world model that: (1) embeds visual latent dynamics in a hyperbolic space aligned with progress order; (2) enforces directional progress along trajectories via hyperbolic entailment learning; (3) reduces ambiguity among locally similar but progress-wise different future states using hyperbolic future discrimination; and (4) uses a progress-aware planning objective that evaluates candidate rollouts jointly by their distance to the goal and their sustained progress across intermediate states.

Result: On four visual goal-reaching benchmarks, ProWorld outperforms the LeWM baseline, achieving an average absolute success-rate improvement of 9.67 points, indicating better long-horizon planning and goal-reaching performance. Specific experimental details are not in the abstract but imply consistent gains across tasks.

Conclusion: Encoding goal-conditioned progress order in a hyperbolic latent space allows visual world models to better capture directional progress in long-horizon tasks, overcoming limitations of purely local next-step prediction. ProWorld’s progress-aware representation learning and planning objective yield substantially improved visual goal-reaching performance, suggesting hyperbolic, progress-structured world models are a promising direction for long-horizon planning.

Abstract: JEPA-style visual world models offer an effective paradigm for visual goal planning by predicting future latent representations. Existing methods typically learn local transition consistency through next-step representation prediction. However, in long-horizon tasks, accurate local prediction alone need not ensure sustained progress toward the goal. First, multi-step rollouts can remain locally plausible while drifting away from goal-relevant trajectories. Second, locally similar future states can correspond to substantially different long-term progress, making them difficult to distinguish in a latent space optimized mainly for local consistency. To address these challenges, we introduce goal-conditioned progress order, a relative ordering of states according to how they advance toward a given goal. This order exhibits an asymmetric, coarse-to-fine structure: early states retain broader future possibilities, while later states concentrate on more specific goal-relevant regions. Such a structure is well suited to hyperbolic geometry. Motivated by this observation, we propose ProWorld, a progress-aware hyperbolic visual world model. ProWorld leverages goal-conditioned progress order to organize visual latent-space dynamics, maintains directional progress within trajectories via hyperbolic entailment learning, and mitigates progress ambiguity among locally similar future states via hyperbolic future discrimination. Furthermore, we design a progress-aware planning objective that scores candidate rollouts by jointly considering proximity to the goal and sustained progress across intermediate states. Experiments on four visual goal-reaching tasks demonstrate that ProWorld achieves an average absolute success-rate gain of 9.67 over LeWM. The code will be released after the paper is accepted.

</details>


### [283] [A Contractualist Argumentation Framework for Moral Decision-Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01937)
*Luis Marcos-Vidal,Giulio Antonio Abbo,Tony Belpaeme*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a formal, argumentation-based framework to model moral decision-making for autonomous agents using Scanlon’s contractualism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous agents in shared environments must make decisions that affect multiple individuals with conflicting interests, and existing decision frameworks often lack an explicit, principled account of moral permissibility grounded in moral philosophy. The authors want a way to formalize and automate moral reasoning that is sensitive to individuals’ reasons and values, and that aligns with a well-established ethical theory.

Method: The authors ground their approach in Scanlon’s contractualism, which judges actions by whether they conform to principles that no one could reasonably reject. To operationalize this in AI, they employ ASPIC+, a structured argumentation framework. They extend ASPIC+ with value-based filtering so that each agent’s values determine which considerations count as morally relevant reasons. This yields a Contractualist Argumentation Framework where reasons for and against actions are represented as arguments, compared, and evaluated using argumentation semantics.

Result: They define the Contractualist Argumentation Framework and show how contractualist moral reasoning can be encoded in structured argumentation with value-based components. They demonstrate its use via a worked example set in a domestic environment (e.g., a home with multiple agents) and compare their framework conceptually with existing value-based argumentation approaches.

Conclusion: The proposed framework provides a principled, formal way to model contractualist moral reasoning for autonomous agents. By combining structured argumentation with value-based filtering, it can represent and evaluate agents’ reasons in line with Scanlon’s contractualism, offering a path toward more transparent and philosophically grounded moral decision-making in multi-agent settings.

Abstract: Autonomous agents operating in shared environments must make decisions that affect multiple individuals with potentially conflicting interests. We propose a formal framework for moral decision-making grounded in Scanlon's contractualism, an ethical theory that evaluates the permissibility of actions in terms of principles that no one could reasonably reject. To operationalise contractualist reasoning, we use ASPIC+, a structured argumentation framework, extended with value-based filtering to model how each agent's values determine which reasons are morally relevant in the first place. The result is a Contractualist Argumentation Framework in which agents' reasons are formally represented, compared, and evaluated through argumentation semantics. We illustrate the approach through a worked example in a domestic setting and discuss its relation to existing value-based argumentation approaches.

</details>


### [284] [Long-Horizon Autonomous Architecture Research with a Language-Model Agent: A Behavioural Case Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01995)
*Aon Safdar,Mohamed Saadeldin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An autonomous single LLM-agent is used as the sole researcher to design and improve a neural architecture (a non-standard Vision Transformer) over ~100 experiments, revealing how workflow and tool design shape research trajectories and outcomes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand whether and how a single general-purpose LLM can autonomously conduct long-horizon machine learning research, and to characterize its behaviour, productivity patterns, and limitations when tasked with a realistic, open-ended neural architecture design problem.

Method: Set up an LLM agent with tools for literature access, code and experiment management, tracking, and persistent memory. Give it a research question, initial hypothesis, and fixed compute budget. Let it autonomously propose, implement, run, and log ~100 sequential experiments on improving a non-standard Vision Transformer. Structure the process into three phases where humans only expand the agent’s tool surface or problem scale at phase transitions, without altering the underlying LLM. Analyze the behavioural trace and performance improvements across small benchmarks and ImageNet-1K.

Result: The agent improves the initial weak ViT baseline to a stronger, more efficient model on small datasets and to a usable, though not state-of-the-art, ImageNet-1K model. The behavioural trace shows: (i) a phase structure of rapid initial gains, a saturation wall after many hypotheses, then recovery when the action surface is expanded; (ii) a single early hypothesis accounts for most accuracy gains, with later improvements following a long-tail distribution; (iii) a strong bias toward greedy, incremental changes, largely induced by the commit-or-discard workflow that mimics hill-climbing, with additional caution due to risk aversion and literature anchoring; and (iv) the agent rediscovers known results and, in the less-charted regime of pure channel attention, challenges a standard architectural design choice.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that an autonomous LLM agent can perform meaningful, extended research in neural architecture design but that its effectiveness is heavily shaped by workflow constraints rather than raw model capability. Workflow elements—such as evaluation rules and available actions—drive greedy search behaviour and limit exploration. The authors suggest future directions like diversified search strategies, explicit budgeted high-risk experiments, branching (forks) in research lines, and regime-aware re-validation to better harness autonomous LLM researchers.

Abstract: We study what happens when a single general-purpose large language model acts as the sole researcher on a long-horizon neural architecture design problem. The agent receives a scientific question, an initial hypothesis and motivation, a compute budget, and research affordances (source and experiment management, experiment tracking, literature access, and persistent memory), then autonomously proposes, implements, evaluates, and records experiments over an extended period. The study comprises three phases, separated by human-declared transitions, that progressively expand the agent's tool surface or problem scale. Across approximately 100 sequential experiments, the agent improves a non-standard Vision Transformer from a weak baseline to a stronger, efficient model on small benchmarks and a usable but sub-SOTA model on ImageNet-1K, while producing a dense behavioural trace. We report four findings.(i)Productivity exhibits a clear phase structure: rapid early gains, a multi-dozen-hypothesis saturation wall, and recovery, with recovery triggered by expanding the action surface rather than changing the underlying model.(ii)A single early hypothesis contributes more to accuracy gain, with later improvements long-tailed.(iii)The preference for greedy, incremental hypotheses is largely workflow-induced: a commit-or-discard evaluation rule is isomorphic to greedy hill-climbing; the remainder reflects risk aversion after bold failures and anchoring on familiar literature. (iv)The agent independently rediscovers established results and, in the unfamiliar regime of pure channel attention, overturns a standard design choice. We conclude that workflow design was at least as influential as agent capability in this study and propose diversified search, budgeted moonshot hypotheses, explicit forks, and regime-aware re-validation as testable directions for future autonomous research.

</details>


### [285] [Evolving in the Agent Jungle via History-Informed Opponent Awareness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02005)
*Zhaofeng Zhang,Linhan Xia,Rui Liu,Yihao Wang,Binrui Shen,Shengxin Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes OASE, a method that lets LLM-based agents adapt strategies in dynamic multi-agent environments by selectively accepting only those skill revisions that show real payoff improvements against historical opponent snapshots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most existing LLM-agent adaptation methods assume a static environment, updating skill libraries using feedback as if the opponents and conditions do not change. In multi-agent scenarios, however, opponents also adapt, making the environment non-stationary and causing naive skill revision to overfit to transient opponent behaviors or obsolete references. There is a need for a mechanism that can distinguish genuinely beneficial strategic updates from short-lived or spurious ones in evolving competitive settings.

Method: OASE (Opponent-Aware Selective Evolution) compares a candidate skill (revised strategy) with the current incumbent skill using paired evaluations under controlled, identical conditions. These conditions are instantiated via historical snapshots of opponent strategies, effectively anchoring comparisons in a stable reference set. OASE estimates the payoff gain of the candidate over the incumbent across these snapshots, and accepts the candidate only if the gain surpasses a pre-defined acceptance threshold. This turns adaptation into a selective evolutionary process that filters out weak or noisy updates.

Result: In experiments on first-price auctions and private-cost Cournot competition, OASE is compared to a Reflexion-style baseline that more liberally revises skills. OASE attains a smaller final equilibrium distance—meaning its strategies come closer to game-theoretic equilibria—while accepting far fewer skill revisions. This shows that OASE maintains or improves performance with less frequent but more meaningful updates, and reduces destabilizing or unproductive strategy changes.

Conclusion: OASE provides a principled, evidence-driven mechanism for strategy adaptation in dynamic multi-agent environments. By anchoring comparisons to historical opponent snapshots and applying a payoff-based acceptance threshold, it mitigates overreaction to non-stationarity and replaces indiscriminate updating with selective evolution. As a result, LLM agents can adapt more stably and efficiently even when opponents are continuously evolving.

Abstract: Learning to adapt strategies through interaction is a key step toward more general and autonomous LLM agents. Existing approaches typically achieve behavioral adaptation by revising skill libraries. However, in multi-agent environments, opponents may simultaneously update their strategies, causing the environment itself to evolve continuously. Applying skill-revision methods designed for static environments in such settings therefore amounts to updating against an obsolete reference. To address this challenge, we introduce OASE (Opponent-Aware Selective Evolution), which identifies and adopts genuinely beneficial skill revisions in dynamic multi-agent environments. Specifically, OASE conducts paired comparisons between a candidate skill and the incumbent under identical conditions anchored by historical snapshots of opponent strategies, and adopts the candidate only when its estimated payoff gain exceeds an acceptance threshold. We evaluate OASE in two decision-making scenarios: first-price auctions and private-cost Cournot competition. Experimental results show that, compared with a Reflexion-style baseline, OASE achieves a lower final equilibrium distance in both environments while accepting substantially fewer skill revisions, thereby suppressing strategy changes that lack sufficient payoff support. OASE therefore replaces blind updating with evidence-anchored selection, allowing agents to adapt stably and efficiently even as opponents continuously evolve.

</details>


### [286] [HALT: Verification-Aware Stopping for Retrieval-Augmented Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02009)
*Daeyoung Roh,Donghee Han*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes HALT, a lightweight, verification-aware stopping policy for retrieval-augmented multi-hop QA agents that stops search when accumulated evidence covers all required intermediate claims, reducing redundant retrieval while preserving answer accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retrieval-augmented multi-hop QA agents often over-retrieve: after they already have enough evidence to answer, they keep issuing search queries. This increases cost and latency and can even hurt answer quality by adding distracting or conflicting context. Existing stopping criteria often rely on the generator’s confidence, which does not directly measure whether the necessary evidence has actually been retrieved. The authors are motivated to design a stopping mechanism grounded in evidence coverage that can be applied to existing systems without retraining.

Method: The authors reframe stopping as an evidence-coverage problem: given a set of expected intermediate “hop claims” that should be supported to answer the question, the system should stop retrieving once every claim has sufficient supporting evidence in the retrieved context. They introduce HALT, a verification-aware stopping policy that operates on top of an existing retrieval-augmented agent. HALT takes as input (i) predicted hop claims (either generated from the question or taken from gold supporting facts for analysis) and (ii) the stream of retrieved evidence passages over hops. It continuously checks whether each hop claim is supported by the cumulative evidence, using a claim–evidence alignment mechanism. When all required claims are verified as covered, HALT halts further retrieval. The core agent, retriever, and generator remain unchanged; HALT is purely a runtime control policy. The paper also compares deployable (generated claims) vs. oracle (gold claims) settings, and runs baseline and ablation studies to isolate the effect of explicit claim–evidence alignment from simpler stopping heuristics like fixed hop limits or lexical overlap thresholds.

Result: On three multi-hop QA benchmarks, HALT significantly reduces redundant retrieval steps (fewer search hops) while largely maintaining exact match accuracy of final answers. In the deployable setting where hop claims are predicted from the input question, HALT yields moderate retrieval savings with negligible loss in exact match. In a diagnostic setting that assumes gold supporting-fact-based claims, HALT achieves larger retrieval reductions, showing the potential upper bound if hop targets are perfectly specified. Baseline comparisons and ablations demonstrate that HALT’s benefits arise from its explicit claim–evidence alignment, outperforming simpler stopping rules based on generic sufficiency, fixed stopping positions, or surface-level lexical overlap. Initial experiments on open-corpus settings further show that HALT tends to abstain from answering when it cannot confidently verify coverage of all required claims.

Conclusion: The study concludes that framing stopping as an evidence-coverage problem provides an effective and practical runtime control signal for multi-hop retrieval-augmented QA agents. HALT, as a lightweight verification-aware stopping layer, can be plugged into existing systems without retraining or modifying the underlying agent and can reduce redundant search while preserving answer quality. The results indicate that accurate hop-claim specification and claim–evidence alignment are key to efficient multi-hop retrieval, and that coverage-based stopping can also naturally support abstention when verification is not possible. Overall, evidence-centric stopping policies like HALT offer a promising direction for making retrieval-augmented agents more efficient, reliable, and deployment-ready.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented search agents answer multi-hop questions by repeatedly issuing search queries and accumulating evidence. This creates a stopping problem: after the necessary evidence has appeared, further retrieval often adds cost, latency, and distracting context rather than useful information. We frame stopping as evidence coverage rather than generator confidence, and introduce HALT, a lightweight verification-aware policy that leaves the search agent unchanged. Given expected hop claims, HALT stops only when cumulative evidence supports each required claim. Across three multi-hop QA benchmarks, HALT reduces redundant search while largely preserving exact match. We separate a deployable setting, where hop claims are generated from the question, from a diagnostic upper bound that uses gold supporting-fact annotations: generated claims give smaller but still exact-match-preserving savings, while gold claims show the larger savings available when hop targets are clean. Baseline comparisons and ablations show that this behavior is driven by claim-evidence alignment rather than generic sufficiency, fixed stop positions, or lexical overlap. Open-corpus pilots further suggest that HALT abstains when coverage cannot be reliably verified. Overall, evidence coverage provides a practical runtime control signal for improving retrieval-augmented agents without retraining or modifying the host agent.

</details>


### [287] [Before Reasoning Fails: Pre-Evidence Procedural Failures in Agentic RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02011)
*Daeyoung Roh,Donghee Han*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies and analyzes a key failure mode in agentic RAG systems where agents retrieve evidence but finalize answers without actually reading it, and shows that enforcing a simple 'read after search' constraint (Read-Gate) significantly improves accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic RAG systems are expected to reason based on retrieved evidence, but in practice they can output answers without adequately inspecting that evidence. Existing evaluations typically conflate evidence gathering with answer reasoning, masking this failure mode. The authors aim to isolate and quantify how often agents fail procedurally (not reading evidence) versus failing after reading, and to test whether simple trajectory-level controls can reduce such failures.

Method: Using saved tool-call traces and logs (including retrieval calls, which passages were actually read, and final answers), the authors analyze 12,000 paired agent trajectories on three multi-hop QA benchmarks: HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue. They decompose wrong answers into two categories: (1) pre-evidence discipline failures, where the agent finalizes without reading retrieved evidence, and (2) post-gold-read failures, where the agent reads relevant evidence but still answers incorrectly. They then propose and evaluate Read-Gate, a minimal runtime invariant that enforces at least one evidence-reading step after search and before finalizing an answer. They also run diagnostics on the effect of increasing the model's hidden thinking budget on evidence inspection behavior.

Result: The analysis shows that pre-evidence discipline failures and post-gold-read failures are largely non-overlapping, with only 11.2–13.1% of cases triggering both types of failure depending on the entity extraction method used. Enforcing the Read-Gate constraint, which forces the agent to perform a reading step before finalizing, improves LLM accuracy by 14.9–19.9 percentage points on trajectories that would otherwise skip reading and by 3.2–9.4 percentage points when considering full minimal-reasoning conditions. Additional diagnostics reveal that simply granting larger hidden thinking budgets does not reliably increase the amount of evidence actually inspected by the agent.

Conclusion: Evidence-gathering behavior in agentic RAG should be treated and evaluated as a distinct trajectory-level control problem, rather than being implicitly bundled with answer-side reasoning quality. A simple procedural invariant like Read-Gate can substantially reduce failures where agents answer without consulting retrieved evidence, but improving overall performance also requires addressing reasoning failures even after evidence is read. More broadly, systems should explicitly monitor and constrain how agents interact with retrieval tools across the trajectory, not just evaluate final answer correctness.

Abstract: Agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems can fail before evidence-conditioned reasoning is tested: an agent may retrieve candidate snippets but finalize without inspecting them. We study this failure mode as a procedural property of the agent trajectory, decomposing wrong answers into pre-evidence discipline failures and post-gold-read failures using saved tool-call traces, retrieved evidence, read passages, and final answers. Across 12,000 paired trajectories on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue, the two failure types are largely non-redundant: the both-trigger rate is in [11.2%, 13.1%] across regex and spaCy entity extractors. We then evaluate Read-Gate, a minimal runtime invariant requiring an agent to read after search and before finalization. Forced reading improves LLM-Acc by 14.9-19.9 points on trajectories that would otherwise skip reading and by 3.2-9.4 points on full minimal-reasoning cells. Additional diagnostics show that larger hidden thinking budgets do not necessarily increase evidence inspection. Together, these results indicate that evidence-gathering should be evaluated as a trajectory-level control problem, separately from answer-side reasoning.

</details>


### [288] [EduZone: A Framework for Evaluating LLM Safety for K-12 Students and Teachers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02024)
*Junyeong Park,Jieun Han,Haneul Yoo,So-Yeon Ahn,Jinsung Yoon,Alice Oh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EduZone is an automated framework to stress-test LLM safety in K-12 educational uses via rich, context-aware adversarial interactions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM safety benchmarks rarely focus on how harms emerge in real student–teacher educational contexts, especially for K-12, where users are minors and risks are unique. The authors aim to fill this gap with a systematic way to evaluate education-specific risks rather than only generic safety categories.

Method: They define an evaluation space that crosses (1) student- vs teacher-facing usage scenarios, (2) detailed curriculum concepts, and (3) a taxonomy of 6 risk categories and 28 subcategories, including education-specific harms. From this space, they automatically generate adversarial interactions in three formats: single-turn prompts, static pre-defined multi-turn dialogues, and dynamically evolving multi-turn conversations. They then test 10 different LLMs on these interactions and score their responses according to four safety outcomes: refusal, safe assistance, risky assistance that includes safety guidance, and fully risky assistance.

Result: Across 10 LLMs, the framework shows models are more vulnerable when dealing with education-specific risks and in dynamic multi-turn conversations. Many existing safety mechanisms that work reasonably on generic benchmarks fail to prevent problematic behavior in these richer educational settings.

Conclusion: EduZone offers a scalable, automated benchmark for probing LLM safety specifically in K-12 educational contexts. It exposes weaknesses in current guardrails, especially for dynamic, context-heavy interactions, and is intended to guide the design and deployment of safer educational LLM systems.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used across diverse tasks in K-12 education, yet existing safety evaluations rarely examine how harmful or inappropriate content appears in interactions between LLMs and students or teachers. To address this, we present EduZone, an evaluation framework for LLM safety across diverse educational scenarios. Our framework systematically combines (1) student- and teacher-facing LLM usage contexts, (2) fine-grained curriculum concepts, and (3) 6 risk categories and 28 subcategories spanning both conventional and education-specific harms to generate contextually grounded adversarial interactions. We construct these interactions in three settings: single-turn requests, static multi-turn conversations, and dynamic multi-turn conversations. Using these interactions, we evaluate ten LLMs using four safety levels: refusal, safe assistance, risky assistance with safety guidance, and fully risky assistance. Our results reveal greater vulnerability to education-specific risks and dynamic multi-turn interactions, while existing safety guardrails fail to adequately address these risks. EduZone advances LLM safety in education by providing an automated, scalable evaluation framework that supports the development and deployment of safer LLMs in K-12 education.

</details>


### [289] [HPFA: Hypergraph-Based Paired Failure Attribution for LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02026)
*Runchuan Zhu,Hongbin Lai,Bowen Jiang,Junrui Zhang,Zhangheng LI,Ostap Kilbasovych,Junyuan Hong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a hypergraph-based paired failure attribution (HPFA) method to pinpoint which reasoning steps cause LLM failures, then trains a lightweight model to automatically do this, improving both attribution and downstream reasoning accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs benefit from reflection on their reasoning traces, but they struggle to identify which specific step caused a failure. Existing attribution approaches are either computationally prohibitive—requiring stepwise counterfactual testing that scales poorly with long chains of thought—or oversimplified, treating the reasoning as a linear sequence and ignoring branching logical dependencies. There is a need for an efficient, scalable, and structurally aware way to localize root causes of failure in complex reasoning trajectories.

Method: The authors model reasoning traces as hypergraphs, where hyperedges capture non-linear logical dependencies between steps. They then introduce Hypergraph-based Paired Failure Attribution (HPFA), which compares the hyperedges along a failing reasoning path with those of a reference successful path for the same task. This paired comparison over a structured hypergraph reduces the search space for potential root causes. Using HPFA, they automatically generate large-scale labeled attribution data and train a compact attributor model through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. This attributor predicts the root-cause steps in new reasoning traces and can be used online during inference to guide reflection and correction.

Result: On mathematical reasoning benchmarks and agent-based coding tasks, HPFA achieves higher attribution accuracy and better computational efficiency than baselines that either rely on step-by-step counterfactual testing or treat reasoning as flat sequences. The learned attributor model, when plugged into reasoning pipelines, consistently improves test-time task performance and outperforms non-graph or non-paired attribution methods in both attribution quality and final reasoning accuracy.

Conclusion: Representing reasoning traces as hypergraphs and using paired comparison between failed and successful trajectories allows efficient, accurate localization of failure causes. The resulting HPFA framework both scales to longer, more complex reasoning and produces high-quality supervision for training a lightweight attributor. This attributor then enhances LLM reasoning performance at inference time, demonstrating that structurally informed, paired failure analysis is a powerful approach for reflection-based reasoning systems.

Abstract: Reflection is a powerful mechanism for LLM reasoning, yet its effectiveness hinges on accurately attributing failures to specific reasoning steps, a capability that current models notably lack. Existing failure attribution methods either require expensive step-by-step counterfactual testing that scales poorly with trajectory length, or treat reasoning traces as flat sequences that ignore the inherent non-linear logical dependencies. We propose a hypergraph-based paired failure attribution (HPFA) framework that attributes the failure root cause by comparing the hyperedges of the targeted failure reasoning path against a reference successful path. By reducing the search space, our method efficiently localizes root causes and enables scalable synthesis of attribution data for training a lightweight attributor model via supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and agentic coding tasks demonstrate that HPFA can dramatically increase attribution accuracy and efficiency, and the trained attributor consistently improves reasoning accuracy at test time, outperforming baselines that lack graph structure or paired analysis.

</details>


### [290] [Cross-Fitted Residual Utility for Primary-Preserving Cognitive Decision Correction in Automatic Modulation Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02063)
*Linzhuo Han,Zongyong Cui,Houbiao Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a cognitive post-inference decision policy that learns when to override a default modulation classifier using residual utilities, yielding consistent accuracy gains and robustness under various channel impairments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automatic modulation classification research focuses on improving classifier accuracy, but practical cognitive receivers must also decide whether and when to override a trusted default prediction based on heterogeneous additional evidence. There is a lack of systematic methods for this post-inference decision-making that can safely exploit auxiliary models without harming the primary classifier’s strengths.

Method: They use a structured KAN-Fourier classifier as a default model providing base probabilities, and add multiple neural and non-neural candidate models as auxiliary evidence sources. They learn candidate-specific residual utilities via cross-fitting, using out-of-fold predictions on the training set to avoid overfitting.
