A separate validation split is then used to fix the decision policy: thresholds for acting, allowed transitions between predictions, conditional routing rules among candidates, and a unified risk mask specifying when not to override the default. This frozen policy is then evaluated on held-out test sets across several datasets and under simulated channel impairments.

Result: On three benchmark datasets (RMLA, RMLB, HISAR), their full cognitive decision system increases overall accuracy by about 2–3 percentage points relative to the KAN-Fourier default: from 63.632% to 66.332%, 65.161% to 66.168%, and 77.769% to 79.867%, respectively. Ablation and controlled comparisons show that simply using a generic out-of-fold meta-learner on the same signals does not consistently outperform baselines; the performance improvements arise from the full evidence-and-action policy design. Statistical tests (paired bootstrap, Holm-corrected McNemar) indicate that these gains are significant. Under stress tests with carrier-frequency offset, I/Q imbalance, and synthetic Rayleigh/Rician fading (11 total conditions), the frozen policy still brings positive gains with all paired 95% confidence intervals above zero.

Conclusion: A carefully designed post-inference cognitive decision policy that treats auxiliary models as evidence and optimizes residual utility can reliably and significantly improve a strong default modulation classifier, including under a variety of channel impairments. The key benefit comes not just from additional models, but from the structured policy that governs when and how to override the default model, providing statistically robust gains without retraining the primary classifier.

Abstract: Automatic modulation classification research has largely emphasized representation accuracy, but a cognitive receiver must also decide when heterogeneous evidence justifies overriding a trusted default prediction. We study this post-inference problem through cross-fitted residual utility and a primary-preserving cognitive decision policy. A structured KAN-Fourier classifier supplies the default probability, while neural and non-neural candidates provide observable evidence. Candidate-specific residual utility is learned from train-split out-of-fold predictions, and a disjoint validation split freezes action thresholds, approved transitions, conditional routes, and a unified risk mask before held-out evaluation. On RMLA, RMLB, and HISAR, the complete system improves overall accuracy from 63.632% to 66.332%, 65.161% to 66.168%, and 77.769% to 79.867%, respectively. Controlled comparisons show that the isolated utility target does not uniformly dominate alternative out-of-fold meta-learners; the consistent gain comes from the complete evidence-and-action policy. Paired bootstrap and Holm-corrected McNemar analyses support the controlled gains. A frozen-policy stress test under carrier-frequency offset, I/Q imbalance, and synthetic Rayleigh/Rician fading yields positive gains in all 11 conditions, with every paired 95\% confidence interval above zero.

</details>


### [291] [Fetch-then-Explore: Decoupling Selection from Extraction over a Persistent Workspace for Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02097)
*Qi Liu,Yiqun Chen,Zidan Chen,Yan Gao,Yi Wu,Yao Hu,Jiaxin Mao,Fengbin Zhu,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a new web-search agent interface, Fetch-then-Explore, that decouples page selection from evidence extraction, stores selected pages persistently, and shows better accuracy than existing interfaces on open-web QA benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based search agents focus on how to find pages rather than how to read and reuse them. Common interfaces either read pages once at fetch time (visit-and-read) or keep only a single page in state (browsing), forcing agents to refetch and reread important pages later. This is inefficient and risks missing evidence that matters at later reasoning steps.

Method: They introduce Fetch-then-Explore, which records fetched pages into a persistent per-question workspace on the filesystem, decoupling selection from extraction. Evidence is extracted on demand as the agent’s hypothesis evolves, and pages are never discarded when moving to new pages. They implement this within a unified ReAct-style agent framework with a fixed search component, and compare it to snippet-only, visit-and-read, and browsing baselines on two open-web QA benchmarks using three different backbone LLM agents.

Result: Fetch-then-Explore outperforms all baselines on BrowseComp for every backbone model and generally matches or surpasses them on WideSearch. Behavioral analysis shows that the key advantage is the ability to revisit previously fetched pages more often than transient interfaces, enabling recovery of evidence missed during earlier passes.

Conclusion: Decoupling page selection from evidence extraction and persisting pages in a workspace improves open-web QA agents. The Fetch-then-Explore interface allows cheap selection, flexible and repeated evidence extraction, and cumulative evidence gathering, leading to higher accuracy—especially through revisiting and re-mining previously seen pages.

Abstract: Search agents now answer questions that take dozens of searches to settle, yet how such an agent reads a page has drawn far less attention than how it finds one. Nearly all of them use one of two document interfaces, and both tie a page to the moment it is opened. \emph{Visit-and-read} injects a reading of the page into the message history at fetch time, fixing that reading before the agent knows which fact it will need. Stateful \emph{browsing} instead extracts on demand from the page in hand, but holds one page at a time and releases it as soon as the agent opens another. Either way, a page that turns out to matter many turns later has to be fetched and rendered into context all over again. We propose \textbf{Fetch-then-Explore}, which separates page selection from evidence extraction and keeps what it selects: pages are recorded in a per-question workspace on the filesystem rather than the context window or a transient session, and evidence is pulled from them on demand later. Selection becomes almost free, extraction can wait until the agent knows what to look for and be repeated as its hypothesis sharpens, and pages are not released when the agent moves on, so evidence accumulates across the trajectory. In a unified ReAct harness with fixed search, we compare Fetch-then-Explore against snippet-only, visit-and-read, and browsing baselines on two open-web benchmarks, BrowseComp and WideSearch, across three agent backbones. It leads BrowseComp accuracy at every backbone and generally matches or exceeds the baselines on WideSearch, and a behavioral analysis traces the gains to the workspace's defining move: returning to a page after leaving it, which it does far more than any transient interface, so evidence missed on a first pass can still be recovered later.

</details>


### [292] [MemArbiter: Decision-Time Memory Arbitration for Long-Horizon LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02113)
*Jiajun Dong,Yutao Hu,Fengrui Fan,Shihan Dou,Yueming Wu,Deqing Zou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces MemArbiter, a function-aware memory arbitration framework that closes the Memory-Action Gap in LLM agents by better structuring and prioritizing accessible memory, leading to significantly improved performance on long-horizon tasks under strict memory budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents tackling long-horizon, multi-step tasks need to carry forward and effectively use information from earlier steps. While prior work focuses on making past information more accessible via retrieval or extended context, action-relevant information often still fails to influence current decisions because it is not properly structured, prioritized, or surfaced at the right time. The authors term this issue the Memory-Action Gap and seek to address the component of this gap caused by suboptimal memory management.

Method: The authors propose MemArbiter, a memory arbitration framework that first decomposes the interaction history into atomic pieces of information. These are then organized into five functional Memory Banks, each associated with different roles. MemArbiter models bank-level demand and item-level relevance, uses distinct focal vs. ambient representations, and employs a temporal presentation gate to decide which memories become salient at each step. This mechanism dynamically selects and presents the most action-relevant memories to the LLM within a fixed token budget.

Result: On the ALFWorld benchmark for long-horizon embodied tasks, MemArbiter is compared to Flat Retrieval and Flat Recency baselines under the same per-step memory token budgets. Using an open-weight model for action generation, MemArbiter obtains success rates of 82.8% and 92.5% for 500- and 750-token budgets, respectively. These results represent gains of 20.9 and 25.4 percentage points over the strongest baseline. Additionally, MemArbiter yields better recovery after failures and reduces the repetition of failed actions and recurring state-action loops.

Conclusion: Function-aware memory arbitration—structuring past interactions into different functional banks and dynamically controlling their salience—substantially narrows the Memory-Action Gap in LLM agents. By ensuring that already-accessible information is better organized and surfaced at the right time, MemArbiter enables LLM agents to use memory more effectively, improving success rates, robustness, and behavioral diversity under constrained memory budgets.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents must retain and use cross-step information to act coherently in long-horizon tasks. Existing methods improve memory accessibility, yet action-relevant information may still fail to guide the current decision because it is poorly formed, organized, prioritized, or presented. We call this post-access failure the Memory-Action Gap. We propose MemArbiter, a function-aware memory arbitration framework that addresses the memory-management-induced component of this gap. MemArbiter decomposes interaction histories into atomic items, organizes them into five functional Memory Banks, and combines bank-level demand, item-level relevance, focal-ambient representations, and a temporal presentation gate to dynamically control memory salience. We evaluate MemArbiter on ALFWorld against Flat Retrieval and Flat Recency under unified per-step memory budgets. With an open-weight action-generation model, MemArbiter achieves success rates of 82.8% and 92.5% under 500- and 750-token budgets, outperforming the strongest baseline by 20.9 and 25.4 percentage points, respectively. It also improves post-failure recovery and reduces failed-action repetition and state-action recurrence. These results show that function-aware memory arbitration enables accessible information to guide actions more effectively.

</details>


### [293] [Beyond Solution-Centric Search: Adaptive Inquiry and Knowledge Revision for Autonomous ML Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02143)
*Shaokang Fu,Yulong Tao,Linbo Jin,Jiarong Zhao,Qiming Shi,Tianjun Pan,Haonan Li,Chengyu Wang,Jia Wu,Chengfu Huo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Iris is a new LLM-based research agent that focuses on managing and updating an explicit information state instead of directly searching over solution candidates, achieving strong performance on long-horizon ML engineering tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon ML engineering tasks require many interdependent decisions under time and resource constraints. Existing LLM agents structure their search around candidate solutions (trees, graphs, chains), which entangles how they explore with how they store and use information, limiting systematic information gathering and reuse. There is a need for agents that reason explicitly about what is known, what is unknown, and what information to acquire next.

Method: The paper introduces the “information paradigm,” where the center object is an evolving information state about the task. They instantiate it as Iris, which runs an inquiry–revision loop: (1) Inquiry: from the current information state, Iris creates local action plans and performs epistemic actions—targeted experiments and probes—specifically to resolve decision-critical unknowns without altering the main solution. (2) Revision: Iris integrates resulting observations into a structured task knowledge base made of revisable claims with explicit scope and status (e.g., hypotheses, confirmed facts). Each decision is then made using a decision context constructed on demand from raw evidence and these structured summaries at an appropriate level of detail. The architecture is evaluated as an LLM-based agent on ML engineering tasks.

Result: On MLE-Bench, a benchmark for ML engineering agents, Iris attains a 64.9% any-medal rate under a 12-hour compute budget, outperforming compared systems. Additionally, when tested on four diverse tasks that include harness engineering and model post-training, Iris maintains strong performance, indicating its ability to generalize across domains.

Conclusion: Organizing an agent around an explicit information state and an inquiry–revision loop leads to more effective long-horizon autonomous research behavior than solution-centric search over candidate solutions. Iris’s structured epistemic actions and knowledge management yield superior performance under budget constraints and generalize beyond the original benchmark tasks, suggesting that the information paradigm is a promising direction for building more capable research agents.

Abstract: Long-horizon autonomous research tasks such as machine learning engineering require systems to make interdependent decisions under a limited budget. Existing LLM-based agents typically organize candidate-solution improvement through tree, graph, or chain structures, meaning that the search process determines how information is acquired and managed. We call this design solution-centric search and propose instead the information paradigm, in which an evolving information state represents the system's understanding of the task and guides solution improvement. We instantiate this paradigm in Iris, an inquiry-revision loop. For information acquisition, Iris generates local action plans from the current information state and uses epistemic actions to probe decision-critical unknowns without modifying the retained solution. For information management, Iris synthesizes observations across experiments into task knowledge composed of revisable claims with explicit scope and status. It updates this knowledge as new evidence arrives and constructs each decision context from raw evidence, structured summaries, or task knowledge at the required level of detail. On MLE-Bench, Iris attains a 64.9% any-medal rate under a 12-hour budget, the highest among compared systems. Across four tasks spanning harness engineering and model post-training, Iris also demonstrates cross-domain generalization.

</details>


### [294] [Beyond the Mean: Multi-Moment Policy Optimization for LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02149)
*Yijun Zhang,Yule Xie,Jiaxin Ding,Xin Ding,Fan Xu,Haoxiang Zhang,Luoyi Fu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a new reinforcement learning framework, Multi-Moment Policy Optimization (MMPO), for improving LLM reasoning by optimizing multiple moments of the failure-probability distribution instead of just one.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most existing RL methods for LLM reasoning focus on reducing average failure probabilities or optimizing a single statistic (moment) of failure across problems. This ignores the full distributional behavior of failures (e.g., variance, tail risks), which limits our understanding and control of how often and how badly models fail. The authors aim to provide a richer, distributional view of policy optimization to better shape LLM reasoning performance.

Method: They model the failure probability on a randomly sampled problem as a random variable and analyze policy objectives via its statistical moments (mean, higher-order moments). They propose MMPO, which jointly minimizes several moments of this failure-probability distribution. They show that MMPO is equivalent to minimizing the expected truncated time to first success, making it operationally interpretable. Additionally, they present a general moment-transformation framework that can generate a wide range of policy optimization objectives by shaping different moment profiles of the failure distribution.

Result: On five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and across LLMs of varying scales, MMPO consistently outperforms strong existing reinforcement-learning-based baselines, indicating that multi-moment optimization leads to better reasoning performance and reliability than single-moment approaches.

Conclusion: Viewing policy optimization for LLM reasoning through the lens of moments of the failure-probability distribution reveals that many existing methods are incomplete, focusing on only one moment. MMPO demonstrates that jointly minimizing multiple moments yields better empirical performance and offers a clear operational meaning. The broader moment-transformation framework provides a unifying, principled way to design new RL objectives for LLM reasoning, potentially guiding future algorithm development.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a central paradigm for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models. Existing methods generally aim to reduce the failure probabilities induced across problems. In this paper, we introduce a moment-based perspective on policy optimization for LLM reasoning by treating the failure probability of a randomly sampled problem as a random variable and characterizing optimization objectives through its moments. Under this perspective, many existing methods optimize only a single moment of the failure-probability distribution, leaving its broader distributional structure largely uncharacterized. We propose \textbf{M}ulti-\textbf{M}oment \textbf{P}olicy \textbf{O}ptimization (MMPO), a novel policy optimization framework that jointly minimizes multiple moments of the failure-probability distribution. MMPO admits a direct operational interpretation as minimizing the expected truncated time required to obtain the first successful response. Beyond MMPO, we further develop a general moment-transformation framework that systematically induces different moment profiles and provides a unified view of a broader family of policy optimization objectives. Experiments across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and models of different scales demonstrate that MMPO consistently outperforms strong baselines. We hope this moment-based perspective offers new insights into the design of policy optimization objectives for LLM reasoning.

</details>


### [295] [Auditing Data Provenance in LLM Fine-tuning via Intrinsic Distributional Fingerprints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02154)
*Zirui Huang,Yunlong Mao,Wei Tong,Tingting Wu,Xin Ge,Sheng Zhong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Distribution Provenance Audit (DPA), a post-hoc, black-box method to detect whether a customized LLM has been fine-tuned on proprietary data, even when attackers try to hide it via paraphrasing or knowledge distillation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Customized LLMs can be secretly fine-tuned on proprietary or copyrighted datasets, causing data IP violations. Existing auditing approaches are weak because they require control during data collection or training and can be bypassed by obfuscating the training data (e.g., paraphrasing). There is a need for a robust, post-hoc method to verify whether proprietary data was used, without needing access to the training process.

Method: They propose Distribution Provenance Audit (DPA), a post-hoc auditing framework that treats the problem as a statistical hypothesis test under a black-box setting. DPA is based on the insight that, to preserve utility, a fine-tuned model must retain a stable intersection between semantic content and lexical expression of the training data, which induces characteristic distributional fingerprints in its outputs. DPA uses unbiased output sampling and statistical testing to detect whether these fingerprints are present, thereby determining if the proprietary data likely contributed to fine-tuning.

Result: On medical and legal fine-tuning tasks, DPA outperforms existing auditing baselines and remains effective even when adversarial trainers attempt to hide training data origins via paraphrasing or knowledge distillation. The experiments indicate that DPA can reliably detect data IP infringement in realistic, hostile settings.

Conclusion: DPA provides a robust, practical framework for post-hoc auditing of data IP misuse in LLM fine-tuning, resistant to common evasion strategies. However, the same detailed distributional fingerprints that enable strong provenance auditing also raise privacy concerns, highlighting a dual-use tension between accountability and potential for privacy attacks.

Abstract: The proliferation of customized Large Language Models (LLMs) poses critical risks of Data Intellectual Property (Data IP) infringement via unauthorized fine-tuning on proprietary data. Existing audit techniques are limited, as they require intervention during data preparation or training and remain fragile under malicious obfuscations such as data paraphrasing and knowledge distillation.
  We propose \textit{Distribution Provenance Audit (DPA)}, a post-hoc framework for auditing data IP infringement in LLM fine-tuning under black-box and malicious settings. DPA is grounded in a critical insight: regardless of fine-tuning tactics to evade provenance, the practical necessity of maintaining utility constrains the model to preserve the fundamental intersection of semantic substance and lexical form. Accordingly, DPA captures this persistent lexical-semantic intersection as intrinsic distributional fingerprints. The framework formulates the audit as a statistical hypothesis test, effectively quantifying these fingerprints via unbiased output sampling to reliably reject the null hypothesis of non-usage.
  Extensive experiments on medical and legal fine-tuning tasks show that DPA consistently outperforms existing baselines, remaining robust against adversarial trainers employing paraphrasing and knowledge distillation. We further highlight a fundamental dual-use tension: the same high-fidelity distributional fingerprints enabling reliable auditing may also facilitate privacy attacks.

</details>


### [296] [From Simple QA to Deep Research: A Verifiable Benchmark Constructed through Iterative Task Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02163)
*Can Wang,Haoran Chen,Haowen Gao,Hao Ding,Zhaoyang Liu,Zhiying Tu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build a new, automatically constructed benchmark of 500 expert-level deep research tasks, each decomposed into verifiable steps for fine-grained, reliable evaluation of AI models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current deep research benchmarks either require costly expert authoring or repurpose existing human materials, and fully automatic methods lack reliable and traceable verification. There is a need for a scalable yet rigorously verifiable benchmark that captures expert-level, multi-step research capabilities and supports stable, human-aligned evaluation.

Method: They automatically construct a 500-task benchmark across 31 topics and 10 categories using an iterative Explorer–Formalizer–Challenger pipeline. This pipeline starts from simple questions and progressively transforms them into complex deep research tasks. Each task is formalized as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of atomic reasoning or research steps, with associated checkpoints and fact-grounded rubrics that co-evolve with the query and DAG, enabling structured, pointwise evaluation.

Result: The resulting benchmark contains 500 deep research tasks, each with an explicit DAG structure and step-level rubrics. Experiments using existing models show the benchmark can clearly distinguish performance across different models and query types, and that its pointwise, fact-grounded rubrics yield fine-grained, human-aligned, and stable evaluations.

Conclusion: A scalable, verifiable deep research benchmark can be constructed automatically by iteratively expanding simple questions into structured, multi-step tasks represented as DAGs with checkpoints. This benchmark provides discriminative and reliable evaluation of AI research capabilities, and all associated data and code are released for public use.

Abstract: Deep research benchmarks require expert-level tasks and reliable evaluation grounded in task-specific knowledge. Existing benchmarks rely heavily on expert authoring or pre-existing human-authored materials, while fully automatic construction struggles to ensure consistent and traceable verification. To address this gap, we introduce a verifiable benchmark of 500 deep research tasks spanning 31 topics and 10 major categories, with three query forms designed to probe complementary capabilities required for deep research. The benchmark is constructed automatically using an iterative Explorer-Formalizer-Challenger pipeline that progressively transforms simple questions into deep research tasks. Each task is represented as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of atomic steps and associated checkpoints, enabling the query, DAG, and rubrics to evolve together in a controlled manner. Experiments demonstrate that the benchmark clearly discriminates among models and query types, while its fact-grounded pointwise rubrics enable fine-grained, human-aligned, and stable evaluation. Our data, implementation, and results are publicly available.

</details>


### [297] [From Profiling to Synthesis: Benchmarking Implicit Behavioral Alignment in Personalized LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02171)
*Jiajia Song,Bobo Li,Haiwen Yi,Zibo Ji,Meishan Zhang,Hao Fei,Min Zhang,Mong-Li Lee,Wynne Hsu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces IBA-Bench, a benchmark and associated agent framework (IBA-Agent) to evaluate and improve how LLM-based agents implicitly align with users’ evolving, noisy preferences over time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing personalization benchmarks for LLM agents mostly use static user profiles, fixed logs, or direct question answering about preferences. These settings do not reflect real-world, evolving, and often implicit user preferences, nor do they test whether agents can translate inferred preferences into behavior during task execution—the "knowledge-to-action" gap. The authors aim to create a more realistic and challenging setting for assessing and improving behavioral alignment of agents to user preferences.

Method: The authors construct IBA-Bench from longitudinal user interaction histories that include noise, implicit cues, and temporal inconsistencies. The benchmark evaluates whether agents can perform tasks while honoring implicit user constraints extracted from these histories. They also design IBA-Agent, an agent framework that uses broad retrieval over past trajectories and trajectory-level alignment mechanisms to resolve conflicting user priorities and guide current decisions.

Result: On IBA-Bench, state-of-the-art LLM agents struggle with effective personalization, showing that current methods have difficulty with implicit, evolving preferences and behavioral alignment. The proposed IBA-Agent achieves substantially better behavioral alignment performance in complex tasks across nine different application domains, outperforming baselines on the benchmark.

Conclusion: IBA-Bench exposes a significant gap between current personalization capabilities of LLM agents and the demands of real-world, evolving user preferences. By leveraging implicit, noisy interaction histories and enforcing preference-conditioned task execution, the benchmark provides a more realistic evaluation of behavioral alignment. IBA-Agent demonstrates that trajectory-level alignment and broad retrieval can significantly improve agents’ ability to satisfy implicit user constraints, but also highlights that personalization remains an open and challenging problem.

Abstract: Large Language Models have enabled increasingly capable autonomous agents, yet personalization remains critical for making such agents practically useful. Recent benchmarks have begun evaluating personalization in agents, but they largely rely on static preference snapshots, fixed interaction logs, or question answering over predefined user profiles. Such designs fail to capture the complexity of evolving user preferences and neglect preference-conditioned task execution-a discrepancy we term as the knowledge-to-action gap. To address this challenge, we introduce IBA-Bench, a benchmark for implicit behavioral alignment constructed from longitudinal interaction histories that contain noise, implicit cues, and temporal inconsistencies. Unlike prior work, IBA-Bench evaluates whether an agent can execute tasks while satisfying implicit user constraints inferred from historical interactions. We further propose IBA-Agent, an agent framework that reconciles conflicting priorities through broad retrieval and trajectory-level alignment. Experiment results on IBA-Bench show that effective personalization remains a significant challenge for state-of-the-art LLM agents, and the proposed IBA-Agent substantially improves behavioral alignment in complex scenarios across nine application domains.

</details>


### [298] [PAC Approximation and DIRECT Optimization for Parametric Markov Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02184)
*Zhiming Chi,Ying Liu,Andrea Turrini,Lijun Zhang,David N. Jansen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They develop efficient, approximate methods to analyze and optimize parametric Markov decision processes by learning a polynomial approximation of property satisfaction and then globally optimizing it with guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Computing exact satisfaction probabilities for temporal-logic properties over parametric MDPs is very costly, especially when the optimal policy changes across parameters. There is a need for scalable, approximate methods with probabilistic guarantees that still allow parameter synthesis and optimization, even for black-box models.

Method: Use the scenario approach: sample parameter valuations, then solve a linear program to fit a polynomial that approximates the true satisfaction function, with PAC-style guarantees on approximation error over most of the parameter space. Combine this PAC approximation with statistical model checking to handle black-box parametric models. Then apply the DIRECT derivative-free global optimization algorithm to the learned approximation, and derive bounds on the optimality gap under Lipschitz and PAC assumptions. Evaluate the approach on 2997 benchmarks, focusing on the DIRECT-based optimization part.

Result: They obtain a PAC polynomial approximation of the satisfaction function for PRCTL properties; they show theoretically that DIRECT, when applied to this approximation under certain assumptions, returns solutions whose value is close to the global optimum up to known bounds. Empirically, on 2997 benchmarks, DIRECT-based optimizers solve fewer instances than the scenario-based optimizer but, where both succeed, DIRECT typically finds slightly better objective values and is usually faster, remaining within the prescribed PAC error margin.

Conclusion: The scenario-based PAC approximation combined with DIRECT provides a practical and theoretically grounded framework for parameter synthesis and optimization in parametric MDPs. While the scenario optimizer is more robust in terms of instance coverage, DIRECT-based variants often yield better and faster solutions on the instances they solve, and their outputs respect the PAC error guarantees.

Abstract: In this paper, we consider the parameter synthesis and optimization problem for parametric Markov decision processes (pMDPs), the extension of classical MDPs where exact probability values are replaced by parametric expressions. Computing the rational function $f_{\lsf}$ that maps parameter valuations to the satisfaction value of a PRCTL property $\lsf$ is a computationally expensive task, particularly for pMDPs where the optimal policy may vary across the parameter space. We adopt the \emph{scenario approach} to efficiently synthesize a probably approximately correct (PAC) approximation $\ApproxFunOfProperty{f}$ of $f_{\lsf}$: by sampling parameter configurations and solving a linear program, we obtain a polynomial approximation whose error margin $\margin$ is guaranteed, with prescribed confidence, for all but an $\errorRate$-fraction of the parameter domain under the sampling distribution. We further show how this PAC framework can be combined with statistical model checking (SMC), enabling the analysis of black-box parametric models. Building on the PAC approximation, we integrate the DIRECT (DIviding RECTangles) algorithm for derivative-free global optimization over the parameter space. We establish conditional optimality-gap guarantees: under explicit Lipschitz and PAC-good-set assumptions, the difference between the true optimum $f_{\lsf}(\parameters^{*})$ and the value found by DIRECT is bounded by a partition-diameter term and, in the PAC case, an additional approximation-error term. An empirical evaluation on 2997 benchmarks focuses on the new DIRECT-based optimization component. The results show that DIRECT variants solve fewer instances than the scenario optimizer, but on their common successful instances they often return slightly better objective values and usually run faster, while remaining close to the scenario values within the PAC margin.

</details>


### [299] [MEGRAG: Multi-Granular Evidence Graphs for Answer-Aware Multi-Hop RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02195)
*Weidong Bao,Yingying Sun,Jun Yang,Yilin Wang,Zili Wei,Yubin Bao,Fangling Leng,Minghe Yu,Tiancheng Zhang,Ge Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces MEGRAG, a multi-hop question answering framework that builds and traverses a multi-granular evidence graph to improve retrieval-augmented generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-hop QA in RAG requires combining evidence scattered across multiple documents. Existing iterative RAG methods typically (1) use a single granularity of evidence per step, which forces a trade-off between having enough information and avoiding noise, and (2) delay answering until all retrieval steps are done, allowing redundant evidence and retrieval errors to accumulate and harm final performance. The authors aim to design a system that can flexibly use different granularities of evidence and decide early when a question is already answerable.

Method: They propose MEGRAG, which represents multi-hop reasoning as a path-structured, multi-granular evidence graph. Offline, it builds a cross-granularity index that explicitly links passages to their constituent sentences and extracted triples. Online, for each step it retrieves passages for the current query, then selects aligned evidence in a coarse-to-fine way: starting from compact triples and only adding sentence or passage context when needed. Using the gathered evidence, it generates an intermediate answer and, based on prior reasoning, assesses whether the initial query has been fully resolved. If not, the system diagnoses what information is missing and formulates a more focused next query; if yes, it halts further retrieval and outputs the answer.

Result: In experiments across multiple benchmarks and RAG baselines, MEGRAG consistently outperforms prior iterative RAG approaches, indicating that its multi-granular evidence representation and answer-aware stopping strategy produce better multi-hop QA performance.

Conclusion: MEGRAG effectively tackles key weaknesses of existing iterative RAG for multi-hop QA by combining a multi-granular evidence graph with answer-aware, stepwise reasoning and early stopping. This leads to more accurate answers with less noise and fewer error cascades, establishing MEGRAG as a stronger framework for retrieval-augmented multi-hop reasoning.

Abstract: Multi-hop question answering is a fundamental challenge in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), because deriving an answer requires integrating dispersed evidence. Iterative RAG (iRAG) is widely used for this challenge, but existing methods have two limitations. First, most methods still support each reasoning step with single-granularity evidence, making it difficult to balance information density and contextual noise. Second, existing methods often answer the original question only after aggregating evidence retrieved across intermediate steps, so redundant evidence and intermediate retrieval errors may accumulate and degrade the final answer. To address these limitations, we propose MEGRAG, an answer-aware framework that represents multi-hop reasoning as a path-structured multi-granular evidence graph. Offline, MEGRAG links passages to their sentences and extracted triples through a cross-granularity index. Online, it retrieves passages for the current query and selects aligned evidence, starting with compact triples and adding sentence or passage context as needed. MEGRAG uses the resulting intermediate answer and prior reasoning to decide whether the Initial Query has been resolved. If not, it identifies the missing information and formulates a focused next query; otherwise, it stops retrieval and returns the answer. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent gains over a diverse set of RAG baselines.

</details>


### [300] [PosterMELD: Multi-Agent Paper-to-Poster Generation for Controllable Design Diversity with Editable Print-Ready Outputs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02218)
*Haojie Hu,Chenhao Dang,Yaojia Liu,Hengrui Kang,Conghui He,Weijia Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PosterMELD is a multi-agent, template-conditioned system that automatically generates editable, high-quality scientific posters from long multimodal papers, achieving a high print-ready rate and strong aesthetic scores at low cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Creating scientific posters from full papers is time-consuming and requires both design and summarization skills. Existing automated systems either generate non-editable images, rely on expensive coding-agent workflows, or evaluate only successful outputs, hiding failure rates. There is a need for a reliable, cost-effective system that produces editable, print-ready posters with explicit design control and transparent quality metrics.

Method: The authors propose PosterMELD, a template-conditioned multi-agent pipeline. First, capacity-aware template slots guide text selection and writing before visual rendering. The system uses deterministic gating rules and a vision-language model (VLM) reviewer to detect failures in geometry, readability, asset integrity, and obvious factual errors, routing problematic cases to bounded repair steps. Successful runs export both editable PPTX files and PNG images, with explicit design parameters enabling multiple variants from the same paper. Quality is evaluated via a Print-Ready Rate (PRR) metric and VLM-based CHE (Craftsmanship-Harmony-Expressiveness) scores for print-ready outputs.

Result: On a benchmark of 621 papers, PosterMELD achieves an 81.3% Print-Ready Rate, which is 3.4× higher than P2P and 5.2× higher than PosterGen. Among methods that can produce multiple print-ready outputs, PosterMELD attains the highest conditional CHE scores. It preserves native editability and explicit design control while keeping the average generation cost at USD 0.38 per request, which is only 3.5% of the cost of the Codex+Skill baseline.

Conclusion: PosterMELD substantially improves automatic scientific poster generation by combining template-aware content planning, deterministic quality gates, and VLM-based review and repair. It delivers a high fraction of print-ready, aesthetically strong, and natively editable posters at a fraction of the cost of coding-agent approaches, while supporting explicit design customization and reproducible evaluation via PRR and CHE metrics.

Abstract: Scientific poster construction compresses a long multimodal paper into a readable, editable canvas. Existing systems hide request-level failures by scoring only completed outputs; direct image generation is not element-editable, while coding-agent workflows are costly. PosterMELD is a template-conditioned multi-agent pipeline: capacity-aware slots guide writing before rendering, and deterministic gates plus vision-language model (VLM) review route failures to bounded repair. Each accepted request exports editable PowerPoint (PPTX) and Portable Network Graphics (PNG) artifacts; explicit design controls yield same-paper variants. Across 621 papers, Print-Ready Rate (PRR) counts requests passing geometric, readability, asset-integrity, and obvious-factual-error checks, with native editability reported separately. A frozen VLM assigns conditional Craftsmanship-Harmony-Expressiveness (CHE) scores to print-ready outputs. PosterMELD attains 81.3% PRR, 3.4 times P2P's rate and 5.2 times PosterGen's, and the highest conditional CHE among generated methods with multiple print-ready outputs. Native editability and explicit design controls are retained at a mean cost of USD 0.38 per request, 3.5% of Codex+Skill's. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/Shannon4Science/PosterMELD.

</details>


### [301] [Trustworthy AI in Digital Health: A Comprehensive Review of Robustness and Explainability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02238)
*Abdullah Mamun,Shovito Barua Soumma,Hassan Ghasemzadeh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A review paper on robustness and explainability as core components of trustworthy AI for digital health, offering a structured synthesis of methods, challenges, and evaluation metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Trustworthy AI is crucial in high-stakes digital health settings, yet existing work is fragmented and lacks a focused synthesis on robustness and explainability tailored to healthcare. The paper aims to fill this gap so researchers and practitioners can better design, evaluate, and deploy reliable AI in clinical contexts.

Method: The authors conduct a structured review of recent literature on trustworthy AI, with emphasis on robustness and explainability in digital health. They organize methods and findings into an accessible framework, examine application-specific trust needs across several medical domains, and categorize technical approaches for robustness under data scarcity and distribution shift, as well as diverse explainable AI techniques.

Result: The review yields a three-part framework: (1) conceptual pillars and challenges of trustworthy AI in digital health; (2) domain-specific trust considerations in areas like intensive care, neonatal, and metabolic health, illustrating how robustness and explainability contribute to trust; and (3) a taxonomy of recent technical advances in robust and explainable AI, along with metrics to evaluate trust-related properties such as validity, fidelity, and diversity.

Conclusion: Trustworthy AI in digital health requires systematic attention to robustness and explainability across the entire AI lifecycle. By synthesizing current methods, domain applications, and evaluation metrics into a coherent framework, the paper provides practical guidance for building and assessing reliable, interpretable AI systems, including in the emerging era of LLM-based healthcare tools.

Abstract: Ensuring trust in AI systems is essential for the safe and ethical integration of machine learning systems into high-stakes domains such as digital health. Key dimensions, including robustness, explainability, fairness, accountability, and privacy, need to be addressed throughout the AI lifecycle, from problem formulation and data collection to model deployment and human interaction. While various contributions address different aspects of trustworthy AI, a focused synthesis on robustness and explainability, especially tailored to the healthcare context, remains limited. This review addresses that need by organizing recent advancements into an accessible framework, highlighting both technical and practical considerations. We present a structured overview of methods, challenges, and solutions, aiming to support researchers and practitioners in developing reliable and explainable AI solutions for digital health. This review article is organized into three main parts. First, we introduce the pillars of trustworthy AI and discuss the technical and ethical challenges, particularly in the context of digital health. Second, we explore application-specific trust considerations across domains such as intensive care, neonatal health, and metabolic health, highlighting how robustness and explainability support trust. Lastly, we present recent advancements in techniques aimed at improving robustness under data scarcity and distributional shifts, as well as explainable AI methods ranging from feature attribution to gradient-based interpretations and counterfactual explanations. This paper is further enriched with detailed discussions of the contributions toward robustness and explainability in digital health, the development of trustworthy AI systems in the era of LLMs, and various evaluation metrics for measuring trust and related parameters such as validity, fidelity, and diversity.

</details>


### [302] [Homebot: A Personal AI Agent for Conversational Home Assistance and Automation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02254)
*Shengyuan Ye,Yixin Zhang,Han Liang,Liekang Zeng,Jiangsu Du,Mu Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Homebot is a locally deployable, voice- and chat-based AI assistant for household tasks that integrates language models with tools and skills, with clear separation of sessions and well-defined interfaces for customization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Households need practical, privacy-preserving AI assistance that works both hands-free and via messaging, can integrate with home automations and tools, and remains configurable for different family members and devices. Existing assistants often mix state between channels, rely on cloud-only services, and provide limited extensibility.

Method: Design and implementation of a shared runtime that connects a language model with registered tools and task-specific skills, while separating request processing from session ownership across messaging and voice channels. The system uses local wake-word detection, streaming speech recognition and synthesis, and a dialogue-state protocol to manage conversation flow, including ending, following up, or continuing interactions. It defines clear contracts for channels, tools, and skills to enable customization.

Result: The resulting system, Homebot, can run locally, accept both instant-messaging and voice requests, maintain channel-scoped histories, and support hands-free operation with wake-word-activated sessions and explicit dialogue-state transitions. The structured interfaces make it feasible to customize Homebot with new tools and skills tailored to household needs.

Conclusion: By combining local speech interfaces, structured dialogue control, and a modular tool/skill architecture under a shared runtime, Homebot provides a practical and customizable AI agent for household assistance and automation, improving privacy, controllability, and multi-modal usability compared to more monolithic assistants.

Abstract: \texttt{Homebot} is a locally deployable AI agent for conversational household assistance and automation. It accepts voice and instant-messaging requests through a shared runtime that combines language-model responses with registered tools and task-specific skills. The design separates common request processing from session ownership: messaging history remains scoped to a channel and chat, whereas voice interaction is bounded by wake-word activation. For hands-free use, \texttt{Homebot} combines local wake-word detection, streaming speech recognition and synthesis, and an explicit dialogue-state protocol for ending, following up, or continuing a conversation. Clear channel, tool, and skill contracts support practical customization for household use.

</details>


### [303] [Self-Certification of Representation Adequacy: Sequential Certification at Minimum Task Loss](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02267)
*Zijie Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies when a compressed state representation for a sequential decision agent is provably adequate, and how an agent can self-certify this from interaction alone, quantifying the cost in task loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In sequential decision problems, agents often operate on compressed or learned representations of their histories rather than full histories. If this representation merges (aliases) distinct histories that require different optimal actions, the agent can suffer unavoidable loss and may not even be able to detect the inadequacy from its own experience. There is a need for a principled framework to define adequacy of such representations and to characterize when and at what cost an agent can certify that its current representation is good enough for decision making.

Method: The authors build a four-layer theoretical framework. (1) A static decision-theoretic layer: they formalize adequacy via a Bayes-risk grouping identity and characterize the minimal total-variation distance required for an external test to distinguish adequate from inadequate representations. (2) A sequential layer: they cast certification as an optimal-stopping problem measured in task loss, introduce an environment-dependent certification complexity constant defined via a covering linear program, and derive an information–task-loss lower bound for any delta-correct certification strategy. (3) They design a concrete Certification Track-and-Stop policy and prove that its expected cost asymptotically matches the lower bound. (4) A boundary layer: they analyze an explicit kernel-switching example to explore limits of their results, and they identify an open problem needed to extend guarantees from fixed kernels to settings with policy switching or representation repair. Full proofs of the main theorems are deferred to the appendices.

Result: They provide: (a) a formal, decision-theoretic notion of representation adequacy and an associated external verification threshold in total variation; (b) an environment-wise certification complexity constant derived from a covering LP; (c) a fundamental lower bound that ties information acquisition to task loss for any delta-correct self-certification strategy; and (d) a Certification Track-and-Stop algorithm whose certification cost matches this bound asymptotically, demonstrating optimality (up to asymptotics) in the fixed-representation setting. They also give a worked kernel-switching example that delineates where their guarantees currently stop.

Conclusion: The paper establishes a structured theory of how an agent can, in principle, certify that its compressed history representation is adequate for optimal decision making, and it quantifies the minimal unavoidable task loss required for such certification in a fixed-kernel setting. While they achieve matching lower and upper bounds for self-certification under a fixed representation, extending these guarantees to scenarios where the agent can switch policies or repair its representation remains open, highlighted by their kernel-switching boundary example.

Abstract: Agents that act on a compressed representation of their history face a structural risk: if the representation aliases histories with different optimal actions, no rule measurable with respect to the representation can avoid an irreducible per-round loss, and the agent may be unable to detect this from its own transcript. This paper develops a four-layer theory of self-certification of representation adequacy. The static layer defines decision-theoretic adequacy through a Bayes-risk grouping identity and prices a one-shot external verification by an exact total-variation threshold. The sequential layer poses certification as an optimal-stopping problem in the currency of task loss: we define an environment-wise certification complexity constant through a covering linear program, prove an information-task-loss lower bound for every delta-correct strategy, and give a Certification Track-and-Stop policy whose cost matches the bound asymptotically. A final boundary layer gives an explicit kernel-switching example and identifies the open theorem needed to cover policy switching or representation repair; it does not claim that the fixed-kernel guarantees extend to representation revision. The proofs of the two main theorems are given in full in the appendices.

</details>


### [304] [Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02276)
*Shuai Shao,Kangning Zhang,Qingyao Li,Shijian Wang,Hao Wang,Wenxiang Jiao,Yuan Lu,Yi Guo,Weiwen Liu,Weinan Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Harness-R1, a system that learns to automatically edit and improve the runtime harness around an LLM agent based on its failures, leading to higher task success across several benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents collect many interaction trajectories during deployment, but their core behavior and the surrounding harness that manages context, tools, and error recovery typically stay fixed. Manually engineering or statically designing these harnesses underuses the rich failure data available from real executions and may not adapt well to diverse or changing tasks. The authors aim to turn the process of harness design and repair into a learned, data-driven capability that continually improves an existing agent without changing its base model weights.

Method: The authors introduce Harness-R1, which learns a dedicated "harness engineer" model that edits the executable runtime (harness) of a frozen target agent. First, they cold-start this engineer with supervised fine-tuning on examples of harness edits. Then they train it online with reinforcement learning using group-relative policy optimization. A 9B-parameter engineer model observes batches of target-agent failures, proposes executable patches to the harness, and reruns the frozen target agent within the same batch. The success or failure of these reruns provides outcome-based rewards that update only the engineer, not the target. This creates a failure-conditioned, lifecycle-wide editing policy over the harness components that construct context, mediate tools, validate actions, and handle recovery.

Result: On three benchmarks—WebShop, ALFWorld, and DBBench—Harness-R1 significantly improves task success of a base Qwen3.5-9B agent. Without changing the target model, adding a generic Harness-R1 engineer boosts average success from 44.3% to 53.6%, a gain of 9.3 percentage points. When the target agent itself is fine-tuned and then paired with a target-specific harness engineer, performance further increases from 59.2% to 64.2%, adding 5.0 points on average.

Conclusion: Harness-R1 demonstrates that learning to edit and improve the runtime harness around an LLM agent—rather than only fine-tuning model weights—can yield substantial gains in task performance. Because the method provides benefits both before and after direct fine-tuning of the target agent, it suggests a promising direction where the harness engineer and the underlying agent co-evolve. This establishes failure-conditioned, RL-trained harness editing as a viable approach for continually enhancing deployed LLM agents using their own interaction trajectories.

Abstract: Agents built around large language models continually accumulate interaction trajectories during deployment, yet their behavior typically remains fixed. Beyond updating model weights, these trajectories can improve the agent harness that constructs context, mediates tools, validates actions, and recovers execution. We introduce Harness-R1, the first method, to our knowledge, that makes failure-conditioned, lifecycle-wide editing of an existing executable runtime a learned capability. It post-trains a dedicated harness engineer with online reinforcement learning so that its edits are optimized for the realized task success they produce, rather than proposed by a fixed editor. A separate 9B engineer converts batches of target-agent failures into validated executable patches; fresh same-batch reruns of the frozen target provide outcome rewards, so training updates only the engineer. Cold-start supervised fine-tuning initializes this editing policy, which is then trained online with group-relative policy optimization. Across WebShop, ALFWorld, and DBBench, Harness-R1 raises vanilla Qwen3.5-9B success from 44.3% to 53.6% (+9.3 percentage points). After direct target-agent fine-tuning, a target-specific engineer raises the average further from 59.2% to 64.2% (+5.0 points); because these gains hold both before and after fine-tuning the target, Harness-R1 points toward co-evolving the harness engineer and the target agent.

</details>


### [305] [SKT: Skill-Use Training at Scale via Verified Synthetic Data Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02287)
*Zelin Tan,Yiqun Zhang,Hao Li,Zhiyao Cui,Hejia Geng,Shao Zhang,Hangfan Zhang,Yang Chen,Xiaosong Wang,Lilong Wang,Zhenfei Yin,Shuyue Hu,Chen Zhang,Lei Bai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes SKT, a verified data synthesis pipeline that creates skill-grounded tasks and trajectories for language-model agents, and shows that training on this data improves agents’ ability to use reusable skills.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language-model agents can be equipped with reusable agent skills (procedural tools or routines), but current models struggle to reliably identify, apply, and coordinate these skills. There is a need for scalable, high-quality training data and evaluation benchmarks specifically focused on skill use, rather than generic tool use or instruction following, to systematically improve and measure agents’ skill-use capabilities.

Method: The authors introduce SKT, a data synthesis pipeline that: (1) takes a large collection of agent skills as input; (2) automatically selects single-skill and multi-skill configurations; (3) synthesizes corresponding tasks that require those skills; (4) uses a combination of rule-based checks and agent-based interaction with feedback-guided repair to verify that tasks are solvable and that trajectories correctly and substantially use each required skill; and (5) retains only successful, verified trajectories. Using 2,000 public skills, they generate 4,000 task packages and 27,164 verified trajectories. They also build SkillEval, a separate, held-out executable benchmark constructed via the same pipeline but from a disjoint skill/test pool, designed to evaluate models’ skill-use performance. They then fine-tune various language models on the SKT trajectories and evaluate performance across different benchmarks and agent harnesses, along with ablation and scaling studies.

Result: SKT produces a large corpus of 4,000 task packages and 27,164 verified trajectories grounded in 2,000 public skills. Supervised fine-tuning of language models on these SKT-generated trajectories consistently improves performance on skill-use tasks across multiple models, benchmarks, and agent interfaces. Ablation experiments show that removing or weakening verification mechanisms reduces performance gains, highlighting the importance of high-quality, verified supervision. Cross-harness evaluations indicate that the benefits of SKT training generalize beyond a single agent framework, and scaling experiments reveal that performance improvements grow with broader skill coverage.

Conclusion: Verified data synthesis focused on skill-grounded tasks and trajectories is an effective, scalable way to train language-model agents to better use reusable skills. SKT both generates high-quality training data and underpins a held-out benchmark, SkillEval, for rigorous evaluation. The consistent gains from fine-tuning on SKT data, their robustness across agent harnesses, and their dependence on rigorous verification collectively support verified data synthesis as a practical approach for improving skill-use capabilities in LLM-based agents.

Abstract: Agent skills have become an important mechanism for equipping language-model agents with reusable procedural knowledge. However, providing skills alone does not guarantee that current models can effectively identify, apply, and coordinate them. To improve skill-use capabilities, we introduce SKT, a verified data synthesis pipeline that constructs skill-grounded tasks and executable trajectories from large collections of agent skills. SKT selects suitable single-skill and multi-skill configurations, synthesizes tasks through rule-based and agent-based verification with feedback-guided repair, and retains only successful trajectories that substantially use every required skill. Using 2,000 public skills, SKT produces 4,000 task packages and 27,164 verified trajectories. Based on the same pipeline and a disjoint test pool, we further construct SkillEval, a held-out executable benchmark for evaluating skill use. Experiments across diverse models, benchmarks, and agent harnesses show that supervised fine-tuning on SKT-generated trajectories consistently improves skill-use performance. Verification ablations, cross-harness evaluation, and scaling experiments further demonstrate that these gains depend on high-quality supervision, extend beyond a single agent interface, and increase with broader skill coverage. Together, these results establish verified data synthesis as an effective and scalable approach for skill-use training.

</details>


### [306] [Shared Prefixes, Better Credit: Adaptive Routing for Multi-Agent Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02291)
*Yiqing Liu,Zihao Wang,Hantao Yao,Wu Liu,Yongdong Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TreeCredit is a credit-assignment and routing framework for multi-agent reasoning that builds shared-prefix collaboration trees to learn which operator to invoke at each state, improving accuracy–cost trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Adaptive multi-agent reasoning systems need to decide which reasoning operator or agent to invoke at each intermediate state. Existing methods typically rely on coarse supervision from query-level labels or trajectory-level returns, which cannot accurately assess the utility of individual operators at specific states in multi-step collaborations. This leads to inefficient or suboptimal routing, harming both accuracy and inference cost. A more fine-grained, state-conditioned credit assignment is needed to guide better operator selection.

Method: TreeCredit builds shared-prefix collaboration trees by branching different candidate operators from the same intermediate reasoning state. Each state–operator pair is evaluated by rolling out its full continuation and assigning a suffix credit that prioritizes final correctness while penalizing additional inference cost. These structured, per-branch credits are then converted into local operator preferences for each state. A lightweight pairwise state router is trained on these preferences to decide, at inference time, which operator to apply next, enabling dynamic, cost-aware MAR.

Result: Across six reasoning benchmarks, TreeCredit achieves modest but consistent accuracy gains while significantly cutting inference cost compared to representative MAR baselines. Overall, it delivers a superior accuracy–cost trade-off, showing that its fine-grained credit assignment and routing decisions lead to more efficient multi-agent reasoning.

Conclusion: By reframing credit assignment in MAR as state-matched downstream comparison over shared-prefix trees, TreeCredit can more precisely estimate operator utility and train an effective routing policy. This yields multi-agent reasoning systems that are not only slightly more accurate but substantially more cost-efficient, demonstrating the value of structured, state-local credit for adaptive collaboration among reasoning operators.

Abstract: Multi-agent reasoning (MAR) improves reasoning reliability through iterative solution exchange and refinement. Existing adaptive MAR methods typically learn routing decisions from query-level labels or trajectory-level returns, but such coarse supervision cannot accurately estimate the state-conditioned utility of individual operators in multi-step collaboration. We propose TreeCredit, a shared-prefix credit assignment framework for efficient adaptive MAR. Its core insight is to estimate operator utility through state-matched downstream comparisons, rather than directly attributing trajectory-level outcomes to preceding decisions. TreeCredit constructs shared-prefix collaboration trees by expanding candidate operators from the same intermediate state and assigns each state--operator pair a correctness-prioritized suffix credit based on the terminal correctness and cumulative additional cost of its complete continuation. These structured credits are converted into state-local operator preferences to train a lightweight pairwise state router, which dynamically selects the next admissible operator during inference. Experiments on six reasoning benchmarks show that TreeCredit modestly improves accuracy while substantially reducing inference cost, achieving a better accuracy--cost trade-off than representative MAR methods.

</details>


### [307] [MechGeo: Autoformalizing and Proving Euclidean Geometry in Lean 4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02295)
*Hao Shen,Junyu Guo,Tian Cui,Yuxuan Xiao,Lihong Zhi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MechGeo is a Mathlib-native framework that combines automatic formalization of informal Euclidean geometry problems with certified proof construction in Lean 4, achieving state-of-the-art, kernel-checked solutions and refutations on challenging IMO-style benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoformalizing informal mathematical problems and producing fully certified proofs in interactive theorem provers is difficult, especially in Euclidean geometry, where existing LLM-based systems struggle with faithfulness, reliability, and tight integration with proof assistants like Lean. The authors aim to build a practical, trustworthy pipeline that takes informal geometry problems, formalizes them accurately, and either proves them or finds certified counterexamples, all checked by Lean’s kernel.

Method: They build MechGeo, a two-agent framework native to Lean/Mathlib. The first agent, GeoFormalizer, converts informal geometry problems into an intermediate representation (GeoIR), then deterministically translates these into Lean 4 statements. It iteratively repairs candidate formalizations using structural diagnostics and semantic evaluation, including counterexample feedback. The second agent, GeoProver, plans and constructs geometric proofs, discovers intermediate lemmas, and selectively reduces appropriate subgoals to algebra via a Lean-verified library. External tools (Singular or SymPy) may generate algebraic certificates, but every proof or counterexample is validated by Lean’s kernel. They evaluate across seven LLM backbones and multiple geometry benchmarks, including IMO problems and LEAP’s Lean-IMO-Bench.

Result: Across seven LLM backbones, MechGeo significantly boosts autoformalization quality, especially for weaker base models. On 43 historical IMO geometry problems, GeoFormalizer produces formal statements that GeoProver can fully prove in 29 cases; in the remaining 14, it automatically finds Lean-verified counterexamples and, after expert correction of the informal statements, proves all repaired versions. Including IMO 2026 Problem 2, this constitutes the largest known collection of automated, kernel-checked Lean proofs for IMO geometry problems. On the 14 geometry statements in LEAP’s Lean-IMO-Bench, MechGeo proves 12 for the first time, formally refutes the other two, and proves both repaired versions.

Conclusion: MechGeo demonstrates that combining counterexample-guided diagnosis, explicit geometric reasoning, and certified symbolic computation yields a practical and trustworthy foundation for formal Euclidean geometry in Lean. The system achieves state-of-the-art performance on demanding IMO-style benchmarks, both proving and refuting problems with full kernel-checked certification, and establishes a scalable approach to faithful autoformalization plus verified proof construction for geometry.

Abstract: We present MechGeo, a Mathlib native agentic framework that jointly addresses faithful autoformalization and certified proof construction for Euclidean geometry. In this framework, GeoFormalizer represents informal problems in GeoIR, deterministically translates them into Lean 4, and iteratively repairs candidate statements using structural diagnostics and semantic evaluation. GeoProver constructs geometric proof plans, derives intermediate lemmas, and selectively algebraizes suitable subgoals through a library verified in Lean. Singular or SymPy may generate algebraic certificates, but all resulting proofs and counterexamples are checked by Lean's kernel. Experiments across seven LLM backbones show substantial improvements in autoformalization, particularly for models with weaker direct translation performance. On 43 historical IMO geometry problems, GeoFormalizer generates formal statements that GeoProver proves in 29 cases; for the remaining 14, it constructs counterexamples verified in Lean and proves all repaired statements after expert correction. Together with IMO 2026 Problem 2, this yields, to the best of our knowledge, the largest reported collection of automated, kernel-checked Lean proofs for IMO geometry problems. On the 14 geometry statements in LEAP's Lean-IMO-Bench, MechGeo proves 12 for the first time, formally refutes the remaining two, and proves both repaired statements. These results establish counterexample guided diagnosis, geometric reasoning, and certified symbolic computation as a practical foundation for trustworthy formal geometry.

</details>


### [308] [Trajectories That Segment Themselves: Agent-Declared Boundaries as a Training Unit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02302)
*Jingxi Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a way for code‑generating agents to mark meaningful segments of their own behavior during data collection, creating better training units than raw actions or whole episodes, and shows these segments are semantically coherent and useful, shifting the research focus to corpus diversity rather than boundary definitions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In long-horizon coding tasks, standard supervision units are poorly aligned with the true structure of problem solving: single actions lack stable value; whole-episode labels conflate useful exploration with dead ends; and fixed-size windows arbitrarily cut through reasoning. This makes it hard to assign accurate credit or blame to particular stretches of behavior. The authors want a data-collection protocol that yields semantically meaningful, causally interpretable segments without needing manual annotation, replay, or external segmenters, and that exposes both successes and the specific failed reasoning that led to later corrections.

Method: They introduce collection-time semantic self-segmentation: during trajectory generation, the acting code agent explicitly declares hypothesized causal phases—structured conjectures about what it is trying to do—and uses these declarations to mark its own phase boundaries online. Each declaration is a falsifiable hypothesis about the governing intent of a block of actions. Because the hypotheses are named, reviewers can later negate specific hypotheses, creating synthetic wrong-cause-then-correction transitions in the data. This yields multiple supervised targets from a single collection: labels for correct phases, explicit negative labels for disproven hypotheses, and fine-grained audit supervision for failure regions that episode-level labels would discard. The authors then remove the textual hypotheses but keep the boundaries and test if models and humans can recover the underlying structure: (1) a model must predict which hypothesis-governed block produced a set of actions; (2) a code-blind annotator must place boundaries; (3) a mechanical rule based on test events is compared. Statistical tests (paired sign test, permutation, lexical controls) assess whether the learned segments are coherent and non-trivial. Finally, they perform a downstream DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) experiment on models fine-tuned with 2,551 phase-boundary preference pairs versus various controls, measuring decision changes on adversarial and matched test items.

Result: The learned segment boundaries prove to be meaningful and non-trivially structured. Given only the cut points (without access to the original hypotheses), a model assigns action blocks to their governing hypotheses at more than twice chance accuracy and significantly better than equal-length block baselines (paired sign test p = 0.0002); this advantage persists under lexical-controls but disappears under label permutation, indicating that performance depends on genuine structure rather than superficial cues. A human annotator without code access correctly matches 24 of 40 boundaries, versus 11.5 expected under random placement, whereas a purely mechanical rule based on test events performs no better than chance across a wide range of thresholds. This shows that the segments reflect coherent semantic phases not easily reproduced by simple heuristics. In downstream DPO, training on 2,551 phase-boundary pairs fails to change model decisions on 91 adversarial held-out items, but on 60 matched-construction items, 4 decisions flip from wrong to right, while two control conditions cause no such improvements. Using 1,825 pairs from a single generator produces similarly limited but positive effects, suggesting that benefits hinge less on refining boundary definitions and more on increasing corpus diversity.

Conclusion: Collection-time semantic self-segmentation lets coding agents declare and bound their own causal hypotheses, generating semantically coherent, variable-length segments that outperform naive fixed windows or mechanical rules and can produce rich supervision, including explicit wrong-cause-then-correction trajectories. Empirical tests show these boundaries encode real, non-trivial structure recognizable by both models and humans. However, in downstream preference-based fine-tuning (DPO), modest gains suggest that segmentation quality is no longer the main bottleneck; expanding and diversifying the dataset of segmented trajectories is likely more important for improving agent behavior than further tweaking how boundaries are drawn.

Abstract: Long-horizon coding-agent trajectories are poorly matched to the credit units available to train on: a single action has no stable value, an episode label merges productive exploration with abandoned directions, and a fixed window cuts where the logging mechanics fall. We introduce collection-time semantic self-segmentation, in which a declarative contract has the acting agent expose its own boundaries while the trajectory is generated. Instantiated with falsifiable causal hypotheses, successive adoptions expose variable-length semantic phases, and no milestone vocabulary, gold patch, environment replay, teacher logits, or retrospective segmenter places a boundary. Because the agent names its conjecture, a reviewer can negate it by name, which lets our protocol manufacture wrong-cause-then-correction transitions that recorded work rarely contains; one collection then yields four supervised targets, including audit supervision from exactly the failed regions an episode label discards. We then ask what survives deleting the declaration. Given the cut points but not the hypothesis, a model attributes action blocks to their governing hypothesis at over twice chance, beating equal-length blocks over the same trajectories (paired sign test $p = 0.0002$), surviving a lexical control and collapsing under label permutation. Asked instead to place boundaries, a code-blind annotator matches 24 of 40 where random placement matches 11.5, while a mechanical test-event rule beats chance at neither end of a strict-to-permissive sweep. The segments are therefore coherent and not cheaply reproducible. Downstream, DPO on 2,551 phase-boundary pairs changes no decision on 91 adversarial held-out items, while four of 60 change on matched-construction items, all wrong to right, where two controls change none: with 1,825 pairs from one generator, the variable to vary next is corpus diversity, not the boundary.

</details>


### [309] [Hard Constraints, Smooth Gradients: Learning Feasible Inventory Policies via Differentiable Projection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02343)
*Patrick Helm,Jan-Niklas Doerr,Joren Gijsbrechts,Stefan Minner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a deep RL framework that enforces complex hard constraints via embedded convex optimization, achieving near-optimal and practically better policies for production-inventory planning with interdependent constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Operational decision problems often involve sequential decisions with large, combinatorial action spaces and complex, interacting constraints. MILPs can handle such constraints but scale poorly in stochastic environments, while standard DRL methods scale but struggle to guarantee feasibility when constraints interact. There is a need for methods that combine the scalability and learning capability of DRL with the strict feasibility handling of MILPs in such settings.

Method: The authors embed a differentiable convex optimization layer inside the RL policy network. A neural network first outputs continuous action targets. These are then projected onto the relaxed feasible set via a quadratic program, and a dual-informed integer mapping converts them into integer actions while preserving feasibility. With a differentiable simulator, the entire pipeline is trained end to end using pathwise gradients. The authors also analyze the feasibility mechanism, proving bounded error relative to exact integer projection and reachability of the full feasible action space.

Result: In multi-echelon production-inventory planning problems with shared resource and material constraints, the learned policy achieves an average optimality gap below 1% on small instances. On larger networks, it outperforms state-of-the-art echelon base-stock policies by up to 9.75% and a rolling-horizon multi-stage stochastic program by at least 7.7%.
