### [328] [AtumAI: A Principled Framework for Agentic Generation of Datacenter Control-Plane Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02569)
*Qiushi Lin,Chaojie Zhang,Íñigo Goiri,Aditya Akella,Ricardo Bianchini,Jovan Stojkovic*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents AtumAI, an agentic AI framework that automatically designs datacenter control-plane policies from natural-language goals, outperforming human baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Datacenter control-plane policies are crucial for efficiency but are increasingly hard and slow to design due to a rapidly growing hardware-software stack, a vast and interdependent design space, and months-long prototyping cycles. Existing agentic/LLM-based approaches are ad hoc: they lack a formal, machine-checkable representation of problems, do not transfer knowledge across tasks, and explore only a narrow region of the design space, often getting stuck in local optima.

Method: AtumAI takes a natural-language goal and uses two main components: (1) a Datacenter Task Compiler that automatically converts the informal request into a formal specification containing objectives, constraints, decision variables, and evaluation methodology; and (2) an Evolutionary Design Discovery Loop that searches this formal space using a combination of LLM proposals, a diffusion model to expand candidate diversity, an evolutionary algorithm to iteratively refine candidates, and a surrogate model to guide search efficiency. The system autonomously proposes, tests (via simulation or evaluation), and refines candidate control-plane policies until constraints are satisfied.

Result: On three representative datacenter control-plane problems—workload placement, resource scaling, and power management—AtumAI-generated policies are empirically evaluated against expert-designed baselines. Across all tasks, the AtumAI policies consistently achieve better performance according to the tasks' objectives, demonstrating both higher efficiency and practical competitiveness. Onboarding new tasks is reduced from months of expert engineering to specifying a textual description that the system compiles and searches over.

Conclusion: AtumAI demonstrates that making agentic AI formal, transferable, and systematic can automate the design of complex datacenter control-plane policies. By compiling natural-language goals into a structured, machine-checkable specification and exploring the resulting design space via an evolutionary, model-guided loop, AtumAI consistently outperforms expert baselines while drastically reducing the effort and time needed to create new control policies.

Abstract: The efficiency of a datacenter rests on its control plane policies. Designing these policies is increasingly hard: the hardware-software stack grows fast, the design space is vast and interdependent, and prototyping a single policy takes months. Agentic AI promises to automate this search. Off the shelf, however, it falls short on three fronts. It is not formal: with no structured, searchable statement of the problem, the search has little structure to exploit and hard constraints are not guaranteed. It is not transferable: each task is solved from scratch, so nothing learned on one task carries to the next. Finally, it is not systematic: relying on the LLM as the sole source of candidates, it explores a narrow slice of the design space and settles into local optima. We introduce AtumAI, a framework that generates datacenter control-plane policies with agentic AI, making the process formal, transferable, and systematic. From a goal stated in plain language, AtumAI autonomously proposes, tests, and refines candidate policies until one satisfies the request. It does so through two components. The Datacenter Task Compiler automates problem formulation: it compiles the request into a formal, machine-checkable, and searchable specification of the task's objectives, constraints, decision variables, and evaluation methodology. The Evolutionary Design Discovery Loop then searches this specification, expanding the search beyond the LLM itself via a diffusion model, an evolutionary algorithm, and a surrogate model. Together, they reduce onboarding a new task from months of engineering to writing its description. We evaluate AtumAI on three control-plane tasks with distinct problem scopes, design spaces, and trade-offs: workload placement, resource scaling, and power management. Across all tasks, the policies generated by AtumAI consistently outperform expert-engineered baselines.

</details>
